articles.title: My judgment is up to me

statement.t: What troubles me rests on my judgment; that judgment is up to me, and when I take it away there is calm.

parts.words: What troubles me rests on my judgment
that judgment is up to me
when I take it away there is calm

statement.kind: A chain: where the trouble is, whose it is, what removing it gives
statement.form: Claim 1 places the trouble in my judgments, claim 2 says the judgment is mine to form or to withhold, and claim 3 says what taking it away gives. The statement joins these three in the order 12.16 itself gives them. Claims 4 and 5 apply it to two cases: my own body, and another person’s words.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the first and the fifth claims gain a second author. Practice gains questions to put to myself and words for facing a feared event, and “when it breaks” gains where false opinions come from and how they are driven out. He limits the first claim (even pain with no opinion added is still slight) and the fourth (the mind is struck by feelings reason cannot rout), and he challenges the fifth: where all is in doubt, he would have me believe what I prefer.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a clause for facing a feared event: if it does happen, perhaps it happens for my best. He limits the first claim, though: even pain with no opinion added is still slight.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Everything depends on opinion; ambition, luxury, greed, hark back to opinion.
piece.follows: Everything depends on opinion, and ambition, luxury and greed go back to it as well.
piece.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness and pain, written to Lucilius, who is ill. “Opinion” is what we tell ourselves about our pain; Seneca extends it to ambition, luxury and greed.
gives: Everything is a matter of judgment

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: It is according to opinion that we suffer.
piece.follows: How much we suffer goes by our opinion.
piece.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness: Seneca tells the sick Lucilius not to make his pain heavier by complaining. “Opinion” is what the sufferer thinks of his own pain.
gives: What troubles me rests on my judgments

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: to strip things of all that disturbs and confuses, and to see what each is at bottom
piece.follows: I should strip from things whatever disturbs and confuses, and see what each one is at bottom.
piece.context: Letter 24: Seneca tells Lucilius to listen calmly when his enemy threatens him over his case. “Things” are what he fears; stripped, they hold nothing fearful but the fear.
gives: I see things as they are

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Let us banish rumour and set a value upon each thing, asking what it is and not what it is called.
piece.follows: We should set rumour aside and value each thing by what it is, not by what it is called.
piece.context: Letter 95, on principles: what opinion we ought to hold about poverty, riches, renown, disgrace and exile. “Each thing” is one of these; “rumour” is what people say of it.
gives: I see things as they are

items.label: practice
items.t: When people around me try to talk me into believing that I am unhappy, I consider what I myself feel and not what I hear. I ask myself whether I am tormented without sufficient reason, and whether I am turning what is not an evil into an evil.
items.why: 4.9 deals with the person who abuses me and wants me to judge as he does. Seneca deals with people who mean well and pity me, and he gives the questions to put to myself; Marcus gives none here.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: when men surround you and try to talk you into believing that you are unhappy, to consider not what you hear but what you yourself feel
support.follows: When others try to persuade me that I am unhappy, I should go by what I feel and not by what I hear.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears. The “men” are people who condole with Lucilius over a trouble he expects; Seneca asks him to consult his own feeling instead of them.
gives: When people around me try to talk me into believing that I am unhappy, I consider what I myself feel and not what I hear

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Put the question voluntarily to yourself: “Am I tormented without sufficient reason, am I morose, and do I convert what is not an evil into what is an evil?”
support.follows: I should ask myself whether I am tormented without reason and am making an evil out of what is not one.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears: the last of the questions Seneca gives Lucilius to ask himself when the people around him tell him that he is unhappy.
gives: I ask myself whether I am tormented without sufficient reason
whether I am turning what is not an evil into an evil

items.label: practice
items.t: When I fear the worst, I say: what if it does happen? Let us see who wins. Perhaps it happens for my best interests.
items.why: 8.47 gives words for a report: say nothing further, or speak as one who recognises what happens in the universe. It gives none for facing an event I fear may come. Seneca does, and his words are again a judgment: he does not grant that the event would be an evil, he judges that it may be for his best.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: You yourself must say: “Well, what if it does happen? Let us see who wins! Perhaps it happens for my best interests; it may be that such a death will shed credit upon my life.”
support.follows: Lucilius is to say: suppose it does happen; let us see who wins; perhaps it is for my best.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears. After the mild remedy, “perhaps the worst will not happen”, Seneca gives the sterner one. “It” is the worst that Lucilius fears.
gives: I say: what if it does happen? Let us see who wins
Perhaps it happens for my best interests

items.label: breaks
items.t: I fail when I agree too quickly with what people say and do not test the things that frighten me. My faults were not born in me: they came from outside and were heaped on me, and with frequent admonitions, from someone who keeps reminding me, I can reject the opinions that din about my ears.
items.why: 7.2 says my principles die when their impressions go out, and that keeping them alight is up to me. Seneca says where the false opinions come from, other people, and that the remedy is to be reminded often, by someone else if need be. Marcus speaks here only of what I do myself.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: we agree too quickly with what people say. We do not put to the test those things which cause our fear
support.follows: We accept what people say too quickly and do not test the things that frighten us.
support.context: Letter 13, on fears of what may happen. Seneca says we are troubled by apprehension and rumour more than by fact; “those things” are the reports that frighten us.
gives: I agree too quickly with what people say and do not test the things that frighten me

support.author: seneca
support.quote: For you are mistaken if you suppose that our faults are inborn in us; they have come from without, have been heaped upon us.
support.follows: Our faults are not inborn; they came from outside and were heaped on us.
support.context: Letter 94 defends the giving of advice. Seneca has just said that parents, slaves and neighbours pass their folly on to us; “from without” means from these people.
gives: My faults were not born in me: they came from outside and were heaped on me

support.author: seneca
support.quote: by receiving frequent admonitions, we can reject the opinions which din about our ears
support.follows: If we are admonished often, we can reject the opinions that are dinned into our ears.
support.context: Letter 94, on the value of advice: we need a guardian to pluck us by the ear and dispel rumours. The “opinions” are those of the crowd around us.
gives: with frequent admonitions, from someone who keeps reminding me, I can reject the opinions that din about my ears

items.t: Seneca leaves a residue. Of bodily pain he says that it is slight when opinion has added nothing to it, not that it is then gone (Ep. 78.13). The same section argues that the weight of pain depends on opinion, and it goes on to advise calling the pain nothing, a trifling matter at most; so this is one argument, and what remains is a slight pain that opinion did not make. This limits the claim that what troubles me rests on my judgments.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Pain is slight if opinion has added nothing to it
support.follows: Pain to which opinion has added nothing is slight.
support.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness, to the sick Lucilius: do not make troubles heavier by complaining. The “pain” is bodily pain; “opinion” is what one tells oneself about it.

items.t: Seneca does not let reason off so cleanly. Even the mind of a man over whom fortune has lost her control will be smitten with a thrill, and he will change colour (Ep. 57.3): there are emotions that no courage can avoid, and such a feeling is not fear but a natural feeling that reason cannot rout (Ep. 57.4). The claim says that the ruling part is undisturbed unless it disturbs itself; here the mind is struck by something it did not do to itself, and reason cannot stop it. This limits the claim and does not contradict it: like Marcus, he calls trembling, pain and turning pale sensations of the body, and he puts what is truly an evil in the mind only if these trials drag the mind down (Ep. 71.29). He is not fully consistent: in Letter 57 the thrill is in the mind, in Letter 71 such things are of the body.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Even such a man’s mind will be smitten with a thrill and he will change colour.
support.follows: Even the mind of a man fortune cannot rule is struck by a shock, and he changes colour.
support.context: Letter 57, on passing through a dark road tunnel. “Such a man” is one over whom fortune has lost her control, not Seneca himself; the “thrill” is the shock of the gloom.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: there are certain emotions, my dear Lucilius, which no courage can avoid
support.follows: Some emotions cannot be avoided by any courage.
support.context: Letter 57: in a dark road tunnel Seneca felt a thrill and a change in himself. The “emotions” are such first shocks, which he says strike even a man fortune cannot rule.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: This is not fear; it is a natural feeling which reason cannot rout.
support.follows: Such a shock is not fear but a natural feeling, and reason cannot drive it out.
support.context: Letter 57, on a journey through a dark tunnel. “This” is frowning at a grim prospect, shuddering at sudden sights and growing dizzy at a precipice, in a brave man.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the wise man will tremble, will feel pain, will turn pale, For all these are sensations of the body. Where, then, is the abode of utter distress, of that which is truly an evil? In the other part of us, no doubt, if it is the mind that these trials drag down
support.follows: Trembling, pain and pallor belong to the body even in the wise man; what is truly an evil is in the mind, and only if these trials drag it down.
support.context: Letter 71, on the supreme good: human virtue does not go beyond nature. “These trials” are the trembling, pain and pallor; “the other part” is the mind.

items.t: Seneca goes further than saying nothing more. Where everything is in doubt, he tells Lucilius to decide in his own favour and believe what he prefers, and to lean toward hope even if fear has the majority (Ep. 13.13). Marcus says to add nothing to what is reported and to see things as they are in truth; a belief chosen because I prefer it is an addition. Seneca does not hold to this himself: a few lines later he says he is ashamed either to admonish Lucilius sternly or to beguile him with such mild remedies, and he goes on to a sterner one (Ep. 13.14).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: whenever all the elements are in doubt, decide in your own favour; believe what you prefer
support.follows: When everything is uncertain, I should decide in my own favour and believe what I prefer.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears: Lucilius is to weigh his hopes against his fears about a trouble that may come. “The elements” are the uncertain signs on either side.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: And if fear wins a majority of the votes, incline in the other direction anyhow, and cease to harass your soul
support.follows: Even if fear has more on its side, I should lean the other way and stop harassing my soul.
support.context: Letter 13, on fears of what may happen. Seneca pictures hopes and fears as voting; even if fear has more votes, Lucilius is to lean toward hope.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: But I am ashamed either to admonish you sternly or to try to beguile you with such mild remedies.
support.follows: Seneca is ashamed either to admonish Lucilius sternly or to try to beguile him with mild remedies like these.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears: said shortly after Seneca advises Lucilius to believe what he prefers. The “mild remedies” are that advice; a sterner one follows.

passages.title: On the healing power of the mind
passages.text: But do not of your own accord make your troubles heavier to bear and burden yourself with complaining. Pain is slight if opinion has added nothing to it; but if, on the other hand, you begin to encourage yourself and say, “It is nothing,—a trifling matter at most; keep a stout heart and it will soon cease”; then in thinking it slight, you will make it slight. Everything depends on opinion; ambition, luxury, greed, hark back to opinion. It is according to opinion that we suffer.

passages.title: On despising death [ 1 ]
passages.text: Therefore, when your enemy threatens, listen unconcernedly. Although your conscience makes you confident, yet, since many things have weight which are outside your case, both hope for that which is utterly just, and prepare yourself against that which is utterly unjust. Remember, however, before all else, to strip things of all that disturbs and confuses, and to see what each is at bottom; you will then comprehend that they contain nothing fearful except the actual fear.

passages.title: On the usefulness of basic principles
passages.text: Next, after considering gods and men, let us see how we should make use of things. It is useless for us to have mouthed out precepts, unless we begin by reflecting what opinion we ought to hold concerning everything—concerning poverty, riches, renown, disgrace, citizenship, exile. Let us banish rumour and set a value upon each thing, asking what it is and not what it is called.

passages.title: On groundless fears
passages.text: Do me the favour, when men surround you and try to talk you into believing that you are unhappy, to consider not what you hear but what you yourself feel, and to take counsel with your feelings and question yourself independently, because you know your own affairs better than anyone else does. Ask: “Is there any reason why these persons should condole with me? Why should they be worried or even fear some infection from me, as if troubles could be transmitted? Is there any evil involved, or is it a matter merely of ill report, rather than an evil?” Put the question voluntarily to yourself: “Am I tormented without sufficient reason, am I morose, and do I convert what is not an evil into what is an evil?”

passages.title: On groundless fears
passages.text: But I am ashamed either to admonish you sternly or to try to beguile you with such mild remedies. Let another say: “Perhaps the worst will not happen.” You yourself must say: “Well, what if it does happen? Let us see who wins! Perhaps it happens for my best interests; it may be that such a death will shed credit upon my life.” Socrates was ennobled by the hemlock draught. Wrench from Cato’s hand his sword, the vindicator of liberty, and you deprive him of the greatest share of his glory.

passages.title: On groundless fears
passages.text: “But,” you say, “something will happen to it.” First of all, consider whether your proofs of future trouble are sure. For it is more often the case that we are troubled by our apprehensions, and that we are mocked by that mocker, rumour, which is wont to settle wars, but much more often settles individuals. Yes, my dear Lucilius; we agree too quickly with what people say. We do not put to the test those things which cause our fear; we do not examine into them; we blench and retreat just like soldiers who are forced to abandon their camp because of a dust-cloud raised by stampeding cattle, or are thrown into a panic by the spreading of some unauthenticated rumour.

passages.title: On the value of advice [ 1 ]
passages.text: We should, therefore, have a guardian, as it were, to pluck us continually by the ear and dispel rumours and protest against popular enthusiasms. For you are mistaken if you suppose that our faults are inborn in us; they have come from without, have been heaped upon us. Hence, by receiving frequent admonitions, we can reject the opinions which din about our ears.

passages.title: On the trials of travel
passages.text: The gloom, however, furnished me with some food for thought; I felt a certain mental thrill, and a transformation unaccompanied by fear, due to the novelty and the unpleasantness of an unusual occurrence. Of course I am not speaking to you of myself at this point, because I am far from being a perfect person, or even a man of middling qualities; I refer to one over whom fortune has lost her control. Even such a man’s mind will be smitten with a thrill and he will change colour.

passages.title: On the trials of travel
passages.text: For there are certain emotions, my dear Lucilius, which no courage can avoid; nature reminds courage how perishable a thing it is. And so he will contract his brow when the prospect is forbidding, will shudder at sudden apparitions, and will become dizzy when he stands at the edge of a high precipice and looks down. This is not fear; it is a natural feeling which reason cannot rout.

passages.title: On the supreme good
passages.text: And now I have reached the point to which your patient waiting summons me. You must not think that our human virtue transcends nature; the wise man will tremble, will feel pain, will turn pale, For all these are sensations of the body. Where, then, is the abode of utter distress, of that which is truly an evil? In the other part of us, no doubt, if it is the mind that these trials drag down, force to a confession of its servitude, and cause to regret its existence.

passages.title: On groundless fears
passages.text: Accordingly, weigh carefully your hopes as well as your fears, and whenever all the elements are in doubt, decide in your own favour; believe what you prefer. And if fear wins a majority of the votes, incline in the other direction anyhow, and cease to harass your soul, reflecting continually that most mortals, even when no troubles are actually at hand or are certainly to be expected in the future, become excited and disquieted. No one calls a halt on himself, when he begins to be urged ahead; nor does he regulate his alarm according to the truth. No one says; “The author of the story is a fool, and he who has believed it is a fool, as well as he who fabricated it.” We let ourselves drift with every breeze; we are frightened at uncertainties, just as if they were certain. We observe no moderation. The slightest thing turns the scales and throws us forthwith into a panic.

claims.t: Everything is a matter of judgment: how anything stands for me depends on how I judge it. What troubles me rests on my judgments. It is not outside me but inside.
claims.shared: 12.16 and 2.13 open with the same words, that all things, or everything, are “judgment”. 9.30 and 9.11 both put what presses on me in “judgment”: 9.30 says the things that trouble me “rest wholly on your judgment”, 9.11 that what hemmed him in was “in my judgments”.
claims.changed: 9.30 says “many” of the things that trouble me rest on judgment; 9.11 says “all that hemmed me in”. The claim says “what troubles me” and leaves the number open. 9.11 speaks of what hemmed him in; the claim uses 9.30’s word “trouble” for both. 12.16 and 2.13 give only the bare saying, “all things are judgment” and “everything is judgment”; the claim says “a matter of” judgment, and the words after the colon, that how anything stands for me depends on how I judge it, are the editor’s reading of the saying, backed by no quote of their own.

support.quote: That all things are judgment
support.follows: All things are a matter of judgment.
gives: Everything is a matter of judgment

support.quote: That everything is judgment.
support.follows: Everything is a matter of judgment.
gives: Everything is a matter of judgment

support.quote: those that trouble you, things that rest wholly on your judgment
support.follows: Many of the things that trouble me are needless and rest wholly on my own judgment.
gives: What troubles me rests on my judgments

support.quote: for it was not outside but inside, in my judgments
support.follows: What hemmed Marcus in was not outside him. It was inside, in his judgments.
gives: What troubles me rests on my judgments
It is not outside me but inside

claims.t: My judgment is up to me. I am able to form the judgment I ought, and free to form none, and I need not be troubled: things themselves do not produce my verdicts, and what is outside my mind is nothing to my mind.
claims.shared: All three passages say that judging lies with me: 12.16 that the judgment “is up to you”, 7.2 “I am able to form the judgment I ought”, 6.47 “One is free to form no judgment”. 7.2 and 6.47 both go on to being disturbed or troubled, and both then turn to “things”: things do not produce our verdicts, and things outside the mind are nothing to it.
claims.changed: 7.2 says “disturbed” and 6.47 “troubled”; the claim says “troubled” for both. The colon stands for the “for” of 6.47, which gives the reason itself. In 7.2 the sentence about things outside the mind only follows the question, without a “for”. Both passages speak of “this”, the matter in front of Marcus; the claim speaks generally.

support.quote: this judgment is up to you
support.follows: The judgment I form is up to me.
gives: My judgment is up to me

support.quote: I am able to form the judgment I ought about this.
support.follows: Marcus is able to form the judgment he ought to form about the matter in front of him.
gives: My judgment is up to me
I am able to form the judgment I ought

support.quote: If I am able, why am I disturbed?
support.follows: Since he is able to judge as he ought, Marcus has no reason to be disturbed.
gives: I need not be troubled

support.quote: One is free to form no judgment about this and not to be troubled in one’s soul
support.follows: A person is free to form no judgment about a matter, and free not to be troubled by it.
gives: My judgment is up to me
free to form none
I need not be troubled

support.quote: things themselves do not have a nature that produces our verdicts
support.follows: Things are not of a kind to make our verdicts for us.
gives: things themselves do not produce my verdicts

support.quote: The things outside my mind are nothing at all to my mind.
support.follows: What is outside Marcus’s mind has no bearing at all on his mind.
gives: what is outside my mind is nothing to my mind

claims.t: When I wish, I can take away my judgment about what seems to distress me, and then I stand in the safest place: there is calm, like a bay without a wave. What hems me in I can throw out, and at once have plenty of open room.
claims.shared: 8.38 and 12.16 both say “take away” the judgment and both say what follows. The shared words are the translation’s: the Greek verbs differ (ἀφέλῃς in 8.38, ἆρον in 12.16) and are close in sense. 9.11 (“threw out”) and 9.30 (“strip away”) both speak of removing what presses on me. All four passages describe the outcome as a place: “the safest place” (8.38), “a bay without a wave” (12.16), “open room” (9.30), being out of “all that hemmed me in” (9.11).
claims.changed: 12.16 says “when you wish” and 8.38 says “if”; the claim keeps “when I wish” and drops the “if”. Only 8.38 and 12.16 name the judgment as the thing removed: in 9.11 what is thrown out is all that hemmed him in, and in 9.30 what is stripped away is needless things among those that trouble me. 9.30 is cut in mid-sentence: the Greek goes on to say by what means the room is made, by taking the whole universe in thought, with endless time and the quick change of each thing. The claim leaves that means out, so its “open room” is not to be read as coming from the removal of a judgment alone. The headland of 12.16 is left out.

support.quote: So take the judgment away when you wish
support.follows: I can take the judgment away whenever I wish.
gives: When I wish
take away my judgment

support.quote: If you take away your judgment about what seems to distress you, you yourself stand in the safest place.
support.follows: Once I take away my judgment about what seems to distress me, I stand in the safest place.
gives: take away my judgment
about what seems to distress me, and then I stand in the safest place

support.quote: just as for someone who has rounded the headland, there is calm: all things steady, and a bay without a wave
support.follows: With the judgment gone there is calm, as for a sailor who has rounded the headland into a bay without a wave.

support.quote: Today I got out of all that hemmed me in, or rather I threw out all that hemmed me in

claims.t: My reason does not trouble or distress itself; it is undisturbed unless it disturbs itself. What happens to my body or to anything else of mine I leave to the part it happens to: the body can say so if it suffers, and whatever else of mine is in a bad way can judge that for itself.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of the judging part acting on “itself”: the ruling part “does not make trouble for itself” (7.13), and reason is not to be the one “to distress itself” (8.38). Both then turn to another part with “let”: let the body say so if it suffers (7.13), let whatever is in a bad way form its own judgment (8.38).
claims.changed: 7.13 says “the ruling part” and 8.38 says “reason”; the claim says “my reason” for both. 7.13 states it as a fact about the ruling part and 8.38 as an instruction; the claim states it as my rule. 8.38 does not name the body; 7.13 does. “Judge that for itself” follows the printed reading of 8.38, “let that form its own judgment about itself”; the translators’ other reading, “let it suppose so about itself”, says much the same: the part that is in a bad way, not reason, is to judge its own state.

support.quote: The ruling part does not make trouble for itself
support.follows: The part of me that rules does not make trouble for itself.
gives: My reason does not trouble or distress itself

support.quote: let reason, for its part, not be the one to distress itself
support.follows: Reason, at least, should not be the one that distresses itself.
gives: My reason does not trouble or distress itself

support.quote: it is undisturbed and unhindered, unless it disturbs and hinders itself
support.follows: The ruling part is undisturbed and unhindered unless it disturbs and hinders itself.
gives: it is undisturbed unless it disturbs itself

support.quote: Let the little body itself take care that it suffers nothing, if it can, and let it say so if it suffers anything.
support.follows: It is for the body to take care that it suffers nothing, and to say so if it does suffer.
gives: I leave to the part it happens to
the body can say so if it suffers

support.quote: if anything else of yours is in a bad way, let that form its own judgment about itself
support.follows: If some other part of me is in a bad way, that part may form its own judgment about itself.

claims.t: I tell myself no more than my first impressions report: if they report that someone speaks ill of me, they have not reported that I am harmed. When someone abuses me, I do not judge things as that person wants me to; I see things as they are.
claims.shared: Both passages take the case of a person who turns on me, one who “is speaking ill of you” (8.47) and one who “abuses you” (4.9). 8.47 answers that case with what has and has not been reported, and uses “see” for its second example, the sick child: “I see it; but that the child is in danger I do not see”. 4.9 answers its case with “see them as they are in truth”. The shared word “see” is the translation’s: the Greek has βλέπω in 8.47 and ἴδε in 4.9, different verbs close in sense. Both refuse a judgment that goes beyond the thing.
claims.changed: In 8.47 the judgment refused is the one I would add from within; in 4.9 it is the one the abuser holds or wants me to hold. The sick child of 8.47 is a second example and is kept only in the quote. 4.9’s “in truth” is left out of the claim. The claim calls the reporters “my first impressions”, the words 8.47 itself uses later for “the impressions that lead the way”.

support.quote: Say nothing more to yourself than what the impressions that lead the way report.
support.follows: I should tell myself only what the first impressions report.
gives: I tell myself no more than my first impressions report

support.quote: It has been reported that so-and-so is speaking ill of you. That has been reported; but that you have been harmed has not been reported.
support.follows: The report is that someone speaks ill of me. That I have been harmed is not part of the report.
gives: if they report that someone speaks ill of me, they have not reported that I am harmed

support.quote: I see that the child is sick. I see it; but that the child is in danger I do not see.
support.follows: Marcus sees that the child is sick. He does not see that the child is in danger.
gives: I see things as they are

support.quote: Do not judge things to be such as the person who abuses you decides they are, or wants you to decide they are
support.follows: I should not take things to be what the person who abuses me decides they are or wants me to decide they are.
gives: When someone abuses me, I do not judge things as that person wants me to

support.quote: see them as they are in truth
support.follows: I should see things as they truly are.
gives: I see things as they are

single.quote: The ruling part, so far as depends on itself, is in need of nothing, unless it makes a need for itself
single.label: No need either
single.t: So far as depends on itself, my ruling part needs nothing, unless it makes a need for itself.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of need. The other passages speak of trouble and distress, so it is not fused.
single.follows: Left to itself, the ruling part needs nothing; any need it has, it makes for itself.

single.quote: Or rather, do say something further, as one who recognises each of the things that happen in the universe.
single.label: Or say this
single.t: Rather than adding nothing to what my first impressions report, I do say something further to myself, as someone who recognises each of the things that happen in the universe.
single.why: Only this passage corrects the rule to say nothing further. It does not spell out what is to be said.
single.follows: Marcus corrects himself: I may say something further, but as one who recognises each thing that happens in the universe.

single.quote: How can the principles be killed, unless the impressions that answer to them are put out, the impressions it is up to you to keep fanning back into flame?
single.label: Principles going out
single.t: My principles can be killed only if the impressions that answer to them are put out, and it is up to me to keep fanning those impressions back into flame.
single.why: Only this passage says how principles are lost and how they are kept alive. It is kept as what failing looks like and the way back.
single.follows: Principles die only when the impressions that answer to them go out, and keeping those alight is up to me.

single.quote: For what is said in answer to Monimus the Cynic is plain; but plain too is the usefulness of the saying, if one takes what is nourishing in it so far as it is true.
single.label: So far as true
single.t: The saying that everything is judgment can be answered, and the answers are plain. Its usefulness is plain too, if I take what is nourishing in it, so far as it is true.
single.why: Only this passage admits that the saying has plain answers and limits it to what is true in it.
single.follows: The replies to Monimus’s saying are plain, and so is its use, if one takes from it what nourishes and only so far as it is true.

single.quote: “Who is ‘yourself’?” Reason. “But I am not reason.” Granted.
single.label: “I am not reason”
single.t: The self that stands in safety is my reason. If I object that I am not reason, I grant it.
single.why: Only this passage raises the objection that I am more than my reason, and it grants it. The item stops where its quote stops. What still holds comes in the passage’s next sentence, which is quoted in the claim on reason and the body: reason is not to be the one that distresses itself.
single.follows: The “yourself” that stands safe is reason. To the objection that he is not reason, Marcus answers: granted.

members.text:
If thou canst but withdraw conceit and opinion concerning that
which may seem hurtful and offensive, thou thyself art as safe, as safe
may be. Thou thyself? and who is that? Thy reason. 'Yea, but I am not
reason.' Well, be it so. However, let not thy reason or understanding
admit of grief, and if there be anything in thee that is grieved, let
that, (whatsoever it be,) conceive its own grief, if it can.
members.english: If you take away your judgment about what seems to distress you, you yourself stand in the safest place. “Who is ‘yourself’?” Reason. “But I am not reason.” Granted. Then let reason, for its part, not be the one to distress itself, and if anything else of yours is in a bad way, let that form its own judgment about itself.
members.greek: Ἐὰν ἀφέλῃς τὴν σὴν ὑπόληψιν περὶ τοῦ λυπεῖν σε δοκοῦντος, αὐτὸς ἐν τῷ ἀσφαλεστάτῳ ἕστηκας.—τίς αὐτός;—ὁ λόγος.—ἀλλ’ οὐκ εἰμὶ λόγος.—ἔστω. οὐκοῦν ὁ μὲν λόγος αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν μὴ λυπείτω, εἰ δέ τι ἄλλο σοι κακῶς ἔχει, ὑπολαβέτω αὐτὸ περὶ αὑτοῦ.

members.text:
What fear is there that thy dogmata, or philosophical resolutions
and conclusions, should become dead in thee, and lose their proper
power and efficacy to make thee live happy, as long as those proper
and correlative fancies, and representations of things on which they
mutually depend (which continually to stir up and revive is in thy
power,) are still kept fresh and alive? It is in my power concerning
this thing that is happened, what soever it be, to conceit that which is
right and true. If it be, why then am I troubled? Those things that are
without my understanding, are nothing to it at all: and that is it only,
which doth properly concern me. Be always in this mind, and thou wilt be
right.
members.english: How can the principles be killed, unless the impressions that answer to them are put out, the impressions it is up to you to keep fanning back into flame? I am able to form the judgment I ought about this. If I am able, why am I disturbed? The things outside my mind are nothing at all to my mind. Learn this and you are upright.
members.greek: Τὰ δόγματα πῶς ἄλλως δύναται νεκρωθῆναι, ἐὰν μὴ αἱ κατάλληλοι αὐτοῖς φαντασίαι σβεσθῶσιν, ἃς διηνεκῶς ἀναζωπυρεῖν ἐπὶ σοί ἐστι. δύναμαι περὶ τούτου ὃ δεῖ ὑπολαμβάνειν· εἰ δύναμαι, τί ταράσσομαι; τὰ ἔξω τῆς ἐμῆς διανοίας οὐδὲν ὅλως πρὸς τὴν ἐμὴν διάνοιαν. τοῦτο μάθε καὶ ὀρθὸς εἶ.

members.text:
It is in thy power absolutely to exclude all manner of conceit
and opinion, as concerning this matter; and by the same means, to
exclude all grief and sorrow from thy soul. For as for the things and
objects themselves, they of themselves have no such power, whereby to
beget and force upon us any opinion at all.
members.english: One is free to form no judgment about this and not to be troubled in one’s soul; for things themselves do not have a nature that produces our verdicts.
members.greek: Ἔξεστι περὶ τούτου μηδὲν ὑπολαμβάνειν καὶ μὴ ὀχλεῖσθαι τῇ ψυχῇ· αὐτὰ γὰρ τὰ πράγματα οὐκ ἔχει φύσιν ποιητικὴν τῶν ἡμετέρων κρίσεων.

members.text:
This may ever be my comfort and security: my understanding, that
ruleth over all, will not of itself bring trouble and vexation upon
itself. This I say; it will not put itself in any fear, it will not lead
itself into any concupiscence. If it be in the power of any other to
compel it to fear, or to grieve, it is free for him to use his power.
But sure if itself do not of itself, through some false opinion or
supposition incline itself to any such disposition; there is no fear.
For as for the body, why should I make the grief of my body, to be the
grief of my mind? If that itself can either fear or complain, let it.
But as for the soul, which indeed, can only be truly sensible of either
fear or grief; to which only it belongs according to its different
imaginations and opinions, to admit of either of these, or of their
contraries; thou mayst look to that thyself, that it suffer nothing.
Induce her not to any such opinion or persuasion. The understanding
is of itself sufficient unto itself, and needs not (if itself doth not
bring itself to need) any other thing besides itself, and by consequent
as it needs nothing, so neither can it be troubled or hindered by
anything, if itself doth not trouble and hinder itself.
members.english: The ruling part does not make trouble for itself; I mean, for example, it does not frighten itself into desire. But if anyone else can frighten or distress it, let them do so; for it will not, by its own judging, turn itself in such directions. Let the little body itself take care that it suffers nothing, if it can, and let it say so if it suffers anything. But the little soul, the thing that fears, that is distressed, that in general forms judgments about these things, will suffer nothing at all; for you will not lead it to such a verdict. The ruling part, so far as depends on itself, is in need of nothing, unless it makes a need for itself; and in the same way it is undisturbed and unhindered, unless it disturbs and hinders itself.
members.greek: Τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν αὐτὸ ἑαυτῷ οὐκ ἐνοχλεῖ, οἷον λέγω, οὐ φοβεῖ ἑαυτὸ εἰς ἐπιθυμίαν. εἰ δέ τις ἄλλος αὐτὸ φοβῆσαι ἢ λυπῆσαι δύναται, ποιείτω· αὐτὸ γὰρ ἑαυτὸ ὑποληπτικῶς οὐ τρέψει εἰς τοιαύτας τροπάς. τὸ σωμάτιον μὴ πάθῃ τι, αὐτὸ μεριμνάτω, εἰ δύναται, καὶ λεγέτω, εἴ τι πάσχει· τὸ δὲ ψυχάριον τὸ φοβούμενον, τὸ λυπούμενον, τὸ περὶ τούτων ὅλως ὑπολαμβάνον, οὐδὲν μὴ πάθῃ· οὐ γὰρ ἄξεις αὐτὸ εἰς κρίσιν τοιαύτην. ἀπροσδεές ἐστιν ὅσον ἐφ’ ἑαυτῷ τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, ἐὰν μὴ ἑαυτῷ ἔνδειαν ποιῇ· κατὰ ταὐτὰ δὲ καὶ ἀτάραχον καὶ ἀνεμπόδιστον, ἐὰν μὴ ἑαυτὸ ταράσσῃ καὶ ἐμποδίζῃ.

members.text:
Many of those things that trouble and straiten thee, it is in thy
power to cut off, as wholly depending from mere conceit and opinion; and
then thou shalt have room enough.
members.english: You can strip away many needless things among those that trouble you, things that rest wholly on your judgment, and you will at once make plenty of open room for yourself.
members.greek: Πολλὰ περισσὰ περιελεῖν τῶν ἐνοχλούντων σοι δύνασαι ὅλα ἐπὶ τῇ ὑπολήψει σου κείμενα, καὶ πολλὴν εὐρυχωρίαν περιποιήσεις ἤδη σεαυτῷ

members.text:
Keep thyself to the first bare and naked apprehensions of things,
as they present themselves unto thee, and add not unto them. It is
reported unto thee, that such a one speaketh ill of thee. Well; that he
speaketh ill of thee, so much is reported. But that thou art hurt
thereby, is not reported: that is the addition of opinion, which thou
must exclude. I see that my child is sick. That he is sick, I see, but
that he is in danger of his life also, I see it not. Thus thou must use
to keep thyself to the first motions and apprehensions of things, as
they present themselves outwardly; and add not unto them from within
thyself through mere conceit and opinion. Or rather add unto them: hut
as one that understandeth the true nature of all things that happen in
the world.
members.english: Say nothing more to yourself than what the impressions that lead the way report. It has been reported that so-and-so is speaking ill of you. That has been reported; but that you have been harmed has not been reported. I see that the child is sick. I see it; but that the child is in danger I do not see. So always stay like this with the first impressions and say nothing further yourself from within, and nothing happens to you. Or rather, do say something further, as one who recognises each of the things that happen in the universe.
members.greek: Μηδὲν πλέον σαυτῷ λέγε ὧν αἱ προηγούμεναι φαντασίαι ἀναγγέλλουσιν. ἤγγελται ὅτι ὁ δεῖνά σε κακῶς λέγει. ἤγγελται τοῦτο· τὸ δέ, ὅτι βέβλαψαι, οὐκ ἤγγελται. βλέπω ὅτι νοσεῖ τὸ παιδίον. βλέπω· ὅτι δὲ κινδυνεύει, οὐ βλέπω. οὕτως οὖν μένε ἀεὶ ἐπὶ τῶν πρώτων φαντασιῶν καὶ μηδὲν αὐτὸς ἔνδοθεν ἐπίλεγε καὶ οὐδέν σοι γίνεται· μᾶλλον δὲ ἐπίλεγε ὡς γνωρίζων ἕκαστα τῶν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ συμβαινόντων.

members.text:
Remember that all is but opinion, and all opinion depends of the
mind. Take thine opinion away, and then as a ship that hath stricken
in within the arms and mouth of the harbour, a present calm; all things
safe and steady: a bay, not capable of any storms and tempests: as the
poet hath it.
members.english: That all things are judgment, and this judgment is up to you. So take the judgment away when you wish, and, just as for someone who has rounded the headland, there is calm: all things steady, and a bay without a wave.
members.greek: Ὅτι πάντα ὑπόληψις καὶ αὕτη ἐπὶ σοί. ἆρον οὖν ὅτε θέλεις τὴν ὑπόληψιν καὶ ὥσπερ κάμψαντι τὴν ἄκραν γαλήνη, σταθερὰ πάντα καὶ κόλπος ἀκύμων.

members.text:
Conceit no such things, as he that wrongeth thee conceiveth,
or would have thee to conceive, but look into the matter itself, and see
what it is in very truth.
members.english: Do not judge things to be such as the person who abuses you decides they are, or wants you to decide they are, but see them as they are in truth.
members.greek: Μὴ τοιαῦτα ὑπολάμβανε, οἷα ὁ ὑβρίζων κρίνει ἢ οἷά σε κρίνειν βούλεται, ἀλλὰ ἴδε αὐτά, ὁποῖα κατʼ ἀλήθειάν ἐστιν.

members.text:
Remember that all is but opinion and conceit, for those things
are plain and apparent, which were spoken unto Monimus the Cynic; and as
plain and apparent is the use that may be made of those things, if that
which is true and serious in them, be received as well as that which is
sweet and pleasing.
members.english: That everything is judgment. For what is said in answer to Monimus the Cynic is plain; but plain too is the usefulness of the saying, if one takes what is nourishing in it so far as it is true.
members.greek: Ὅτι πᾶν ὑπόληψις. δῆλα μὲν γὰρ τὰ πρὸς τὸν Κυνικὸν Μόνιμον λεγόμενα· δῆλον δὲ καὶ τὸ χρήσιμον τοῦ λεγομένου, ἐάν τις αὐτοῦ τὸ νόστιμον μέχρι τοῦ ἀληθοῦς δέχηται.

members.text:
This day I did come out of all my trouble. Nay I have cast out all
my trouble; it should rather be for that which troubled thee, whatsoever
it was, was not without anywhere that thou shouldest come out of it, but
within in thine own opinions, from whence it must be cast out, before
thou canst truly and constantly be at ease.
members.english: Today I got out of all that hemmed me in, or rather I threw out all that hemmed me in; for it was not outside but inside, in my judgments.
members.greek: Σήμερον ἐξῆλθον πάσης περιστάσεως, μᾶλλον δὲ ἐξέβαλον πᾶσαν περίστασιν· ἔξω γὰρ οὐκ ἦν, ἀλλὰ ἔνδον ἐν ταῖς ὑπολήψεσιν.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay those of 1634. In modern editions 8.38 is 8.40, 6.47 is 6.52, 7.13 is 7.16, 9.30 is the opening of 9.32, 8.47 is 8.49, 12.16 is 12.22, 4.9 is 4.11, 2.13 is 2.15 and 9.11 is 9.13; 7.2 is the first part of 7.2.

Reads “reason” (8.38) and “the ruling part” (7.13) as the same thing and calls both “my reason” in claim 4. Reads the unnamed “anything else of yours” of 8.38 beside the “little body” of 7.13; the Greek of 8.38 does not name the body.

The statement says “what troubles me” without “all” or “many”. 9.30 says many of the things that trouble me rest on judgment, 9.11 says all that hemmed him in was in his judgments, and 2.13 holds “everything is judgment” only so far as it is true.

Uses “trouble” in the statement and in claims 1 and 2 for three of the translation’s words: “trouble” (9.30, 6.47), “disturbed” (7.2) and “hemmed in” (9.11). “Distress” is kept as it is in claims 3 and 4. The quotes keep the difference.

Fuses 8.47 and 4.9 into claim 5 although they share few words: both take a person who speaks against me, and both answer with “see” in the translation. The words “I see things as they are” rest on 4.9; 8.47 backs them only by its example of the sick child.

Quotes 9.30 although the passage is cut in mid-sentence. The Greek goes on to say that the open room is made by taking the whole universe in thought; claim 3 quotes only the room, and says where it lists what the fusion changed that the room is not to be read as coming from removing a judgment alone. Also leaves out “it does not frighten itself into desire” (7.13), where the translators’ note says the Greek text has been doubted, and the “little soul” of the same passage.
articles.limit: 12.16 feeds three of the five claims and two of the three parts of the statement, so the article leans on one short passage. The passages do not agree on what to do with a judgment: 6.47 says I may form none, 7.2 that I can form the one I ought, 8.47 first says to add nothing and then to add something. Claim 2 keeps 6.47 and 7.2 side by side, and claim 5 and the said-once item on 8.47’s correction keep the two halves of 8.47; the article settles neither. Article 2 already says that I take care in my judgments and that reason is not to be overpowered by the senses. What this article adds is that the trouble itself rests on the judgment, and that the judgment can be taken away.

articles.title: What happens can be borne and does not harm me

statement.t: Nothing happens to me that I cannot bear; what happens harms me only if I judge it bad, and it does not stop me from being good and just.

parts.words: Nothing happens to me that I cannot bear
what happens harms me only if I judge it bad
it does not stop me from being good and just

statement.kind: Two grounds, what follows from them, and rules for the moment
statement.form: Claims 1 and 2 are the grounds: what happens is within what I am fitted to bear, and the harm lies in my judgment. Claims 3 and 4 say what follows for the body and for conduct. Claims 5 and 6 are exercises for the moment a thing strikes. The statement joins the two grounds and claim 4 with no step of the editor’s.

groups.name: Why
groups.asks: The ground for the statement.

groups.name: In action
groups.asks: What follows for what I do.

groups.name: Practice
groups.asks: An exercise I can repeat.

groups.name: When it breaks
groups.asks: What failing looks like, and the way back.

groups.name: If I doubt it

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, five of the six claims gain a second witness: nothing is beyond my power to bear, I suffer according to opinion, pain is a sensation of the body, whatever I am given is material for virtue, and pain is slight when opinion adds nothing to it. The article gains a way of turning the mind from pain, a question that catches the sorrow I add myself, and a reason to go on living when I could leave. He challenges the first claim: a pain I cannot bear may come, though it is short. He limits the third: the mind is steady only once virtue is complete.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement is challenged in its first part. That part does not stand as it is worded: Seneca, like Marcus in 10.3, allows a pain I cannot bear, and says only that it will not last, though elsewhere he says nothing is beyond my power to bear. The rest of the statement stands.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: none of these things is an evil, none is beyond your power to bear, or is burdensome
piece.follows: None of the things Seneca has listed is an evil, and none is beyond a person’s power to bear.
piece.context: After the fire that destroyed Lyons, Seneca tells Lucilius what everyone must suffer. “These things” are pain, thirst, hunger, old age, sickness, loss and death.
gives: Nothing happens to me that I cannot bear

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: It is according to opinion that we suffer.
piece.follows: How much we suffer depends on our opinion.
piece.context: Letter 78 is to Lucilius, who is ill, on bearing pain. “Opinion” is what we tell ourselves about our trouble; Seneca has just said that everything depends on it.
gives: my own judgment

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: for a man there is no misery unless there be something in the universe which he thinks miserable
piece.follows: A person is miserable only if there is something that he thinks miserable.
piece.context: Letter 96: Seneca answers a Lucilius who chafes and complains, and lists his own illness and losses. The one real evil in such things, he says, is the complaining.
gives: my own judgment
that it is bad

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: the wise man will tremble, will feel pain, will turn pale, For all these are sensations of the body
piece.follows: Even the wise man trembles, feels pain and turns pale, because these are sensations of the body.
piece.context: Letter 71 argues that the honourable is the only good. Seneca grants that virtue does not rise above nature, and places real distress in the mind, if trials drag it down.
gives: the pain is for the body and its senses to see to

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Therefore a high-minded and sensible man divorces soul from body, and dwells much with the better or divine part, and only as far as he must with this complaining and frail portion.
piece.follows: A sensible person keeps the soul apart from the body and stays with the complaining body only as far as he must.
piece.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness: the inexperienced cannot stand bodily pain because they live too close to the body. The “complaining and frail portion” is the body.
gives: the pain is for the body and its senses to see to

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: If you had given him marble, or a still meaner material, he would have made of it the best statue that the material would permit. So the wise man will develop virtue, if he may, in the midst of wealth, or, if not, in poverty
piece.follows: As a sculptor makes the best statue his material allows, the wise man develops virtue in wealth or in poverty.
piece.context: Letter 85 defends the view that poverty and pain do not harm the wise man: he makes use of evils. “Him” is the sculptor Phidias, who worked in ivory and in bronze.
gives: What comes to hand is material
for virtue

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Pain is slight if opinion has added nothing to it
piece.follows: Pain is slight when opinion has added nothing to it.
piece.context: Letter 78, to Lucilius, who is ill: do not make troubles heavier by complaining. “Opinion” is what a person adds to the pain by what he says of it to himself.
gives: I take a hardship bare, by itself, and add nothing to it
not my opinion

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Two elements must therefore be rooted out once for all,—the fear of future suffering, and the recollection of past suffering; since the latter no longer concerns me, and the former concerns me not yet.
piece.follows: Fear of suffering to come and memory of suffering past must both go: the past no longer concerns me and the future does not yet.
piece.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness: Seneca wants an end to laments over what one has suffered. “The latter” is past suffering; “the former” is suffering still to come.
gives: not the rest of my life

items.label: practice
items.t: When I am in pain I turn my mind aside to other things: to the honourable and brave things I have done, and to the brave men who have conquered pain. If pain can be conquered by a smile, it can be conquered by reason.
items.why: Marcus gives rules to recall and one example, Epicurus, who went on with philosophy in illness. Seneca makes a method of it: turn the mind away from the pain, toward my own good deeds and toward those who have beaten it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: This, too, will help—to turn the mind aside to thoughts of other things and thus to depart from pain.
support.follows: It helps to turn the mind to other thoughts and so to leave the pain.
support.context: Letter 78, to Lucilius who is ill: having argued that pain is bearable or short, Seneca lists further helps. “This” is turning the mind to other thoughts.
gives: I turn my mind aside to other things

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Call to mind what honourable or brave deeds you have done; consider the good side of your own life.
support.follows: In pain I should recall my own honourable and brave deeds and the good side of my life.
support.context: Letter 78, Seneca’s advice to the sick Lucilius on where to turn the mind when in pain: first to what he himself has done well.
gives: the honourable and brave things I have done

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Then think of all the brave men who have conquered pain
support.follows: I should think of all the brave men who have conquered pain.
support.context: Letter 78, to the sick Lucilius: Seneca goes on to name such men, one who read a book during surgery and one who kept smiling at his torturers.
gives: the brave men who have conquered pain

support.author: seneca
support.quote: If pain can be conquered by a smile, will it not be conquered by reason?
support.follows: If a smile can conquer pain, reason can.
support.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness: Seneca has just told of a man who kept smiling under torture, and argues from him to what reason can do against pain.
gives: If pain can be conquered by a smile, it can be conquered by reason

items.label: breaks
items.role: Three ways I add to it
items.t: When a sorrow torments me more than it should, before it should, or when it should not at all, I am exaggerating it, imagining it or anticipating it. I ask myself: am I tormented without sufficient reason, and am I turning what is not an evil into an evil?
items.why: Marcus names one way I add to a hardship, by taking in the past and the future along with it (8.34), and says not to add to it by opinion (7.35). Seneca names three ways, and gives a question that catches them.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Accordingly, some things torment us more than they ought; some torment us before they ought; and some torment us when they ought not to torment us at all. We are in the habit of exaggerating, or imagining, or anticipating, sorrow.
support.follows: Some things torment us too much, some too early, some with no cause: we exaggerate, imagine or anticipate sorrow.
support.context: Letter 13 is on groundless fears; Seneca has just said that we suffer more often in imagination than in reality. “We” is people in general.
gives: When a sorrow torments me more than it should, before it should, or when it should not at all
I am exaggerating it, imagining it or anticipating it

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Am I tormented without sufficient reason, am I morose, and do I convert what is not an evil into what is an evil?
support.follows: I should ask whether I am tormented without reason and whether I am making an evil of what is not one.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears: when others try to persuade Lucilius that he is unhappy, he is to consult his own feeling and put this question to himself.
gives: am I tormented without sufficient reason
am I turning what is not an evil into an evil

items.label: doubt
items.t: Before I leave a life I could bravely leave, I ask who would not be able to bear the loss of me. Sometimes it is an act of bravery even to live.
items.why: 8.45 lets me leave life in a kindly spirit when it is not worth living. Seneca, who had the same impulse in a long illness, adds what held him back: his father, who could not have borne the loss.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: For I reflected, not how bravely I had the power to die, but how little power he had to bear bravely the loss of me.
support.follows: Seneca weighed not how bravely he could die but how badly his father could bear losing him.
support.context: Letter 78: Seneca recalls a long illness of his youth in which he often wanted to end his life. “He” is his old father, the thought of whom held him back.
gives: I ask who would not be able to bear the loss of me

support.author: seneca
support.quote: And so I commanded myself to live. For sometimes it is an act of bravery even to live.
support.follows: Seneca ordered himself to live; sometimes living is itself the brave act.
support.context: Letter 78: Seneca on the illness of his youth. He wanted to end his life and did not, for his father’s sake; his studies and his friends then consoled him.
gives: Sometimes it is an act of bravery even to live

items.t: Seneca gives the steady mind to the person whose virtue is complete. He agrees that pain belongs to the body and that the rational part cannot be conquered (Ep. 71.27, 71.29), but he says that until the good is fully attained the mind wavers, and that someone still on the way will slip back at times. This limits the claim and does not contradict it: Marcus says that the mind can keep its calm; Seneca says who can count on it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Before this is completely attained, the mind wavers in uncertainty; only when it is fully achieved is the mind fixed and steady.
support.follows: Until the supreme good is fully attained the mind wavers; only then is it fixed and steady.
support.context: Letter 71: the wise man feels pain, with an irrational part that can be hurt and a rational part that cannot be conquered. “This” is the supreme good, in the rational part.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: one will retrograde at times and there will be a certain slackening of mental effort
support.follows: A person who is not yet perfect will slip back at times and slacken.
support.context: Letter 71, on the honourable as the only good. “One” is a person who has just begun or is still on the way to virtue, set against the man whose virtue is complete.

items.t: Seneca disagrees with “Nothing happens to me that I cannot bear”, which is also the statement’s first part. He says that nature has made pain either endurable or short, and he tells Pain to its face that it is slight if he can bear it and short if he cannot: so a pain I cannot bear may come, and what he promises is only that it will not last. Marcus’s own 10.3 allows the same case (“it will perish once it has used you up”). Seneca is inconsistent with himself here: in Letter 91 he says that none of these things, pain among them, is beyond my power to bear (Ep. 91.19), and in Letter 96 that he will not endure himself on the day he finds anything unendurable (Ep. 96.1).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: No man can suffer both severely and for a long time; Nature, who loves us most tenderly, has so constituted us as to make pain either endurable or short.
support.follows: No one suffers both severely and for long: nature has made pain either endurable or short.
support.context: Letter 78, to Lucilius who is ill: of the three hard things in disease Seneca takes up bodily pain, and says that extreme pain must come to an end.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Slight thou art, if I can bear thee; short thou art if I cannot bear thee!
support.follows: Pain is slight if I can bear it and short if I cannot.
support.context: Letter 24, on fears: Seneca strips the masks from Death and Pain and speaks to each. “Thou” is Pain, which the gouty man scorns and the woman in labour bears bravely.

passages.title: On the lesson to be drawn from the burning of lyons [ 1 ]
passages.text: Nevertheless, you should not believe those whose noisy clamour surrounds you; none of these things is an evil, none is beyond your power to bear, or is burdensome. It is only by common opinion that there is anything formidable in them. Your fearing death is therefore like your fear of gossip. But what is more foolish than a man afraid of words? Our friend Demetrius is wont to put it cleverly when he says: “For me the talk of ignorant men is like the rumblings which issue from the belly. For,” he adds, “what difference does it make to me whether such rumblings come from above or from below?”

passages.title: On the healing power of the mind
passages.text: But do not of your own accord make your troubles heavier to bear and burden yourself with complaining. Pain is slight if opinion has added nothing to it; but if, on the other hand, you begin to encourage yourself and say, “It is nothing,—a trifling matter at most; keep a stout heart and it will soon cease”; then in thinking it slight, you will make it slight. Everything depends on opinion; ambition, luxury, greed, hark back to opinion. It is according to opinion that we suffer.

passages.title: On facing hardships
passages.text: Spite of all do you still chafe and complain, not understanding that, in all the evils to which you refer, there is really only one—the fact that you do chafe and complain? If you ask me, I think that for a man there is no misery unless there be something in the universe which he thinks miserable. I shall not endure myself on that day when I find anything unendurable. I am ill; but that is a part of my lot. My slaves have fallen sick, my income has gone off, my house is rickety, I have been assailed by losses, accidents, toil, and fear; this is a common thing. Nay, that was an understatement; it was an inevitable thing.

passages.title: On the supreme good
passages.text: And now I have reached the point to which your patient waiting summons me. You must not think that our human virtue transcends nature; the wise man will tremble, will feel pain, will turn pale, For all these are sensations of the body. Where, then, is the abode of utter distress, of that which is truly an evil? In the other part of us, no doubt, if it is the mind that these trials drag down, force to a confession of its servitude, and cause to regret its existence.

passages.title: On the healing power of the mind
passages.text: This is, accordingly, a consolation for excessive pain,—that you cannot help ceasing to feel it if you feel it to excess. The reason, however, why the inexperienced are impatient when their bodies suffer is, that they have not accustomed themselves to be contented in spirit. They have been closely associated with the body. Therefore a high-minded and sensible man divorces soul from body, and dwells much with the better or divine part, and only as far as he must with this complaining and frail portion.

passages.title: On some vain syllogisms
passages.text: Do you suppose that he is weighed down by evils? He makes use of them. It was not of ivory only that Phidias knew how to make statues; he also made statues of bronze. If you had given him marble, or a still meaner material, he would have made of it the best statue that the material would permit. So the wise man will develop virtue, if he may, in the midst of wealth, or, if not, in poverty; if possible, in his own country—if not, in exile; if possible, as a commander—if not, as a common soldier; if possible, in sound health—if not, enfeebled. Whatever fortune he finds, he will accomplish therefrom something noteworthy.

passages.title: On the healing power of the mind
passages.text: A man is as wretched as he has convinced himself that he is. I hold that we should do away with complaint about past sufferings and with all language like this: “None has ever been worse off than I. What sufferings, what evils have I endured! No one has thought that I shall recover. How often have my family bewailed me, and the physicians given me over! Men who are placed on the rack are not torn asunder with such agony!” However, even if all this is true, it is over and gone. What benefit is there in reviewing past sufferings, and in being unhappy, just because once you were unhappy? Besides, every one adds much to his own ills, and tells lies to himself. And that which was bitter to bear is pleasant to have borne; it is natural to rejoice at the ending of one’s ills. Two elements must therefore be rooted out once for all,—the fear of future suffering, and the recollection of past suffering; since the latter no longer concerns me, and the former concerns me not yet.

passages.title: On the healing power of the mind
passages.text: This, too, will help—to turn the mind aside to thoughts of other things and thus to depart from pain. Call to mind what honourable or brave deeds you have done; consider the good side of your own life. Run over in your memory those things which you have particularly admired. Then think of all the brave men who have conquered pain: of him who continued to read his book as he allowed the cutting out of varicose veins; of him who did not cease to smile, though that very smile so enraged his torturers that they tried upon him every instrument of their cruelty. If pain can be conquered by a smile, will it not be conquered by reason?

passages.title: On groundless fears
passages.text: Accordingly, some things torment us more than they ought; some torment us before they ought; and some torment us when they ought not to torment us at all. We are in the habit of exaggerating, or imagining, or anticipating, sorrow. The first of these three faults may be postponed for the present, because the subject is under discussion and the case is still in court, so to speak. That which I should call trifling, you will maintain to be most serious; for of course I know that some men laugh while being flogged, and that others wince at a box on the ear. We shall consider later whether these evils derive their power from their own strength, or from our own weakness.

passages.title: On groundless fears
passages.text: Do me the favour, when men surround you and try to talk you into believing that you are unhappy, to consider not what you hear but what you yourself feel, and to take counsel with your feelings and question yourself independently, because you know your own affairs better than anyone else does. Ask: “Is there any reason why these persons should condole with me? Why should they be worried or even fear some infection from me, as if troubles could be transmitted? Is there any evil involved, or is it a matter merely of ill report, rather than an evil?” Put the question voluntarily to yourself: “Am I tormented without sufficient reason, am I morose, and do I convert what is not an evil into what is an evil?”

passages.title: On the healing power of the mind
passages.text: I often entertained the impulse of ending my life then and there; but the thought of my kind old father kept me back. For I reflected, not how bravely I had the power to die, but how little power he had to bear bravely the loss of me. And so I commanded myself to live. For sometimes it is an act of bravery even to live.

passages.title: On the supreme good
passages.text: I do not withdraw the wise man from the category of man, nor do I deny to him the sense of pain as though he were a rock that has no feelings at all. I remember that he is made up of two parts: the one part is irrational,—it is this that may be bitten, burned, or hurt; the other part is rational,—it is this which holds resolutely to opinions, is courageous, and unconquerable. In the latter is situated man’s Supreme Good. Before this is completely attained, the mind wavers in uncertainty; only when it is fully achieved is the mind fixed and steady.

passages.title: On the supreme good
passages.text: And so when one has just begun, or is on one’s way to the heights and is cultivating virtue, or even if one is drawing near the perfect good but has not yet put the finishing touch upon it, one will retrograde at times and there will be a certain slackening of mental effort. For such a man has not yet traversed the doubtful ground; he is still standing in slippery places. But the happy man, whose virtue is complete, loves himself most of all when his bravery has been submitted to the severest test, and when he not only, endures but welcomes that which all other men regard with fear, if it is the price which he must pay for the performance of a duty which honour imposes, and he greatly prefers to have men say of him: “how much more noble!” rather than “how much more lucky!”

passages.title: On the healing power of the mind
passages.text: Let us now return to the consideration of the characteristic disadvantage of disease: it is accompanied by great suffering. The suffering, however, is rendered endurable by interruptions; for the strain of extreme pain must come to an end. No man can suffer both severely and for a long time; Nature, who loves us most tenderly, has so constituted us as to make pain either endurable or short.

passages.title: On despising death [ 1 ]
passages.text: “Why dost thou hold up before my eyes swords, fires, and a throng of executioners raging about thee? Take away all that vain show, behind which thou lurkest and scarest fools! Ah! thou art naught but Death, whom only yesterday a manservant of mine and a maid-servant did despise! Why dost thou again unfold and spread before me, with all that great display, the whip and the rack? Why are those engines of torture made ready, one for each several member of the body, and all the other innumerable machines for tearing a man apart piecemeal? Away with all such stuff, which makes us numb with terror! And thou, silence the groans, the cries, and the bitter shrieks ground out of the victim as he is torn on the rack! Forsooth thou are naught but Pain, scorned by yonder gout-ridden wretch, endured by yonder dyspeptic in the midst of his dainties, borne bravely by the girl in travail. Slight thou art, if I can bear thee; short thou art if I cannot bear thee!”

claims.t: Nothing happens to me that I cannot bear. I am fitted by nature to bear whatever my own judgment can make bearable. What happens to me is the kind of thing that happens to human beings, usual and natural, and I do not resent it.
claims.shared: 5.16 and 8.45 both say it of everything that happens and both end on bearing: nothing happens that a person is not “fitted by nature to bear” (5.16), nature brought nothing “that could not be borne” (8.45). 10.3 uses 5.16’s phrase, “fitted by nature to bear”, and says with 8.45 not to “resent it”.
claims.changed: 5.16 says “anyone” and 8.45 says “you”; the claim says “me”. 5.16 and 8.45 say it of everything that happens; 10.3 says only that I am fitted to bear whatever my own judgment can make bearable, and allows a second case, a thing I am not fitted to bear. The claim keeps 10.3’s condition in its second sentence and does not say that everything is within my judgment’s reach; the second case stands under “If I doubt it”. The ox, the vine and the stone of 8.45 are dropped.

claims.t: What troubles or harms me is not the thing outside me but my own judgment that it is bad. Unless I make that judgment I have not been harmed, and it is in my power not to make it, or to wipe it out once it is made.
claims.shared: All five passages put the trouble in the one who judges and not in the thing: “your own verdict” (8.45), “that which judges about bad things” (4.32), “unless I judge” (7.11), “the judgment” (4.7), and things that “do not touch the soul” (5.16). 7.11 and 4.7 share the words “been harmed”. 8.45 and 7.11 both say that something about the judgment is open to me (“in your power”, “possible for me”): 7.11 not to judge, 8.45 to wipe out a verdict already made.
claims.changed: “Verdict” (8.45) and “judgment” (4.7) translate two Greek words; the claim uses “judgment” for both. 4.32 speaks of what is bad for me, 8.45 of what troubles me, 7.11 and 4.7 of harm; the claim says “troubles or harms”. 7.11 says “not yet been harmed”; the claim says “not been harmed”.

claims.t: Even if my body is cut, burned or torn apart, the pain is for the body and its senses to see to. Nothing from outside touches my mind: it can keep its own calm, and it does not add the judgment that this is bad.
claims.shared: 4.32 and 7.39 both take the worst that can be done to the body (“is cut, is burned”; “tearing apart the little limbs”) and both leave the mind where it was. 7.39 and 8.26 share the word “calm”. 8.26 and 5.20 name the one thing the mind must not do: “judge that it is a bad thing” (8.26), “add … the judgment that it is something good or bad” (5.20). 8.26, 8.39 and 5.20 hand the pain to the body or to sensation.
claims.changed: The claim says “my mind” where the passages say “the soul” (8.26), “the mind” (7.39), “the ruling part” (5.20) and “what is the mind’s own” (8.39). 5.20 speaks of pleasure as well as pain and says “good or bad”; the claim keeps pain and “bad”. 5.20 also grants that the feeling does reach the mind; that sentence stands as a said-once item under “In action”.

claims.t: Nothing that happens prevents me from being good and just; that is in my power everywhere. What comes to hand is material for virtue: using it rightly makes me better, and to bear it nobly is good fortune.
