support.quote: “What is there in this task that is unbearable and not to be endured?” For you will be ashamed to admit it.
support.follows: Asked what is unbearable in the task in front of me, I would be ashamed to name anything.
gives: it is not unbearable

single.quote: That is, let it decide that nothing is either bad or good which can happen equally to a bad man and a good one.
single.label: Good and bad alike
single.t: Nothing is bad or good that can happen equally to a bad man and a good one.
single.why: Only this passage argues from the fact that the same things happen to good people and bad. It is a separate ground, and no second passage of the section gives it.
single.follows: What can happen equally to a bad man and a good one is neither bad nor good.

single.quote: Do not be swept off wholesale by the impression, but help as far as you are able and as far as is deserved, even if it is in the middle things that they are coming off worse; do not, however, form the impression that it is a harm, for that is a bad habit.
single.label: Help without alarm
single.t: When other people lose things that are neither good nor bad, I help as far as I am able and as far as is deserved. I do not form the impression that their loss is a harm.
single.why: Only this passage turns from my own hardship to other people’s losses. It keeps the help and withholds the judgment.
single.follows: I should help as far as I can even when the loss is in indifferent things, but I should not form the impression that it is a harm.

single.quote: So do the same as he did, in illness, if you are ill, and in any other circumstance. For not to stand away from philosophy in anything whatever that befalls
single.label: In illness
single.t: In illness, and in any other circumstance, I do as Epicurus did when he was ill: I keep to philosophy, whatever befalls.
single.why: Only this passage gives an example to copy. By his own account Epicurus, when ill, did not talk about his body’s sufferings and went on inquiring into nature. The sentence that begins with “For” is cut off in the passage.
single.follows: In illness, and in any other circumstance, I should do as Epicurus did and not stand away from philosophy, whatever befalls.

single.quote: many things that are the same as pain go unnoticed as such, though we resent them, such as being drowsy, being overheated and having no appetite. So when you are displeased at any of these, say to yourself: “You are giving in to pain.”
single.label: Pain unnoticed
single.t: Being drowsy, overheated or without appetite is the same as pain, though I do not notice it as such. When one of these displeases me, I say to myself: “You are giving in to pain.”
single.why: Only this passage names the small discomforts and gives words to say when I resent them. It shows what failing looks like on an ordinary day.
single.follows: Drowsiness, heat and loss of appetite are forms of pain; being displeased at them is giving in to pain.

single.quote: Did something come to stand in the way of your impulse? If your impulse was without reservation, then it is already a bad thing for you as a rational being. But if you accept the common lot, you have not yet been harmed or hindered.
single.label: An unconditional impulse
single.t: If I set out on something unconditionally, without keeping in mind “if nothing prevents it”, and something comes to stand in its way, that is already a bad thing for me as a rational being. If I accept the common lot, I have not yet been harmed or hindered.
single.why: Only this passage says when an obstacle does harm me: when I wanted the thing unconditionally. It gives the failure and the way back.
single.follows: A blocked impulse is already bad for me if it was without reservation; if I accept the common lot I have not yet been harmed or hindered.

single.quote: But when they pass up into the mind by the other shared feeling, as in a body that is one, then one should not try to go against the sensation, which is natural
single.label: The feeling is natural
single.t: When the body’s feelings do pass up into my mind, I do not try to go against the sensation, which is natural.
single.why: Only this passage grants that the line between body and mind is crossed. It says what I do then: I let the sensation be and withhold only the judgment.
single.follows: When bodily feelings reach the mind, one should not fight the sensation, which is natural.

single.quote: The same things happen to someone else, and either because they do not know that it has happened, or because they are showing off greatness of mind, they stand firm and remain unhurt. It is a terrible thing, then, that ignorance and the wish to please should be stronger than wisdom.
single.label: Outdone by ignorance
single.t: Other people stand firm and unhurt under the same things, because they do not know what has happened or because they are showing off. It is a terrible thing if ignorance and the wish to please are stronger than wisdom.
single.why: Only this passage compares me with people who bear the same things for worse reasons. It is a rebuke for the moment I give way.
single.follows: Others bear the same things out of ignorance or to show off; it is terrible if those are stronger than wisdom.

single.quote: And if in a way you are not fitted by nature to bear, do not resent it: for it will perish once it has used you up.
single.label: If I cannot bear it
single.t: If something happens that I am not fitted by nature to bear, I do not resent that either: it will perish once it has used me up. When it has consumed me, it comes to an end with me.
single.why: Only this passage allows that something may be more than I can bear. It is the section’s own answer to a doubt about the first claim.
single.follows: What I am not fitted to bear ends once it has used me up, so it too is not to be resented.

single.quote: “But something stronger stands in the way.” Then do not be distressed, for the cause of its not being done does not lie with you. “But life is not worth living if this is not done.” Then leave life in a kindly spirit, just as the one who is doing it dies too, and at the same time gracious towards the things that stand in the way.
single.label: If I am blocked
single.t: If something stronger keeps me from doing what seems sound to me, I am not distressed, for the cause does not lie with me. If life is not worth living without it, I leave life in a kindly spirit, gracious towards what stands in the way.
single.why: Only this passage follows the objection to its end: an obstacle that cannot be removed, and a life judged not worth living without the thing. 10.33 also speaks of not going on living, but as the price of not being good, not as the answer to an obstacle.
single.follows: If something stronger blocks the act, the cause is not mine and I need not be distressed; if life is not worth living without it, I may leave life kindly.

members.text:
Nothing can happen unto thee, which is not incidental unto thee, as
thou art a man. As nothing can happen either to an ox, a vine, or to
a stone, which is not incidental unto them; unto every one in his own
kind. If therefore nothing can happen unto anything, which is not both
usual and natural; why art thou displeased? Sure the common nature
of all would not bring anything upon any, that were intolerable. If
therefore it be a thing external that causes thy grief, know, that it is
not that properly that doth cause it, but thine own conceit and opinion
concerning the thing: which thou mayest rid thyself of, when thou wilt.
But if it be somewhat that is amiss in thine own disposition, that doth
grieve thee, mayest thou not rectify thy moral tenets and opinions. But
if it grieve thee, that thou doest not perform that which seemeth unto
thee right and just, why doest not thou choose rather to perform it than
to grieve? But somewhat that is stronger than thyself doth hinder thee.
Let it not grieve thee then, if it be not thy fault that the thing is
not performed. 'Yea but it is a thing of that nature, as that thy life
is not worth the while, except it may be performed.' If it be so, upon
condition that thou be kindly and lovingly disposed towards all men,
thou mayest be gone. For even then, as much as at any time, art thou in
a very good estate of performance, when thou doest die in charity with
those, that are an obstacle unto thy performance.
members.english:
Nothing can happen to any human being that is not a human occurrence, nor to an ox that is not of the ox kind, nor to a vine that is not of the vine kind, nor to a stone that is not proper to a stone. So if what happens to each is what is both usual and natural, why would you resent it? For the common nature was bringing you nothing that could not be borne.

If you are distressed because of something outside you, it is not that thing that troubles you but your own verdict about it, and to wipe that out at once is in your power. But if what distresses you is something in your own disposition, who prevents you from putting your principle right? In the same way, if you are distressed because you are not doing some particular thing that seems sound to you, why not do it rather than be distressed? “But something stronger stands in the way.” Then do not be distressed, for the cause of its not being done does not lie with you. “But life is not worth living if this is not done.” Then leave life in a kindly spirit, just as the one who is doing it dies too, and at the same time gracious towards the things that stand in the way.
members.greek:
Ἀνθρώπῳ οὐδενὶ συμβαίνειν τι δύναται ὃ οὐκ ἔστιν ἀνθρωπικὸν σύμπτωμα, οὐδὲ βοὶ ὃ οὐκ ἔστι βοικόν, οὐδὲ ἀμπέλῳ ὃ οὐκ ἔστιν ἀμπελικόν, οὐδὲ λίθῳ ὃ οὐκ ἔστι λίθου ἴδιον. εἰ οὖν ἑκάστῳ συμβαίνει ὃ καὶ εἴωθε καὶ πέφυκε, τί ἂν δυσχεραίνοις; οὐ γὰρ ἀφόρητόν σοι ἔφερεν ἡ κοινὴ φύσις.

Εἰ μὲν διά τι τῶν ἐκτὸς λυπῇ, οὐκ ἐκεῖνό σοι ἐνοχλεῖ, ἀλλὰ τὸ σὸν περὶ αὐτοῦ κρῖμα, τοῦτο δὲ ἤδη ἐξαλεῖψαι ἐπὶ σοί ἐστιν. εἰ δὲ λυπεῖ σέ τι τῶν ἐν τῇ σῇ διαθέσει, τίς ὁ κωλύων διορθῶσαι τὸ δόγμα; ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ εἰ λυπῇ ὅτι οὐχὶ τόδε τι ἐνεργεῖς ὑγιές σοι φαινόμενον, τί οὐχὶ μᾶλλον ἐνεργεῖς ἢ λυπῇ;—ἀλλὰ ἰσχυρότερόν τι ἐνίσταται.—μὴ οὖν λυποῦ· οὐ γὰρ παρὰ σὲ ἡ αἰτία τοῦ μὴ ἐνεργεῖσθαι.—ἀλλὰ οὐκ ἄξιον ζῆν μὴ ἐνεργουμένου τούτου.—ἄπιθι οὖν ἐκ τοῦ ζῆν εὐμενής, ᾗ καὶ ὁ ἐνεργῶν ἀποθνῄσκει, ἅμα ἵλεως τοῖς ἐνισταμένοις.

members.text:
Let it not be in any man's power, to say truly of thee, that
thou art not truly simple, or sincere and open, or not good. Let him be
deceived whosoever he be that shall have any such opinion of thee. For
all this doth depend of thee. For who is it that should hinder thee from
being either truly simple or good? Do thou only resolve rather not to
live, than not to be such. For indeed neither doth it stand with reason
that he should live that is not such. What then is it that may upon this
present occasion according to best reason and discretion, either be said
or done? For whatsoever it be, it is in thy power either to do it, or
to say it, and therefore seek not any pretences, as though thou wert
hindered. Thou wilt never cease groaning and complaining, until such
time as that, what pleasure is unto the voluptuous, be unto thee, to do
in everything that presents itself, whatsoever may be done conformably
and agreeably to the proper constitution of man, or, to man as he is a
man. For thou must account that pleasure, whatsoever it be, that thou
mayest do according to thine own nature. And to do this, every place
will fit thee. Unto the _cylindrus_, or roller, it is not granted to
move everywhere according to its own proper motion, as neither unto
the water, nor unto the fire, nor unto any other thing, that either is
merely natural, or natural and sensitive; but not rational for many
things there be that can hinder their operations. But of the mind and
understanding this is the proper privilege, that according to its own
nature, and as it will itself, it can pass through every obstacle that
it finds, and keep straight on forwards. Setting therefore before thine
eyes this happiness and felicity of thy mind, whereby it is able to pass
through all things, and is capable of all motions, whether as the fire,
upwards; or as the stone downwards, or as the _cylindrus_ through that
which is sloping: content thyself with it, and seek not after any other
thing. For all other kind of hindrances that are not hindrances of thy
mind either they are proper to the body, or merely proceed from the
opinion, reason not making that resistance that it should, but basely,
and cowardly suffering itself to be foiled; and of themselves can
neither wound, nor do any hurt at all. Else must he of necessity,
whosoever he be that meets with any of them, become worse than he was
before. For so is it in all other subjects, that that is thought hurtful
unto them, whereby they are made worse. But here contrariwise, man (if
he make that good use of them that he should) is rather the better
and the more praiseworthy for any of those kind of hindrances, than
otherwise. But generally remember that nothing can hurt a natural
citizen, that is not hurtful unto the city itself, nor anything hurt
the city, that is not hurtful unto the law itself. But none of these
casualties, or external hindrances, do hurt the law itself; or, are
contrary to that course of justice and equity, by which public societies
are maintained: neither therefore do they hurt either city or citizen.
members.english:
Let it not be possible for anyone to say truthfully of you that you are not straightforward or that you are not good, but let anyone who is going to judge any of these things about you be mistaken. All of this is in your power: for who prevents you from being good and straightforward? You have only to decide not to go on living unless you are going to be such a person, for reason does not require you to live either, if you are not such.

With this material, what is it that can be done or said in the soundest way? For whatever it is, it is possible to do it or say it, and do not make the excuse that you are being prevented. You will not stop groaning until this has come over you: that what luxury is to those who live for pleasure, that is what it is for you to do, with the material that is supplied and comes to hand, the things that belong to the way a human being is made. For one must judge everything that it is possible to do in accordance with one’s own nature to be an enjoyment. And it is possible everywhere. Now a cylinder is not granted everywhere to be carried along in its own motion, nor is water, nor fire, nor the other things that are governed by nature or by a soul without reason: for the things that bar them and stand in their way are many. But mind and reason can make their way through everything that falls against them, in the way their nature is and in the way they wish. Set this ease before your eyes, the ease with which reason will be carried through all things as fire is carried up, as a stone down, as a cylinder down a slope, and look for nothing more. For the remaining obstacles either belong to the little body, the dead thing, or, without a judgment and the giving in of reason itself, they break no one and do nothing bad at all. Otherwise the one affected would themselves at once become bad. At any rate with all other made things, whatever bad thing happens to any of them, the thing affected itself becomes worse because of it. But here, if it must be said, the human being becomes both better and more praiseworthy by using rightly the things that befall them. In general, remember that nothing harms one who is by nature a citizen that does not harm the city, and nothing harms the city that does not harm the law. And of these so-called strokes of bad luck not one harms the law. So what does not harm the law harms neither city nor citizen.
members.greek:
Μηδενὶ ἐξέστω εἰπεῖν ἀληθεύοντι περὶ σοῦ ὅτι οὐχ ἁπλοῦς ἢ ὅτι οὐκ ἀγαθός, ἀλλὰ ψευδέσθω, ὅστις τούτων τι περὶ σοῦ ὑπολήψεται. πᾶν δὲ τοῦτο ἐπὶ σοί· τίς γὰρ ὁ κωλύων ἀγαθὸν εἶναί σε καὶ ἁπλοῦν; σὺ μόνον κρῖνον μηκέτι ζῆν, εἰ μὴ τοιοῦτος ἔσῃ· οὐδὲ γὰρ αἱρεῖ λόγος μὴ τοιοῦτον ὄντα.

Τί ἐστι τὸ ἐπὶ ταύτης τῆς ὕλης δυνάμενον κατὰ τὸ ὑγιέστατον πραχθῆναι ἢ ῥηθῆναι; ὅ τι γὰρ ἂν τοῦτο ᾖ, ἔξεστιν αὐτὸ πρᾶξαι ἢ εἰπεῖν καὶ μὴ προφασίζου ὡς κωλυόμενος. Οὐ πρότερον παύσῃ στένων πρὶν ἢ τοῦτο πάθῃς, ὅτι οἷόν ἐστι τοῖς ἡδυπαθοῦσιν ἡ τρυφή; τοιοῦτό σοι τὸ ἐπὶ τῆς ὑποβαλλομένης καὶ ὑποπιπτούσης ὕλης ποιεῖν τὰ οἰκεῖα τῇ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου κατασκευῇ· ἀπόλαυσιν γὰρ δεῖ ὑπολαμβάνειν πᾶν ὃ ἔξεστι κατὰ τὴν ἰδίαν φύσιν ἐνεργεῖν. πανταχοῦ δὲ ἔξεστι. τῷ μὲν οὖν κυλίνδρῳ οὐ πανταχοῦ δίδοται φέρεσθαι τὴν ἰδίαν κίνησιν οὐδὲ τῷ ὕδατι οὐδὲ πυρὶ οὐδὲ τοῖς ἄλλοις ὅσα ὑπὸ φύσεως ἢ ψυχῆς ἀλόγου διοικεῖται· τὰ γὰρ διείργοντα καὶ ἐνιστάμενα πολλά· νοῦς δὲ καὶ λόγος διὰ παντὸς τοῦ ἀντιπίπτοντος οὕτως πορεύεσθαι δύναται ὡς πέφυκε καὶ ὡς θέλει. ταύτην τὴν ῥᾳστώνην πρὸ ὀμμάτων τιθέμενος, καθ’ ἣν ἐνεχθήσεται ὁ λόγος διὰ πάντων ὡς πῦρ ἄνω, ὡς λίθος κάτω, ὡς κύλινδρος κατὰ πρανοῦς, μηκέτι μηδὲν ἐπιζήτει· τὰ γὰρ λοιπὰ ἐγκόμματα ἤτοι τοῦ σωματίου ἐστὶ τοῦ νεκροῦ, ἢ χωρὶς ὑπολήψεως καὶ τῆς αὐτοῦ τοῦ λόγου ἐνδόσεως οὐ θραύει οὐδὲ ποιεῖ κακὸν οὐδ’ ὁτιοῦν. ἐπεί τοι καὶ ὁ πάσχων αὐτὸς κακὸς ἂν εὐθὺς ἐγίνετο· ἐπὶ γοῦν τῶν ἄλλων κατασκευασμάτων πάντων, ὅ τι ἂν κακόν τινι αὐτῶν συμβῇ, παρὰ τοῦτο χεῖρον γίνεται αὐτὸ τὸ πάσχον, ἐνταῦθα δέ, εἰ δεῖ εἰπεῖν, καὶ κρείττων γίνεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος καὶ ἐπαινετώτερος, ὀρθῶς χρώμενος τοῖς προσπίπτουσιν. ὅλως δὲ μέμνησο ὅτι τὸν φύσει πολίτην οὐδὲν βλάπτει ὃ πόλιν οὐ βλάπτει, οὐδέ γε πόλιν βλάπτει ὃ νόμον οὐ βλάπτει· τούτων δὲ τῶν καλουμένων ἀκληρημάτων οὐδὲν βλάπτει νόμον. ὃ τοίνυν νόμον οὐ βλάπτει, οὔτε πόλιν οὔτε πολίτην.

members.text:
Free from all compulsion in all cheerfulness and alacrity thou
mayst run out thy time, though men should exclaim against thee never so
much, and the wild beasts should pull in sunder the poor members of thy
pampered mass of flesh. For what in either of these or the like cases
should hinder the mind to retain her own rest and tranquillity,
consisting both in the right judgment of those things that happen unto
her, and in the ready use of all present matters and occasions? So that
her judgment may say, to that which is befallen her by way of cross:
this thou art in very deed, and according to thy true nature:
notwithstanding that in the judgment of opinion thou dust appear
otherwise: and her discretion to the present object; thou art that,
which I sought for. For whatsoever it be, that is now present, shall
ever be embraced by me as a fit and seasonable object, both for my
reasonable faculty, and for my sociable, or charitable inclination to
work upon. And that which is principal in this matter, is that it may be
referred either unto the praise of God, or to the good of men. For
either unto God or man, whatsoever it is that doth happen in the world
hath in the ordinary course of nature its proper reference; neither is
there anything, that in regard of nature is either new, or reluctant and
intractable, but all things both usual and easy.
members.english: To live life through unforced and in the greatest gladness, even if everyone is shouting whatever they like against you, even if the wild beasts are tearing apart the little limbs of this lump of dough that has thickened around you. For what, in all of this, prevents the mind from keeping itself in calm, in a true verdict on what stands around it, and in a ready use of what is put before it, so that the verdict says to what befalls, “This is what you are in reality, even if in opinion you look like something else,” and the use says to what comes to hand, “You are what I was looking for. For to me what is present is always material for rational and civic virtue, and in general for the craft of a human being or a god”? For everything that happens is made akin to a god or a human being, and is neither new nor hard to handle, but familiar and easy to work.
members.greek: Ἀβιάστως διαζῆσαι ἐν πλείστῃ θυμηδίᾳ, κἂν πάντες καταβοῶσιν ἅτινα βούλονται, κἂν τὰ θηρία διασπᾷ τὰ μελύδρια τοῦ περιτεθραμμένου τούτου φυράματος. τί γὰρ κωλύει ἐν πᾶσι τούτοις τὴν διάνοιαν σῴζειν ἑαυτὴν ἐν γαλήνῃ καὶ κρίσει τῇ περὶ τῶν περιεστηκότων ἀληθεῖ καὶ χρήσει τῶν ὑποβεβλημένων ἑτοίμῃ, ὥστε τὴν μὲν κρίσιν λέγειν τῷ προσπίπτοντι· τοῦτο ὑπάρχεις κατ’ οὐσίαν, κἂν κατὰ δόξαν ἀλλοῖον φαίνῃ· τὴν δὲ χρῆσιν λέγειν τῷ ὑποπίπτοντι· σὲ ἐζήτουν· ἀεὶ γάρ μοι τὸ παρὸν ὕλη ἀρετῆς λογικῆς καὶ πολιτικῆς καὶ τὸ σύνολον τέχνης ἀνθρώπου ἢ θεοῦ· πᾶν γὰρ τὸ συμβαῖνον θεῷ ἢ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐξοικειοῦται καὶ οὔτε καινὸν οὔτε δυσμεταχείριστον, ἀλλὰ γνώριμον καὶ εὐεργές.

members.text:
Where the matter may be effected agreeably to that reason, which
both unto the Gods and men is common, there can be no just cause of
grief or sorrow. For where the fruit and benefit of an action well begun
and prosecuted according to the proper constitution of man may be reaped
and obtained, or is sure and certain, it is against reason that any
damage should there be suspected. In all places, and at all times, it is
in thy power religiously to embrace whatsoever by God's appointment is
happened unto thee, and justly to converse with those men, whom thou
hast to do with, and accurately to examine every fancy that presents
itself, that nothing may slip and steal in, before thou hast rightly
apprehended the true nature of it.
members.english:
Where a piece of work can be completed in accordance with the reason that gods and human beings have in common, there is nothing to fear there. For where it is possible to gain benefit through an activity that travels a good road and goes forward in accordance with the way we are made, no harm is to be suspected there.

Everywhere and without a break it is in your power to be well content, in reverence for the gods, with the present turn of events, to behave justly towards the people present, and to work with a craftsman’s care on the present impression, so that nothing slips in that has not been grasped.
members.greek:
Ὅπου ἔργον ἐπιτελεῖσθαι δύναται κατὰ τὸν κοινὸν θεοῖς καὶ ἀνθρώποις λόγον, ἐκεῖ οὐδὲν δεινόν· ὅπου γὰρ ὠφελείας τυχεῖν ἔξεστι διὰ τῆς εὐοδούσης καὶ κατὰ τὴν κατασκευὴν προιούσης ἐνεργείας, ἐκεῖ οὐδεμίαν βλάβην ὑφορατέον.

Πανταχοῦ καὶ διηνεκῶς ἐπὶ σοί ἐστι καὶ τῇ παρούσῃ συμβάσει θεοσεβῶς εὐαρεστεῖν καὶ τοῖς παροῦσιν ἀνθρώποις κατὰ δικαιοσύνην προσφέρεσθαι καὶ τῇ παρούσῃ φαντασίᾳ ἐμφιλοτεχνεῖν, ἵνα μή τι ἀκατάληπτον παρεισρυῇ.

members.text:
In another man's mind and understanding thy evil Cannot subsist,
nor in any proper temper or distemper of the natural constitution of thy
body, which is but as it were the coat or cottage of thy soul. Wherein
then, but in that part of thee, wherein the conceit, and apprehension
of any misery can subsist? Let not that part therefore admit any such
conceit, and then all is well. Though thy body which is so near it
should either be cut or burnt, or suffer any corruption or putrefaction,
yet let that part to which it belongs to judge of these, be still at
rest; that is, let her judge this, that whatsoever it is, that equally
may happen to a wicked man, and to a good man, is neither good nor evil.
For that which happens equally to him that lives according to nature,
and to him that doth not, is neither according to nature, nor against
it; and by consequent, neither good nor bad.
members.english: What is bad for you does not have its existence in another’s ruling part, nor yet in any turn and alteration of what surrounds you. Where, then? In the place where you have that which judges about bad things. So let that not judge, and all is well. Even if what is nearest to it, the little body, is cut, is burned, festers, rots, still let the part that judges about these things keep quiet. That is, let it decide that nothing is either bad or good which can happen equally to a bad man and a good one. For what happens equally to the one who lives against nature and to the one who lives in accordance with nature is neither in accordance with nature nor against nature.
members.greek: Ἐν ἀλλοτρίῳ ἡγεμονικῷ κακὸν σὸν οὐχ ὑφίσταται οὐδὲ μὴν ἔν τινι τροπῇ καὶ ἑτεροιώσει τοῦ περιέχοντος. ποῦ οὖν; ὅπου τὸ περὶ κακῶν ὑπολαμβάνον σοί ἐστι. τοῦτο οὖν μὴ ὑπολαμβανέτω καὶ πάντα εὖ ἔχει. κἂν τὸ ἐγγυτάτω αὐτοῦ, τὸ σωμάτιον, τέμνηται, καίηται, διαπυίσκηται, σήπηται, ὅμως τὸ ὑπολαμβάνον περὶ τούτων μόριον ἡσυχαζέτω· τουτέστι, κρινέτω μήτε κακόν τι εἶναι μήτε ἀγαθόν, ὃ ἐπίσης δύναται κακῷ ἀνδρὶ καὶ ἀγαθῷ συμβαίνειν. ὃ γὰρ καὶ τῷ παρὰ φύσιν καὶ τῷ κατὰ φύσιν βιοῦντι ἐπίσης συμβαίνει, τοῦτο οὔτε κατὰ φύσιν ἐστὶν οὔτε παρὰ φύσιν.

members.text:
Oh, wretched I, to whom this mischance is happened! nay, happy I,
to whom this thing being happened, I can continue without grief; neither
wounded by that which is present, nor in fear of that which is to come.
For as for this, it might have happened unto any man, but any man having
such a thing befallen him, could not have continued without grief. Why
then should that rather be an unhappiness, than this a happiness? But
however, canst thou, O man! term that unhappiness, which is no mischance
to the nature of man I Canst thou think that a mischance to the nature
of man, which is not contrary to the end and will of his nature? What
then hast thou learned is the will of man's nature? Doth that then which
hath happened unto thee, hinder thee from being just? or magnanimous? or
temperate? or wise? or circumspect? or true? or modest? or free? or from
anything else of all those things in the present enjoying and possession
whereof the nature of man, (as then enjoying all that is proper unto
her,) is fully satisfied? Now to conclude; upon all occasion of sorrow
remember henceforth to make use of this dogma, that whatsoever it is
that hath happened unto thee, is in very deed no such thing of itself,
as a misfortune; but that to bear it generously, is certainly great
happiness.
members.english: “I am unfortunate, because this has happened to me.” No, rather: “I am fortunate, because although this has happened to me I go on undistressed, neither broken by what is present nor afraid of what is coming.” For a thing of this kind could have happened to anyone, but not everyone would have gone on undistressed at it. Why then is that a misfortune rather than this a piece of good fortune? And do you call anything at all a human being’s misfortune that is not a failure of the human being’s nature? And does anything seem to you to be a failure of the human being’s nature that is not against what that nature wills? Well then: you have learned what it wills. Surely this that has happened does not prevent you from being just, great-hearted, self-controlled, sensible, not rash, not deceived, modest, free, and the rest, the things with which, when they are present together, the human being’s nature has in full what is its own? From now on, remember, at everything that leads you towards distress, to use this principle: not “this is a misfortune”, but “to bear it nobly is good fortune.”
members.greek: Ἀτυχὴς ἐγώ, ὅτι τοῦτό μοι συνέβη. οὐμενοῦν ἀλλʼ εὐτυχὴς ἐγώ, ὅτι τούτου μοι συμβεβηκότος ἄλυπος διατελῶ, οὔτε ὑπὸ παρόντος θραυόμενος οὔτε ἐπιὸν φοβούμενος. συμβῆναι μὲν γὰρ τὸ τοιοῦτο παντὶ ἐδύνατο, ἄλυπος δὲ οὐ πᾶς ἐπὶ τούτῳ ἂν διετέλεσε. διὰ τί οὖν ἐκεῖνο μᾶλλον ἀτύχημα ἢ τοῦτο εὐτύχημα; λέγεις δὲ ὅλως ἀτύχημα ἀνθρώπου, ὃ οὐκ ἔστιν ἀπότευγμα τῆς φύσεως τοῦ ἀνθρώπου; ἀπότευγμα δὲ τῆς φύσεως τοῦ ἀνθρώπου εἶναι δοκεῖ σοι, ὃ μὴ παρὰ τὸ βούλημα τῆς φύσεως αὐτοῦ ἐστι; τί οὖν; τὸ βούλημα μεμάθηκας· μήτι οὖν τὸ συμβεβηκὸς τοῦτο κωλύει σε δίκαιον εἶναι, μεγαλόψυχον, σώφρονα, ἔμφρονα, ἀπρόπτωτον, ἀδιάψευστον, αἰδήμονα, ἐλεύθερον, τἄλλα, ὧν συμπαρόντων ἡ φύσις ἡ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἀπέχει τὰ ἴδια; μέμνησο λοιπὸν ἐπὶ παντὸς τοῦ εἰς λύπην σε προαγομένου τούτῳ χρῆσθαι τῷ δόγματι· οὐχ ὅτι τοῦτο ἀτύχημα, ἀλλὰ τὸ φέρειν αὐτὸ γενναίως εὐτύχημα.

members.text:
That which doth not hurt the city itself; cannot hurt any citizen.
This rule thou must remember to apply and make use of upon every conceit
and apprehension of wrong. If the whole city be not hurt by this,
neither am I certainly. And if the whole be not, why should I make it
my private grievance? consider rather what it is wherein he is overseen
that is thought to have done the wrong. Again, often meditate how
swiftly all things that subsist, and all things that are done in the
world, are carried away, and as it were conveyed out of sight: for both
the substance themselves, we see as a flood, are in a continual flux;
and all actions in a perpetual change; and the causes themselves,
subject to a thousand alterations, neither is there anything almost,
that may ever be said to be now settled and constant. Next unto this,
and which follows upon it, consider both the infiniteness of the time
already past, and the immense vastness of that which is to come, wherein
all things are to be resolved and annihilated. Art not thou then a
very fool, who for these things, art either puffed up with pride, or
distracted with cares, or canst find in thy heart to make such moans as
for a thing that would trouble thee for a very long time? Consider the
whole universe whereof thou art but a very little part, and the whole
age of the world together, whereof but a short and very momentary
portion is allotted unto thee, and all the fates and destinies together,
of which how much is it that comes to thy part and share! Again: another
doth trespass against me. Let him look to that. He is master of his own
disposition, and of his own operation. I for my part am in the meantime
in possession of as much, as the common nature would have me to possess:
and that which mine own nature would have me do, I do.
members.english:
What is not harmful to the city does not harm the citizen either. At every impression of having been harmed, apply this rule: if the city is not harmed by this, I have not been harmed either. And if the city is harmed, one should not be angry, but should show the one who harms the city what it is that is being overlooked.

Think often of the speed with which the things that are and the things that come to be are carried past and drawn away. For the substance of things is like a river in unbroken flow, the activities are in continual changes, the causes in countless turns, and almost nothing stands still, even what is close at hand. And the boundlessness of the past and of the future is a yawning gulf in which all things vanish. How then is a person not a fool who, among these things, is puffed up, or torn about, or complains bitterly, as though at something that troubled them for a time, and a long one?

Remember the whole substance of things, of which you have the smallest share; and the whole of time, of which a brief, momentary interval has been marked off for you; and fate, of which you are how small a part?

Someone else does me some wrong? That is for them to see to: they have their own disposition, their own activity. I now have what the common nature wants me to have now, and I do what my own nature wants me to do now.

members.text:
What pain soever thou art in, let this presently come to thy mind,
that it is not a thing whereof thou needest to be ashamed, neither is it
a thing whereby thy understanding, that hath the government of all,
can be made worse. For neither in regard of the substance of it, nor
in regard of the end of it (which is, to intend the common good) can
it alter and corrupt it. This also of Epicurus mayst thou in most pains
find some help of, that it is 'neither intolerable, nor eternal;' so
thou keep thyself to the true bounds and limits of reason and give not
way to opinion. This also thou must consider, that many things there be,
which oftentimes unsensibly trouble and vex thee, as not armed against
them with patience, because they go not ordinarily under the name of
pains, which in very deed are of the same nature as pain; as to slumber
unquietly, to suffer heat, to want appetite: when therefore any of these
things make thee discontented, check thyself with these words: Now hath
pain given thee the foil; thy courage hath failed thee.
members.english: At every pain, have this ready to hand: that it is not shameful and does not make the mind at the helm any worse, for it does not ruin it either in so far as it is rational or in so far as it is social. With most pains, though, let Epicurus’s saying help you as well: that it is neither unbearable nor everlasting, if you remember the limits and do not add to it by opinion. And remember this too: that many things that are the same as pain go unnoticed as such, though we resent them, such as being drowsy, being overheated and having no appetite. So when you are displeased at any of these, say to yourself: “You are giving in to pain.”
members.greek: Ἐπὶ μὲν παντὸς πόνου πρόχειρον ἔστω ὅτι οὐκ αἰσχρὸν οὐδὲ τὴν διάνοιαν τὴν κυβερνῶσαν χείρω ποιεῖ· οὔτε γὰρ καθὸ λογική ἐστιν οὔτε καθὸ κοινωνικὴ διαφθείρει αὐτήν. ἐπὶ μέντοι τῶν πλείστων πόνων καὶ τὸ τοῦ Ἐπικούρου σοι βοηθείτω, ὅτι οὔτε ἀφόρητον οὔτε αἰώνιον, ἐὰν τῶν ὅρων μνημονεύῃς καὶ μὴ προσδοξάζῃς. κἀκείνου δὲ μέμνησο, ὅτι πολλὰ πόνῳ τὰ αὐτὰ ὄντα λανθάνει, δυσχεραινόμενα· οἷον τὸ νυστάζειν καὶ τὸ καυματίζεσθαι καὶ τὸ ἀνορεκτεῖν· ὅταν οὖν τινι τούτων δυσαρεστῇς, λέγε ἑαυτῷ, ὅτι πόνῳ ἐνδίδως.

members.text:
Let not the general representation unto thyself of the
wretchedness of this our mortal life, trouble thee. Let not thy mind
wander up and down, and heap together in her thoughts the many troubles
and grievous calamities which thou art as subject unto as any other. But
as everything in particular doth happen, put this question unto thyself,
and say: What is it that in this present matter, seems unto thee so
intolerable? For thou wilt be ashamed to confess it. Then upon this
presently call to mind, that neither that which is future, nor that
which is past can hurt thee; but that only which is present. (And that
also is much lessened, if thou dost lightly circumscribe it:) and then
check thy mind if for so little a while, (a mere instant), it cannot
hold out with patience.
members.english: Do not let the impression of your whole life confound you. Do not take in, in one sweep of thought, what hardships and how many are likely to have come on you. Instead, at each of the things present, ask yourself: “What is there in this task that is unbearable and not to be endured?” For you will be ashamed to admit it. Then remind yourself that it is neither the future nor the past that weighs on you, but always the present; and this shrinks if you mark it off by itself alone and convict your mind if it cannot hold out against this, stripped bare.
members.greek: Μή σε συγχείτω ἡ τοῦ ὅλου βίου φαντασία, μὴ συμπερινόει ἐπίπονα οἷα καὶ ὅσα πιθανὸν ἐπιγεγενῆσθαι, ἀλλὰ καθ’ ἕκαστον τῶν παρόντων ἐπερώτα σεαυτόν· τί τοῦ ἔργου τὸ ἀφόρητον καὶ ἀνύποιστον; αἰσχυνθήσῃ γὰρ ὁμολογῆσαι. ἔπειτα ἀναμίμνῃσκε σεαυτὸν ὅτι οὔτε τὸ μέλλον οὔτε τὸ παρῳχηκὸς βαρεῖ σε, ἀλλ’ ἀεὶ τὸ παρόν, τοῦτο δὲ κατασμικρύνεται, ἐὰν αὐτὸ μόνον περιορίσῃς καὶ ἀπελέγχῃς τὴν διάνοιαν, εἰ πρὸς τοῦτο ψιλὸν ἀντέχειν μὴ δύναται.

members.text:
To desire things impossible is the part of a mad man. But it is a
thing impossible, that wicked man should not commit some such things.
Neither doth anything happen to any man, which in the ordinary course
of nature as natural unto him doth not happen. Again, the same things
happen unto others also. And truly, if either he that is ignorant that
such a thing hath happened unto him, or he that is ambitious to be
commended for his magnanimity, can be patient, and is not grieved: is it
not a grievous thing, that either ignorance, or a vain desire to please
and to be commended, should be more powerful and effectual than true
prudence? As for the things themselves, they touch not the soul, neither
can they have any access unto it: neither can they of themselves any
ways either affect it, or move it. For she herself alone can affect and
move herself, and according as the dogmata and opinions are, which she
doth vouchsafe herself; so are those things which, as accessories, have
any co-existence with her.
members.english:
To chase after impossible things is madness. And it is impossible that bad people should not do things of this kind.

Nothing happens to anyone that they are not fitted by nature to bear. The same things happen to someone else, and either because they do not know that it has happened, or because they are showing off greatness of mind, they stand firm and remain unhurt. It is a terrible thing, then, that ignorance and the wish to please should be stronger than wisdom.

Things themselves do not touch the soul in any way at all, nor do they have a way in to the soul, nor can they turn or move the soul. But it alone turns and moves itself, and whatever verdicts it thinks itself worthy to pass, it makes the things that stand before it to be of that kind for itself.
members.greek:
Τὸ τὰ ἀδύνατα διώκειν μανικόν· ἀδύνατον δὲ τὸ τοὺς φαύλους μὴ τοιαῦτά τινα ποιεῖν.

Οὐδὲν οὐδενὶ συμβαίνει ὃ οὐχὶ πέφυκε φέρειν. ἄλλῳ τὰ αὐτὰ συμβαίνει καὶ ἤτοι ἀγνοῶν ὅτι συμβέβηκεν, ἢ ἐπιδεικνύμενος μεγαλοφροσύνην, εὐσταθεῖ καὶ ἀκάκωτος μένει. δεινὸν οὖν ἄγνοιαν καὶ ἀρέσκειαν ἰσχυροτέρας εἶναι φρονήσεως.

Τὰ πράγματα αὐτὰ οὐδ’ ὁπωστιοῦν ψυχῆς ἅπτεται οὐδὲ ἔχει εἴσοδον πρὸς ψυχὴν οὐδὲ τρέψαι οὐδὲ κινῆσαι ψυχὴν δύναται, τρέπει δὲ καὶ κινεῖ αὐτὴ ἑαυτὴν μόνη καὶ οἵων ἂν κριμάτων καταξιώσῃ ἑαυτήν, τοιαῦτα ἑαυτῇ ποιεῖ τὰ προσυφεστῶτα.

members.text:
Let not that chief commanding part of thy soul be ever subject to
any variation through any corporal either pain or pleasure, neither
suffer it to be mixed with these, but let it both circumscribe itself,
and confine those affections to their own proper parts and members.
But if at any time they do reflect and rebound upon the mind and
understanding (as in an united and compacted body it must needs;) then
must thou not go about to resist sense and feeling, it being natural.
However let not thy understanding to this natural sense and feeling,
which whether unto our flesh pleasant or painful, is unto us nothing
properly, add an opinion of either good or bad and all is well.
members.english: Let the ruling and governing part of your soul not be turned by the smooth or rough motion in the flesh, and let it not be blended in, but let it draw a line around itself and confine those feelings within the parts of the body. But when they pass up into the mind by the other shared feeling, as in a body that is one, then one should not try to go against the sensation, which is natural; but let the ruling part not add, from itself, the judgment that it is something good or bad.
members.greek: Τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν καὶ κυριεῦον τῆς ψυχῆς σου μέρος ἄτρεπτον ἔστω ὑπὸ τῆς ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ λείας ἢ τραχείας κινήσεως καὶ μὴ συγκρινέσθω, ἀλλὰ περιγραφέτω αὑτὸ καὶ περιοριζέτω τὰς πείσεις ἐκείνας ἐν τοῖς μορίοις. ὄταν δὲ ἀναδιδῶνται κατὰ τὴν ἑτέραν συμπάθειαν εἰς τὴν διάνοιαν ὡς ἐν σώματι ἡνωμένῳ, τότε πρὸς μὲν τὴν αἴσθησιν φυσικὴν οὖσαν οὐ πειρατέον ἀντιβαίνειν, τὴν δὲ ὑπόληψιν τὴν ὡς περὶ ἀγαθοῦ ἢ κακοῦ μὴ προστιθέτω τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ.

members.text:
Whatsoever doth happen unto thee, thou art naturally by thy natural
constitution either able, or not able to bear. If thou beest able, be
not offended, but bear it according to thy natural constitution, or as
nature hath enabled thee. If thou beest not able, be not offended. For
it will soon make an end of thee, and itself, (whatsoever it be) at the
same time end with thee. But remember, that whatsoever by the strength
of opinion, grounded upon a certain apprehension of both true profit and
duty, thou canst conceive tolerable; that thou art able to bear that by
thy natural constitution.
members.english: Everything that happens either happens in such a way that you are fitted by nature to bear it, or in such a way that you are not fitted by nature to bear it. So if it happens to you in a way you are fitted by nature to bear, do not resent it, but bear it as you are fitted by nature to do. And if in a way you are not fitted by nature to bear, do not resent it: for it will perish once it has used you up. Remember, though, that you are fitted by nature to bear everything that it rests with your own judgment to make bearable and endurable, through the impression that it is good for you, or is your duty, to do so.
members.greek: Πᾶν τὸ συμβαῖνον ἤτοι οὕτω συμβαίνει ὡς πέφυκας αὐτὸ φέρειν ἢ ὡς οὐ πέφυκας αὐτὸ φέρειν. εἰ μὲν οὖν συμβαίνει σοι ὡς πέφυκας φέρειν. μὴ δυσχέραινε, ἀλλ’ ὡς πέφυκας φέρε. εἰ δὲ ὡς μὴ πέφυκας φέρειν, μὴ δυσχέραινε· φθαρήσεται γάρ σε ἀπαναλῶσαν. μέμνησο μέντοι ὅτι πέφυκας φέρειν πᾶν, περὶ οὗ ἐπὶ τῇ ὑπολήψει ἐστὶ τῇ σῇ φορητὸν καὶ ἀνεκτὸν αὐτὸ ποιῆσαι κατὰ φαντασίαν τοῦ συμφέρειν ἢ καθήκειν σεαυτῷ τοῦτο ποιεῖν.

members.text:
Of things that are external, happen what will to that which can
suffer by external accidents. Those things that suffer let them complain
themselves, if they will; as for me, as long as I conceive no such
thing, that that which is happened is evil, I have no hurt; and it is in
my power not to conceive any such thing.
members.english: Let whatever likes fall from outside on the things that are able to be affected by this falling. For those things, once affected, will complain if they like. But I, unless I judge that what has happened is bad, have not yet been harmed. And it is possible for me not to judge so.
members.greek: Ὃ θέλει, ἔξωθεν προσπιπτέτω τοῖς παθεῖν ἐκ τῆς προσπτώσεως ταύτης δυναμένοις. ἐκεῖνα γάρ, ἐὰν θελήσῃ, μέμψεται τὰ παθόντα, ἐγὼ δέ, ἐὰν μὴ ὑπολάβω ὅτι κακὸν τὸ συμβεβηκός, οὔπω βέβλαμμαι· ἔξεστι δέ μοι μὴ ὑπολαβεῖν.

members.text:
That which is a hindrance of the senses, is an evil to the
sensitive nature. That which is a hindrance of the appetitive and
prosecutive faculty, is an evil to the sensitive nature. As of the
sensitive, so of the vegetative constitution, whatsoever is a hindrance
unto it, is also in that respect an evil unto the same. And so likewise,
whatsoever is a hindrance unto the mind and understanding, must needs
be the proper evil of the reasonable nature. Now apply all those things
unto thyself. Do either pain or pleasure seize on thee? Let the senses
look to that. Hast thou met with Some obstacle or other in thy purpose
and intention? If thou didst propose without due reservation and
exception now hath thy reasonable part received a blow indeed But if in
general thou didst propose unto thyself what soever might be, thou art
not thereby either hurt, nor properly hindered. For in those things that
properly belong unto the mind, she cannot be hindered by any man. It
is not fire, nor iron; nor the power of a tyrant nor the power of a
slandering tongue; nor anything else that can penetrate into her.
members.english: A hindrance to sensation is a bad thing for an animal nature. A hindrance to impulse is likewise a bad thing for an animal nature. And there is something else that likewise hinders, and is a bad thing for, the way a plant is made. In the same way, then, a hindrance to mind is a bad thing for a nature that has mind. Now carry all of this over to yourself. Does pain, does pleasure touch you? That is for sensation to see to. Did something come to stand in the way of your impulse? If your impulse was without reservation, then it is already a bad thing for you as a rational being. But if you accept the common lot, you have not yet been harmed or hindered. What is the mind’s own, however, no one else is in the habit of hindering: for neither fire, nor iron, nor a tyrant, nor slander, nor anything whatever touches it,
members.greek: Ἐμποδισμὸς αἰσθήσεως κακὸν ζωτικῆς φύσεως. ἐμποδισμὸς ὁρμῆς ὁμοίως κακὸν ζωτικῆς φύσεως. ἔστι δέ τι ἄλλο ὁμοίως ἐμποδιστικὸν καὶ κακὸν τῆς φυτικῆς κατασκευῆς. οὕτως τοίνυν ἐμποδισμὸς νοῦ κακὸν νοερᾶς φύσεως. πάντα δὴ ταῦτα ἐπὶ σεαυτὸν μετάφερε. πόνος, ἡδονὴ ἅπτεταί σου; ὄψεται ἡ αἴσθησις. ὁρμήσαντι ἔνστημα ἐγένετο; εἰ μὲν ἀνυπεξαιρέτως ὥρμας, ἤδη ὡς λογικοῦ κακόν, εἰ δὲ τὸ κοινὸν λαμβάνεις, οὔπω βέβλαψαι οὐδὲ ἐμπεπόδισαι. τὰ μέντοι τοῦ νοῦ ἴδια οὐδεὶς ἄλλος εἴωθεν ἐμποδίζειν· τούτου γὰρ οὐ πῦρ, οὐ σίδηρος, οὐ τύραννος, οὐ βλασφημία, οὐχ ὁτιοῦν ἅπτεται,

members.text:
'In my sickness' (saith Epicurus of himself:) 'my discourses were
not concerning the nature of my disease, neither was that, to them that
came to visit me, the subject of my talk; but in the consideration and
contemplation of that, which was of especial weight and moment, was all
my time bestowed and spent, and among others in this very thing, how my
mind, by a natural and unavoidable sympathy partaking in some sort with
the present indisposition of my body, might nevertheless keep herself
free from trouble, and in present possession of her own proper
happiness. Neither did I leave the ordering of my body to the physicians
altogether to do with me what they would, as though I expected any
great matter from them, or as though I thought it a matter of such great
consequence, by their means to recover my health: for my present estate,
methought, liked me very well, and gave me good content.' Whether
therefore in sickness (if thou chance to sicken) or in what other kind
of extremity soever, endeavour thou also to be in thy mind so affected,
as he doth report of himself: not to depart from thy philosophy for
anything that can befall thee, nor to give ear to the discourses of
silly people, and mere naturalists.
members.english: Epicurus says: “In my illness my conversations were not about the sufferings of the little body, nor,” he says, “did I talk about such things to those who came in. Instead I went on inquiring into the leading questions of nature, and stayed on this very point: how the mind, though it has its share in such motions in the bit of flesh, stays untroubled, keeping its own good. Nor did I give the doctors the chance,” he says, “to put on airs as though they were doing something. Rather, life went on well and nobly.” So do the same as he did, in illness, if you are ill, and in any other circumstance. For not to stand away from philosophy in anything whatever that befalls, and not to chatter along with someone who is a layman and has not studied nature,
members.greek: Ὁ Ἐπίκουρος λέγει ὅτι· ʽἐν τῇ νόσῳ οὐκ ἦσάν μοι αἱ ὁμιλίαι περὶ τῶν τοῦ σωματίου παθῶν οὐδὲ πρὸς τοὺς εἰσιόντας τοιαῦτά τινα, φησίν, ἐλάλουν, ἀλλὰ τὰ προηγούμενα φυσιολογῶν διετέλουν καὶ πρὸς αὐτῷ τούτῳ ὤν, πῶς ἡ διάνοια συμμεταλαμβάνουσα τῶν ἐν τῷ σαρκιδίῳ τοιούτων κινήσεων ἀταρακτεῖ τὸ ἴδιον ἀγαθὸν τηροῦσα. οὐδὲ τοῖς ἰατροῖς ἐμπαρεῖχον, φησί, καταφρυάττεσθαι ὥς τι ποιοῦσιν, ἀλλ’ ὁ βίος ἤγετο εὖ καὶ καλῶς.ʼ ταὐτὰ οὖν ἐκείνῳ, ἐν νόσῳ, ἐὰν νοσῇς καὶ ἐν ἄλλῃ τινὶ περιστάσει· τὸ γὰρ μὴ ἀφίστασθαι φιλοσοφίας ἐν οἷς δήποτε τοῖς προσπίπτουσι μηδὲ ἰδιώτῃ καὶ ἀφυσιολόγῳ συμφλυαρεῖν,

members.text:
If this neither be my wicked act, nor an act anyways depending
from any wickedness of mine, and that by it the public is not hurt; what
doth it concern me? And wherein can the public be hurt? For thou must
not altogether be carried by conceit and common opinion: as for help
thou must afford that unto them after thy best ability, and as occasion
shall require, though they sustain damage, but in these middle or
worldly things; but however do not thou conceive that they are truly
hurt thereby: for that is not right. But as that old foster-father
in the comedy, being now to take his leave doth with a great deal of
ceremony, require his foster-child's rhombus, or rattle-top, remembering
nevertheless that it is but a rhombus; so here also do thou likewise.
For indeed what is all this pleading and public bawling for at the
courts? O man, hast thou forgotten what those things are! yea but they
are things that others much care for, and highly esteem of. Wilt thou
therefore be a fool too? Once I was; let that suffice.
members.english:
If this is neither badness of mine nor an activity that comes from badness of mine, and the community is not harmed, why am I upset over it? And what harm is there to the community?

Do not be swept off wholesale by the impression, but help as far as you are able and as far as is deserved, even if it is in the middle things that they are coming off worse; do not, however, form the impression that it is a harm, for that is a bad habit. But as the old man, on leaving, asked for his foster-child’s top, remembering that it was a top, so too in this case. Otherwise you become someone calling out on the Rostra. Man, have you forgotten what these things were? “Yes, but they are much sought after by these people.” And is that a reason for you to become a fool as well? I once was,
members.greek:
Εἰ μήτε κακία ἐστὶ τοῦτο ἐμὴ μήτε ἐνέργεια κατὰ κακίαν ἐμὴν μήτε τὸ κοινὸν βλάπτεται, τί ὑπὲρ αὐτοῦ διαφέρομαι, τίς δὲ βλάβη τοῦ κοινοῦ;

Μὴ ὁλοσχερῶς τῇ φαντασίᾳ συναρπάζεσθαι, ἀλλὰ βοηθεῖν μὲν κατὰ δύναμιν καὶ κατ’ ἀξίαν, κἂν εἰς τὰ μέσα ἐλαττῶνται, μὴ μέντοι βλάβην αὐτὸ φαντάζεσθαι· κακὸν γὰρ ἔθος. ἀλλ’ ὡς ὁ γέρων ἀπελθὼν τὸν τοῦ θρεπτοῦ ῥόμβον ἀπῄτει, μεμνημένος ὅτι ῥόμβος, οὕτως οὖν καὶ ὧδε. ἐπεί τοι γίνῃ καλῶν ἐπὶ τῶν ἐμβόλων. ἄνθρωπε, ἐπελάθου τί ταῦτα ἦν;—ναί· ἀλλὰ τούτοις περισπούδαστα.—διὰ τοῦτ’ οὖν καὶ σὺ μωρὸς γένῃ; Ἐγενόμην ποτέ,

members.why: Says what gladdens Marcus: a sound ruling part that turns away from nothing that happens and uses each thing according to its worth. The use of what happens is already in claim 4 from 10.33 and 7.39, and its first sentence, on not causing himself distress, is a different thought.
members.text:
Why should I grieve myself; who never did willingly grieve any
other! One thing rejoices one and another thing another. As for me, this
is my joy, if my understanding be right and sound, as neither averse
from any man, nor refusing any of those things which as a man I am
subject unto; if I can look upon all things in the world meekly and
kindly; accept all things and carry myself towards everything according
to to true worth of the thing itself.
members.english:
I do not deserve to cause myself distress, for I have never yet willingly distressed anyone else.

One thing gladdens one person, another another. What gladdens me is if I have my ruling part sound: not turning away from any human being or from any of the things that happen to human beings, but looking at everything with kindly eyes, accepting it, and using each thing according to its worth.
members.greek:
Οὐκ εἰμὶ ἄξιος ἐμαυτὸν λυπεῖν· οὐδὲ γὰρ ἄλλον πώποτε ἑκὼν ἐλύπησα.

Εὐφραίνει ἄλλον ἄλλο, ἐμὲ δέ, ἐὰν ὑγιὲς ἔχω τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, μὴ ἀποστρεφόμενον μήτε ἄνθρωπόν τινα μήτε τι τῶν ἀνθρώποις συμβαινόντων, ἀλλὰ πᾶν εὐμενέσιν ὀφθαλμοῖς ὁρῶν τε καὶ δεχόμενον καὶ χρώμενον ἑκάστῳ κατ’ ἀξίαν.

members.text:
If pain be an evil, either it is in regard of the body; (and that
cannot be, because the body of itself is altogether insensible:) or in
regard of the soul But it is in the power of the soul, to preserve her
own peace and tranquillity, and not to suppose that pain is evil. For
all judgment and deliberation; all prosecution, or aversation is from
within, whither the sense of evil (except it be let in by opinion)
cannot penetrate.
members.english: Pain is either a bad thing for the body, and then let the body declare it so, or for the soul. But it is possible for the soul to keep its own clear sky and calm, and not to judge that it is a bad thing. For every verdict and impulse and desire and aversion is inside, and nothing climbs up to here.
members.greek: Ὁ πόνος ἤτοι τῷ σώματι κακόν· οὐκοῦν ἀποφαινέσθω· ἢ τῇ ψυχῇ· ἀλλ’ ἔξεστιν αὐτῇ τὴν ἰδίαν αἰθρίαν καὶ γαλήνην διαφυλάσσειν καὶ μὴ ὑπολαμβάνειν ὅτι κακόν. πᾶσα γὰρ κρίσις καὶ ὁρμὴ καὶ ὄρεξις καὶ ἔκκλισις ἔνδον καὶ οὐδὲν ὧδε ἀναβαίνει.

members.text:
Let opinion be taken away, and no man will think himself wronged.
If no man shall think himself wronged, then is there no more any such
thing as wrong. That which makes not man himself the worse, cannot
make his life the worse, neither can it hurt him either inwardly
or outwardly. It was expedient in nature that it should be so, and
therefore necessary.
members.english:
Take away the judgment, and “I have been harmed” is taken away. Take away “I have been harmed”, and the harm is taken away.

What does not make a human being worse than they were does not make their life worse either, and does not harm them either from outside or from within.

The nature of what is beneficial is bound by necessity to do this.
members.greek:
Ἆρον τὴν ὑπόληψιν, ἦρται τὸ βέβλαμμαι· ἆρον τὸ βέβλαμμαι, ἦρται ἡ βλάβη.

Ὃ χείρω αὐτὸν ἑαυτοῦ ἄνθρωπον οὐ ποιεῖ, τοῦτο οὐδὲ τὸν βίον αὐτοῦ χείρω ποιεῖ οὐδὲ βλάπτει οὔτε ἔξωθεν οὔτε ἔνδοθεν.

Ἠνάγκασται ἡ τοῦ συμφέροντος φύσις τοῦτο ποιεῖν.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of the 1634 edition, given here with the modern number in pairs: 8.45 is 8.46–47, 10.33 is 10.32–33, 7.39 is 7.68, 7.29 is 7.53–54, 4.32 is 4.39, 4.41 is 4.49b, 5.19 is 5.22–25, 7.35 is 7.64, 8.34 is 8.36, 5.16 is 5.17–19, 5.20 is 5.26, 7.11 is 7.14, 8.39 is 8.41a, 9.41 is 9.41a, 5.29 is 5.35–36a, 8.41 is 8.42–43, 8.26 is 8.28 and 4.7 is 4.7–9; 10.3 is 10.3 in both.

Widens the title from “Nothing happens that a human being cannot bear” to “What happens can be borne and does not harm me”. More passages of the section speak of harm and of the judgment that makes it than of bearing.

States “Nothing happens to me that I cannot bear” without a condition, as 5.16 and 8.45 do. 10.3 allows a second case, a thing I am not fitted to bear; the article puts that case, and 8.45’s exit from life, under “If I doubt it” and not into the statement.
Treats “verdict” (8.45, 8.26), “judgment” (4.7, 7.11, 5.20, 10.3) and “opinion” (7.35) as one act of the mind. The translation keeps them apart because the Greek uses different words.
articles.limit: Other articles say parts of this one from their own sections: Article 2 that pain is not bad for me; Article 3 that none of what happens is unusual; Article 7 that what troubles me rests on my judgment, that the body’s pain is the body’s, and that I tell myself no more than my first impressions report (claims 2, 3 and 6 here); Article 11 that I keep my principles ready and that my situation is material for my reason (claims 5 and 4); Article 13 that no one can prevent me from living well and acting justly (claim 4); and Article 21 that an impulse is made with a reservation and that my mind, gathered into itself, cannot be harmed (8.39c and claim 3). What this article adds is that I am fitted to bear what happens, that harm and not only trouble lies in my judgment, and this section’s own rules: the city and the citizen, what does not make me worse, and the hardship taken bare. Its first claim is asserted and not argued: 10.3 itself allows that something may come that I cannot bear, and Seneca, with Letter 78 and Letter 24, challenges it on the same point.

articles.title: Keeping the few names I have given myself

statement.t: I keep to the few names I have given myself, do each thing as someone about to leave life, and need no one as witness.

parts.words: I keep to the few names I have given myself
do each thing as someone about to leave life
need no one as witness

statement.kind: A rule, the way it is carried out, and what it does not need
statement.form: Claim 1 is the rule: a few names, kept. Claim 4 says how each act is done under it and claim 3 what it does not need; they give the statement its second and third parts. Claim 2 is the ground, claim 5 a check on the past, and claim 6 what happens when the rule is lost. The third part takes its words from 3.5, where the witness stands beside an oath and is someone who vouches for a man; 10.8 backs its sense, not its words. The statement joins its parts with “and” only, so it holds no inference of the editor’s.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, five of the six claims gain a second author; only the review of my conduct does not. Practice gains a daily review with a test of steadiness, action gains a warning against making a show of plainness, and the side on what failing looks like gains what Seneca says of those who are not yet one person. He limits two claims: until I respect myself I keep a witness in mind, and a day is lived as one that might be my last, not snatched at as the last. The side on doubt stays empty.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a clause for the one who has not yet arrived: though more of the road to wisdom remains than lies behind me, the greater part of progress is the desire to progress.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: it is more important for you to keep the resolutions you have already made than to go on and make noble ones
piece.follows: Keeping the resolutions already made matters more than making new and noble ones.
piece.context: Letter 16 opens: no happy life without wisdom, an idea to deepen by daily reflection. The “resolutions” are those Lucilius has already made, to be held until they become settled purpose.
gives: I keep myself in them

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: You should therefore force yourself to maintain to the very end of life’s drama the character which you assumed at the beginning.
piece.follows: I should force myself to keep, to the end of my life, the character I took up at its beginning.
piece.context: The close of Letter 120, on how we learn what virtue is: its mark is being always the same. The “character” is the one part a person has taken up, set against changing masks.
gives: I struggle to remain this kind of person

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Would you win over the gods? Then be a good man. Whoever imitates them, is worshipping them sufficiently.
piece.follows: The way to win the gods is to be good; whoever imitates them worships them enough.
piece.context: Letter 95 turns from rules of ritual to the right idea of the gods, who need no servants and do good by nature. “Them” are the gods; to imitate them is to be a good man.
gives: for rational beings to become like them

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Those who wish their virtue to be advertised are not striving for virtue but for renown.
piece.follows: Whoever wants his virtue made known is after renown, not virtue.
piece.context: The end of Letter 113, where Seneca says justice should have nothing to do with ambition and reputation. “Advertised” means made known to other people.
gives: without craving that others call me by them

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: it makes no difference how many persons are acquainted with your uprightness
piece.follows: How many people know that I am upright makes no difference.
piece.context: Seneca’s closing charge to Lucilius in Letter 113, after saying one must be just without reward. “Your uprightness” is your being just, whether or not anyone knows of it.
gives: any human being as witness

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: let us so order our minds as if we had come to the very end
piece.follows: I should put my mind in order as if I had reached the end of my life.
piece.context: Letter 101, on the futility of planning far ahead: death stands at our side and no one knows how near his fixed limit is. “The very end” is the end of life.
gives: as someone about to leave life
set myself in order

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: I have looked upon every day as if it were my last
piece.follows: Seneca has treated every day as if it were his last.
piece.context: Letter 93, on a man whose life was short but complete: a life is measured by what is done in it. Seneca speaks of himself; he never counted on the days he hoped for.
gives: as someone about to leave life

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: That which is short of perfection must necessarily be unsteady, at one time progressing, at another slipping or growing faint; and it will surely slip back unless it keeps struggling ahead
piece.follows: Whatever is short of perfection is unsteady and slips back unless it keeps struggling forward.
piece.context: Letter 71, on those who follow wisdom but have not reached it. “That which is short of perfection” is their progress, which goes backward as soon as effort slackens.
gives: I fall short

items.label: breaks
items.t: Nobody but the wise man can be one person; the rest of us often change masks. A philosopher may not always keep the same pace, but he can always travel the same path. More of the road remains than lies behind me, and the greater part of progress is the desire to progress.
items.why: Marcus says what to do when the names are lost: go back to them quickly, or go to a corner where I will prevail (10.8). Seneca adds what Marcus does not say here: that not being one person is the common case, his own included; that the path can be kept at an uneven pace; and that wanting to progress is most of progress. The three sentences come from three letters, and setting them side by side is the editor’s.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: But nobody can be one person except the wise man; the rest of us often shift our masks.
support.follows: Only the wise man can be one person; everyone else, Seneca included, often changes masks.
support.context: The close of Letter 120: the foolish mind is never like itself. To “be one person” is to keep one character; “the rest of us” counts Seneca among those who change.
gives: Nobody but the wise man can be one person; the rest of us often change masks

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I do not say that the philosopher can always keep the same pace. But he can always travel the same path.
support.follows: A philosopher may not always keep the same pace, but he can always keep to the same path.
support.context: Letter 20 asks that deed and word agree and that a man be always the same. Asked who can keep this standard, Seneca answers that very few can, and then says this of the philosopher.
gives: A philosopher may not always keep the same pace, but he can always travel the same path

support.author: seneca
support.quote: There remains much more of the road than we have put behind us; but the greater part of progress is the desire to progress.
support.follows: More of the road lies ahead than behind, but wanting to progress is the greater part of progressing.
support.context: Letter 71, just after Seneca says that progress slips back unless one struggles ahead. The “road” is the way to wisdom, which he says he desires with all his heart.
gives: More of the road remains than lies behind me
the greater part of progress is the desire to progress

items.label: practice
items.role: A daily review, and a test
items.t: I watch myself continually and review each day. To find out whether I have accomplished anything, I ask whether I want the same things today that I wanted yesterday.
items.why: Marcus looks back once over his whole conduct up to now (5.25). Seneca makes the review a habit of every day, and gives a test of whether I am holding steady that Marcus does not give here.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I shall keep watching myself continually, and—a most useful habit—shall review each day.
support.follows: Seneca will watch himself continually and review each day, which he calls a most useful habit.
support.context: In Letter 83 Lucilius has asked for an account of each of Seneca’s days. Seneca agrees, and says that what makes people wicked is that no one looks back over his own life.
gives: I watch myself continually and review each day

support.author: seneca
support.quote: when you would find out whether you have accomplished anything, consider whether you desire the same things to-day that you desired yesterday
support.follows: To see whether I have achieved anything, I should ask whether I want today what I wanted yesterday.
support.context: In Letter 35 Seneca urges Lucilius to make progress and above all to be consistent with himself. This is the test he gives: a will that shifts shows a mind adrift.
gives: To find out whether I have accomplished anything
I ask whether I want the same things today that I wanted yesterday

items.label: action
items.t: I make no show of plainness either: rough dress, an unkempt beard, open scorn of silver and a bed on the bare earth are another kind of self-display. Inwardly I am different in every respect, and outwardly I live as the people around me do.
items.why: Marcus drops the show of a court and draws himself in toward a private person’s life (1.14). Seneca warns of the opposite show, which Marcus does not mention here: plainness worn in order to be noticed.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Repellent attire, unkempt hair, slovenly beard, open scorn of silver dishes, a couch on the bare earth, and any other perverted forms of self-display, are to be avoided.
support.follows: Rough dress, unkempt hair and beard, scorn of silver and sleeping on the ground are self-display and should be avoided.
support.context: Letter 5 warns Lucilius, who studies philosophy, against those who want to be conspicuous rather than to improve. The list is of ways of flaunting an austere life.
gives: I make no show of plainness either
rough dress, an unkempt beard, open scorn of silver and a bed on the bare earth are another kind of self-display

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Inwardly, we ought to be different in all respects, but our exterior should conform to society.
support.follows: We should differ from others inwardly in everything, while our outward life conforms to theirs.
support.context: From Letter 5, on not parading philosophy in dress or habits. “We” are those who pursue philosophy; “society” is the people among whom they live.
gives: Inwardly I am different in every respect, and outwardly I live as the people around me do

items.t: Seneca does not send the witness away so soon. Until I have come to respect myself, he has me set the authority of some man over myself as a guard; only after that may I dismiss him. This limits the claim and does not contradict it: Marcus’s man who needs no human witness has already set himself in order (3.5), and Marcus keeps a model of his own, Antoninus (6.28). Seneca’s witness is a person I picture for my own correction, not an audience whose praise I want.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: And when you have progressed so far that you have also respect for yourself, you may send away your attendant; but until then, set as a guard over yourself the authority of some man
support.follows: Until I have come to respect myself I should keep some man’s authority over me as a guard; after that I may dismiss him.
support.context: Letter 25 passes on Epicurus’s advice to act as if a great man were watching. The “attendant” is that imagined guardian, a Cato, a Scipio or a Laelius, kept in mind.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: We can get rid of most sins, if we have a witness who stands near us when we are likely to go wrong.
support.follows: Most wrongdoing can be got rid of if a witness stands by when we are likely to go wrong.
support.context: Letter 11 ends with Epicurus’s advice to keep a man of high character before one’s eyes. The “witness” is that man, pictured as present; he is not an actual onlooker.

items.t: Seneca draws a line that Marcus does not draw. He lives each day as a complete life and regards it as one that might be his last, but he says he does not snatch at it as if it were his last. The difference is small, and he does not always keep to it himself: in Letter 93 he says he has looked upon every day as if it were his last (Ep. 93.6).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I do not indeed snatch it up as if it were my last; I do regard it, however, as if it might even be my last.
support.follows: Seneca does not seize a day as if it were his last; he regards it as one that might be.
support.context: In Letter 61 Seneca, now old, writes that his one task is to end his long-standing faults. “It” is each day, which he tries to live as a complete life.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I am endeavouring to live every day as if it were a complete life.
support.follows: Seneca tries to live every day as if it were a whole life.
support.context: The opening of Letter 61, on meeting death gladly. Seneca describes his own practice in old age; the letter itself, he says next, is written as if death might call him away.
