passages.title: On philosophy, the guide of life
passages.text: It is clear to you, I am sure, Lucilius, that no man can live a happy life, or even a supportable life, without the study of wisdom; you know also that a happy life is reached when our wisdom is brought to completion, but that life is at least endurable even when our wisdom is only begun. This idea, however, clear though it is, must be strengthened and implanted more deeply by daily reflection; it is more important for you to keep the resolutions you have already made than to go on and make noble ones. You must persevere, must develop new strength by continuous study, until that which is only a good inclination becomes a good settled purpose.

passages.title: More about virtue
passages.text: That is how a foolish mind is most clearly demonstrated: it shows first in this shape and then in that, and is never like itself—which is, in my opinion, the most shameful of qualities. Believe me, it is a great rôle—to play the rôle of one man. But nobody can be one person except the wise man; the rest of us often shift our masks. At times you will think us thrifty and serious, at other times wasteful and idle. We continually change our characters and play a part contrary to that which we have discarded. You should therefore force yourself to maintain to the very end of life’s drama the character which you assumed at the beginning. See to it that men be able to praise you; if not, let them at least identify you. Indeed, with regard to the man whom you saw but yesterday, the question may properly be asked: “Who is he?” So great a change has there been! Farewell.

passages.title: On the usefulness of basic principles
passages.text: The first way to worship the gods is to believe in the gods; the next to acknowledge their majesty, to acknowledge their goodness without which there is no majesty. Also, to know that they are supreme commanders in the universe, controlling all things by their power and acting as guardians of the human race, even though they are sometimes unmindful of the individual. They neither give nor have evil but they do chasten and restrain certain persons and impose penalties, and sometimes punish by bestowing that which seems good outwardly. Would you win over the gods? Then be a good man. Whoever imitates them, is worshipping them sufficiently.

passages.title: On the vitality of the soul and its attributes
passages.text: Fasten deep in your mind that which I remarked a short space above: that it makes no difference how many persons are acquainted with your uprightness. Those who wish their virtue to be advertised are not striving for virtue but for renown. Are you not willing to be just without being renowned? Nay, indeed you must often be just and be at the same time disgraced. And then, if you are wise, let ill repute, well won, be a delight. Farewell.

passages.title: On the futility of planning ahead
passages.text: Yet what is more foolish than to wonder that something which may happen every day has happened on any one day? There is indeed a limit fixed for us, just where the remorseless law of Fate has fixed it; but none of us knows how near he is to this limit. Therefore, let us so order our minds as if we had come to the very end. Let us postpone nothing. Let us balance life’s account every day.

passages.title: The epistles of seneca
passages.text: And yet I would not on that account decline for myself a few additional years; although, if my life’s space be shortened, I shall not say that I have lacked aught that is essential to a happy life. For I have not planned to live up to the very last day that my greedy hopes had promised me; nay, I have looked upon every day as if it were my last. Why ask the date of my birth, or whether I am still enrolled on the register of the younger men? What I have is my own.

passages.title: On the supreme good
passages.text: That which is short of perfection must necessarily be unsteady, at one time progressing, at another slipping or growing faint; and it will surely slip back unless it keeps struggling ahead; for if a man slackens at all in zeal and faithful application, he must retrograde. No one can resume his progress at the point where he left off.

passages.title: On practising what you preach
passages.text: Far different is the purpose of those who are speech-making and trying to win the approbation of a throng of hearers, far different that of those who allure the ears of young men and idlers by many-sided or fluent argumentation; philosophy teaches us to act, not to speak; it exacts of every man that he should live according to his own standards, that his life should not be out of harmony with his words, and that, further, his inner life should be of one hue and not out of harmony with all his activities. This, I say, is the highest duty and the highest proof of wisdom,—that deed and word should be in accord, that a man should be equal to himself under all conditions, and always the same. “But,” you reply, “who can maintain this standard?” Very few, to be sure; but there are some. It is indeed a hard undertaking, and I do not say that the philosopher can always keep the same pace. But he can always travel the same path.

passages.title: On the supreme good
passages.text: Therefore let us press on and persevere. There remains much more of the road than we have put behind us; but the greater part of progress is the desire to progress. I fully understand what this task is. It is a thing which I desire, and I desire it with all my heart. I see that you also have been aroused and are hastening with great zeal towards infinite beauty. Let us, then, hasten; only on these terms will life be a boon to us; otherwise, there is delay, and indeed disgraceful delay, while we busy ourselves with revolting things. Let us see to it that all time belongs to us. This, however, cannot be unless first of all our own selves begin to belong to us.

passages.title: On drunkenness
passages.text: I shall therefore do as you bid, and shall gladly inform you by letter what I am doing, and in what sequence. I shall keep watching myself continually, and—a most useful habit—shall review each day. For this is what makes us wicked: that no one of us looks back over his own life. Our thoughts are devoted only to what we are about to do. And yet our plans for the future always depend on the past.

passages.title: On the friendship of kindred minds
passages.text: Hasten to find me, but hasten to find yourself first. Make progress, and, before all else, endeavour to be consistent with yourself. And when you would find out whether you have accomplished anything, consider whether you desire the same things to-day that you desired yesterday. A shifting of the will indicates that the mind is at sea, heading in various directions, according to the course of the wind. But that which is settled and solid does not wander from its place. This is the blessed lot of the completely wise man, and also, to a certain extent, of him who is progressing and has made some headway. Now what is the difference between these two classes of men? The one is in motion, to be sure, but does not change its position; it merely tosses up and down where it is; the other is not in motion at all. Farewell.

passages.title: The philosopher’s mean
passages.text: Repellent attire, unkempt hair, slovenly beard, open scorn of silver dishes, a couch on the bare earth, and any other perverted forms of self-display, are to be avoided. The mere name of philosophy, however quietly pursued, is an object of sufficient scorn; and what would happen if we should begin to separate ourselves from the customs of our fellow-men? Inwardly, we ought to be different in all respects, but our exterior should conform to society.

passages.title: On reformation
passages.text: And when you have progressed so far that you have also respect for yourself, you may send away your attendant; but until then, set as a guard over yourself the authority of some man, whether your choice be the great Cato or Scipio, or Laelius,—or any man in whose presence even abandoned wretches would check their bad impulses. Meantime, you are engaged in making of yourself the sort of person in whose company you would not dare to sin. When this aim has been accomplished and you begin to hold yourself in some esteem, I shall gradually allow you to do what Epicurus, in another passage, suggests: “The time when you should most of all withdraw into yourself is when you are forced to be in a crowd.”

passages.title: On the blush of modesty
passages.text: Such, my dear Lucilius, is the counsel of Epicurus; he has quite properly given us a guardian and an attendant. We can get rid of most sins, if we have a witness who stands near us when we are likely to go wrong. The soul should have someone whom it can respect,—one by whose authority it may make even its inner shrine more hallowed. Happy is the man who can make others better, not merely when he is in their company, but even when he is in their thoughts! And happy also is he who can so revere a man as to calm and regulate himself by calling him to mind! One who can so revere another, will soon be himself worthy of reverence.

passages.title: On meeting death cheerfully
passages.text: Let us cease to desire that which we have been desiring. I, at least, am doing this: in my old age I have ceased to desire what I desired when a boy. To this single end my days and my nights are passed; this is my task, this the object of my thoughts,—to put an end to my chronic ills. I am endeavouring to live every day as if it were a complete life. I do not indeed snatch it up as if it were my last; I do regard it, however, as if it might even be my last.

claims.t: I hold myself to a few things, the names I have given myself, among them good, dignified, just, affectionate and without pretence. I keep myself in them, I take care never to bear other names, and I struggle to remain this kind of person.
claims.shared: All three passages give a short list of qualities and tell the reader to keep to it. 2.2 and 6.27 both name dignity, affection and justice, and both rule out pretence (“unfeigned”, “unpretentious”); 6.27 and 10.8 both say “good” and “keep yourself”; 2.2 and 10.8 both say “few” and “take care”.
claims.changed: The claim names only the qualities that two lists share, and says “among them” because each list has more. Left out are freedom (2.2); simple, unspoiled, reverent, kindly, strong for fitting work (6.27); modest, truthful and the three names ending in “minded” (10.8), which have an item of their own. 2.2 speaks of “things” and 6.27 of a “kind of person”; the claim calls them names, 10.8’s word. “Unpretentious” in 6.27 stands for a Greek word meaning “without polish”, so its match with 2.2’s “unfeigned” is closer in the English than in the Greek.

support.quote: At every hour take firm care
support.follows: Care is to be taken at every hour, and firmly.
gives: I take care

support.quote: to do what is in hand with exact and unfeigned dignity, affection, freedom and justice
support.follows: What is in hand is to be done with dignity, affection, freedom and justice, exactly and without feigning.
gives: dignified
just
affectionate
without pretence

support.quote: You see how few the things are
support.follows: The things that have to be mastered are few.
gives: a few things

support.quote: keep yourself simple, good, unspoiled, dignified, unpretentious, a friend of what is just, reverent toward the gods, kindly, warmly affectionate
support.follows: I should keep myself simple, good, dignified, unpretentious, just, reverent, kindly and affectionate.
gives: I keep myself in them
good
dignified
just
affectionate
without pretence

support.quote: Struggle to remain the kind of person philosophy wanted to make you.
support.follows: Remaining the person philosophy meant to make me takes a struggle.
gives: I struggle to remain this kind of person

support.quote: Having given yourself these names: good, modest, truthful, clear-minded, like-minded, high-minded, take care that you never come to bear other names
support.follows: Marcus has given himself six names and must take care that he does not end up bearing others.
gives: the names I have given myself
good
I take care
never to bear other names

support.quote: if you keep yourself in these names
support.follows: The names are something a person keeps himself in.
gives: I keep myself in them

support.quote: So put yourself aboard these few names, and if you can stay on them, stay
support.follows: The names are few; I should put myself aboard them and stay on them if I can.
gives: a few things
I keep myself in them

claims.t: Keeping to these few things lets me live a different life, one that flows smoothly. The gods ask nothing more of me. What they want is not to be flattered, but for rational beings to become like them and for a human being to do the work of a human being.
claims.shared: Both passages say that keeping to the few things leads to a life: in 2.2 the few things, once mastered, “let a person live a life that flows smoothly”; in 10.8 whoever keeps himself in the names “will enter a different life”. Both then say what the gods ask of a person: 2.2 that they demand nothing more, 10.8 what it is they want.
claims.changed: The claim takes the weaker verb, 2.2’s “let a person live”; 10.8 says outright “you will enter”. 2.2 adds that the life is god-fearing, and 10.8 that the person becomes a different person; the claim leaves both out. 10.8 lists the fig tree, the dog and the bee before the human being; the claim keeps the human being.

support.quote: once mastered, let a person live a life that flows smoothly and is god-fearing
support.follows: The few things, once mastered, let a person live a life that flows smoothly and is god-fearing.
gives: Keeping to these few things lets me live
one that flows smoothly

support.quote: for the gods will demand nothing more of whoever keeps to these
support.follows: The gods will demand nothing more of anyone who keeps to these few things.
gives: The gods ask nothing more of me

support.quote: if you keep yourself in these names, without craving to have others call you by them, you will be a different person and will enter a different life
support.follows: Whoever keeps himself in these names becomes a different person and enters a different life.
gives: Keeping to these few things lets me live
a different life

support.quote: what they want is not to be flattered, but for all rational beings to become like them, and for the fig tree to do the work of a fig tree, the dog the work of a dog, the bee the work of a bee, and the human being the work of a human being
support.follows: The gods do not want flattery; they want rational beings to become like them and each thing, the human being included, to do its own work.
gives: What they want is not to be flattered
for rational beings to become like them
for a human being to do the work of a human being

claims.t: I keep these names without craving that others call me by them. I need neither show nor any human being as witness.
claims.shared: 1.14 and 3.5 both say “need neither … nor”: at a court one need have no bodyguards, marked clothes or similar show, and the man who has set himself in order needs no oath and no human witness. 3.5 and 10.8 both do without other people’s word: no human being to witness for me, no craving that others use the names of me.
claims.changed: The words two passages share here are only the frame “need neither”; what is not needed differs. 1.14 lists bodyguards, clothes that mark one out, torches and statues; the claim keeps its summing word, “show”. 1.14 says this is possible at a court and reports it as a thought Marcus was brought to; the claim states it of myself. 3.5’s oath is dropped; standing beside an oath, its witness is someone who vouches for a man, not an audience.

support.quote: it is possible to live at a court and need neither bodyguards, nor clothes that mark one out, nor torches and statues of this sort and similar show
support.follows: The ruler and father Marcus was placed under brought him to think that one can live at a court without guards, marked clothes or similar show.
gives: I need neither
show

support.quote: needing neither an oath nor any human being as witness
support.follows: The man who has set himself in order needs no oath and no human witness.
gives: I need neither
any human being as witness

support.quote: without craving to have others call you by them
support.follows: The names are to be kept without craving that other people use them of me.
gives: without craving that others call me by them

claims.t: I want my last hour to come upon me with a good conscience. As a Roman and a man, I set myself in order and do each thing as someone about to leave life, waiting for the signal to withdraw. I carry out each action as the last of my life.
claims.shared: 2.2 and 3.5 both name who is acting, “a Roman” and a man (3.5: “male”), and both set him at the edge of life: 2.2 has each action done “as the last of your life”, 3.5 has him waiting for the signal “to withdraw from life”. 2.2 and 6.28 share the word “last”.
claims.changed: 3.5 adds that the man is old, engaged in public affairs and a ruler; the claim keeps what 2.2 also says. In 6.28 the good conscience at the last hour is the aim of following Antoninus; the claim states the aim without its model, who has an item of his own.

support.quote: so that your last hour may come upon you with a conscience as good as his
support.follows: Following Antoninus is meant to bring me to my last hour with a conscience as good as his.
gives: I want my last hour to come upon me with a good conscience

support.quote: as a Roman and a man
support.follows: The care over what is in hand is to be taken as a Roman and a man.
gives: As a Roman and a man

support.quote: a living being that is male, old, engaged in public affairs, a Roman and a ruler, who has set himself in order
support.follows: The god within is to guard a being that is male, old, in public life, a Roman and a ruler, and that has set himself in order.
gives: As a Roman and a man
set myself in order

support.quote: as someone would be who is waiting for the signal to withdraw from life, easily released
support.follows: The man described is to be like someone who waits for the signal to withdraw from life and is easily released.
gives: as someone about to leave life
waiting for the signal to withdraw

support.quote: carry out each action as the last of your life
support.follows: Each action is to be carried out as if it were the last of my life.
gives: as someone about to leave life
each action as the last of my life

claims.t: I ask myself how I have behaved up to now toward my parents, my teachers, my friends and those close to me, and whether I have done nothing wrong to any of them.
claims.shared: Both passages go through the same people (parents, teachers, friends, those close to me) and both speak of wrong done to them: 5.25 asks whether I have “done nothing wrong to anyone”, and 1.14 gives thanks that I was “not carried away into any offence against any of them”.
claims.changed: 5.25 asks the question; 1.14 answers it for the past and thanks the gods. The claim keeps the question. It drops the gods, brothers, wife, children, those who brought me up and household slaves of 5.25, and the grandfathers, sister and relatives of 1.14, which the other list does not have.

support.quote: How have you behaved up to now toward the gods, your parents, your brothers, your wife, your children, your teachers, those who brought you up, your friends, those close to you, your household slaves?
support.follows: Marcus asks himself how he has behaved up to now toward the gods, his family, teachers, friends, those close to him and his household.
gives: I ask myself how I have behaved up to now
my parents, my teachers, my friends and those close to me

support.quote: Does this hold of you up to now, toward all of them: “to have done nothing wrong to anyone, nor said anything wrong”?
support.follows: Marcus asks whether, toward all the people he has listed, he has done nothing wrong and said nothing wrong.
gives: I have done nothing wrong to any of them

support.quote: that I had good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good people close to me, relatives, friends, nearly all of them
support.follows: Marcus thanks the gods that nearly all his family, teachers, friends and those close to him were good.
gives: my parents, my teachers, my friends and those close to me

support.quote: I was not carried away into any offence against any of them
support.follows: Marcus was not carried away into any offence against his family, teachers, friends or those close to him.
gives: I have done nothing wrong to any of them

claims.t: These names can be lost. It happens that a person is turned into a Caesar, made over by the office he holds. I fall short by my own fault. When I lose the names, I go back to them quickly.
claims.shared: 10.8 and 1.14 both admit a falling: “falling away and not prevailing” from the names, and “I still fall short” of the life according to nature. 6.27 and 10.8 both warn of becoming something else than what was to be kept: being turned into a Caesar “happens”, and the names can be lost.
claims.changed: In 1.14 what Marcus falls short of is living according to nature; in 10.8 it is the names. The claim treats them as one falling short. The word “fall” is shared only in the English: 10.8’s verb is “fall out” (ἐκπίπτεις) and 1.14’s is “be left behind” (ἀπολείπεσθαι). 6.27 says that being turned into a Caesar happens; it does not say that names are lost. “Made over by the office he holds” is the editor’s gloss: Caesar is Marcus’s own title as emperor.

support.quote: if you do lose these names, go back to them quickly
support.follows: The names can be lost; if they are, I should go back to them quickly.
gives: These names can be lost
When I lose the names, I go back to them quickly

support.quote: Take care that you are not turned into a Caesar, that you are not dyed: for it happens.
support.follows: Being turned into a Caesar is something that happens, and care must be taken against it.
gives: It happens that a person is turned into a Caesar

support.quote: if you sense that you are falling away and are not prevailing
support.follows: A person can sense that he is falling away from the names and not prevailing.
gives: I fall short

support.quote: that I still fall short of this is by my own fault and by not keeping to the reminders from the gods
support.follows: That Marcus still falls short of living according to nature is his own fault: he has not kept to the gods’ reminders.
gives: I fall short
by my own fault

single.quote: Life is short. There is one fruit of living on earth: a pious disposition and social actions.
single.label: The one fruit
single.t: Life is short. There is one fruit of living on earth: a pious disposition and social actions, that is, actions done for the community.
single.why: Only this passage says that life has a single fruit. No second passage of the section says it, so it is not fused. “Actions done for the community” is the translators’ gloss of “social actions”.
single.follows: Life is short, and the one thing to be had from it is a pious disposition and actions done for the community.

single.quote: one may draw oneself in until one is very nearly a private person and not, on that account, be more lowly or more slack in what has to be done as a leader for the common good
single.label: Leading without the show
single.t: I can draw myself in until I am very nearly a private person, and be no lowlier and no slacker for it in what I have to do as a leader for the common good.
single.why: Only this passage says it, as a thought Marcus was brought to by the ruler and father he was placed under. Its words on needing no show are fused in the claim on show and witness.
single.follows: Marcus’s ruler and father showed him that one can live almost as a private person and be no lowlier or slacker in a leader’s work for the common good.

single.quote: Love the little trade you have learned, and rest in it; and go through what is left of your life having entrusted everything that is yours to the gods with your whole soul, and making yourself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any human being.
single.label: The trade I learned
single.t: I love the little trade I have learned, and I rest in it. For what is left of my life I entrust everything that is mine to the gods with my whole soul, and I make myself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any human being.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of a trade to love, and of being neither tyrant nor slave. It does not say which trade, so it is not fused with the names.
single.follows: I should love the trade I learned and rest in it, entrust what is mine to the gods, and be neither tyrant nor slave to anyone.

single.quote: Do not act unwillingly, or unsocially, or without examining, or while pulled the other way. Do not let elegance dress up your thought. Do not be a person of many words or a busybody.
single.label: How not to act
single.t: I do not act unwillingly, or unsocially, or without examining, or while pulled the other way. I do not let elegance dress up my thought, and I am not a person of many words or a busybody.
single.why: Only this passage gives this list. 2.2 has its own list of what each action should be rid of, but the two lists share no words.
single.follows: Acting unwillingly, unsocially, unexamined or divided is ruled out, and so are dressed-up thought, many words and meddling.

single.quote: Remember that “clear-minded” was to mean for you a discerning attention to each thing, and not letting things go unheeded; “like-minded”, the willing acceptance of what the common nature assigns; and “high-minded”, the lifting high of the part that has mind, above the smooth or rough movement of the flesh, above petty reputation, above death and everything of that kind.
single.label: Three further names
single.t: Three further names I have given myself are clear-minded, like-minded and high-minded, and I remember what each was to mean. Clear-minded: a discerning attention to each thing, letting nothing go unheeded. Like-minded: willingly accepting what the common nature assigns. High-minded: lifting the part of me that has mind above the smooth or rough movement of the flesh, that is, pleasure and pain, above petty reputation, and above death.
single.why: Only this passage has these three names and defines them. No other list in the section has them, so they are not among the names of the first claim; the definitions are kept as something to recall. “Pleasure and pain” is the translators’ gloss of the movement of the flesh.
single.follows: The three names mean attention to each thing, willing acceptance of what nature assigns, and a mind lifted above the flesh, reputation and death.

single.quote: Everything as a pupil of Antoninus: his vigour on behalf of what is done according to reason, his evenness everywhere, his piety, the calm of his face, his gentleness, his freedom from vanity, and his ambition to grasp matters
single.label: A model
single.t: I do everything as a pupil of Antoninus, the emperor who adopted me. I recall his vigour on behalf of what is done according to reason, his evenness everywhere, his piety, the calm of his face, his gentleness, his freedom from vanity and his ambition to grasp matters.
single.why: Only this passage sets up a person as the model. Its long list describes Antoninus and is not the list of names, so it is not fused. That Antoninus is Antoninus Pius, who adopted Marcus, is the translators’ note.
single.follows: Marcus is to do everything as a pupil of Antoninus, whose traits he lists, beginning with these seven.

single.quote: Call to mind, too, what things you have passed through and what things you have been strong enough to endure; and that the story of your life is now full and your service complete; and how many fine things you have seen; and how many pleasures and pains you have looked down on, how many honours you have looked past, and to how many inconsiderate people you have been considerate.
single.label: What I have come through
single.t: I call to mind what I have passed through and have been strong enough to endure; that the story of my life is now full and my service complete; how many fine things I have seen; how many pleasures and pains I have looked down on, how many honours I have looked past; and to how many inconsiderate people I have been considerate.
single.why: Only this passage looks back on what was endured and calls the life full. The question about wrongdoing in the same passage is fused in the review of my conduct.
single.follows: Marcus is to recall what he has endured, seen and looked past, and that his life’s story is full and his service complete.

single.quote: although I had a disposition from which, if it had so happened, I might well have done something of the kind; but it is the gods’ kindness that no combination of circumstances came about that would have shown me up
single.label: A rider to the review
single.t: I remember that my clean record toward those close to me is partly the gods’ kindness: I had a disposition from which I might well have offended them, and no circumstances came about that would have shown me up.
single.why: Only this passage says it. It sits under Practice as a rider to the review of my conduct: what I recall when the review comes out clean, that the record is partly good fortune.
single.follows: Marcus had it in him to offend those close to him, and thanks the gods that no circumstances arose to bring it out.

single.quote: It is shameful that, in a life in which your body does not give out, your soul should give out first.
single.label: The soul giving out
single.t: It is shameful if my soul gives out in a life in which my body has not yet given out.
single.why: Only this passage says it. It names the failure as a giving out of the soul; the other passages speak of losing names or falling short.
single.follows: It is shameful for the soul to give out before the body does.

single.quote: For to go on being such as you have been up to now, and to be torn and soiled in a life like this, is the mark of someone thoroughly senseless and clinging to life, someone like the half-eaten beast-fighters who, full of wounds and gore, still beg to be kept until tomorrow, to be thrown, just as they are, to the same claws and bites.
single.label: What failing looks like
single.t: To go on being as I have been up to now, torn and soiled in a life like this, is senseless clinging to life. It is like the half-eaten beast-fighters who, full of wounds, still beg to be kept until tomorrow, to be thrown to the same claws and bites.
single.why: Only this passage gives a picture of what not changing is like.
single.follows: Going on unchanged in a life that tears and soils me is senseless clinging to life, like a mauled beast-fighter begging for one more day.

single.quote: go away with a good heart to some corner where you will prevail
single.label: If I am not prevailing
single.t: If I am not prevailing in keeping these names where I am, I go away with a good heart to some corner where I will prevail.
single.why: Only this passage says where to go when the names cannot be kept. It goes on to a second way out, leaving life altogether, which the article does not turn into a rule (see the editor’s decisions).
single.follows: Someone who is not prevailing should withdraw, in good heart, to a corner where he will prevail.

members.text:
Let it be thy earnest and incessant care as a Roman and a man to
perform whatsoever it is that thou art about, with true and unfeigned
gravity, natural affection, freedom and justice: and as for all other
cares, and imaginations, how thou mayest ease thy mind of them. Which
thou shalt do; if thou shalt go about every action as thy last action,
free from all vanity, all passionate and wilful aberration from reason,
and from all hypocrisy, and self-love, and dislike of those things,
which by the fates or appointment of God have happened unto thee. Thou
seest that those things, which for a man to hold on in a prosperous
course, and to live a divine life, are requisite and necessary, are not
many, for the gods will require no more of any man, that shall but keep
and observe these things.
members.english: At every hour take firm care, as a Roman and a man, to do what is in hand with exact and unfeigned dignity, affection, freedom and justice, and to win yourself respite from all other impressions. You will win it if you carry out each action as the last of your life, rid of all aimlessness, of turning away in passion from what reason decides, of pretence, of self-love and of discontent with what has been allotted to you. You see how few the things are which, once mastered, let a person live a life that flows smoothly and is god-fearing: for the gods will demand nothing more of whoever keeps to these.
members.greek: Πάσης ὥρας φρόντιζε στιβαρῶς ὡς Ῥωμαῖος καὶ ἄρρην τὸ ἐν χερσὶ μετὰ τῆς ἀκριβοῦς καὶ ἀπλάστου σεμνότητος καὶ φιλοστοργίας καὶ ἐλευθερίας καὶ δικαιότητος πράσσειν καὶ σχολὴν σαυτῷ ἀπὸ πασῶν τῶν ἄλλων φαντασιῶν πορίζειν. ποριεῖς δέ, ἂν ὡς ἐσχάτην τοῦ βίου ἑκάστην πρᾶξιν ἐνεργῇς, ἀπηλλαγμένος πάσης εἰκαιότητος καὶ ἐμπαθοῦς ἀποστροφῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ αἱροῦντος λόγου καὶ ὑποκρίσεως καὶ φιλαυτίας καὶ δυσαρεστήσεως πρὸς τὰ συμμεμοιραμένα. ὁρᾷς πῶς ὀλίγα ἐστίν, ὧν κρατήσας τις δύναται εὔρουν καὶ θεουδῆ βιῶσαι βίον· καὶ γὰρ οἱ θεοὶ πλέον οὐδὲν ἀπαιτήσουσι παρὰ τοῦ ταῦτα φυλάσσοντος.

members.text:
If in this kind of life thy body be able to hold out, it is a
shame that thy soul should faint first, and give over, take heed, lest
of a philosopher thou become a mere Cæsar in time, and receive a new
tincture from the court. For it may happen if thou dost not take heed.
Keep thyself therefore, truly simple, good, sincere, grave, free
from all ostentation, a lover of that which is just, religious, kind,
tender-hearted, strong and vigorous to undergo anything that becomes
thee. Endeavour to continue such, as philosophy (hadst thou wholly and
constantly applied thyself unto it) would have made, and secured thee.
Worship the Gods, procure the welfare of men, this life is short.
Charitable actions, and a holy disposition, is the only fruit of this
earthly life.
members.english:
It is shameful that, in a life in which your body does not give out, your soul should give out first.

Take care that you are not turned into a Caesar, that you are not dyed: for it happens. So keep yourself simple, good, unspoiled, dignified, unpretentious, a friend of what is just, reverent toward the gods, kindly, warmly affectionate, strong for the work that is fitting. Struggle to remain the kind of person philosophy wanted to make you. Stand in awe of the gods, keep people safe. Life is short. There is one fruit of living on earth: a pious disposition and social actions.
members.greek:
Αἰσχρόν ἐστιν, ἐν ᾧ βίῳ τὸ σῶμά σοι μὴ ἀπαυδᾷ, ἐν τούτῳ τὴν ψυχὴν προαπαυδᾶν.

Ὅρα μὴ ἀποκαισαρωθῇς, μὴ βαφῇς· γίνεται γάρ. τήρησον οὖν σεαυτὸν ἁπλοῦν, ἀγαθόν, ἀκέραιον, σεμνόν, ἄκομψον, τοῦ δικαίου φίλον, θεοσεβῆ, εὐμενῆ, φιλόστοργον, ἐρρωμένον πρὸς τὰ πρέποντα ἔργα. ἀγώνισαι, ἵνα τοιοῦτος συμμείνῃς, οἷόν σε ἠθέλησε ποιῆσαι φιλοσοφία. αἰδοῦ θεούς, σῷζε ἀνθρώπους. βραχὺς ὁ βίος· εἶς καρπὸς τῆς ἐπιγείου ζωῆς, διάθεσις ὁσία καὶ πράξεις κοινωνικαί.

members.text:
Now that thou hast taken these names upon thee of good, modest,
true; of ἔμφρων, σύμφρων, ὑπέρφρων; take heed lest at any times by
doing anything that is contrary, thou be but improperly so called, and
lose thy right to these appellations. Or if thou do, return unto them
again with all possible speed. And remember, that the word ἔμφρων notes
unto thee an intent and intelligent consideration of every object that
presents itself unto thee, without distraction. And the word σύμφρων, a
ready and contented acceptation of whatsoever by the appointment of the
common nature, happens unto thee. And the word ὑπέρφρων, a
super-extension, or a transcendent, and outreaching disposition of thy
mind, whereby it passeth by all bodily pains and pleasures, honour and
credit, death and whatsoever is of the same nature, as matters of
absolute indifferency, and in no wise to be stood upon by a wise man.
These then if inviolably thou shalt observe, and shalt not be ambitious
to be so called by others, both thou thyself shalt become a new man,
and thou shalt begin a new life. For to continue such as hitherto thou
hast been, to undergo those distractions and distempers as thou must
needs for such a life as hitherto thou hast lived, is the part of one
that is very foolish, and is overfond of his life. Whom a man might
compare to one of those half-eaten wretches, matched in the
amphitheatre with wild beasts; who as full as they are all the body
over with wounds and blood, desire for a great favour, that they may be
reserved till the next day, then also, and in the same estate to be
exposed to the same nails and teeth as before. Away therefore, ship
thyself; and from the troubles and distractions of thy former life
convey thyself as it were unto these few names; and if thou canst abide
in them, or be constant in the practice and possession of them,
continue there as glad and joyful as one that were translated unto some
such place of bliss and happiness as that which by Hesiod and Plato is
called the Islands of the Blessed, by others called the Elysian Fields.
And whensoever thou findest thyself; that thou art in danger of a
relapse, and that thou art not able to master and overcome those
difficulties and temptations that present themselves in thy present
station: get thee into any private corner, where thou mayst be better
able. Or if that will not serve forsake even thy life rather. But so
that it be not in passion but in a plain voluntary modest way: this
being the only commendable action of thy whole life that thus thou art
departed, or this having been the main work and business of thy whole
life, that thou mightest thus depart. Now for the better remembrance of
those names that we have spoken of, thou shalt find it a very good
help, to remember the Gods as often as may be: and that, the thing
which they require at our hands of as many of us, as are by nature
reasonable creation is not that with fair words, and outward show of
piety and devotion we should flatter them, but that we should become
like unto them: and that as all other natural creatures, the fig tree
for example; the dog the bee: both do, all of them, and apply
themselves unto that which by their natural constitution, is proper
unto them; so man likewise should do that, which by his nature, as he
is a man, belongs unto him.
members.english: Having given yourself these names: good, modest, truthful, clear-minded, like-minded, high-minded, take care that you never come to bear other names; and if you do lose these names, go back to them quickly. Remember that “clear-minded” was to mean for you a discerning attention to each thing, and not letting things go unheeded; “like-minded”, the willing acceptance of what the common nature assigns; and “high-minded”, the lifting high of the part that has mind, above the smooth or rough movement of the flesh, above petty reputation, above death and everything of that kind. So if you keep yourself in these names, without craving to have others call you by them, you will be a different person and will enter a different life. For to go on being such as you have been up to now, and to be torn and soiled in a life like this, is the mark of someone thoroughly senseless and clinging to life, someone like the half-eaten beast-fighters who, full of wounds and gore, still beg to be kept until tomorrow, to be thrown, just as they are, to the same claws and bites. So put yourself aboard these few names, and if you can stay on them, stay, like someone who has moved to some Islands of the Blessed. But if you sense that you are falling away and are not prevailing, go away with a good heart to some corner where you will prevail, or even leave life altogether, not in anger, but simply, freely and modestly, having at least done this one thing, and only this, in your life: to leave it in this way. Toward remembering the names, though, it will help you greatly to remember the gods, and that what they want is not to be flattered, but for all rational beings to become like them, and for the fig tree to do the work of a fig tree, the dog the work of a dog, the bee the work of a bee, and the human being the work of a human being.
members.greek: Ὀνόματα θέμενος σαυτῷ ταῦτα· ἀγαθός, αἰδήμων, ἀληθής, ἔμφρων, σύμφρων, ὑπέρφρων, πρόσεχε μήποτε μετονομάζῃ, κἂν ἀπολλύῃς ταῦτα τὰ ὀνόματα, καὶ ταχέως ἐπάνιθι ἐπ’ αὐτά. μέμνησο δὲ ὅτι τὸ μὲν ἔμφρων ἐβούλετό σοι σημαίνειν τὴν ἐφ’ ἕκαστα διαληπτικὴν ἐπίστασιν καὶ τὸ ἀπαρενθύμητον· τὸ δὲ σύμφρων τὴν ἑκούσιον ἀπόδεξιν τῶν ὑπὸ τῆς κοινῆς φύσεως ἀπονεμομένων· τὸ δὲ ὑπέρφρων τὴν ὑπέρτασιν τοῦ φρονοῦντος μορίου ὑπὲρ λείαν ἣ τραχεῖαν κίνησιν τῆς σαρκὸς καὶ τὸ δοξάριον καὶ τὸν θάνατον καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα. ἐὰν οὖν διατηρῇς σεαυτὸν ὲν τούτοις τοῖς ὀνόμασι μὴ γλιχόμενος τοῦ ὑπ’ ἄλλων κατὰ ταῦτα ὀνομάζεσθαι, ἔσῃ ἕτερος καὶ εἰς βίον εἰσελεύσῃ ἕτερον. τὸ γὰρ ἔτι τοιοῦτον εἶναι οἷος μέχρι νῦν γέγονας, καὶ ἐν βίῳ τοιούτῳ σπαράσσεσθαι καὶ μολύνεσθαι, λίαν ἐστὶν ἀναισθήτου καὶ φιλοψύχου καὶ ὁμοίου τοῖς ἡμιβρώτοις θηριομάχοις, οἵτινες μεστοὶ τραυμάτων καὶ λύθρου παρακαλοῦσιν ὅμως εἰς τὴν αὔριον φυλαχθῆναι, παραβληθησόμενοι τοιοῦτοι τοῖς αὐτοῖς ὄνυξι καὶ δήγμασιν. ἐμβίβασον οὖν σαυτὸν εἰς τὰ ὀλίγα ταῦτα ὀνόματα, κἂν μὲν ἐπ’ αὐτῶν μένειν δύνῃ, μένε ὥσπερ εἰς μακάρων τινὰς νήσους μετῳκισμένος· ἐὰν δὲ αἴσθῃ ὅτι ἐκπίπτεις καὶ οὐ περικρατεῖς, ἄπιθι θαρρῶν εἰς γωνίαν τινά, ὅπου κρατήσεις, ἢ καὶ παντάπασιν ἔξιθι τοῦ βίου, μὴ ὀργιζόμενος, ἀλλὰ ἁπλῶς καὶ ἐλευθέρως καὶ αἰδημόνως, ἕν γε τοῦτο μόνον πράξας ἐν τῷ βίῳ τὸ οὕτως ἐξελθεῖν. πρὸς μέντοι τὸ μεμνῆσθαι τῶν ὀνομάτων μεγάλως συλλήψεταί σοι τὸ μεμνῆσθαι θεῶν καὶ ὅτιπερ οὐ κολακεύεσθαι οὗτοι θέλουσιν, ἀλλὰ ἐξομοιοῦσθαι ἑαυτοῖς τὰ λογικὰ πάντα καὶ εἶναι τὴν μὲν συκῆν τὰ συκῆς ποιοῦσαν, τὸν δὲ κύνα τὰ κυνός, τὴν δὲ μέλισσαν τὰ μελίσσης, τὸν δὲ ἄνθρωπον τὰ ἀνθρώπου.

members.text:
Do nothing against thy will, nor contrary to the community, nor
without due examination, nor with reluctancy. Affect not to set out thy
thoughts with curious neat language. Be neither a great talker, nor a
great undertaker. Moreover, let thy God that is in thee to rule over
thee, find by thee, that he hath to do with a man; an aged man; a
sociable man; a Roman; a prince; one that hath ordered his life, as
one that expecteth, as it were, nothing but the sound of the trumpet,
sounding a retreat to depart out of this life with all expedition. One
who for his word or actions neither needs an oath, nor any man to be a
witness.
members.english: Do not act unwillingly, or unsocially, or without examining, or while pulled the other way. Do not let elegance dress up your thought. Do not be a person of many words or a busybody. Further, let the god in you be the guardian of a living being that is male, old, engaged in public affairs, a Roman and a ruler, who has set himself in order, as someone would be who is waiting for the signal to withdraw from life, easily released, needing neither an oath nor any human being as witness.
members.greek: Μήτε ἀκούσιος ἐνέργει μήτε ἀκοινώνητος μήτε ἀνεξέταστος μήτε ἀνθελκόμενος· μήτε κομψεία τὴν διάνοιάν σου καλλωπιζέτω· μήτε πολυρρήμων μήτε πολυπράγμων ἔσο. ἔτι δὲ ὁ ἐν σοὶ θεὸς ἔστω προστάτης ζῴου ἄρρενος καὶ πρεσβύτου καὶ πολιτικοῦ καὶ Ῥωμαίου καὶ ἄρχοντος, ἀνατεταχότος ἑαυτόν, οἷος ἂν εἴη τις περιμένων τὸ ἀνακλητικὸν ἐκ τοῦ βίου εὔλυτος, μήτε ὅρκου δεόμενος μήτε ἀνθρώπου τινὸς μάρτυρος.

members.text:
How hast thou carried thyself hitherto towards the Gods? towards
thy parents? towards thy brethren? towards thy wife? towards thy
children? towards thy masters? thy foster-fathers? thy friends? thy
domestics? thy servants? Is it so with thee, that hitherto thou hast
neither by word or deed wronged any of them? Remember withal through how
many things thou hast already passed, and how many thou hast been able
to endure; so that now the legend of thy life is full, and thy charge is
accomplished. Again, how many truly good things have certainly by thee
been discerned? how many pleasures, how many pains hast thou passed over
with contempt? how many things eternally glorious hast thou despised?
towards how many perverse unreasonable men hast thou carried thyself
kindly, and discreetly?
members.english: How have you behaved up to now toward the gods, your parents, your brothers, your wife, your children, your teachers, those who brought you up, your friends, those close to you, your household slaves? Does this hold of you up to now, toward all of them: “to have done nothing wrong to anyone, nor said anything wrong”? Call to mind, too, what things you have passed through and what things you have been strong enough to endure; and that the story of your life is now full and your service complete; and how many fine things you have seen; and how many pleasures and pains you have looked down on, how many honours you have looked past, and to how many inconsiderate people you have been considerate.
members.greek: Πῶς προσενήνεξαι μέχρι νῦν θεοῖς, γονεῦσιν, ἀδελφοῖς, γυναικί, τέκνοις, διδασκάλοις, τροφεῦσι, φίλοις, οἰκείοις, οἰκέταις· εἰ πρὸς πάντας σοι μέχρι νῦν ἐστι τό· μήτε τινὰ ῥέξαι ἐξαίσιον μήτε τι εἰπεῖν. ἀναμιμνῄσκου δὲ καὶ δι’ οἵων διελήλυθας καὶ οἷα ἤρκεσας ὑπομεῖναι καὶ ὅτι πλήρης ἤδη σοι ἡ ἱστορία τοῦ βίου καὶ τελεία ἡ λειτουργία καὶ πόσα ὦπται καλὰ καὶ πόσων μὲν ἡδονῶν καὶ πόνων ὑπερεῖδες, πόσα δὲ ἔνδοξα παρεῖδες, εἰς ὅσους δὲ ἀγνώμονας εὐγνώμων ἐγένου.

members.text:
Do all things as becometh the disciple of Antoninus Pius.
Remember his resolute constancy in things that were done by him
according to reason, his equability in all things, his sanctity; the
cheerfulness of his countenance, his sweetness, and how free he was from
all vainglory; how careful to come to the true and exact knowledge of
matters in hand, and how he would by no means give over till he did
fully, and plainly understand the whole state of the business; and how
patiently, and without any contestation he would bear with them, that
did unjustly condemn him: how he would never be over-hasty in anything,
nor give ear to slanders and false accusations, but examine and observe
with best diligence the several actions and dispositions of men. Again,
how he was no backbiter, nor easily frightened, nor suspicious, and in
his language free from all affectation and curiosity: and how easily he
would content himself with few things, as lodging, bedding, clothing,
and ordinary nourishment, and attendance. How able to endure labour, how
patient; able through his spare diet to continue from morning to evening
without any necessity of withdrawing before his accustomed hours to
the necessities of nature: his uniformity and constancy in matter of
friendship. How he would bear with them that with all boldness and
liberty opposed his opinions; and even rejoice if any man could better
advise him: and lastly, how religious he was without superstition. All
these things of him remember, that whensoever thy last hour shall
come upon thee, it may find thee, as it did him, ready for it in the
possession of a good conscience.
members.english: Everything as a pupil of Antoninus: his vigour on behalf of what is done according to reason, his evenness everywhere, his piety, the calm of his face, his gentleness, his freedom from vanity, and his ambition to grasp matters; and how he would not let anything at all go by without first looking into it very well and understanding it clearly; and how he bore with those who blamed him unjustly, without blaming them in return; and how he hurried toward nothing; and how he did not accept slanders; and how exact an examiner he was of characters and actions, and not one to reproach, not one to jump at a noise, not suspicious, not a sophist; and how he was content with little, for example in housing, bedding, clothing, food and service; and how hard-working he was and how patient; and that he was the kind of man who could stay at the same thing until evening, not even needing, because of his plain diet, to pass his waste except at the usual hour; and his being firm and always the same in his friendships; and his putting up with those who openly opposed his opinions, and being glad if anyone showed him something better; and how he was reverent toward the gods without superstition; so that your last hour may come upon you with a conscience as good as his.
members.greek: πάντα ὡς Ἀντωνίνου μαθητής· τὸ ὑπὲρ τῶν κατὰ λόγον πρασσομένων εὔτονον ἐκείνου καὶ τὸ ὁμαλὲς πανταχοῦ καὶ τὸ ὅσιον καὶ τὸ εὔδιον τοῦ προσώπου καὶ τὸ μειλίχιον καὶ τὸ ἀκενόδοξον καὶ τὸ περὶ τὴν κατάληψιν τῶν πραγμάτων φιλότιμον· καὶ ὡς ἐκεῖνος οὐκ ἄν τι ὅλως παρῆκε μὴ πρότερον εὖ μάλα κατιδὼν καὶ σαφῶς νοήσας· καὶ ὡς ἔφερεν ἐκεῖνος τοὺς ἀδίκως αὐτὸν μεμφομένους μὴ ἀντιμεμφόμενος· καὶ ὡς ἐπ’ οὐδὲν ἔσπευδεν· καὶ ὠς διαβολὰς οὐκ ἐδέχετο· καὶ ὡς ἀκριβὴς ἦν ἐξεταστὴς ἠθῶν καὶ πράξεων καὶ οὐκ ὀνειδιστής, οὐ ψοφοδεής, οὐχ ὑπόπτης, οὐ σοφιστής· καὶ ὡς ὀλίγοις ἀρκούμενος, οἷον οἰκήσει, στρωμνῇ, ἐσθῆτι, τροφῇ, ὑπηρεσίᾳ· καὶ ὡς φιλόπονος καὶ μακρόθυμος· καὶ οἷος μένειν ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ μέχρι ἑσπέρας, διὰ τὴν λιτὴν δίαιταν μηδὲ τοῦ ἀποκρίνειν τὰ περιττώματα παρὰ τὴν συνήθη ὥραν χρῄζων· καὶ τὸ βέβαιον καὶ ὅμοιον ἐν ταῖς φιλίαις αὐτοῦ· καὶ τὸ ἀνέχεσθαι τῶν ἀντιβαινόντων παρρησιαστικῶς ταῖς γνώμαις αὐτοῦ καὶ χαίρειν εἴ τίς τι δεικνύοι κρεῖττον· καὶ ὡς θεοσεβὴς χωρὶς δεισιδαιμονίας· ἵν’ οὕτως εὐσυνειδήτῳ σοι ἐπιστῇ ἠ τελευταία ὥρα ὡς ἐκείνῳ.

members.text:
What art and profession soever thou hast learned, endeavour to
affect it, and comfort thyself in it; and pass the remainder of thy life
as one who from his whole heart commits himself and whatsoever belongs
unto him, unto the gods: and as for men, carry not thyself either
tyrannically or servilely towards any.
members.english: Love the little trade you have learned, and rest in it; and go through what is left of your life having entrusted everything that is yours to the gods with your whole soul, and making yourself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any human being.
members.greek: Τὸ τεχνίον ὃ ἔμαθες φίλει, τούτῳ προσαναπαύου· τὸ δὲ ὑπόλοιπον τοῦ βίου διέξελθε ὡς θεοῖς μὲν ἐπιτετροφὼς τὰ σεαυτοῦ πάντα ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς, ἀνθρώπων δὲ μηδενὸς μήτε τύραννον μήτε δοῦλον σεαυτὸν καθιστάς.

members.text:
From the gods I received that I had good grandfathers, and parents,
a good sister, good masters, good domestics, loving kinsmen, almost all
that I have; and that I never through haste and rashness transgressed
against any of them, notwithstanding that my disposition was such,
as that such a thing (if occasion had been) might very well have been
committed by me, but that It was the mercy of the gods, to prevent such
a concurring of matters and occasions, as might make me to incur this
blame. That I was not long brought up by the concubine of my father;
that I preserved the flower of my youth. That I took not upon me to be
a man before my time, but rather put it off longer than I needed. That
I lived under the government of my lord and father, who would take
away from me all pride and vainglory, and reduce me to that conceit and
opinion that it was not impossible for a prince to live in the court
without a troop of guards and followers, extraordinary apparel, such
and such torches and statues, and other like particulars of state and
magnificence; but that a man may reduce and contract himself almost to
the state of a private man, and yet for all that not to become the more
base and remiss in those public matters and affairs, wherein power and
authority is requisite. That I have had such a brother, who by his own
example might stir me up to think of myself; and by his respect and
love, delight and please me. That I have got ingenuous children, and
that they were not born distorted, nor with any other natural deformity.
That I was no great proficient in the study of rhetoric and poetry, and
of other faculties, which perchance I might have dwelt upon, if I had
found myself to go on in them with success. That I did by times prefer
those, by whom I was brought up, to such places and dignities, which
they seemed unto me most to desire; and that I did not put them off with
hope and expectation, that (since that they were yet but young) I would
do the same hereafter. That I ever knew Apollonius and Rusticus, and
Maximus. That I have had occasion often and effectually to consider and
meditate with myself, concerning that life which is according to nature,
what the nature and manner of it is: so that as for the gods and such
suggestions, helps and inspirations, as might be expected from them,
nothing did hinder, but that I might have begun long before to live
according to nature; or that even now that I was not yet partaker and
in present possession of that life, that I myself (in that I did not
observe those inward motions, and suggestions, yea and almost plain and
apparent instructions and admonitions of the gods,) was the only cause
of it. That my body in such a life, hath been able to hold out so long.
That I never had to do with Benedicta and Theodotus, yea and afterwards
when I fell into some fits of love, I was soon cured. That having been
often displeased with Rusticus, I never did him anything for which
afterwards I had occasion to repent. That it being so that my mother was
to die young, yet she lived with me all her latter years. That as often
as I had a purpose to help and succour any that either were poor, or
fallen into some present necessity, I never was answered by my officers
that there was not ready money enough to do it; and that I myself never
had occasion to require the like succour from any other. That I have
such a wife, so obedient, so loving, so ingenuous. That I had choice of
fit and able men, to whom I might commit the bringing up of my children.
That by dreams I have received help, as for other things, so in
particular, how I might stay my casting of blood, and cure my dizziness,
as that also that happened to thee in Cajeta, as unto Chryses when he
prayed by the seashore. And when I did first apply myself to philosophy,
that I did not fall into the hands of some sophists, or spent my time
either in reading the manifold volumes of ordinary philosophers, nor in
practising myself in the solution of arguments and fallacies, nor dwelt
upon the studies of the meteors, and other natural curiosities. All
these things without the assistance of the gods, and fortune, could not
have been.
members.english: From the gods: that I had good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good people close to me, relatives, friends, nearly all of them; and that I was not carried away into any offence against any of them, although I had a disposition from which, if it had so happened, I might well have done something of the kind; but it is the gods’ kindness that no combination of circumstances came about that would have shown me up. And that I was not brought up for longer with my grandfather’s concubine; and that I preserved the bloom of my youth; and that I was not made a man before the season, but even took some time more. That I was placed under a ruler and father who was to take all the conceit out of me and bring me to the thought that it is possible to live at a court and need neither bodyguards, nor clothes that mark one out, nor torches and statues of this sort and similar show; but that one may draw oneself in until one is very nearly a private person and not, on that account, be more lowly or more slack in what has to be done as a leader for the common good. That I happened to have such a brother, able by his character to rouse me to take care of myself, and at the same time gladdening me with his respect and affection. That my children were not born lacking in natural gifts, nor deformed in their little bodies. That I did not make more progress in rhetoric, in poetry and in the other pursuits, in which I might perhaps have been held fast, if I had felt myself getting on easily. That I was quick to set those who brought me up in the rank they seemed to me to desire, and did not put it off with the hope that, since they were still young, I would do it later. That I came to know Apollonius, Rusticus, Maximus. That I had an impression, clearly and often, of the life according to nature, of what kind of life it is, so that, as far as it rests with the gods and with the gifts, help and inspirations that come from there, nothing prevents me from living according to nature already, and that I still fall short of this is by my own fault and by not keeping to the reminders from the gods, which are all but teachings. That my body has held out so long in a life like this. That I touched neither Benedicta nor Theodotus, but that later too, when I fell into the passions of love, I recovered. That, though I was often angry with Rusticus, I did nothing more that I would have regretted. That my mother, who was to die young, still lived with me in her last years. That whenever I wanted to help someone who was poor or in need of something else, I was never told that I had no money to do it with; and that no similar need befell me myself, so as to take from another. That my wife is as she is, so compliant, so warmly affectionate, so unaffected. That I had no lack of suitable people to bring up my children. That remedies were given me through dreams, among others against spitting blood and against dizziness; and of this, at Caieta, as you will use. That, when I set my heart on philosophy, I did not fall into the hands of some sophist, nor sit down to writing, or to resolving syllogisms, or to busying myself with the things in the sky. For all these things “need the gods’ help and fortune.”
members.greek: Παρὰ τῶν θεῶν τὸ ἀγαθοὺς πάππους, ἀγαθοὺς γονέας, ἀγαθὴν ἀδελφήν, ἀγαθοὺς διδασκάλους, ἀγαθοὺς οἰκείους, συγγενεῖς, φίλους σχεδὸν ἅπαντας ἔχειν· καὶ ὅτι περὶ οὐδένα αὐτῶν προέπεσον πλημμελῆσαί τι, καίτοι διάθεσιν ἔχων τοιαύτην, ἀφ’ ἧς, εἰ ἔτυχε, κἂν ἔπραξά τι τοιοῦτο· τῶν θεῶν δὲ εὐποιία τὸ μηδεμίαν συνδρομὴν πραγμάτων γενέσθαι, ἥτις ἔμελλέ με ἐλέγξειν. καὶ τὸ μὴ ἐπὶ πλέον τραφῆναι παρὰ τῇ παλλακῇ τοῦ πάππου καὶ τὸ τὴν ὥραν διασῶσαι καὶ τὸ μὴ πρὸ ὥρας ἀνδρωθῆναι, ἀλλ’ ἔτι καὶ ἐπιλαβεῖν τοῦ χρόνου. τὸ ἄρχοντι καὶ πατρὶ ὑποταχθῆναι, ὃς ἔμελλε πάντα τὸν τῦφον ἀφαιρήσειν μου καὶ εἰς ἔννοιαν ἄξειν τοῦ ὅτι δυνατόν ἐστιν ἐν αὐλῇ βιοῦντα μήτε δορυφορήσεων χρῄζειν μήτε ἐσθήτων σημειωδῶν μήτε λαμπάδων καὶ ἀνδριάντων τοιῶνδέ τινων καὶ τοῦ ὁμοίου κόμπου, ἀλλʼ ἔξεστιν ἐγγυτάτω ἰδιώτου συστέλλειν ἑαυτὸν καὶ μὴ διὰ τοῦτο ταπεινότερον ἢ ῥᾳθυμότερον ἔχειν πρὸς τὰ ὑπὲρ τῶν κοινῶν ἡγεμονικῶς πραχθῆναι δέοντα. τὸ ἀδελφοῦ τοιούτου τυχεῖν, δυναμένου μὲν διὰ ἤθους ἐπεγεῖραί με πρὸς ἐπιμέλειαν ἐμαυτοῦ, ἅμα δὲ καὶ τιμῇ καὶ στοργῇ εὐφραίνοντός με· τὸ παιδία μοι ἀφυῆ μὴ γενέσθαι μηδὲ κατὰ τὸ σωμάτιον διάστροφα. τὸ μὴ ἐπὶ πλέον με προκόψαι ἐν ῥητορικῇ καὶ ποιητικῇ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἐπιτηδεύμασιν, ἐν οἷς ἴσως ἂν κατεσχέθην, εἰ ᾐσθόμην ἐμαυτὸν εὐόδως προιόντα. τὸ φθάσαι τοὺς τροφέας ἐν ἀξιώματι καταστῆσαι, οὗ δὴ ἐδόκουν μοι ἐπιθυμεῖν, καὶ μὴ ἀναβαλέσθαι ἐλπίδι τοῦ με, ἐπεὶ νέοι ἔτι ἦσαν, ὕστερον αὐτὸ πράξειν. τὸ γνῶναι Ἀπολλώνιον, Ῥούστικον, Μάξιμον. τὸ φαντασθῆναι περὶ τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν βίου ἐναργῶς καὶ πολλάκις οἷός τίς ἐστιν, ὥστε, ὅσον ἐπὶ τοῖς θεοῖς καὶ ταῖς ἐκεῖθεν διαδόσεσι καὶ συλλήψεσι καὶ ἐπιπνοίαις, μηδὲν κωλύειν ἤδη κατὰ φύσιν ζῆν με, ἀπολείπεσθαι δὲ ἔτι τούτου παρὰ τὴν ἐμὴν αἰτίαν καὶ παρὰ τὸ μὴ διατηρεῖν τὰς ἐκ τῶν θεῶν ὑπομνήσεις καὶ μονονουχὶ διδασκαλίας· τὸ ἀντισχεῖν μοι τὸ σῶμα ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον ἐν τοιούτῳ βίῳ· τὸ μήτε Βενεδίκτης ἅψασθαι μήτε Θεοδότου, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὕστερον ἐν ἐρωτικοῖς πάθεσι γενόμενον ὑγιᾶναι· τὸ χαλεπήναντα πολλάκις Ῥουστίκῳ μηδὲν πλέον πρᾶξαι, ἐφ’ ᾧ ἂν μετέγνων· τὸ μέλλουσαν νέαν τελευτᾶν τὴν τεκοῦσαν ὅμως οἰκῆσαι μετ’ ἐμοῦ τὰ τελευταῖα ἔτη. τὸ ὁσάκις ἐβουλήθην ἐπικουρῆσαί τινι πενομένῳ ἢ εἰς ἄλλο τι χρῄζοντι, μηδέποτε ἀκοῦσαί με, ὅτι οὐκ ἔστι μοι χρήματα, ὅθεν γένηται, καὶ τὸ αὐτῷ ἐμοὶ χρείαν ὁμοίαν, ὡς παρ’ ἑτέρου μεταλαβεῖν, μὴ συμπεσεῖν· τὸ τὴν γυναῖκα τοιαύτην εἶναι, οὑτωσὶ μὲν πειθήνιον, οὕτω δὲ φιλόστοργον, οὕτω δὲ ἀφελῆ· τὸ ἐπιτηδείων τροφέων εἰς τὰ παιδία εὐπορῆσαι. τὸ δι’ ὀνειράτων βοηθήματα δοθῆναι ἄλλα τε καὶ ὡς μὴ πτύειν αἷμα καὶ μὴ ἰλιγγιᾶν, καὶ τούτου ἐν Καιήτῃ ὥσπερ χρήσῃ· τὸ ὅπως ἐπεθύμησα φιλοσοφίας, μὴ ἐμπεσεῖν εἴς τινα σοφιστὴν μηδὲ ἀποκαθίσαι ἐπὶ τὸ συγγράφειν ἢ συλλογισμοὺς ἀναλύειν ἢ περὶ τὰ μετεωρολογικὰ καταγίνεσθαι. πάντα γὰρ ταῦτα ʽθεῶν βοηθῶν καὶ τύχης δεῖται.ʼ

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay those of the 1634 edition. In modern editions 2.2 is 2.5, 6.27 is 6.29 with the first part of 6.30, 6.28 is the rest of 6.30, 3.5 is the first part of 3.5, 5.25 is 5.31, 4.26 is 4.31 and 1.14 is 1.17; 10.8 is the same.

Reads the qualities of 2.2, the list of 6.27 and the names of 10.8 as one short list. The first claim names only the qualities that two of the three lists have, and says “among them”; three of 10.8’s own names (clear-minded, like-minded, high-minded) stand in an item of their own with their meanings. Calling the qualities of 2.2 and 6.27 “names” is 10.8’s word, extended by the editor.

Leaves the second way out of 10.8 out of the first-person text. After “go away to some corner where you will prevail” Marcus adds “or even leave life altogether, not in anger, but simply, freely and modestly”. The article does not write “I leave life” as a rule of life; the words stay in the passage for the reader to see.

Reads the last sentence of 10.8 as saying what the gods want (the fig tree doing a fig tree’s work, the human being a human being’s). The translators note that it can also depend on “remember”, as a statement of what makes each thing what it is.

Uses 1.14, a list of thanks to the gods, only where it states something Marcus holds or admits: no offence against those close to him, a court without show, falling short by his own fault. The rest of its thanks are not turned into rules.

Words the third part of the statement after 3.5 (“nor any human being as witness”). 10.8 backs its sense, not its words: it says “without craving to have others call you by them” and has neither “need” nor “witness”.
articles.limit: The article leans on 10.8, which feeds four of the six claims, and three of its joins are loose: “without pretence” rests partly on the English of 6.27, the claim on show and witness shares only the frame “need neither”, and the claim on falling short shares the word “fall” only in the English. Much of it is said in other articles: Article 5 has the human being’s own work, Article 3 accepting what is allotted, Articles 10 and 17 doing each thing as if it were the last (Article 10 on the same Ep. 101.7, Article 17 also without pretence), and Article 11 the good life in very few things, no show and no witness (on the same Ep. 113.32) and coming back after a failure. What this section adds is a short list of names I have given myself, kept without wanting others to call me by them, and each act done as a Roman and a man who waits for the signal to withdraw and wants a good conscience at the last hour.

articles.title: Living now as one about to die

statement.t: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere, so I live the present justly, as one already at the end, and wait for death cheerfully.

parts.words: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere
I live the present justly
as one already at the end
wait for death cheerfully

inferences.why: No passage says that I live justly because I shall soon be gone; 4.21 only sets “life is short” beside turning the present to profit.

statement.kind: A ground, the conduct that answers it, and the stance toward the end
statement.form: Claim 1 is the ground: I shall soon be gone and I live only the present. Claims 2 and 3 are the conduct: living as one already at the end, and what is enough meanwhile. Claim 4 is the stance toward death itself; claim 5 is the exercise that keeps the ground in view, and claim 6 says what failing would be.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, living as one already at the end gains three witnesses, waiting for death gains three, and what is enough and the view from above gain one each. Practice gains a nightly exercise and the reminder that a cheerful death is long prepared; When it breaks gains a name for the failure, a life always postponed. He limits leaving the past behind, and he challenges the claim that being remembered is of no account. His allowance for ending one’s own life, which differs from waiting for the natural end, is left out of this article.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a daily exercise: each night I say “I have lived”, and every morning after that is a bonus. He limits one claim, on leaving the past behind, and disagrees with another, on being remembered. A third difference is left out of this article: he allows a wise man to end his own life (Ep. 70.5), where claim 4 waits for the natural end.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: let us so order our minds as if we had come to the very end
piece.follows: I should set my mind in order as if I had already reached the end of my life.
piece.context: Letter 101 follows the sudden death of Cornelius Senecio amid his plans: a limit is fixed for each of us and none knows how near it is. “The very end” is that limit.
gives: as someone already at the end of life

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: he has won his honourable discharge and is free,—who still lives after his life has been completed
piece.follows: The person who goes on living after his life is complete has his discharge and is free.
piece.context: Seneca’s prayer for Lucilius: a mind at rest that has no need of added years. A “completed” life is one that already has what is truly good, however long it then lasts.
gives: I live what is left
as someone already at the end of life

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: The present letter is written to you with this in mind,—as if death were about to call me away in the very act of writing.
piece.follows: Seneca writes this letter as if death might call him away while he is writing it.
piece.context: Seneca, now old, has just said that he tries to live every day as a complete life and to regard it as possibly his last. “This” is that thought.
gives: knowing that I may leave life at this very moment

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: To have lived long enough depends neither upon our years nor upon our days, but upon our minds.
piece.follows: Whether I have lived long enough is settled by my mind, not by the number of my years or days.
piece.context: The end of Letter 61, on being ready to die: life is well enough furnished, but we are greedy and always find something lacking in it.
gives: how long I do it does not matter

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: she but resolves that which she has compounded, and compounds again that which she has resolved
piece.follows: Nature only takes apart what she put together, and puts together again what she took apart.
piece.context: From the letter on the old and dying Bassus: death’s rule is fixed and equal for everyone. “She” is Nature, whose law for us is the same as her own.
gives: a dissolving
it is according to nature

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: I have lived, my dear friend Lucilius, long enough. I have had my fill; I await death.
piece.follows: Seneca says he has lived long enough, has had his fill, and now awaits death.
piece.context: The last words of Letter 61, written in old age, where Seneca has said that dying well means dying gladly and that one should reflect on one’s end without sadness.
gives: I wait for it

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: And what is death? It is either the end, or a process of change.
piece.follows: Death is one of two things: the end, or a change into another state.
piece.context: The close of Letter 65: the soul should rule the body as God rules matter, so we should be brave. Seneca goes on to say he fears neither ceasing to exist nor changing state.
gives: whether it is an extinguishing or a move elsewhere

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: you will indeed look down from above upon all that men regard as most lofty
piece.follows: Whoever reaches the height of wisdom looks down from above on everything people consider most lofty.
piece.context: The end of Letter 84: what is conspicuous in human affairs is really petty. The height is wisdom once reached, a peak above Fortune; it is a place arrived at, not an exercise.
gives: I look down on human affairs as if from high above
The things people prize

items.label: practice
items.t: I order each day as if it completed my life. I go to sleep gladly, saying “I have lived”; then every morning I wake to is a bonus.
items.why: 7.31 tells me to live what is left as a surplus and gives no way of doing it day by day. Seneca gives one: close each day as a finished life, so that the next day comes as a bonus.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: every day ought to be regulated as if it closed the series, as if it rounded out and completed our existence
support.follows: Each day should be ordered as if it were the last of the series and completed my life.
support.context: Letter 12 is on old age. Seneca goes on to Pacuvius, who held his own funeral feast every evening. “The series” is the series of one’s days.
gives: I order each day as if it completed my life

support.author: seneca
support.quote: let us go to our sleep with joy and gladness; let us say: I have lived; the course which Fortune set for me Is finished.
support.follows: At bedtime I should say, gladly, that I have lived and that the course Fortune set me is finished.
support.context: Pacuvius had himself carried from dinner to bed each night as if to burial. Seneca says to do from a good motive what he did from a bad one; the words to say are a line of verse.
gives: I go to sleep gladly, saying “I have lived”

support.author: seneca
support.quote: When a man has said: “I have lived!”, every morning he arises he receives a bonus.
support.follows: Whoever has said “I have lived” receives each new morning as a bonus.
support.context: The close of Seneca’s point in Letter 12 about ending each day as a finished life: if God adds another day, it is welcomed gladly. The “bonus” is that added day.
gives: every morning I wake to is a bonus

items.label: practice
items.t: Leaving life calmly when the hour comes is something I can learn only by long practice. I shall welcome death cheerfully when it comes only if I have long since composed myself for it.
items.why: Marcus says to wait for death cheerfully and gives the reasons. He does not say here that this has to be learned, or how long it takes. Seneca says it needs long practice.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: This is a great accomplishment, Lucilius, and one which needs long practice to learn,—to depart calmly when the inevitable hour arrives.
support.follows: Departing calmly at the inevitable hour is a great thing, and it takes long practice to learn.
support.context: Seneca describes his old friend Bassus, who is dying of age and looks on his own end with courage. “This” is what Bassus is doing: facing his death calmly.
gives: Leaving life calmly when the hour comes is something I can learn only by long practice

support.author: seneca
support.quote: when death comes to meet him, no one welcomes it cheerfully, except the man who has long since composed himself for death
support.follows: Only someone long prepared for death welcomes it cheerfully when it comes.
support.context: From the letter on the dying Bassus. Seneca contrasts men who rush at death in a fit of rage with those who meet it calmly; “him” is anyone to whom death comes unsought.
gives: I shall welcome death cheerfully when it comes only if I have long since composed myself for it

items.label: breaks
items.t: The great flaw is a life that is never finished, with part of it always put off. Some people begin to live only when it is time to stop, and some stop before they have begun. I postpone nothing and settle life’s account every day.
items.why: 12.1 names the fear of never beginning to live according to nature and does not say how that comes about. Seneca says how: by postponing, so that the life is always unfinished. He also gives the way back, which is to settle the account daily.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The greatest flaw in life is that it is always imperfect, and that a certain part of it is postponed.
support.follows: The worst fault in a life is that it is never complete, because part of it is always put off.
support.context: Letter 101 follows the sudden death of Cornelius Senecio in the middle of his plans. “Imperfect” here means unfinished: part of the life is left for later.
gives: The great flaw is a life that is never finished, with part of it always put off

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Some men, indeed, only begin to live when it is time for them to leave off living. And if this seems surprising to you, I shall add that which will surprise you still more: Some men have left off living before they have begun.
support.follows: Some people start living only when it is time to stop, and some stop living before they have started.
support.context: Seneca comments on Epicurus’s saying that they live ill who are always beginning to live: such a life is always incomplete, and cannot be ready for death.
gives: Some people begin to live only when it is time to stop, and some stop before they have begun

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Let us postpone nothing. Let us balance life’s account every day.
support.follows: I should put nothing off and settle the account of my life each day.
support.context: From Letter 101: a limit is fixed for each of us and no one knows how near it is. To “balance life’s account” is to leave nothing of one’s life owing at the end of the day.
gives: I postpone nothing and settle life’s account every day

items.t: Seneca does not hold that being remembered is of no account. He agrees that time will roll over everyone and that the dead do not feel what posterity says, but he promises Lucilius a name among later generations (Ep. 21.5) and tells him to have regard to the thousands of years to come (Ep. 79.17). He is not consistent: his good man, told that his deed will soon be forgotten, answers that this lies outside his task (Ep. 76.29).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: some few great men will raise their heads above it, and, though destined at the last to depart into the same realms of silence, will battle against oblivion and maintain their ground for long
support.follows: Time covers everyone, but a few great men hold out against oblivion for a long while before they too fall silent.
support.context: Seneca tells Lucilius that his name will last through these letters, as Epicurus’s letters kept the name of Idomeneus alive. “It” is the deep flood of time that rolls over us.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I shall find favour among later generations; I can take with me names that will endure as long as mine.
support.follows: Seneca expects to be read by later generations and to make the names he writes down last as long as his own.
support.context: Seneca promises Lucilius what Epicurus promised his friend Idomeneus: a name preserved by being written into letters that later generations will read.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Many thousands of years and many thousands of peoples will come after you; it is to these that you should have regard.
support.follows: I should have regard to the many peoples and years that come after me, not only to my own generation.
support.context: On virtue that goes unrecognised in its own time, as with Epicurus: a day will reveal it. “These” are the later peoples, who will judge without malice or favour.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: We ourselves, indeed, shall not be affected by the talk of posterity; nevertheless, posterity will cherish and celebrate us even though we are not conscious thereof.
support.follows: The dead are not touched by what posterity says, yet posterity will honour them all the same.
support.context: The close of Seneca’s argument in Letter 79 that virtue is never lost to view. “We” are those who followed virtue without recognition in their own lifetime.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: you may say: “Your deed will speedily be forgotten,” or “Your fellow-citizens will offer you scant thanks.” He will answer: “All these matters lie outside my task. My thoughts are on the deed itself.
support.follows: Told that his deed will soon be forgotten, the good man answers that this is outside his task and that he thinks only of the deed.
support.context: Seneca argues that the honourable is the only good. “He” is the good man who goes to his death rightly and dutifully, with no reward and no joy in prospect.

items.t: Seneca does not leave all the past behind. Consoling a mourner, he calls the past ours and the most secure thing we have, and says that people narrow their enjoyments if they take pleasure only in the present (Ep. 99.4–5). This limits the claim and does not overturn it: he means good things once had, and elsewhere he says that we torment ourselves over what is past and that the present alone makes no one wretched (Ep. 5.9).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The past is ours, and there is nothing more secure for us than that which has been.
support.follows: The past belongs to us, and nothing we have is safer than what has already been.
support.context: A letter of consolation quoted in Letter 99: grief forgets how much was gained. “The past” is the years already had with the one who has died.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: People set a narrow limit to their enjoyments if they take pleasure only in the present; both the future and the past serve for our delight
support.follows: Whoever takes pleasure only in the present narrows his enjoyment; the past and the future give delight as well.
support.context: Seneca, consoling a mourner, says we are ungrateful for past gains because we hope for the future. The delight the past gives is memory, which is certain.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The present alone can make no man wretched.
support.follows: Nothing in the present moment alone makes a person wretched.
support.context: The close of Letter 5: animals fear only the danger they see, while people are tormented by memory of the past and by anticipation of the future.

amend.t: ; each night I say “I have lived”, and every morning after that is a bonus
; but what has been is still mine, and nothing I have is more secure
; yet a few names hold out long against oblivion, and I should have regard to the thousands of years after me

passages.title: On the futility of planning ahead
passages.text: Yet what is more foolish than to wonder that something which may happen every day has happened on any one day? There is indeed a limit fixed for us, just where the remorseless law of Fate has fixed it; but none of us knows how near he is to this limit. Therefore, let us so order our minds as if we had come to the very end. Let us postpone nothing. Let us balance life’s account every day.
