being mentioned upon the stage were merrily, and with great applause of
the multitude, scoffed at with this jest, that they that possessed them
had not in all the world of their own, (such was their affluence and
plenty) so much as a place where to avoid their excrements. Whether, I
say, those ought not also in very deed to be much respected, and
esteemed of, as the only things that are truly good.
members.english: What kind of things they are that seem good to most people, you can gather from this as well. For if a person had in mind certain things that truly are good, such as wisdom, self-control, justice, courage, then with these in mind first they could not listen to the words “because of the good things”, for it will not fit. But a person who has first in mind the things that appear good to most people will listen, and will readily accept what the comic poet said as a fitting thing to add. So even most people have an impression of the difference. For otherwise this line would not jar and be refused in the one case, while when it is said of wealth and of the pieces of good luck that make for luxury or reputation we accept it as aptly and wittily said. Go on, then, and ask whether one should honour and judge to be good the kind of things which, when they have first been brought to mind, can fittingly be followed by the line that their owner, because of the plenty, “has nowhere to shit”.
members.greek: Ὁποῖά τινά ἐστι τὰ τοῖς πολλοῖς δοκοῦντα ἀγαθά, κἂν ἐντεῦθεν λάβοις. εἰ γάρ τις ἐπινοήσειεν ὑπάρχοντά τινα ὡς ἀληθῶς ἀγαθά, οἷον φρόνησιν, σωφροσύνην, δικαιοσύνην, ἀνδρείαν, οὐκ ἂν ταῦτα προεπινοήσας ἐπακοῦσαι δυνηθείη τό· ʽὑπὸ τῶν ἀγαθῶνʼ, οὐ γὰρ ἐφαρμόσει. τὰ δέ γε τοῖς πολλοῖς φαινόμενα ἀγαθὰ προεπινοήσας τις ἐπακούσεται καὶ ῥᾳδίως δέξεται ὡς οἰκείως ἐπιλεγόμενον τὸ ὑπὸ τοῦ κωμικοῦ εἰρημένον. οὕτως καὶ οἱ πολλοὶ φαντάζονται τὴν διαφοράν· οὐ γὰρ ἂν τοῦτο μὲν οὐ προσέκοπτε καὶ ἀπηξιοῦτο, τὸ δὲ ἐπὶ τοῦ πλούτου καὶ τῶν πρὸς τρυφὴν ἢ δόξαν εὐκληρημάτων παρεδεχόμεθα ὡς ἱκνουμένως καὶ ἀστείως εἰρημένον. πρόιθι οὖν καὶ ἐρώτα, εἰ τιμητέον καὶ ἀγαθὰ ὑποληπτέον τὰ τοιαῦτα, ὧν προεπινοηθέντων οἰκείως ἂν ἐπιφέροιτο τὸ τὸν κεκτημένον αὐτὰ ὑπὸ τῆς εὐπορίας ʽοὐκ ἔχειν ὅποι χέσῃʼ.

members.text:
How clearly doth it appear unto thee, that no other course of thy
life could fit a true philosopher's practice better, than this very
course, that thou art now already in?
members.english: How plainly it comes home that there is no other situation in life so suited to philosophy as this one in which you now happen to be.
members.greek: Πῶς ἐναργὲς προσπίπτει τὸ μὴ εἶναι ἄλλην βίου ὑπόθεσιν εἰς τὸ φιλοσοφεῖν οὕτως ἐπιτήδειον ὡς ταύτην, ἐν ᾗ νῦν ὢν τυγχάνεις.

members.text:
As physicians and chirurgeons have always their instruments ready
at hand for all sudden cures; so have thou always thy dogmata in a
readiness for the knowledge of things, both divine and human: and
whatsoever thou dost, even in the smallest things that thou dost, thou
must ever remember that mutual relation, and connection that is between
these two things divine, and things human. For without relation unto
God, thou shalt never speed in any worldly actions; nor on the other
side in any divine, without some respect had to things human.
members.english: As doctors always have their instruments and blades at hand for emergency treatments, so have your principles ready for knowing things divine and human, and for doing everything, even the smallest thing, as one who remembers the bond that ties the two to each other. For you will not do any human thing well without referring it at the same time to the divine, nor the other way round.
members.greek: Ὥσπερ οἱ ἰατροὶ ἀεὶ τὰ ὄργανα καὶ σιδήρια πρόχειρα ἔχουσι πρὸς τὰ αἰφνίδια τῶν θεραπευμάτων, οὕτω τὰ δόγματα σὺ ἕτοιμα ἔχε πρὸς τὸ τὰ θεῖα καὶ ἀνθρώπινα εἰδέναι, καὶ πᾶν καὶ τὸ μικρότατον οὕτω ποιεῖν ὡς τῆς ἀμφοτέρων πρὸς ἄλληλα συνδέσεως μεμνημένον. οὔτε γὰρ ἀνθρώπινόν τι ἄνευ τῆς ἐπὶ τὰ θεῖα συναναφορᾶς εὖ πράξεις οὔτ’ ἔμπαλιν.

members.why: Says that what moves a person is hidden inside and that the body is its tool. Nothing in it is about principles, their use or falling short; it belongs with the passages on the ruling part and the body.
members.text:
Remember, that that which sets a man at work, and hath power
over the affections to draw them either one way, or the other way, is
not any external thing properly, but that which is hidden within every
man's dogmata, and opinions: That, that is rhetoric; that is life; that
(to speak true) is man himself. As for thy body, which as a vessel, or
a case, compasseth thee about, and the many and curious instruments
that it hath annexed unto it, let them not trouble thy thoughts. For
of themselves they are but as a carpenter's axe, but that they are born
with us, and naturally sticking unto us. But otherwise, without the
inward cause that hath power to move them, and to restrain them, those
parts are of themselves of no more use unto us, than the shuttle is
of itself to the weaver, or the pen to the writer, or the whip to the
coachman.
members.english: Remember that what pulls the strings is that thing hidden inside. That is oratory, that is life, that, if one must say it, is the human being. Never picture along with it the vessel-like thing that surrounds it and these little tools moulded around it. For they are like a carpenter’s axe, differing only in being grown on. For without the cause that moves them and holds them in check these parts are in fact of no more use than the weaver’s shuttle, the writer’s pen and the charioteer’s little whip.
members.greek: Μέμνησο ὅτι τὸ νευροσπαστοῦν ἐστιν ἐκεῖνο τὸ ἔνδον ἐγκεκρυμμένον· ἐκεῖνο ῥητορεία, ἐκεῖνο ζωή, ἐκεῖνο, εἰ δεῖ εἰπεῖν, ἄνθρωπος. μηδέποτε συμπεριφαντάζου τὸ περικείμενον ἀγγειῶδες καὶ τὰ ὀργάνια ταῦτα τὰ περιπεπλασμένα· ὅμοια γάρ ἐστι σκεπάρνῳ, μόνον διαφέροντα, καθότι προσφυῆ ἐστιν. ἐπεί τοι οὐ μᾶλλόν τι τούτων ὄφελός ἐστι τῶν μορίων χωρὶς τῆς κινούσης καὶ ἰσχούσης αὐτὰ αἰτίας, ἢ τῆς κερκίδος τῇ ὑφαντρίᾳ καὶ τοῦ καλάμου τῷ γράφοντι καὶ τοῦ μαστιγίου τῷ ἡνιόχῳ.

members.text:
Do not ever conceive anything impossible to man, which by thee
cannot, or not without much difficulty be effected; but whatsoever in
general thou canst Conceive possible and proper unto any man, think that
very possible unto thee also.
members.english: Do not, if something is hard for you yourself to carry out, judge it impossible for a human being; but if something is possible for a human being and proper to them, consider it within your own reach too.
members.greek: Μή, εἴ τι αὐτῷ σοὶ δυσκαταπόνητον, τοῦτο ἀνθρώπῳ ἀδύνατον ὑπολαμβάνειν, ἀλλ’ εἴ τι ἀνθρώπῳ δυνατὸν καὶ οἰκεῖον, τοῦτο καὶ σεαυτῷ ἐφικτὸν νόμιζε.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of the 1634 edition. In modern editions 5.9 is 5.9 with the first part of 5.10, 12.6 is 12.7 to 12.9, 6.11 is 6.13, 9.28 is 9.29, 10.32 is 10.31, 7.38 is 7.67, 11.4 is 11.4 and 11.5, 11.6 is 11.7, 3.14 is 3.13 and 6.18 is 6.19; 8.1, 10.9, 3.11 and 10.11 keep their numbers.

Joins in claim 1 what philosophy asks with its not needing to be seen, because 5.9, 8.1, 9.28 and 7.38 each say both within a few lines. “It does not need to be seen” is the editor’s summary of 7.38 and 9.28, not words of either.

Reads “situation” (8.1, 11.6) and “subject” (10.32) as one thing in claim 2, because the Greek has the same word in all three. The translators note that its sense differs: in 8.1 and 11.6 it is the footing of a life, in 10.32 a subject set before one to work on. The contrast between a situation that fights against a philosopher’s reputation and one that suits philosophy is drawn by the editor, and no passage says what the situation is.
Uses 9.28 for my own progress although it is about public affairs and about other people, whose principles no one will change.
Puts the second paragraph of 5.9 under doubt. It says that every assent can shift and then turns to the objects; that this is what holds when I doubt is the editor’s reading.
articles.limit: The article leans on two passages: 8.1 feeds four of the five claims, and 5.9 feeds two claims and two said-once items. Much of it is said elsewhere: claim 1 comes near Article 2, claim 4 (doing my work is living by my nature) and Article 9, claims 2 and 3 (a few things are enough; I need no show and no witness); claim 2 near Article 8, claim 4 (what comes to hand is material for virtue) and Article 25, claim 1 (philosophy makes the court bearable), and Seneca’s Ep. 53.9, 62.1 and 72.3 limit claim 2 here and are marked as a challenge to Article 25’s claim 1; claim 3 near Article 8, claim 5 and Article 12’s said-once 4.3f (rules and truths kept ready), and Articles 23 and 24 (living as a craft); claim 4 is the exercise of Article 20, claims 1 and 2, and its 12.6 quote that of Article 4, claim 4; claim 5 and the said-once 5.9c come near Article 9, claim 6 and Article 25, claims 1 and 3 (I go back quickly, to philosophy as to a mother), and Seneca’s limit on claim 5 near Article 1’s warning that return grows harder. What this section adds is the rule for falling short of philosophy: it asks nothing beyond what my nature asks, failing is no reason to give up, a part is enough, and the principles I come back to are kept at hand.

articles.title: The retreat within

statement.t: At any hour I can retreat into myself, and I keep to my own mind rather than to what others say and do.

parts.words: At any hour I can retreat into myself
I keep to my own mind
rather than to what others say and do

statement.kind: A place, how I keep to it, and the way back
statement.form: Claims 1 and 4 say where the retreat is and why the mind is mine. Claims 2, 5 and 6 say how I keep to it: away from other people’s doings and praise, in the present, and with an aim when I act. Claim 3 says what being disturbed is and how it stops.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the retreat of claim 1 gains a second author for its hour and its place, the praise of claim 2 and the target of claim 6 gain one each; the practice gains a way to keep my mind within amid noise, and what failing looks like gains two signs: travelling to escape my own gloom, and starting at every sound. He sets two limits on the retreat: one goes into the statement (it is right only for someone already good), and one into claim 1 (a mind not yet sound is harmed by some places).
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands with a condition: retreating into myself is right only if I am already good, calm and self-controlled; otherwise, alone, I am too close to a rascal.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: the mere place avails little for this purpose, unless the mind is fully master of itself, and can, at its pleasure, find seclusion even in the midst of business
piece.follows: A place does little for the mind unless the mind can find seclusion in itself whenever it wishes, even amid business.
piece.context: Letter 104, written from Seneca’s country house where his health has mended: the place itself does little for peace of mind; the mind must find its own seclusion.
gives: at any hour
I can retreat into myself

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: The place where one lives, however, can contribute little towards tranquillity; it is the mind which must make everything agreeable to itself.
piece.follows: Where I live does little for my calm; my mind has to make every place agreeable to itself.
piece.context: Letter 55: Seneca passes the seaside villa where the rich Vatia hid in leisure, and says the villa could not give calm; only the mind can.
gives: I do not need a country place, a seashore or a mountain

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Lay these words to heart, Lucilius, that you may scorn the pleasure which comes from the applause of the majority.
piece.follows: I should scorn the pleasure that comes from the applause of the majority.
piece.context: End of Letter 7, on avoiding crowds. “These words” are three sayings he has just quoted, each content with an audience of one or none.
gives: I set no store by the praise of the many

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Our plans miscarry because they have no aim. When a man does not know what harbour he is making for, no wind is the right wind.
piece.follows: Plans go wrong when they have no aim; if I do not know where I am heading, no wind helps me.
piece.context: Letter 71, on the supreme good: everything we do should be set by one chief purpose of life, as an archer must know what he is trying to hit.
gives: I give my impulses a target

items.label: breaks
items.t: When I am troubled, going somewhere else does not help, because I always take myself with me. What I need is a change of soul, not a change of climate.
items.why: Marcus says the place where I am is just like a country place, but not what happens to someone who keeps going elsewhere. Seneca says it: the trouble travels with me, and only a change in me ends it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Why do you wonder that globe-trotting does not help you, seeing that you always take yourself with you?
support.follows: Travelling cannot help me, because I take myself wherever I go.
support.context: Letter 28, on travel as a cure for discontent: Seneca repeats Socrates’s answer to a man who complained that his travels had not cured his gloom.
gives: going somewhere else does not help, because I always take myself with me

support.author: seneca
support.quote: You need a change of soul rather than a change of climate.
support.follows: What a gloomy mind needs is a change in itself, not a change of country.
support.context: Opening of Letter 28: Lucilius has travelled far and changed scene often, and still cannot shake off the gloom and heaviness of his mind.
gives: What I need is a change of soul, not a change of climate

items.label: practice
items.t: When there is noise all around me, I make my mind concentrate and keep it from straying to things outside itself. Outside may be bedlam, so long as there is no disturbance within: a quiet neighbourhood is no use if my feelings are in an uproar.
items.why: 4.3 says no place is quieter than my own soul, but gives no exercise for a noisy place. Seneca, lodging over a bath house, trains himself to keep his mind on its work through the noise.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: For I force my mind to concentrate, and keep it from straying to things outside itself; all outdoors may be bedlam, provided that there is no disturbance within
support.follows: Seneca makes his mind concentrate and keeps it on itself; the noise outside does not matter if nothing is in turmoil within.
support.context: Letter 56: Seneca lodges over a public bath and lists its noises. Here he says how he studies through them by holding his mind to itself.
gives: I make my mind concentrate and keep it from straying to things outside itself
Outside may be bedlam, so long as there is no disturbance within

support.author: seneca
support.quote: For of what benefit is a quiet neighbourhood, if our emotions are in an uproar?
support.follows: A quiet place is no use to someone whose feelings are in an uproar.
support.context: Letter 56, after listing the noises of the bath house below his lodgings: the uproar that matters is fear and desire fighting within, not the noise outside.
gives: a quiet neighbourhood is no use if my feelings are in an uproar

items.label: breaks
items.t: If a word or a chance sound makes me start, my mind has not yet withdrawn into itself. I know I am at peace with myself when no noise reaches me and no word, of flattery or of threat, shakes me out of myself.
items.why: Marcus tells me to retreat into myself and does not say how I can tell whether I have. Seneca gives the sign of failing and the sign of success.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The mind which starts at words or at chance sounds is unstable and has not yet withdrawn into itself
support.follows: A mind that starts at words or chance sounds is unsteady and has not yet withdrawn into itself.
support.context: Letter 56, on quiet and study: Seneca says that a mind shaken by noises still holds fear within it, and so has not truly retired.
gives: If a word or a chance sound makes me start, my mind has not yet withdrawn into itself

support.author: seneca
support.quote: You may therefore be sure that you are at peace with yourself, when no noise reaches you, when no word shakes you out of yourself, whether it be of flattery or of threat
support.follows: I am at peace with myself when no noise reaches me and no flattering or threatening word shakes me out of myself.
support.context: Letter 56: after Virgil’s hero who fears every sound for the load he carries, Seneca gives the test of a mind that has really withdrawn into itself.
gives: I know I am at peace with myself when no noise reaches me and no word, of flattery or of threat, shakes me out of myself

items.t: Seneca allows the retreat into oneself only to someone already good, calm and self-controlled. Until then he gives the opposite advice: almost any company is better than one’s own, for alone one is too close to a rascal. Marcus comes near this in 4.3, where the ease within belongs above all to someone with the right things within; Seneca makes it a condition and says what to do before it is met. This limits the claim and does not contradict it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Yes, provided that you are a good, tranquil, and self-restrained man; otherwise, you had better withdraw into a crowd in order to get away from your self. Alone, you are too close to a rascal.
support.follows: Withdrawing into myself is right only if I am good, calm and self-controlled; otherwise I am better off in company, away from myself.
support.context: End of Letter 25: Seneca grants Epicurus’s saying “withdraw into yourself most of all when you are forced to be in a crowd”, and here sets its condition.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: while it is not yet safe to withdraw into solitude, seek out certain individuals; for everyone is better off in the company of somebody or other,—no matter who,—than in his own company alone.
support.follows: Until it is safe to be alone, I should seek out some people, since almost any company is better than my own.
support.context: Letter 25, on reforming oneself: Lucilius is still making himself into someone in whose company he would not dare to do wrong.

items.t: Seneca agrees that the person matters more than the place, but not that every place is alike. A mind that is recovering but not yet sound is harmed by some places; and he himself, having tested himself against the noise of a bath house, decides that it is simpler to move. Marcus says the place where I am is just like a country place; Seneca keeps that for a mind already sound, and moves when he can. This limits the claim and does not contradict it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: For just as pestilential places assail even the strongest constitution, so there are some places which are also unwholesome for a healthy mind which is not yet quite sound, though recovering from its ailment.
support.follows: Some places harm a mind that is recovering but not yet quite sound, as unhealthy places harm even a strong body.
support.context: Letter 28, on travel: Seneca has said one can live quietly even in the Forum if one must, but that he would keep far from it if he could choose.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: “What then?” you say, “is it not sometimes a simpler matter just to avoid the uproar?” I admit this. Accordingly, I shall change from my present quarters.
support.follows: It is sometimes simpler just to avoid the noise, and Seneca will move from his lodgings.
support.context: End of Letter 56: Seneca has shown he can study over the noise of a bath house; he says he only wanted to test himself, and will now move.

amend.t: ; the retreat is right only if I am good, calm and self-controlled, for otherwise, alone, I am too close to a rascal
; yet some places harm a mind not yet sound, and it is sometimes simpler just to move away from a noisy place

passages.title: On care of health and peace of mind
passages.text: But the mere place avails little for this purpose, unless the mind is fully master of itself, and can, at its pleasure, find seclusion even in the midst of business; the man, however, who is always selecting resorts and hunting for leisure, will find something to distract his mind in every place. Socrates is reported to have replied, when a certain person complained of having received no benefit from his travels: “It serves you right! You travelled in your own company!”

passages.title: On vatia’s villa
passages.text: The place where one lives, however, can contribute little towards tranquillity; it is the mind which must make everything agreeable to itself. I have seen men despondent in a gay and lovely villa, and I have seen them to all appearance full of business in the midst of a solitude. For this reason you should not refuse to believe that your life is well-placed merely because you are not now in Campania. But why are you not there? Just let your thoughts travel, even to this place.

passages.title: On crowds
passages.text: Lay these words to heart, Lucilius, that you may scorn the pleasure which comes from the applause of the majority. Many men praise you; but have you any reason for being pleased with yourself, if you are a person whom the many can understand? Your good qualities should face inwards. Farewell.

passages.title: On the supreme good
passages.text: The archer must know what he is seeking to hit; then he must aim and control the weapon by his skill. Our plans miscarry because they have no aim. When a man does not know what harbour he is making for, no wind is the right wind. Chance must necessarily have great influence over our lives, because we live by chance.

passages.title: On travel as a cure for discontent
passages.text: Socrates made the same remark to one who complained; he said: “Why do you wonder that globe-trotting does not help you, seeing that you always take yourself with you? The reason which set you wandering is ever at your heels.” What pleasure is there in seeing new lands? Or in surveying cities and spots of interest? All your bustle is useless. Do you ask why such flight does not help you? It is because you flee along with yourself. You must lay aside the burdens of the mind; until you do this, no place will satisfy you.

passages.title: On travel as a cure for discontent
passages.text: Do you suppose that you alone have had this experience? Are you surprised, as if it were a novelty, that after such long travel and so many changes of scene you have not been able to shake off the gloom and heaviness of your mind? You need a change of soul rather than a change of climate. Though you may cross vast spaces of sea, and though, as our Vergil remarks, Lands and cities are left astern, your faults will follow you whithersoever you travel.

passages.title: On quiet and study
passages.text: Furthermore, an intermittent noise upsets me more than a steady one. But by this time I have toughened my nerves against all that sort of thing, so that I can endure even a boatswain marking the time in high-pitched tones for his crew. For I force my mind to concentrate, and keep it from straying to things outside itself; all outdoors may be bedlam, provided that there is no disturbance within, provided that fear is not wrangling with desire in my breast, provided that meanness and lavishness are not at odds, one harassing the other. For of what benefit is a quiet neighbourhood, if our emotions are in an uproar?

passages.title: On quiet and study
passages.text: The mind which starts at words or at chance sounds is unstable and has not yet withdrawn into itself; it contains within itself an element of anxiety and rooted fear, and this makes one a prey to care, as our Vergil says: I, whom of yore no dart could cause to flee, Nor Greeks, with crowded lines of infantry. Now shake at every sound, and fear the air, Both for my child and for the load I bear.

passages.title: On quiet and study
passages.text: Select anyone you please from among your favourites of Fortune, trailing their many responsibilities, carrying their many burdens, and you will behold a picture of Vergil’s hero, “fearing both for his child and for the load he bears.” You may therefore be sure that you are at peace with yourself, when no noise reaches you, when no word shakes you out of yourself, whether it be of flattery or of threat, or merely an empty sound buzzing about you with unmeaning din.

passages.title: On reformation
passages.text: You ought to make yourself of a different stamp from the multitude. Therefore, while it is not yet safe to withdraw into solitude, seek out certain individuals; for everyone is better off in the company of somebody or other,—no matter who,—than in his own company alone. “The time when you should most of all withdraw into yourself is when you are forced to be in a crowd.” Yes, provided that you are a good, tranquil, and self-restrained man; otherwise, you had better withdraw into a crowd in order to get away from your self. Alone, you are too close to a rascal. Farewell.

passages.title: On travel as a cure for discontent
passages.text: Can there be any spot so full of confusion as the Forum? Yet you can live quietly even there, if necessary. Of course, if one were allowed to make one’s own arrangements, I should flee far from the very sight and neighbourhood of the Forum. For just as pestilential places assail even the strongest constitution, so there are some places which are also unwholesome for a healthy mind which is not yet quite sound, though recovering from its ailment.

passages.title: On quiet and study
passages.text: “What then?” you say, “is it not sometimes a simpler matter just to avoid the uproar?” I admit this. Accordingly, I shall change from my present quarters. I merely wished to test myself and to give myself practice. Why need I be tormented any longer, when Ulysses found so simple a cure for his comrades even against the songs of the Sirens? Farewell.

claims.t: I do not need a country place, a seashore or a mountain: where I am is just like them, and at any hour I can retreat into myself. No place is quieter than my own mind; there it can be at ease, that is, in good order, and when it acts justly it has calm.
claims.shared: 4.3 and 10.24 both name the country place, the seashore and the mountain, and both say I need none of them: 4.3 calls the longing for them untrained, 10.24 says the place where I am is just like them. 4.3 and 7.20 both send me into myself (“retreat into yourself”, “Draw in upon yourself”) and both say what I find there: ease that is good order (4.3), and calm when the ruling part acts justly (7.20).
claims.changed: 4.3 says the ease belongs above all to someone who has the right things within; the claim keeps only that ease means good order. 10.24 goes on to Plato’s herdsman in his sheepfold, which the claim leaves out.

support.quote: People look for retreats for themselves: country places, seashores, mountains. You too are in the habit of longing very much for such things. But all of this is the mark of someone with no training at all, when you are free, at whatever hour you wish, to retreat into yourself.
support.follows: Longing for a retreat in the country, by the sea or in the mountains is untrained, since I can retreat into myself whenever I wish.
gives: I do not need a country place, a seashore or a mountain
at any hour
I can retreat into myself

support.quote: Let it always be clear that the country place over there is just like this, and how everything here is the same as on the top of the mountain or on the seashore or wherever you like.
support.follows: The place where I am is no different from a country place, a mountain top or a seashore.
gives: I do not need a country place, a seashore or a mountain
where I am is just like them

support.quote: Draw in upon yourself.
support.follows: Marcus tells himself to draw in upon himself.
gives: I can retreat into myself

support.quote: nowhere that a person retreats to is quieter or freer from business than their own soul
support.follows: No place a person can retreat to is quieter or freer from business than their own soul.
gives: No place is quieter than my own mind

support.quote: they are at once in complete ease; and by ease I mean nothing other than good order
support.follows: Looking within, such a person is at once at ease, and Marcus means by ease nothing but good order.
gives: at ease, that is, in good order

support.quote: It is the nature of the rational ruling part to be content with itself when it acts justly and by that very fact has calm.
support.follows: When the rational ruling part acts justly, it is content with itself and, by that very fact, calm.
gives: when it acts justly it has calm

claims.t: Unless it serves the common good, I do not spend my life guessing what other people are saying, doing or thinking; I look at what I am doing and keep watch over what is within me. And I set no store by the praise of the many.
claims.shared: 3.4 and 4.15 both name the same three things not to look at: what another is saying, doing and thinking (3.4: “what they are saying, and what they have in mind”; 4.15: “what their neighbour said or did or thought”). 3.4 and 2.11 both set against this the care of what is within: “watching over your own ruling part” (3.4), “keep only to the guardian spirit within them” (2.11). 3.4 and 6.15 both set no value on praise.
claims.changed: 3.4 keeps the good opinion of those who live in agreement with nature and sets no store only by the praise of the others; 6.15 speaks of “the many”, and the claim follows 6.15. The guardian spirit of 2.11 and the ruling part of 3.4 are both called “what is within me”.

support.quote: Do not wear away the part of your life that is left in impressions about other people, when you are not referring them to something of common benefit
support.follows: I should not use up what is left of my life on impressions of other people, unless they serve some common benefit.
gives: Unless it serves the common good, I do not spend my life

support.quote: forming impressions of what so-and-so is doing, and for what purpose, and what they are saying, and what they have in mind, and what they are contriving, and all such things as make you wander away from watching over your own ruling part
support.follows: Picturing what others do, say, mean and plot draws me away from watching over my own ruling part.
gives: what other people are saying, doing or thinking
keep watch over what is within me

support.quote: looks by guesswork for what is in the souls of their neighbours, but does not notice that it is enough to keep only to the guardian spirit within them and to serve it truly
support.follows: Guessing at what is in other people’s souls is wretched; it is enough to keep to the guardian spirit within me and serve it.
gives: guessing
keep watch over what is within me

support.quote: How much leisure a person gains who does not look at what their neighbour said or did or thought, but only at what they themselves are doing
support.follows: Whoever looks only at what they are doing, not at what a neighbour said, did or thought, gains much leisure.
gives: what other people are saying, doing or thinking
I look at what I am doing

support.quote: So he sets no store either by praise that comes from such people, who are not even pleased with themselves.
support.follows: The good man sets no store by praise from people who do not live by nature and are not even pleased with themselves.
gives: I set no store by the praise

support.quote: Being clapped? No. Then not being clapped by tongues either; for the praises of the many are a clapping of tongues. So you have let petty fame go as well.
support.follows: Applause has no value, and the praise of the many is only applause by tongues, so petty fame has no value either.
gives: I set no store by the praise of the many

claims.t: The things I chase and run from do not come to me: they stay outside, unmoving, and my turmoil comes from my own judgment about them. When I let that judgment be quiet, I neither chase them nor run from them.
claims.shared: Both passages say that the things which disturb me do not reach me (4.3: “things do not touch the soul”; 11.10: they “do not come to you”), and both put what matters in my judgment about them. Both call the things “unmoving”: 4.3 as a standing fact, 11.10 as what follows when my judgment is quiet.
claims.changed: 11.10 adds that “in a way you yourself go to them”; the claim keeps only that they do not come to me. 4.3 speaks of “disturbances”, 11.10 of “turmoil”; the claim uses “turmoil”. 4.3 says the disturbance comes “only” from the judgment; the claim says “from my own judgment about them”. Only 4.3 says “unmoving” as a standing fact; in 11.10 the things stay unmoving as a consequence, when my judgment about them is quiet.

support.quote: The things whose pursuit and avoidance throw you into turmoil do not come to you, but in a way you yourself go to them.
support.follows: The things I chase or flee do not come to me; in a way I go to them.
gives: The things I chase and run from
do not come to me

support.quote: things do not touch the soul but stand outside it, unmoving, and disturbances come only from the judgment within
support.follows: Things stay outside the soul and do not touch it; every disturbance comes from the judgment within.
gives: do not come to me
they stay outside
unmoving
my turmoil comes from my own judgment about them

support.quote: At least let your judgment about them be quiet, and they will stay unmoving, and you will be seen neither pursuing nor avoiding.
support.follows: If my judgment about these things is quiet, they stay where they are, and I neither pursue nor avoid them.
gives: unmoving
