claims.t: Of body, breath and mind, only my mind is properly mine; the other two are mine to take care of. I keep my mind apart from them: once it has drawn back and knows its own power, it does not mix with the breath, and it is not to be fused with my body so that it is swayed whichever way my body is swayed.
claims.shared: All three passages set the mind apart from the body and its breath: 4.3 says the mind “does not mix with the breath”, 12.2 tells me to separate from my thought what comes from “the little body” and “the little breath”, and 10.24 asks with misgiving whether the ruling part has been “melted into the bit of flesh”.
claims.changed: 10.24 is a question; the claim turns it into what the question hopes for. 12.2 puts the separating as an “if” that leads to an untroubled life; the claim states it as what I do. 10.24’s image of melting into the flesh is given in plain words: fused with my body and swayed as it is swayed.

support.quote: There are three things of which you are made up: a little body, a little breath, mind. Of these the other two are yours so far as you must take care of them, but only the third is properly yours.
support.follows: Of body, breath and mind, only the mind is properly mine; body and breath are mine to care for.
gives: Of body, breath and mind, only my mind is properly mine; the other two are mine to take care of

support.quote: So if you separate from yourself, that is, from your thought, all that others do or say, or all that you yourself have done or said, and all that troubles you as something to come, and all that belongs to you, without your choosing it, from the little body that surrounds you or the little breath born with you
support.follows: Marcus tells himself to separate from his thought, among other things, all that comes to him unchosen from his body and breath.
gives: I keep my mind apart from them

support.quote: the mind does not mix with the breath, whether that moves smoothly or roughly, once the mind has taken itself back and come to know its own power
support.follows: Once the mind has drawn back and knows its own power, it does not mix with the breath, whether that moves smoothly or roughly.
gives: I keep my mind apart from them
once it has drawn back and knows its own power, it does not mix with the breath

support.quote: Can it be melted into the bit of flesh and blended with it, so that it turns as the flesh turns?
support.follows: Marcus asks, with misgiving, whether his ruling part has been melted into the flesh, so that it turns as the flesh turns.
gives: it is not to be fused with my body so that it is swayed whichever way my body is swayed

claims.t: I keep to what is present: I practise living only the present, I do not think of absent things as if they were already mine but count up the best of what I have, and I am content with my present state and take pleasure in it.
claims.shared: All three passages turn me to what is present: 12.2 to living “only what you are living, that is, the present”, 7.20 to “the best of the things that are present” instead of absent things, and 10.1 to being “content with your present state”.
claims.changed: 10.1 is a question Marcus puts to his soul (“Will you ever …?”); the claim states what the question longs for. 7.20 says “already there”; the claim says “already mine”, the other reading the translators give.

support.quote: practise living only what you are living, that is, the present
support.follows: Marcus tells himself to practise living only what he is living now, the present.
gives: I keep to what is present
I practise living only the present

support.quote: Not to think of absent things as already there, but to reckon up the best of the things that are present
support.follows: I should not treat absent things as already there, but count up the best of what is present.
gives: I keep to what is present
I do not think of absent things as if they were already mine but count up the best of what I have

support.quote: But will you be content with your present state and take pleasure in all that is present
support.follows: Marcus asks his soul whether it will ever be content with its present state and take pleasure in all that is present.
gives: I keep to what is present
I am content with my present state and take pleasure in it

claims.t: I give my impulses a target and go straight toward it: I look at what has to be done and, when I see it clearly, go that way without turning back, not drifting and not thrown this way and that.
claims.shared: 4.15 and 10.13 both say to go straight on: “run straight along the line” (4.15), go “that way with good will and without turning back” (10.13). 2.4 and 4.15 both name the opposite: “drifting” (2.4), being “thrown this way and that” (4.15).
claims.changed: 10.13 adds what to do when I do not see clearly: hold off and use the best advisers. 4.15 says the aim is that what I do be just and holy. Both are left out. 2.4’s “drifting” and 4.15’s “not thrown this way and that” are near-synonyms, joined into one phrase that both passages back; each passage says one half of it.

support.quote: But now there is the other kind of drifting to guard against as well. For people play the fool through their actions too, those who are worn out by life and have no target at which to direct every impulse and, in general, every impression.
support.follows: People with no target for their impulses play the fool in what they do, and this drifting has to be guarded against.
gives: I give my impulses a target
not drifting and not thrown this way and that

support.quote: What need is there of guessing, when you are free to look at what has to be done, and, if you see it clearly, to go that way with good will and without turning back
support.follows: Instead of guessing, I can look at what has to be done and, if I see it clearly, go that way without turning back.
gives: go straight toward it
I look at what has to be done and, when I see it clearly, go that way without turning back

support.quote: not to look round at a dark character, but to run straight along the line, not thrown this way and that
support.follows: I should not look round at a bad character but run straight along my line, not thrown from side to side.
gives: go straight toward it
not drifting and not thrown this way and that

single.quote: So give yourself this retreat continually, and renew yourself. And let the things be short and elementary which, as soon as they meet you, will be enough to wash away all distress and to send you back without resentment at the things you are returning to.
single.label: Renewing the retreat
single.t: I give myself this retreat again and again and renew myself there. I keep a few short, basic truths ready, enough to wash away all distress and to send me back without resentment to what I return to.
single.why: Only 4.3 says to make the retreat a habit and to carry short truths into it. The other passages that send me inward give no such store of truths.
single.follows: The retreat should be taken continually, with a few short truths that wash away distress and send me back without resentment.

single.quote: And you must accustom yourself to form only those impressions about which, if someone suddenly asked, “What are you thinking now?”, you would answer at once and frankly, “This, and this”
single.label: A test for my thoughts
single.t: I make a habit of having only such thoughts that, if someone suddenly asked what I was thinking, I could answer at once and frankly.
single.why: Only 3.4 gives this test of answering frankly at once. 10.24 also checks the mind, but with different questions.
single.follows: I should form only impressions I could name at once and frankly if someone suddenly asked what I was thinking.

single.quote: What is my ruling part to me, and what kind of thing am I making it now, and what am I using it for now?
single.label: Three questions
single.t: I ask myself what my mind, the part of me that rules, is to me, what I am making it into now, and what I am using it for now.
single.why: Only 10.24 puts these questions. They are kept as a practice I can repeat.
single.follows: Marcus asks himself what his ruling part is to him, what he is making of it now and what he is using it for.

single.quote: To serve it is to keep it clean of passion and aimlessness and discontent with what comes from the gods and from people.
single.label: Serving what is within
single.t: I serve the guardian spirit within me by keeping it clean of passion, of aimlessness, and of discontent with what comes from the gods and from people.
single.why: 12.2 also calls the freed mind clean, but only 2.11 says what serving the spirit within consists of, so it is not fused.
single.follows: Serving the guardian spirit within means keeping it free of passion, aimlessness and discontent with what gods and people send.

single.quote: Will you not stop valuing many other things as well? Then you will be neither free nor sufficient to yourself nor without passion. For you are bound to envy, to be jealous, to look with suspicion on those who can take those things away, to plot against those who have what you value. In short, anyone who is in need of any of those things is bound to be in confusion, and what is more to find much fault even with the gods. But respect for your own mind, and the value you set on it, will make you pleasing to yourself
single.label: Valuing other things
single.t: If I go on valuing many things outside my mind, I am not free or sufficient to myself: I envy and suspect those who can take them away. Respect for my own mind makes me pleasing to myself.
single.why: Only 6.15 says what valuing outside things does to me and that respect for my own mind is the way back.
single.follows: Valuing many outside things leaves me unfree, envious and confused; respect for my own mind makes me pleasing to myself.

single.quote: be on your guard that through being so glad of them you do not accustom yourself to prize them so much that, if ever they are not present, you will be troubled.
single.label: A caution
single.t: Glad as I am of what I have now, I take care not to prize it so much that I would be troubled if it were ever gone.
single.why: Only 7.20 warns that taking pleasure in what is present can become a dependence on it.
single.follows: Being glad of what I have, I should not get used to prizing it so much that losing it would trouble me.

members.text:
They seek for themselves private retiring
places, as country villages, the sea-shore, mountains; yea thou thyself
art wont to long much after such places. But all this thou must know
proceeds from simplicity in the highest degree. At what time soever thou
wilt, it is in thy power to retire into thyself, and to be at rest, and
free from all businesses. A man cannot any whither retire better than
to his own soul; he especially who is beforehand provided of such
things within, which whensoever he doth withdraw himself to look in, may
presently afford unto him perfect ease and tranquillity. By tranquillity
I understand a decent orderly disposition and carriage, free from
all confusion and tumultuousness. Afford then thyself this retiring
continually, and thereby refresh and renew thyself. Let these precepts
be brief and fundamental, which as soon as thou dost call them to mind,
may suffice thee to purge thy soul throughly, and to send thee away well
pleased with those things whatsoever they be, which now again after this
short withdrawing of thy soul into herself thou dost return unto. For
what is it that thou art offended at? Can it be at the wickedness of
men, when thou dost call to mind this conclusion, that all reasonable
creatures are made one for another? and that it is part of justice to
bear with them? and that it is against their wills that they offend?
and how many already, who once likewise prosecuted their enmities,
suspected, hated, and fiercely contended, are now long ago stretched
out, and reduced unto ashes? It is time for thee to make an end. As for
those things which among the common chances of the world happen unto
thee as thy particular lot and portion, canst thou be displeased with
any of them, when thou dost call that our ordinary dilemma to mind,
either a providence, or Democritus his atoms; and with it, whatsoever we
brought to prove that the whole world is as it were one city? And as for
thy body, what canst thou fear, if thou dost consider that thy mind and
understanding, when once it hath recollected itself, and knows its own
power, hath in this life and breath (whether it run smoothly and gently,
or whether harshly and rudely), no interest at all, but is altogether
indifferent: and whatsoever else thou hast heard and assented unto
concerning either pain or pleasure? But the care of thine honour and
reputation will perchance distract thee? How can that be, if thou
dost look back, and consider both how quickly all things that are, are
forgotten, and what an immense chaos of eternity was before, and will
follow after all things: and the vanity of praise, and the inconstancy
and variableness of human judgments and opinions, and the narrowness of
the place, wherein it is limited and circumscribed? For the whole earth
is but as one point; and of it, this inhabited part of it, is but a very
little part; and of this part, how many in number, and what manner of
men are they, that will commend thee? What remains then, but that thou
often put in practice this kind of retiring of thyself, to this little
part of thyself; and above all things, keep thyself from distraction,
and intend not anything vehemently, but be free and consider all things,
as a man whose proper object is Virtue, as a man whose true nature is
to be kind and sociable, as a citizen, as a mortal creature. Among
other things, which to consider, and look into thou must use to withdraw
thyself, let those two be among the most obvious and at hand. One, that
the things or objects themselves reach not unto the soul, but stand
without still and quiet, and that it is from the opinion only which is
within, that all the tumult and all the trouble doth proceed. The next,
that all these things, which now thou seest, shall within a very little
while be changed, and be no more: and ever call to mind, how many
changes and alterations in the world thou thyself hast already been an
eyewitness of in thy time. This world is mere change, and this life,
opinion.
members.english: People look for retreats for themselves: country places, seashores, mountains. You too are in the habit of longing very much for such things. But all of this is the mark of someone with no training at all, when you are free, at whatever hour you wish, to retreat into yourself. For nowhere that a person retreats to is quieter or freer from business than their own soul, above all for someone who has such things within that, on bending to look into them, they are at once in complete ease; and by ease I mean nothing other than good order. So give yourself this retreat continually, and renew yourself. And let the things be short and elementary which, as soon as they meet you, will be enough to wash away all distress and to send you back without resentment at the things you are returning to. For what will you resent? The badness of people? Think over the conclusion: that rational animals have come to be for the sake of one another, and that forbearance is a part of justice, and that they go wrong against their will, and how many before now, after feuding, suspecting, hating, fighting with spears, have been laid out and turned to ash; and then stop at last. Or will you also resent what is dealt out from the whole? Renew for yourself the either-or, “either providence or atoms”, and all the grounds on which it was proved that the universe is, as it were, a city. Or will the things of the body still touch you? Consider that the mind does not mix with the breath, whether that moves smoothly or roughly, once the mind has taken itself back and come to know its own power; and, for the rest, all that you have heard and agreed to about pain and pleasure. Or will petty fame distract you? Look at how fast everything is forgotten, and at the gulf of endless time on either side, and the emptiness of the echo, and how changeable and undiscerning those are who seem to give praise, and the narrowness of the place in which that petty fame is confined. For the whole earth is a point, and how small a corner of it is this dwelling place? And here, how many are there, and what sort of people, who will give the praise? For the rest, then, remember the withdrawal into this little country place of your own; and before everything do not be torn about and do not strain, but be free, and look at things as a man, as a human being, as a citizen, as a mortal animal. And among the things readiest to hand, which you will bend to look into, let there be these two. One, that things do not touch the soul but stand outside it, unmoving, and disturbances come only from the judgment within. The other, that all these things you see will change in almost no time and will no longer be; and keep thinking of how many things you have yourself already seen change. The universe is alteration; life is judgment.
members.greek: Ἀναχωρήσεις αὑτοῖς ζητοῦσιν ἀγροικίας καὶ αἰγιαλοὺς καὶ ὄρη, εἴωθας δὲ καὶ σὺ τὰ τοιαῦτα μάλιστα ποθεῖν. ὅλον δὲ τοῦτο ἰδιωτικώτατόν ἐστιν ἐξόν, ἧς ἂν ὥρας ἐθελήσῃς, εἰς ἑαυτὸν ἀναχωρεῖν. οὐδαμοῦ γὰρ οὔτε ἡσυχιώτερον οὔτε ἀπραγμονέστερον ἄνθρωπος ἀναχωρεῖ ἢ εἰς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχήν, μάλισθʼ ὅστις ἔχει ἔνδον τοιαῦτα, εἰς ἃ ἐγκύψας ἐν πάσῃ εὐμαρείᾳ εὐθὺς γίνεται· τὴν δὲ εὐμάρειαν οὐδὲν ἄλλο λέγω ἢ εὐκοσμίαν. συνεχῶς οὖν δίδου σεαυτῷ ταύτην τὴν ἀναχώρησιν καὶ ἀνανέου σεαυτόν· βραχέα δὲ ἔστω καὶ στοιχειώδη ἃ εὐθὺς ἀπαντήσαντα ἀρκέσει εἰς τὸ πᾶσαν λύπην ἀποκλύσαι καὶ ἀποπέμψαι σε μὴ δυσχεραίνοντα ἐκείνοις ἐφʼ ἃ ἐπανέρχῃ. τίνι γὰρ δυσχερανεῖς; τῇ τῶν ἀνθρώπων κακίᾳ; ἀναλογισάμενος τὸ κρῖμα, ὅτι τὰ λογικὰ ζῷα ἀλλήλων ἕνεκεν γέγονε καὶ ὅτι τὸ ἀνέχεσθαι μέρος τῆς δικαιοσύνης καὶ ὅτι ἄκοντες ἁμαρτάνουσι καὶ πόσοι ἤδη διεχθρεύσαντες, ὑποπτεύσαντες, μισήσαντες, διαδορατισθέντες ἐκτέτανται, τετέφρωνται, παύου ποτέ. ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς ἐκ τῶν ὅλων ἀπονεμομένοις δυσχερανεῖς; ἀνανεωσάμενος τὸ διεζευγμένον τό· ἤτοι πρόνοια ἢ ἄτομοι, καὶ ἐξ ὅσων ἀπεδείχθη ὅτι ὁ κόσμος ὡσανεὶ πόλις. ἀλλὰ τὰ σωματικά σου ἅψεται ἔτι; ἐννοήσας ὅτι οὐκ ἐπιμίγνυται λείως ἢ τραχέως κινουμένῳ πνεύματι ἡ διάνοια, ἐπειδὰν ἅπαξ ἑαυτὴν ἀπολάβῃ καὶ γνωρίσῃ τὴν ἰδίαν ἐξουσίαν, καὶ λοιπὸν ὅσα περὶ πόνου καὶ ἡδονῆς ἀκήκοας καὶ συγκατέθου. ἀλλὰ τὸ δοξάριόν σε περισπάσει; ἀπιδὼν εἰς τὸ τάχος τῆς πάντων λήθης καὶ τὸ χάος τοῦ ἐφʼ ἑκάτερα ἀπείρου αἰῶνος καὶ τὸ κενὸν τῆς ἀπηχήσεως καὶ τὸ εὐμετάβολον καὶ ἄκριτον τῶν εὐφημεῖν δοκούντων καὶ τὸ στενὸν τοῦ τόπου, ἐν ᾧ περιγράφεται· ὅλη τε γὰρ ἡ γῆ στιγμὴ καὶ ταύτης πόστον γωνίδιον ἡ κατοίκησις αὕτη; καὶ ἐνταῦθα πόσοι καὶ οἷοί τινες οἱ ἐπαινεσόμενοι; λοιπὸν οὖν μέμνησο τῆς ὑποχωρήσεως τῆς εἰς τοῦτο τὸ ἀγρίδιον ἑαυτοῦ καὶ πρὸ παντὸς μὴ σπῶ μηδὲ κατεντείνου, ἀλλὰ ἐλεύθερος ἔσο καὶ ὅρα τὰ πράγματα ὡς ἀνήρ, ὡς ἄνθρωπος, ὡς πολίτης, ὡς θνητὸν ζῷον. ἐν δὲ τοῖς προχειροτάτοις, εἰς ἃ ἐγκύψεις, ταῦτα ἔστω τὰ δύο· ἕν μέν, ὅτι τὰ πράγματα οὐχ ἅπτεται τῆς ψυχῆς, ἀλλʼ ἔξω ἕστηκεν ἀτρεμοῦντα, αἱ δὲ ὀχλήσεις ἐκ μόνης τῆς ἔνδον ὑπολήψεως· ἕτερον δέ, ὅτι πάντα ταῦτα, ὅσα ὁρᾷς, ὅσον οὐδέπω μεταβαλεῖ καὶ οὐκ ἔτι ἔσται· καὶ ὅσων ἤδη μεταβολαῖς αὐτὸς παρατετύχηκας, συνεχῶς διανοοῦ. ὁ κόσμος ἀλλοίωσις, ὁ βίος ὑπόληψις.

members.text:
Spend not the remnant of thy days in thoughts and fancies concerning
other men, when it is not in relation to some common good, when by it
thou art hindered from some other better work. That is, spend not thy
time in thinking, what such a man doth, and to what end: what he saith,
and what he thinks, and what he is about, and such other things or
curiosities, which make a man to rove and wander from the care and
observation of that part of himself, which is rational, and overruling.
See therefore in the whole series and connection of thy thoughts, that
thou be careful to prevent whatsoever is idle and impertinent: but
especially, whatsoever is curious and malicious: and thou must use
thyself to think only of such things, of which if a man upon a sudden
should ask thee, what it is that thou art now thinking, thou mayest
answer This, and That, freely and boldly, that so by thy thoughts it may
presently appear that in all thee is sincere, and peaceable; as becometh
one that is made for society, and regards not pleasures, nor gives way
to any voluptuous imaginations at all: free from all contentiousness,
envy, and suspicion, and from whatsoever else thou wouldest blush to
confess thy thoughts were set upon. He that is such, is he surely that
doth not put off to lay hold on that which is best indeed, a very priest
and minister of the gods, well acquainted and in good correspondence
with him especially that is seated and placed within himself, as in
a temple and sacrary: to whom also he keeps and preserves himself
unspotted by pleasure, undaunted by pain; free from any manner of wrong,
or contumely, by himself offered unto himself: not capable of any evil
from others: a wrestler of the best sort, and for the highest prize,
that he may not be cast down by any passion or affection of his own;
deeply dyed and drenched in righteousness, embracing and accepting with
his whole heart whatsoever either happeneth or is allotted unto him. One
who not often, nor without some great necessity tending to some public
good, mindeth what any other, either speaks, or doth, or purposeth: for
those things only that are in his own power, or that are truly his own,
are the objects of his employments, and his thoughts are ever taken
up with those things, which of the whole universe are by the fates or
Providence destinated and appropriated unto himself. Those things that
are his own, and in his own power, he himself takes order, for that they
be good: and as for those that happen unto him, he believes them to be
so. For that lot and portion which is assigned to every one, as it is
unavoidable and necessary, so is it always profitable. He remembers
besides that whatsoever partakes of reason, is akin unto him, and that
to care for all men generally, is agreeing to the nature of a man: but
as for honour and praise, that they ought not generally to be admitted
and accepted of from all, but from such only, who live according to
nature. As for them that do not, what manner of men they be at home,
or abroad; day or night, how conditioned themselves with what manner of
conditions, or with men of what conditions they moil and pass away
the time together, he knoweth, and remembers right well, he therefore
regards not such praise and approbation, as proceeding from them, who
cannot like and approve themselves.
members.english: Do not wear away the part of your life that is left in impressions about other people, when you are not referring them to something of common benefit (for in truth you are deprived of other work). That is, forming impressions of what so-and-so is doing, and for what purpose, and what they are saying, and what they have in mind, and what they are contriving, and all such things as make you wander away from watching over your own ruling part. So you must avoid, in the chain of your impressions, even what is random and to no purpose, but far the most what is meddling and malicious. And you must accustom yourself to form only those impressions about which, if someone suddenly asked, “What are you thinking now?”, you would answer at once and frankly, “This, and this”; so that from them it would be plain straight away that everything is simple and kindly and belongs to a social animal, one that cares nothing for imaginings of pleasure or of enjoyment in general, or for any rivalry, or envy and suspicion, or anything else that you would blush to explain you had in your mind. For a man of this kind, who no longer puts off being, so to speak, among the best already, is a kind of priest and servant of the gods. He also makes use of what is enshrined within him, which makes the person unstained by pleasures, unwounded by any pain, untouched by any insult, insensible to any wickedness, an athlete in the greatest contest, the contest not to be thrown by any passion, dyed deep in justice, welcoming with his whole soul everything that happens and is dealt out, and not often, nor without a great need that serves the common benefit, forming an impression of what another person is saying or doing or thinking. For it is only what is his own that he has for his activity, and what is spun for him out of the whole he thinks of without a break; and the first he makes fine, and the second he is convinced are good. For the lot dealt to each person is carried along with them and carries them along with it. He remembers too that everything rational is kin, and that to care for all human beings is in keeping with the nature of a human being, but that the good opinion to hold on to is not that of everyone, but only of those who live in agreement with nature. As for those who do not live so, he keeps in mind all the time what sort of people they are at home and outside the house, by night and by day, and what they are like and with what kind of people they are mixed up. So he sets no store either by praise that comes from such people, who are not even pleased with themselves.
members.greek: Μὴ κατατρίψῃς τὸ ὑπολειπόμενον τοῦ βίου μέρος ἐν ταῖς περὶ ἑτέρων φαντασίαις, ὁπόταν μὴ τὴν ἀναφορὰν ἐπί τι κοινωφελὲς ποιῇ (ἤτοι γὰρ ἄλλου ἔργου στέρῃ). τουτέστι φανταζόμενος τί ὁ δεῖνα πράσσει καὶ τίνος ἕνεκεν καὶ τί λέγει καὶ τί ἐνθυμεῖται καὶ τί τεχνάζεται καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα ποιεῖ ἀπορρέμβεσθαι τῆς τοῦ ἰδίου ἡγεμονικοῦ παρατηρήσεως. χρὴ μὲν οὖν καὶ τὸ εἰκῇ καὶ μάτην ἐν τῷ εἱρμῷ τῶν φαντασιῶν περιίστασθαι, πολὺ δὲ μάλιστα τὸ περίεργον καὶ κακόηθες καὶ ἐθιστέον ἑαυτὸν μόνα φαντάζεσθαι, περὶ ὧν εἴ τις ἄφνω ἐπανέροιτο· τί νῦν διανοῇ; μετὰ παρρησίας παραχρῆμα ἂν ἀποκρίναιο ὅτι τὸ καὶ τό· ὡς ἐξ αὐτῶν εὐθὺς δῆλα εἶναι, ὅτι πάντα ἁπλᾶ καὶ εὐμενῆ καὶ ζῴου κοινωνικοῦ καὶ ἀμελοῦντος ἡδονικῶν ἢ καθάπαξ ἀπολαυστικῶν φαντασμάτων ἢ φιλονεικίας τινὸς ἢ βασκανίας καὶ ὑποψίας ἢ ἄλλου τινός, ἐφ’ ᾧ ἂν ἐρυθριάσειας ἐξηγούμενος, ὅτι ἐν νῷ αὐτὸ εἶχες. ὁ γάρ τοι ἀνὴρ ὁ τοιοῦτος, οὐκέτι ὑπερτιθέμενος τὸ ὡς ἐν ἀρίστοις ἤδη εἶναι, ἱερεύς τίς ἐστι καὶ ὑπουργὸς θεῶν, χρώμενος καὶ τῷ ἔνδον ἱδρυμένῳ αὐτῷ, ὃ παρέχεται τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἄχραντον ἡδονῶν, ἄτρωτον ὑπὸ παντὸς πόνου, πάσης ὕβρεως ἀνέπαφον, πάσης ἀναίσθητον πονηρίας, ἀθλητὴν ἄθλου τοῦ μεγίστου, τοῦ ὑπὸ μηδενὸς πάθους καταβληθῆναι, δικαιοσύνῃ βεβαμμένον εἰς βάθος, ἀσπαζόμενον μὲν ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς τὰ συμβαίνοντα καὶ ἀπονεμόμενα πάντα, μὴ πολλάκις δὲ μηδὲ χωρὶς μεγάλης καὶ κοινωφελοῦς ἀνάγκης φανταζόμενον τί ποτε ἄλλος λέγει ἢ πράσσει ἢ διανοεῖται. μόνα γὰρ τὰ ἑαυτοῦ πρὸς ἐνέργειαν † ἔχει καὶ τὰ ἑαυτῷ ἐκ τῶν ὅλων συγκλωθόμενα διηνεκῶς ἐννοεῖ κἀκεῖνα μὲν καλὰ παρέχεται, ταῦτα δὲ ἀγαθὰ εἶναι πέπεισται· ἡ γὰρ ἑκάστῳ νεμομένη μοῖρα συνεμφέρεταί τε καὶ συνεμφέρει. μέμνηται δὲ καὶ ὅτι συγγενὲς πᾶν τὸ λογικόν, καὶ ὅτι κήδεσθαι μὲν πάντων ἀνθρώπων κατὰ τὴν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου φύσιν ἐστί, δόξης δὲ οὐχὶ τῆς παρὰ πάντων ἀνθεκτέον, ἀλλὰ τῶν ὁμολογουμένως τῇ φύσει βιούντων μόνων. οἱ δὲ μὴ οὕτως βιοῦντες ὁποῖοί τινες οἴκοι τε καὶ ἔξω τῆς οἰκίας καὶ νύκτωρ καὶ μεθʼ ἡμέραν, οἷοι μεθʼ οἵων φύρονται, μεμνημένος διατελεῖ. οὐ τοίνυν οὐδὲ τὸν παρὰ τῶν τοιούτων ἔπαινον ἐν λόγῳ τίθεται, οἵγε οὐδὲ αὐτοὶ ἑαυτοῖς ἀρέσκονται.

members.text:
God beholds our minds and understandings, bare and naked from these
material vessels, and outsides, and all earthly dross. For with His
simple and pure understanding, He pierceth into our inmost and purest
parts, which from His, as it were by a water pipe and channel, first
flowed and issued. This if thou also shalt use to do, thou shalt
rid thyself of that manifold luggage, wherewith thou art round about
encumbered. For he that does regard neither his body, nor his clothing,
nor his dwelling, nor any such external furniture, must needs gain unto
himself great rest and ease. Three things there be in all, which thou
doest consist of; thy body, thy life, and thy mind. Of these the two
former, are so far forth thine, as that thou art bound to take care for
them. But the third alone is that which is properly thine. If then thou
shalt separate from thyself, that is from thy mind, whatsoever other men
either do or say, or whatsoever thou thyself hast heretofore either
done or said; and all troublesome thoughts concerning the future, and
whatsoever, (as either belonging to thy body or life:) is without the
jurisdiction of thine own will, and whatsoever in the ordinary course
of human chances and accidents doth happen unto thee; so that thy
mind (keeping herself loose and free from all outward coincidental
entanglements; always in a readiness to depart:) shall live by herself,
and to herself, doing that which is just, accepting whatsoever doth
happen, and speaking the truth always; if, I say, thou shalt separate
from thy mind, whatsoever by sympathy might adhere unto it, and all time
both past and future, and shalt make thyself in all points and respects,
like unto Empedocles his allegorical sphere, 'all round and circular,'
&c., and shalt think of no longer life than that which is now present:
then shalt thou be truly able to pass the remainder of thy days without
troubles and distractions; nobly and generously disposed, and in good
favour and correspondency, with that spirit which is within thee.
members.english:
God sees all ruling parts bare of their material vessels and husks and refuse. For with only the part of himself that is of mind he touches only what has flowed out of himself into these and been channelled off. If you too make a habit of doing this, you will strip away most of your distraction. For someone who does not look at the surrounding scraps of flesh is hardly likely to busy themselves with gazing at clothing and a house and reputation and that kind of wrapping and stage scenery.

There are three things of which you are made up: a little body, a little breath, mind. Of these the other two are yours so far as you must take care of them, but only the third is properly yours. So if you separate from yourself, that is, from your thought, all that others do or say, or all that you yourself have done or said, and all that troubles you as something to come, and all that belongs to you, without your choosing it, from the little body that surrounds you or the little breath born with you, and all that the whirl streaming round outside sets spinning, so that the power of mind, lifted clear of what is bound up with it by fate, and clean, lives set loose by itself, doing what is just and willing what happens and saying what is true; if, I say, you separate from this ruling part the things fastened onto it by attachment, and what of time lies ahead or has gone by, and make yourself like the sphere of Empedocles, “rounded, rejoicing in its encircling solitude”, and practise living only what you are living, that is, the present: then what is left until you die, at least, you will be able to live through untroubled, kindly, and gracious toward your own guardian spirit.
members.greek:
Ὁ θεὸς πάντα τὰ ἡγεμονικὰ γυμνὰ τῶν ὑλικῶν ἀγγείων καὶ φλοιῶν καὶ καθαρμάτων ὁρᾷ· μόνῳ γὰρ τῷ ἑαυτοῦ νοερῷ μόνων ἅπτεται τῶν ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ εἰς ταῦτα ἐρρυηκότων καὶ ἀπωχετευμένων. ἐὰν δὲ καὶ σὺ τοῦτο ἐθίσῃς ποιεῖν, τὸν πολὺν περισπασμὸν σεαυτοῦ περιαιρήσεις· ὁ γὰρ μὴ τὰ περικείμενα κρεᾴδια ὁρῶν, ἦ πού γε ἐσθῆτα καὶ οἰκίαν καὶ δόξαν καὶ τὴν τοιαύτην περιβολὴν καὶ σκηνὴν θεώμενος, ἀσχολήσεται.

Τρία ἐστὶν ἐξ ὧν συνέστηκας· σωμάτιον, πνευμάτιον, νοῦς. τούτων τἄλλα μέχρι τοῦ ἐπιμελεῖσθαι δεῖν σά ἐστι, τὸ δὲ τρίτον μόνον κυρίως σόν. ὃ ἐὰν χωρίσῃς ἀπὸ σεαυτοῦ, τουτέστιν ἀπὸ τῆς σῆς διανοίας, ὅσα ἄλλοι ποιοῦσιν ἢ λέγουσιν ἢ ὅσα αὐτὸς ἐποίησας ἢ εἶπας καὶ ὅσα ὡς μέλλοντα ταράσσει σε καὶ ὅσα τοῦ περικειμένου σοι σωματίου ἢ τοῦ συμφύτου πνευματίου ἀπροαίρετα πρόσεστιν καὶ ὅσα ἡ ἔξωθεν περιρρέουσα δίνη ἑλίσσει, ὥστε τῶν συνειμαρμένων ἐξῃρημένην καὶ καθαρὰν τὴν νοερὰν δύναμιν ἀπόλυτον ἐφ’ ἑαυτῆς ζῆν, ποιοῦσαν τὰ δίκαια καὶ θέλουσαν τὰ συμβαίνοντα καὶ λέγουσαν τἀληθῆ· ἐὰν χωρίσῃς, φημί, τοῦ ἡγεμονικοῦ τούτου τὰ προσηρτημένα ἐκ προσπαθείας καὶ τοῦ χρόνου τὰ ἐπέκεινα ἢ τὰ παρῳχηκότα, ποιήσῃς τε σεαυτόν, οἷος ὁ Ἐμπεδόκλειος σφαῖρος κυκλοτερὴς μονίῃ περιηγέι γαίων, μόνον τε ζῆν ἐκμελετήσῃς ὃ ζῇς, τουτέστι τὸ παρόν· δυνήσῃ τό γε μέχρι τοῦ ἀποθανεῖν ὑπολειπόμενον ἀταράκτως καὶ εὐμενῶς καὶ ἵλεως τῷ σαυτοῦ δαίμονι διαβιῶναι.

members.text:
Consider with thyself how man, and by what part of his, is joined
unto God, and how that part of man is affected, when it is said to be
diffused. There is nothing more wretched than that soul, which in a kind
of circuit compasseth all things, searching (as he saith) even the very
depths of the earth; and by all signs and conjectures prying into the
very thoughts of other men's souls; and yet of this, is not sensible,
that it is sufficient for a man to apply himself wholly, and to confine
all his thoughts and cares to the tendance of that spirit which is
within him, and truly and really to serve him. His service doth consist
in this, that a man keep himself pure from all violent passion and
evil affection, from all rashness and vanity, and from all manner of
discontent, either in regard of the gods or men. For indeed whatsoever
proceeds from the gods, deserves respect for their worth and excellency;
and whatsoever proceeds from men, as they are our kinsmen, should by us
be entertained, with love, always; sometimes, as proceeding from their
ignorance, of that which is truly good and bad, (a blindness no less,
than that by which we are not able to discern between white and black:)
with a kind of pity and compassion also.
members.english:
How a human being touches god, and with what part of themselves, and in what state this part of the human being is when that happens.

Nothing is more wretched than a person who goes round everything in a circle and, as it is said, “searches into the things beneath the earth”, and looks by guesswork for what is in the souls of their neighbours, but does not notice that it is enough to keep only to the guardian spirit within them and to serve it truly. To serve it is to keep it clean of passion and aimlessness and discontent with what comes from the gods and from people. For what comes from the gods deserves reverence because of their excellence; and what comes from people is dear because of kinship, and sometimes also, in a way, pitiable because of their ignorance of what is good and bad. This disability is no less than the one that takes away the power to tell white from black.
members.greek:
πῶς ἅπτεται θεοῦ ἄνθρωπος καὶ κατὰ τί ἑαυτοῦ μέρος καὶ ὅταν πῶς ἔχῃ διακέηται τὸ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τοῦτο μόριον.

Οὐδὲν ἀθλιώτερον τοῦ πάντα κύκλῳ ἐκπεριερχομένου καὶ ʽτὰ νέρθεν γᾶς (φησὶν) ἐρευνῶντοςʼ καὶ τὰ ἐν ταῖς ψυχαῖς τῶν πλησίον διὰ τεκμάρσεως ζητοῦντος, μὴ αἰσθομένου δέ, ὅτι ἀρκεῖ πρὸς μόνῳ τῷ ἔνδον ἑαυτοῦ δαίμονι εἶναι καὶ τοῦτον γνησίως θεραπεύειν. θεραπεία δὲ αὐτοῦ, καθαρὸν πάθους διατηρεῖν καὶ εἰκαιότητος καὶ δυσαρεστήσεως τῆς πρὸς τὰ ἐκ θεῶν καὶ ἀνθρώπων γινόμενα. τὰ μὲν γὰρ ἐκ θεῶν αἰδέσιμα δι’ ἀρετήν· τὰ δὲ ἐξ ἀνθρώπων φίλα διὰ συγγένειαν, ἔστι δὲ ὅτε καὶ τρόπον τινὰ ἐλεεινὰ δι’ ἄγνοιαν ἀγαθῶν καὶ κακῶν· οὐκ ἐλάττων ἡ πήρωσις αὕτη τῆς στερισκούσης τοῦ διακρίνειν τὰ λευκὰ καὶ μέλανα.

members.text:
Fancy not to thyself things future, as though they were present
but of those that are present, take some aside, that thou takest most
benefit of, and consider of them particularly, how wonderfully thou
wouldst want them, if they were not present. But take heed withal, lest
that whilst thou dust settle thy contentment in things present, thou
grow in time so to overprize them, as that the want of them (whensoever
it shall so fall out) should be a trouble and a vexation unto thee. Wind
up thyself into thyself. Such is the nature of thy reasonable
commanding part, as that if it exercise justice, and have by that means
tranquillity within itself, it doth rest fully satisfied with itself
without any other thing.
members.english:
Not to think of absent things as already there, but to reckon up the best of the things that are present, and on their account to remind yourself how they would be sought after if they were not present. At the same time, though, be on your guard that through being so glad of them you do not accustom yourself to prize them so much that, if ever they are not present, you will be troubled.

Draw in upon yourself. It is the nature of the rational ruling part to be content with itself when it acts justly and by that very fact has calm.
members.greek:
Μὴ τὰ ἀπόντα ἐννοεῖν ὡς ἤδη ὄντα, ἀλλὰ τῶν παρόντων τὰ δεξιώτατα ἐκλογίζεσθαι καὶ τούτων χάριν ὑπομιμνῄσκεσθαι πῶς ἂν ἐπεζητεῖτο, εἰ μὴ παρῆν. ἅμα μέντοι φυλάσσου, μὴ διὰ τοῦ οὕτως ἀσμενίζειν αὐτοῖς ἐθίσῃς ἐκτιμᾶν αὐτά, ὥστε, ἐάν ποτε μὴ παρῇ, ταραχθήσεσθαι.

Εἰς σαυτὸν συνειλοῦ· φύσιν ἔχει τὸ λογικὸν ἡγεμονικὸν ἑαυτῷ ἀρκεῖσθαι δικαιοπραγοῦντι καὶ παρ’ αὐτὸ τοῦτο γαλήνην ἔχοντι.

members.text:
Let it always appear and be manifest unto thee that solitariness,
and desert places, by many philosophers so much esteemed of and
affected, are of themselves but thus and thus; and that all things are
them to them that live in towns, and converse with others as they are
the same nature everywhere to be seen and observed: to them that have
retired themselves to the top of mountains, and to desert havens, or
what other desert and inhabited places soever. For anywhere it thou wilt
mayest thou quickly find and apply that to thyself; which Plato saith of
his philosopher, in a place: as private and retired, saith he, as if he
were shut up and enclosed about in some shepherd's lodge, on the top of
a hill. There by thyself to put these questions to thyself or to enter
in these considerations: What is my chief and principal part, which hath
power over the rest? What is now the present estate of it, as I use it;
and what is it, that I employ it about? Is it now void of reason ir no?
Is it free, and separated; or so affixed, so congealed and grown
together as it were with the flesh, that it is swayed by the motions and
inclinations of it?
members.english:
Let it always be clear that the country place over there is just like this, and how everything here is the same as on the top of the mountain or on the seashore or wherever you like. For you will find exactly what Plato says: “putting a sheepfold round himself on a mountain,” he says, “and milking the bleaters.”

What is my ruling part to me, and what kind of thing am I making it now, and what am I using it for now? Can it be empty of mind? Can it be cut loose and torn away from community? Can it be melted into the bit of flesh and blended with it, so that it turns as the flesh turns?
members.greek:
Ἐναργὲς ἔστω ἀεὶ τὸ ὅτι τοιοῦτο ἐκεῖνο ὁ ἀγρός ἐστι καὶ πῶς πάντα ἐστὶ τὰ αὐτὰ ἐνθάδε τοῖς ἐν ἄκρῳ τῷ ὄρει ἢ ἐπὶ τοῦ αἰγιαλοῦ ἢ ὅπου θέλεις. ἄντικρυς γὰρ εὑρήσεις τὰ τοῦ Πλάτωνος· ʽσηκὸν ἐν ὄρει, φησί, περιβαλλόμενος καὶ βδάλλων βληχήματα.ʼ

Τί ἐστί μοι τὸ ἡγεμονικόν μου καὶ ποῖόν τι αὐτὸ ἐγὼ ποιῶ νῦν καὶ πρὸς τί ποτε αὐτῷ νῦν χρῶμαι; μήτι κενὸν νοῦ ἐστι; μήτι ἀπόλυτον καὶ ἀπεσπασμένον κοινωνίας; μήτι προστετηκὸς καὶ ἀνακεκραμένον τῷ σαρκιδίῳ, ὥστε τούτῳ συντρέπεσθαι;

members.text:
Not vegetative spiration, it is not surely (which plants have) that
in this life should be so dear unto us; nor sensitive respiration, the
proper life of beasts, both tame and wild; nor this our imaginative
faculty; nor that we are subject to be led and carried up and down by
the strength of our sensual appetites; or that we can gather, and live
together; or that we can feed: for that in effect is no better, than
that we can void the excrements of our food. What is it then that should
be dear unto us? to hear a clattering noise? if not that, then neither
to be applauded by the tongues of men. For the praises of many tongues,
is in effect no better than the clattering of so many tongues. If then
neither applause, what is there remaining that should be dear unto thee?
This I think: that in all thy motions and actions thou be moved,
and restrained according to thine own true natural constitution and
Construction only. And to this even ordinary arts and professions do
lead us. For it is that which every art doth aim at, that whatsoever it
is, that is by art effected and prepared, may be fit for that work that
it is prepared for. This is the end that he that dresseth the vine, and
he that takes upon him either to tame colts, or to train up dogs,
doth aim at. What else doth the education of children, and all learned
professions tend unto? Certainly then it is that, which should be dear
unto us also. If in this particular it go well with thee, care not for
the obtaining of other things. But is it so, that thou canst not but
respect other things also? Then canst not thou truly be free? then canst
thou not have self-content: then wilt thou ever be subject to passions.
For it is not possible, but that thou must be envious, and jealous, and
suspicious of them whom thou knowest can bereave thee of such things;
and again, a secret underminer of them, whom thou seest in present
possession of that which is dear unto thee. To be short, he must of
necessity be full of confusion within himself, and often accuse the
Gods, whosoever stands in need of these things. But if thou shalt
honour and respect thy mind only, that will make thee acceptable
towards thyself, towards thy friends very tractable; and conformable
and concordant with the Gods; that is, accepting with praises whatsoever
they shall think good to appoint and allot unto thee.
members.english: It is not breathing through the surface as plants do that is of value, nor breathing as cattle and wild beasts do, nor being stamped by an impression, nor being pulled on strings by impulse, nor herding together, nor taking in food; for this last is like passing out the waste from the food. What then is of value? Being clapped? No. Then not being clapped by tongues either; for the praises of the many are a clapping of tongues. So you have let petty fame go as well. What is left that is of value? I think it is this: to move and to hold back in keeping with the way one is oneself made, which is also where tending and the crafts lead. For every craft aims at this, that the thing made should be fit for the work it was made for. The planter and the one who tends the vine, the breaker of colts and the one who tends the dog are after this. And the upbringing of children, and teaching: what are they pressing towards? Here, then, is what is of value. And if this is in a good state, you will not be acquiring any of the other things for yourself. Will you not stop valuing many other things as well? Then you will be neither free nor sufficient to yourself nor without passion. For you are bound to envy, to be jealous, to look with suspicion on those who can take those things away, to plot against those who have what you value. In short, anyone who is in need of any of those things is bound to be in confusion, and what is more to find much fault even with the gods. But respect for your own mind, and the value you set on it, will make you pleasing to yourself, well fitted to your fellows and in tune with the gods, that is, praising all that they deal out and have arranged.
members.greek: Οὔτε τὸ διαπνεῖσθαι ὡς τὰ φυτὰ τίμιον οὔτε τὸ ἀναπνεῖν ὡς τὰ βοσκήματα καὶ τὰ θηρία οὔτε τὸ τυποῦσθαι κατὰ φαντασίαν οὔτε τὸ νευροσπαστεῖσθαι καθ’ ὁρμὴν οὔτε τὸ συναγελάζεσθαι οὔτε τὸ τρέφεσθαι· τοῦτο γὰρ ὅμοιον τῷ ἀποκρίνειν τὰ περιττώματα τῆς τροφῆς. τί οὖν τίμιον; τὸ κροτεῖσθαι; οὐχί. οὐκοῦν οὐδὲ τὸ ὑπὸ γλωσσῶν κροτεῖσθαι· αἱ γὰρ παρὰ τῶν πολλῶν εὐφημίαι κρότος γλωσσῶν. ἀφῆκας οὖν καὶ τὸ δοξάριον· τί καταλείπεται τίμιον; δοκῶ μὲν τὸ κατὰ τὴν ἰδίαν κατασκευὴν κινεῖσθαι καὶ ἴσχεσθαι, ἐφ’ ὅ καὶ αἱ ἐπιμέλειαι ἄγουσι καὶ αἱ τέχναι. ἥ τε γὰρ τέχνη πᾶσα τούτου στοχάζεται, ἵνα τὸ κατασκευασθὲν ἐπιτηδείως ἔχῃ πρὸς τὸ ἔργον πρὸς ὅ κατεσκεύασται· ὅ τε φυτουργὸς καὶ ὁ ἐπιμελούμενος τῆς ἀμπέλου, καὶ ὁ πωλοδάμνης καὶ ὁ τοῦ κυνὸς ἐπιμελούμενος τοῦτο ζητεῖ. αἱ δὲ παιδαγωγίαι, αἱ δὲ διδασκαλίαι ἐπὶ τί σπεύδουσιν; ὧδε οὖν τὸ τίμιον καὶ τοῦτο μὲν ἂν εὖ ἔχῃ, οὐδὲν τῶν ἄλλων περιποιήσεις σεαυτῷ. οὐ παύσῃ καὶ ἄλλα πολλὰ τιμῶν; οὔτ’ οὖν ἐλεύθερος ἔσῃ οὔτε αὐτάρκης οὔτε ἀπαθής· ἀνάγκη γὰρ φθονεῖν, ζηλοτυπεῖν, ὑφορᾶσθαι τοὺς ἀφελέσθαι ἐκεῖνα δυναμένους, ἐπιβουλεύειν τοῖς ἔχουσι τὸ τιμώμενον ὑπὸ σοῦ. ὅλως πεφύρθαι ἀνάγκη τὸν ἐκείνων τινὸς ἐνδεῆ, προσέτι δὲ πολλὰ καὶ τοῖς θεοῖς μέμφεσθαι. ἡ δὲ τῆς ἰδίας διανοίας αἰδὼς καὶ τιμὴ σεαυτῷ τε ἀρεστόν σε ποιήσει καὶ τοῖς κοινωνοῖς εὐάρμοστον καὶ τοῖς θεοῖς σύμφωνον, τουτέστιν ἐπαινοῦντα ὅσα ἐκεῖνοι διανέμουσι καὶ διατετάχασιν.

members.text:
O my soul, the time I trust will be, when thou shalt be good, simple,
single, more open and visible, than that body by which it is enclosed.
Thou wilt one day be sensible of their happiness, whose end is love, and
their affections dead to all worldly things. Thou shalt one day be full,
and in want of no external thing: not seeking pleasure from anything,
either living or insensible, that this world can afford; neither wanting
time for the continuation of thy pleasure, nor place and opportunity,
nor the favour either of the weather or of men. When thou shalt have
content in thy present estate, and all things present shall add to thy
content: when thou shalt persuade thyself, that thou hast all things;
all for thy good, and all by the providence of the Gods: and of things
future also shalt be as confident, that all will do well, as tending to
the maintenance and preservation in some sort, of his perfect welfare
and happiness, who is perfection of life, of goodness, and beauty; who
begets all things, and containeth all things in himself, and in himself
doth recollect all things from all places that are dissolved, that of
them he may beget others again like unto them. Such one day shall be thy
disposition, that thou shalt be able, both in regard of the Gods, and
in regard of men, so to fit and order thy conversation, as neither
to complain of them at any time, for anything that they do; nor to do
anything thyself, for which thou mayest justly be condemned.
members.english: Will you ever, soul, be good and simple and one and bare, plainer to see than the body wrapped round you? Will you ever taste the loving and affectionate disposition? Will you ever be full and in need of nothing, longing for nothing and desiring nothing, whether living or lifeless, for the enjoyment of pleasures? Nor time in which to enjoy them longer? Nor a place or a country or a mild climate? Nor people who suit you well? But will you be content with your present state and take pleasure in all that is present, and persuade yourself that all things are present to you, from the gods, that all things are well with you and will be well, all that pleases them and all that they are going to give for the preservation of the perfect living being, the good and just and beautiful one, which begets all things and holds them together and surrounds them and takes them into itself as they are dissolved for the birth of others like them? Will you ever be such as to live as a fellow citizen with gods and human beings in such a way that you neither find any fault with them nor are condemned by them?
members.greek: Ἔσῃ ποτὲ ἆρα, ὦ ψυχή, ἀγαθὴ καὶ ἁπλῆ καὶ μία καὶ γυμνή, φανερωτέρα τοῦ περικειμένου σοι σώματος; γεύσῃ ποτὲ ἆρα τῆς φιλητικῆς καὶ στερκτικῆς διαθέσεως; ἔσῃ ποτὲ ἆρα πλήρης καὶ ἀνενδεὴς καὶ οὐδὲν ἐπιποθοῦσα οὐδὲ ἐπιθυμοῦσα οὐδενὸς οὔτε ἐμψύχου οὔτε ἀψύχου πρὸς ἡδονῶν ἀπολαύσεις; οὐδὲ χρόνου, ἐν ᾧ ἐπὶ μακρότερον ἀπολαύσεις; οὐδὲ τόπου ἢ χώρας ἢ ἀέρων εὐκρασίας; οὐδὲ ἀνθρώπων εὐαρμοστίας; ἀλλὰ ἀρκεσθήσῃ τῇ παρούσῃ καταστάσει καὶ ἡσθήσῃ τοῖς παροῦσι πᾶσι καὶ συμπείσεις σεαυτὴν ὅτι πάντα σοι παρὰ τῶν θεῶν πάρεστι, πάντα σοι εὖ ἔχει καὶ εὖ ἕξει, ὅσα φίλον αὐτοῖς καὶ ὅσα μέλλουσι δώσειν ἐπὶ σωτηρίᾳ τοῦ τελείου ζῴου, τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ καὶ δικαίου καὶ καλοῦ καὶ γεννῶντος πάντα καὶ συνέχοντος καὶ περιέχοντος καὶ περιλαμβάνοντος διαλυόμενα εἰς γένεσιν ἑτέρων ὁμοίων; ἔσῃ ποτὲ ἆρα τοιαύτη, οἵα θεοῖς τε καὶ ἀνθρώποις οὕτως συμπολιτεύεσθαι ὡς μήτε μέμφεσθαί τι αὐτοῖς μήτε καταγινώσκεσθαι ὑπ’ αὐτῶν;

members.text:
Why should any of these things that happen externally, so much
distract thee? Give thyself leisure to learn some good thing, and cease
roving and wandering to and fro. Thou must also take heed of another
kind of wandering, for they are idle in their actions, who toil and
labour in this life, and have no certain scope to which to direct all
their motions, and desires.
members.english: Do the things that fall on you from outside distract you at all? Then give yourself leisure to learn some further good thing, and stop wandering. But now there is the other kind of drifting to guard against as well. For people play the fool through their actions too, those who are worn out by life and have no target at which to direct every impulse and, in general, every impression.
members.greek: Περισπᾷ τί σε τὰ ἔξωθεν ἐμπίπτοντα; καὶ σχολὴν πάρεχε σεαυτῷ τοῦ προσμανθάνειν ἀγαθόν τι καὶ παῦσαι ῥεμβόμενος. ἤδη δὲ καὶ τὴν ἑτέραν περιφορὰν φυλακτέον· ληροῦσι γὰρ καὶ διὰ πράξεων οἱ κεκμηκότες τῷ βίῳ καὶ μὴ ἔχοντες σκοπόν, ἐφ’ ὃν πᾶσαν ὁρμὴν καὶ καθάπαξ φαντασίαν ἀπευθύνουσιν.

members.text:
What use is there of suspicion at all? or, why should thoughts
of mistrust, and suspicion concerning that which is future, trouble thy
mind at all? What now is to be done, if thou mayest search and inquiry
into that, what needs thou care for more? And if thou art well able to
perceive it alone, let no man divert thee from it. But if alone thou
doest not so well perceive it, suspend thine action, and take advice
from the best. And if there be anything else that doth hinder thee, go
on with prudence and discretion, according to the present occasion
and opportunity, still proposing that unto thyself, which thou doest
conceive most right and just. For to hit that aright, and to speed in
the prosecution of it, must needs be happiness, since it is that only
which we can truly and properly be said to miss of, or miscarry in.
members.english: What need is there of guessing, when you are free to look at what has to be done, and, if you see it clearly, to go that way with good will and without turning back; and if you do not see it clearly, to hold off and use the best advisers; and if some other things stand in the way of this, to go forward as present means allow, in a considered way, holding to what appears just? For to reach this is best, since failure, at any rate, is falling away from this.
members.greek: Τίς ὑπονοίας χρεία παρὸν σκοπεῖν τί δεῖ πραχθῆναι, κἂν μὲν συνορᾷς, εὐμενῶς, ἀμεταστρεπτὶ ταύτῃ χωρεῖν· ἐὰν δὲ μὴ συνορᾷς, ἐπέχειν καὶ συμβούλοις τοῖς ἀρίστοις χρῆσθαι· ἐὰν δὲ ἕτερά τινα πρὸς ταῦτα ἀντιβαίνῃ, προιέναι κατὰ τὰς παρούσας ἀφορμὰς λελογισμένως, ἐχόμενον τοῦ φαινομένου δικαίου; ἄριστον γὰρ κατατυγχάνειν τούτου, ἐπεί τοι ἥ γε ἀπόπτωσις ἀπὸ τούτου ἐστίν.

members.text:
The things themselves (which either to get or to avoid thou art put
to so much trouble) come not unto thee themselves; but thou in a manner
goest unto them. Let then thine own judgment and opinion concerning
those things be at rest; and as for the things themselves, they stand
still and quiet, without any noise or stir at all; and so shall all
pursuing and flying cease.
members.english: The things whose pursuit and avoidance throw you into turmoil do not come to you, but in a way you yourself go to them. At least let your judgment about them be quiet, and they will stay unmoving, and you will be seen neither pursuing nor avoiding.
members.greek: Εἰ μὲν Οὐκ ἔρχεται ἐπὶ σὲ τὰ πράγματα ὧν αἱ διώξεις καὶ φυγαὶ θορυβοῦσί σε, ἀλλὰ τρόπον τινὰ αὐτὸς ἐπʼ ἐκεῖνα ἔρχῃ· τὸ γοῦν κρῖμα τὸ περὶ αὐτῶν ἡσυχαζέτω κἀκεῖνα μενεῖ ἀτρεμοῦντα καὶ οὔτε διώκων οὔτε φεύγων ὀφθήσῃ.

members.text:
Now much time and leisure doth he gain, who is not curious to know
what his neighbour hath said, or hath done, or hath attempted, but only
what he doth himself, that it may be just and holy? or to express it in
Agathos' words, Not to look about upon the evil conditions of others,
but to run on straight in the line, without any loose and extravagant
agitation.
members.english: How much leisure a person gains who does not look at what their neighbour said or did or thought, but only at what they themselves are doing, so that this very thing may be just and holy, or in keeping with the good man: not to look round at a dark character, but to run straight along the line, not thrown this way and that.
members.greek: Ὅσην εὐσχολίαν κερδαίνει ὁ μὴ βλέπων τί ὁ πλησίον εἶπεν ἢ ἔπραξεν ἢ διενοήθη, ἀλλὰ μόνον τί αὐτὸς ποιεῖ, ἵνα αὐτὸ τοῦτο δίκαιον ᾖ καὶ ὅσιον ἢ † κατὰ τὸν ἀγαθὸν· μὴ μέλαν ἦθος περιβλέπεσθαι, ἀλλʼ ἐπὶ τῆς γραμμῆς τρέχειν ὀρθόν, μὴ διερριμμένον.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 2.11 is 2.12–13, 7.20 is 7.27–28, 10.24 is 10.23–24, 6.15 is 6.16, 2.4 is 2.7, 10.13 is 10.12, 11.10 is 11.11, 4.15 is 4.18 and 12.2 is 12.2–3; 4.3, 3.4 and 10.1 are the same.

Reads the soul (4.3), the ruling part (3.4, 7.20, 10.24), the guardian spirit within (2.11) and the mind (4.3, 12.2) as one thing, called “my mind” or “what is within me”. This section does not say that the guardian spirit is the mind; the identification is the editor’s.

Puts praise into claim 2 with not watching other people. 3.4 sets no store only by the praise of those who do not live by nature; the claim follows 6.15’s “the many”. 4.3’s own reasons against petty fame (forgetting, the earth a point) are not quoted.

Keeps claim 6, acting with an aim, though its passages do not speak of retreat. 2.4 begins with distraction from outside and 4.15 with the leisure gained by not watching a neighbour; the editor reads them as where the retreat sends me back to.
articles.limit: The section holds together less well than its title: 2.4, 10.13 and 4.15 are about aim rather than retreat, and 4.3 feeds three claims, so much rests on one long passage. Much of it is said elsewhere: going back into myself, and doing it continually (claim 1 and the item from 4.3), is in Article 25’s claims 1 and 3; that the place makes no difference is Article 17’s claim 4 and Article 18’s claim 1; claim 3 repeats Articles 7 and 8; claim 4 comes near Article 2’s claim on the body; claim 5 comes near Articles 10 and 16; and asking what my mind is being used for (10.24) and going straight toward a target (claim 6) are in Article 31’s claims 3 and 6, with holding to one aim and going straight on in Articles 1 and 2. Articles 22, 26 and 27 turn my attention to other people’s minds for a purpose, which claim 2’s exception for the common good may allow, though no passage here says so; what this article adds is the retreat as a place I can reach at any hour, keeping to my own mind instead of to what others say and do, and, in claim 6, seeing clearly what has to be done and not being thrown about.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, three claims gain a second author: the good that is my own, keeping to what is necessary, and what pulls me away from it. “Why” gains his argument that reason is a human being’s own good, and “In action” gains where the good in a choice lies. He limits the claim that no one can prevent me from living well: nothing can break the happiness of the wise, but mine can be broken off while I am short of perfection, and old age can shatter the mind.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a ground: each thing is judged by its own good, and a human being’s own good is reason brought to perfection. Its second half is narrowed in the second claim: he grants it fully only to the wise.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: come back to the Good that is really yours
piece.follows: There is a good that is truly my own, and I should come back to it.
piece.context: Letter 124, on the good grasped by reason. Seneca tells Lucilius to stop rivalling animals in strength and looks; “the Good” is a clear, flawless mind: perfect reason.
gives: That is the good that is my own

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: how pleasant and unimpeded life is for those who follow these laws, but how bitter and perplexed it is for those who have put their trust in opinion rather than in nature
piece.follows: Life is easy and unhindered for those who follow nature’s laws, and bitter and confused for those who trust opinion.
piece.context: Letter 48, against logic games. Philosophy should show people what nature makes necessary and what superfluous; “these laws” are nature’s simple laws on that.
gives: spares me toil and trouble

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Abandon those pursuits which heretofore have caused you to run hither and thither.
piece.follows: The pursuits that have kept me running here and there are to be given up.
piece.context: Letter 84: reason’s voice, as Seneca imagines it, on making the mind one whole. “Those pursuits” are the riches, pleasures and office she tells one to give up next.
gives: it pulls me about

items.label: why
items.role: Why reason is my own good
items.t: Everything is judged by its own good, as a vine is valued for its wine and a stag for its speed. Strength, beauty and speed I share with animals; reason brought to perfection is the good that is my own as a human being.
items.why: Marcus says that nothing is better than the spirit within and its virtue, and does not say why. Seneca argues it: each thing is judged by what is its own, and what is a human being’s own is reason, which no animal shares.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Everything is estimated by the standard of its own good. The vine is valued for its productiveness and the flavour of its wine, the stag for his speed.
support.follows: Each thing is valued by the good that is its own, as a vine for its wine and a stag for its speed.
support.context: Letter 76 sets out to prove that there is only one good. Each thing, vine, stag or dog, is valued for the quality it was brought into being for.
gives: Everything is judged by its own good
as a vine is valued for its wine and a stag for its speed

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Man is strong; so is the lion. Man is comely; so is the peacock. Man is swift; so is the horse.
support.follows: Strength, beauty and speed a human being shares with the lion, the peacock and the horse.
support.context: Letter 76, in the argument that there is only one good: qualities a human being shares with animals, which therefore cannot be his own good.
gives: Strength, beauty and speed I share with animals

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Perfect reason is therefore the good peculiar to man; all other qualities he shares in some degree with animals and plants.
support.follows: Perfect reason is the good peculiar to a human being; every other quality animals or plants share.
support.context: Letter 76, in the argument that there is only one good: what is best in a human being is reason, by which he surpasses the animals.
gives: reason brought to perfection is the good that is my own as a human being

items.label: action
items.role: Where the good lies in a choice
items.t: I may seek health, rest and freedom from pain, not because they are goods but because they are according to nature. What is good is not the thing I choose but the quality of my choice.
items.why: 10.2 says I am to take up what my animal nature asks for unless it makes me worse as a rational being, and 3.7 says to admit it when a benefit is only an animal’s. Neither says what is good in such a choice. Seneca says: not the thing chosen but the choosing.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Of course I shall seek them, but not because they are goods,—I shall seek them because they are according to nature
support.follows: Health, rest and freedom from pain may be sought because they are according to nature, not because they are goods.
support.context: Letter 92, on the happy life. An objector asks whether health, rest and freedom from pain, which do not hinder virtue, should be sought; “them” are those three.
gives: I may seek health, rest and freedom from pain
not because they are goods but because they are according to nature

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the good is not in the thing selected, but in the quality of the selection
support.follows: The good lies not in what is chosen but in how well it is chosen.
support.context: Letter 92, on choosing neat clothing: the choice of it is a good, the clothing is not. “The thing selected” is whatever is chosen, clothing or health.
gives: What is good is not the thing I choose but the quality of my choice

items.t: Seneca agrees that nothing from outside can break the happiness of the wise man (Ep. 72.4), but he grants this only to the wise: the happiness of anyone still short of perfection can be broken off. He also names a case Marcus does not name here, old age shattering the mind (Ep. 58.35). He gives it as the premise of his rule on when to leave life, not as an objection, and old age is not plainly a thing from outside. This narrows the claim; it does not deny it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: It is those who are still short of perfection whose happiness can be broken off; the joy of a wise man, on the other hand, is a woven fabric, rent by no chance happening and by no change of fortune
support.follows: The happiness of one not yet perfect can be broken off; the wise man’s joy no chance can tear.
support.context: Letter 72, on business crowding out philosophy. Someone says that something will hinder him; Seneca answers that only the happiness of the imperfect can be broken off.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: if old age begins to shatter my mind, and to pull its various faculties to pieces
support.follows: Old age can begin to shatter the mind and pull its faculties apart.
support.context: Letter 58 ends on when one may leave life. Seneca will keep his old age while it leaves his mind intact; what may shatter the mind is old age.

; but while I am short of perfection my happiness can be broken off, and old age can shatter my mind

passages.title: On the true good as attained by reason
passages.text: Are you not willing to abandon all these details—wherein you must acknowledge defeat, striving as you are for something that is not your own—and come back to the Good that is really yours? And what is this Good? It is a clear and flawless mind, which rivals that of God, raised far above mortal concerns, and counting nothing of its own to be outside itself. You are a reasoning animal. What Good, then, lies within you? Perfect reason. Are you willing to develop this to its farthest limits—to its greatest degree of increase?

passages.title: On quibbling as unworthy of the philosopher
passages.text: Tell them what nature has made necessary, and what superfluous; tell them how simple are the laws that she has laid down, how pleasant and unimpeded life is for those who follow these laws, but how bitter and perplexed it is for those who have put their trust in opinion rather than in nature. I should deem your games of logic to be of some avail in relieving men’s burdens, if you could first show me what part of these burdens they will relieve. What among these games of yours banishes lust? Or controls it? Would that I could say that they were merely of no profit! They are positively harmful. I can make it perfectly clear to you whenever you wish, that a noble spirit when involved in such subtleties is impaired and weakened.

passages.title: On gathering ideas [ 1 ]
passages.text: “How,” you ask, “can this be accomplished?” By constant effort, and by doing nothing without the approval of reason. And if you are willing to hear her voice, she will say to you: “Abandon those pursuits which heretofore have caused you to run hither and thither. Abandon riches, which are either a danger or a burden to the possessor. Abandon the pleasures of the body and of the mind; they only soften and weaken you. Abandon your quest for office; it is a swollen, idle, and empty thing, a thing that has no goal, as anxious to see no one outstrip it as to see no one at its heels. It is afflicted with envy, and in truth with a twofold envy; and you see how wretched a man’s plight is if he who is the object of envy feels envy also.”

passages.title: On learning wisdom in old age
passages.text: Everything is estimated by the standard of its own good. The vine is valued for its productiveness and the flavour of its wine, the stag for his speed. We ask, with regard to beasts of burden, how sturdy of back they are; for their only use is to bear burdens. If a dog is to find the trail of a wild beast, keenness of scent is of first importance; if to catch his quarry, swiftness of foot; if to attack and harry it, courage. In each thing that quality should be best for which the thing is brought into being and by which it is judged.

passages.title: On learning wisdom in old age
passages.text: And what quality is best in man? It is reason; by virtue of reason he surpasses the animals, and is surpassed only by the gods. Perfect reason is therefore the good peculiar to man; all other qualities he shares in some degree with animals and plants. Man is strong; so is the lion. Man is comely; so is the peacock. Man is swift; so is the horse. I do not say that man is surpassed in all these qualities. I am not seeking to find that which is greatest in him, but that which is peculiarly his own. Man has body; so also have trees. Man has the power to act and to move at will; so have beasts and worms. Man has a voice; but how much louder is the voice of the dog, how much shriller that of the eagle, how much deeper that of the bull, how much sweeter and more melodious that of the nightingale!

passages.title: On the happy life [ 1 ]
passages.text: “What, then,” comes the retort, “if good health, rest, and freedom from pain are not likely to hinder virtue, shall you not seek all these?” Of course I shall seek them, but not because they are goods,—I shall seek them because they are according to nature and because they will be acquired through the exercise of good judgment on my part. What, then, will be good in them? This alone,—that it is a good thing to choose them. For when I don suitable attire, or walk as I should, or dine as I ought to dine, it is not my dinner, or my walk, or my dress that are goods, but the deliberate choice which I show in regard to them, as I observe, in each thing I do, a mean that conforms with reason.

passages.title: On the happy life [ 1 ]
passages.text: Let me also add that the choice of neat clothing is a fitting object of a man’s efforts; for man is by nature a neat and well-groomed animal. Hence the choice of neat attire, and not neat attire in itself, is a good; since the good is not in the thing selected, but in the quality of the selection. Our actions are honourable, but not the actual things which we do.

passages.title: On business as the enemy of philosophy
passages.text: He says: “Something will happen to hinder me.” No, not in the case of the man whose spirit, no matter what his business may be, is happy and alert. It is those who are still short of perfection whose happiness can be broken off; the joy of a wise man, on the other hand, is a woven fabric, rent by no chance happening and by no change of fortune; at all times and in all places he is at peace. For his joy depends on nothing external and looks for no boon from man or fortune. His happiness is something within himself; it would depart from his soul if it entered in from the outside; it is born there.

passages.title: On being
passages.text: Do not hear me with reluctance, as if my statement applied directly to you, but weigh what I have to say. It is this: that I shall not abandon old age, if old age preserves me intact for myself, and intact as regards the better part of myself; but if old age begins to shatter my mind, and to pull its various faculties to pieces, if it leaves me, not life, but only the breath of life, I shall rush out of a house that is crumbling and tottering.

claims.t: I prefer the spirit within me and its virtue to everything else: nothing in human life is better than justice, truth, self-control and courage. That is the good that is my own. Everything else is small beside it, and I chase after none of it and run from none of it.
claims.shared: Both 3.7 and 3.8 put the spirit within first: in 3.7 nothing appears better than “the spirit itself that is seated in you”, in 3.8 the good person “has preferred their own mind and spirit, and the rites of its virtue”. 3.7 and 5.28 both name a good that is one’s own (“that good which is proper to you and is yours”; “to have its good in a just disposition and just action”), and 3.8 and 3.13 both say the person flees nothing (“neither pursuing nor fleeing”; “waiting for nothing and fleeing nothing”).
claims.changed: 3.7 puts it as a test, “if nothing appears better”; the claim states the answer that 3.7 expects. 3.8 says “neither pursuing nor fleeing” and 3.13 “waiting for nothing and fleeing nothing”, with no object; the claim limits both to the things set below the spirit, so it does not forbid choosing the better and holding on to it. 5.28 speaks of every rational being; the claim says “me”.

support.quote: But if nothing appears better than the spirit itself that is seated in you
support.follows: If nothing appears better than the spirit seated within me, that spirit is the best thing I have.
gives: I prefer the spirit within me and its virtue to everything else

support.quote: whoever has preferred their own mind and spirit, and the rites of its virtue
support.follows: Whoever has preferred their own mind and spirit and its virtue does not make a tragedy of things and does not groan.
gives: I prefer the spirit within me and its virtue to everything else

support.quote: If you find in human life anything better than justice, truth, self-control, courage
support.follows: Justice, truth, self-control and courage are the standard that anything better in human life would have to beat.
gives: nothing in human life is better than justice, truth, self-control and courage

support.quote: that good which is proper to you and is yours
support.follows: There is a good that belongs to me as my own, and I am to honour it above everything else.
gives: That is the good that is my own

support.quote: to have its good in a just disposition and just action, and to have its desire stop there
support.follows: A rational being’s good lies in being just and acting justly, and its desire should go no further than that.
gives: That is the good that is my own

support.quote: if you find everything else smaller and cheaper than this, give room to nothing else
support.follows: If everything else looks smaller and cheaper than the spirit within, nothing else should be given room.
gives: Everything else is small beside it

support.quote: Greatest of all, they will live neither pursuing nor fleeing.
support.follows: Whoever prefers their own mind and spirit lives without chasing things and without running from them.
gives: I chase after none of it and run from none of it
run from none of it

support.quote: waiting for nothing and fleeing nothing
support.follows: Living well requires, among other things, waiting for nothing and running from nothing.
gives: run from none of it

claims.t: No one can prevent me from living well, or from doing and saying what is according to nature. Nothing from outside stands in the way of my acting justly, with self-control and good sense.
claims.shared: Four passages say that no one can prevent it: “there is no one who can prevent this” (3.13), “there is no one who prevents you” (2.6), “No one will prevent you” (6.53), “no one at all can prevent you” (8.30). 3.13 and 11.15 both speak of living well and say it is in my power; 2.6 and 6.53 both say what is unpreventable is what accords with nature.
claims.changed: The four passages name different things that no one can prevent: living well (3.13), doing and saying what fits the nature of the whole (2.6), living by the reason of my own nature (6.53), each action doing its part (8.30). The claim puts living well first and names doing and saying after it. 2.6 speaks of the nature of which I am a part, 6.53 of my own nature; the claim says “according to nature” and does not choose between them. 8.30 says “at least” of acting justly, with self-control and good sense, and grants that some other activity may be prevented; the claim keeps that second sentence to those three.

support.quote: you will live well. And there is no one who can prevent this.
support.follows: Whoever does the present work by right reason and keeps their spirit pure will live well, and no one can prevent it.
gives: No one can prevent me
living well

support.quote: To live life through in the finest way: this power is in the soul
support.follows: The power to live in the finest way lies in the soul itself.
gives: living well

support.quote: there is no one who prevents you from always doing and saying what is in keeping with the nature of which you are a part
support.follows: No one can stop me from always doing and saying what fits the nature of the whole I am part of.

claims.t: In all I say and do, I keep to what is necessary, what reason requires of a being made for life among fellow citizens, and I strip away the rest, needless impressions as well as needless acts. Keeping to it is taking the short road, the one according to nature, and it spares me toil and trouble.
claims.shared: Both passages are about everything one says and does (4.20: “most of what we say and do”; 4.43: “say and do everything in the soundest way”), and both say that keeping to the right course frees one from burden: 4.20 “more leisure and be less troubled”, 4.43 “frees you from toil”.
claims.changed: 4.20 puts this as a cautious question (“Might it not be better…?”) that suggests its answer; the claim states the answer. 4.20 says doing only what is necessary leaves one “less troubled”; 4.43 says the short road “frees you from toil and from hanging back, and from all contriving and affectation”. The claim says “spares me toil and trouble” for both, and drops hanging back, contriving and affectation. That the necessary road and the short road are the same road is the editor’s reading.

support.quote: For most of what we say and do is not necessary, and if a person strips it away they will have more leisure and be less troubled.

gives: I keep to what is necessary, what reason requires of a being made for life among fellow citizens

support.quote: For a purpose of this kind frees you from toil and from hanging back, and from all contriving and affectation.

claims.t: When something seems to benefit me, I ask whether it benefits me as a rational being or as an animal. If as an animal, I admit plainly that it is only an animal’s benefit, and I take what my animal nature asks for only if it does not make me worse as a rational being. What is rational in me is also made for life among fellow citizens.
claims.shared: Both passages tell apart what I am as an animal and what I am as a rational being, and both put the rational first: 3.7 “If it benefits you as a rational being, keep to that. But if as an animal, say so”; 10.2 “unless your nature as a rational animal is going to be put in a worse state”. Both also join the rational to the civic: 3.7 “the rational and civic good”, 10.2 “what is rational is by that very fact also civic”.
claims.changed: 10.2 speaks of what my animal nature asks for, not of a benefit, and asks no question; that the two passages speak of one thing is the editor’s reading. 10.2 begins one step lower, with what I need simply as a growing body, and climbs to the animal and then to the rational; the claim keeps only the last step. 3.7 answers a speaker who says “the better is what benefits”; the claim makes the question my own. “Civic” in both passages is put as “made for life among fellow citizens”.

support.quote: “But the better is what benefits.” If it benefits you as a rational being, keep to that. But if as an animal, say so
support.follows: If something benefits me as a rational being I should keep to it; if only as an animal, I should admit that.
gives: When something seems to benefit me, I ask whether it benefits me

claims.t: I put my life together one action at a time. I carry through what lies before me step by step, as I would spell out a name letter by letter, and I join one good to the next without leaving a gap.
claims.shared: 5.28 and 6.24 both say “step by step”: to “judge and act step by step, as along a road” (5.28) and to “carry through step by step what lies before you” (6.24). 8.30 says something near it of a whole life: “put your life together one action at a time”.
claims.changed: 6.24 speaks of each duty, 8.30 of a life, 5.28 of the road a life travels; the claim speaks of my life. The link between “step by step” and 8.30’s “one action at a time” leans on the translation: in 5.28 and 6.24 the Greek is an idiom for “methodically, in due order”, rendered “step by step”. 12.22 adds the joining of one good to the next.

support.quote: You must put your life together one action at a time

claims.t: If I lean toward anything other than the good that is my own and count it as a benefit to me, such as praise, office, wealth or pleasure, it pulls me about, takes control of me and carries me off course. I count nothing as a benefit that will force me to break faith, to hate or to play a part. The way back is to choose the better, simply and freely, and hold on to it.
claims.shared: Both passages warn against giving weight to what is not my own good: 3.7 against having “tipped and turned aside toward anything else”, 3.8 against valuing “as a benefit to yourself” what will one day harm me.
claims.changed: 3.8 does not say that praise or wealth forces anyone to break faith; it forbids counting as a benefit whatever will. The claim keeps that as a rule of its own. 3.8 lists seven things such a benefit forces: to break faith, abandon self-respect, hate, suspect, curse, play a part, and want what must be hidden behind walls and curtains; the claim keeps three. “The way back” is the editor’s name for 3.7’s command to choose the better.

support.quote: Once you have tipped and turned aside toward anything else, you will no longer be able, without being pulled about, to honor above all else

it pulls me about
