single.quote: if, I say, you see anything better than this, turn to it with your whole soul and enjoy what is found to be best
single.label: If I find better
single.t: If I ever see anything better than this, I shall turn to it with my whole soul and enjoy what I have found to be best.
single.why: Only 3.7 allows that something might be better than justice and the spirit within, and says what to do then. No other passage of the section considers it.
single.follows: If something better than justice and a mind content with itself is ever seen, one should turn to it wholeheartedly.

single.quote: keep your own spirit standing pure, as if you had to give it back this very moment
single.label: Keeping it pure
single.t: I keep my own spirit pure, as if I had to give it back this very moment.
single.why: Only 3.13 speaks of keeping the spirit pure and of giving it back. 3.8 shares the readiness (“even if they have to depart this moment”) but not the purity or the giving back, so it is not fused.
single.follows: I should keep my spirit pure as though I had to hand it back right now.

single.quote: none of them puts a judgment about itself into us, nor comes to us, but the things stay still, and it is we who produce the verdicts about them and, as it were, write them in ourselves, when it is in our power not to write them, and in our power, even if one somehow escapes notice, to wipe it out at once
single.label: Wiping out a verdict
single.t: Things do not put judgments about themselves into me; I write the verdicts myself. I need not write them, and if one gets written without my noticing, I can wipe it out at once.
single.why: Only 11.15 says where my verdicts about things come from and that I can wipe one out. It is kept as a way back when a wrong verdict has been written.
single.follows: Things do not judge themselves in me; I write the verdicts, and I can refuse to write them or wipe one out at once.

single.quote: if they are contrary to nature, look for what there is for you that is according to your own nature and hurry toward that, even if it brings no reputation
single.label: When things go against nature
single.t: When what I meet is contrary to nature, I look for what there is for me that is according to my own nature and hurry toward it, even if it brings me no reputation.
single.why: Only 11.15 says what to do when things are contrary to nature. In 11.15 “they” are the indifferent things just named, and the translators note that the sentence before is obscure.
single.follows: When things are contrary to nature, I should seek what accords with my own nature and go for it, even if it brings no fame.

members.text:
If thou shalt find anything in this mortal life better than
righteousness, than truth, temperance, fortitude, and in general better
than a mind contented both with those things which according to right
and reason she doth, and in those, which without her will and knowledge
happen unto thee by the providence; if I say, thou canst find out
anything better than this, apply thyself unto it with thy whole heart,
and that which is best wheresoever thou dost find it, enjoy freely. But
if nothing thou shalt find worthy to be preferred to that spirit which
is within thee; if nothing better than to subject unto thee thine own
lusts and desires, and not to give way to any fancies or imaginations
before thou hast duly considered of them, nothing better than to
withdraw thyself (to use Socrates his words) from all sensuality, and
submit thyself unto the gods, and to have care of all men in general: if
thou shalt find that all other things in comparison of this, are but
vile, and of little moment; then give not way to any other thing, which
being once though but affected and inclined unto, it will no more be in
thy power without all distraction as thou oughtest to prefer and to
pursue after that good, which is thine own and thy proper good. For it
is not lawful, that anything that is of another and inferior kind and
nature, be it what it will, as either popular applause, or honour, or
riches, or pleasures; should be suffered to confront and contest as it
were, with that which is rational, and operatively good. For all these
things, if once though but for a while, they begin to please, they
presently prevail, and pervert a man's mind, or turn a man from the
right way. Do thou therefore I say absolutely and freely make choice of
that which is best, and stick unto it. Now, that they say is best, which
is most profitable. If they mean profitable to man as he is a rational
man, stand thou to it, and maintain it; but if they mean profitable, as
he is a creature, only reject it; and from this thy tenet and conclusion
keep off carefully all plausible shows and colours of external
appearance, that thou mayest be able to discern things rightly.
members.english: If you find in human life anything better than justice, truth, self-control, courage, and, in a word, than your thought being content with itself in the things where it has you acting according to right reason, and in fate, in the things that are allotted without your choosing; if, I say, you see anything better than this, turn to it with your whole soul and enjoy what is found to be best. But if nothing appears better than the spirit itself that is seated in you, which has put its own impulses under itself, which examines the impressions, which has pulled itself away, as Socrates used to say, from the feelings of the senses, and has put itself under the gods, and cares for human beings; if you find everything else smaller and cheaper than this, give room to nothing else. Once you have tipped and turned aside toward anything else, you will no longer be able, without being pulled about, to honor above all else that good which is proper to you and is yours. For it is not permitted that anything whatever of a different kind, such as praise from the many, or offices, or wealth, or the enjoyment of pleasures, should take up a position against the rational and civic good. All these, even if for a little while they seem to fit, suddenly take control and carry you off course. But you, I say, simply and freely choose the better and hold on to it. “But the better is what benefits.” If it benefits you as a rational being, keep to that. But if as an animal, say so, and guard your verdict without conceit. Only see that you make the examination without slipping.
members.greek: Εἰ μὲν κρεῖττον εὑρίσκεις ἐν τῷ ἀνθρωπίνῳ βίῳ δικαιοσύνης, ἀληθείας, σωφροσύνης, ἀνδρείας καὶ καθάπαξ τοῦ ἀρκεῖσθαι ἑαυτῇ τὴν διάνοιάν σου, ἐν οἷς κατὰ τὸν λόγον τὸν ὀρθὸν πράσσοντά σε παρέχεται, καὶ ἐν τῇ εἱμαρμένῃ ἐν τοῖς ἀπροαιρέτως ἀπονεμομένοις· εἰ τούτου, φημί, κρεῖττόν τι ὁρᾷς, ἐπʼ ἐκεῖνο ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς τραπόμενος τοῦ ἀρίστου εὑρισκομένου ἀπόλαυε. εἰ δὲ μηδὲν κρεῖττον φαίνεται αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἐνιδρυμένου ἐν σοὶ δαίμονος, τάς τε ἰδίας ὁρμὰς ὑποτεταχότος ἑαυτῷ καὶ τὰς φαντασίας ἐξετάζοντος καὶ τῶν αἰσθητικῶν πείσεων, ὡς ὁ Σωκράτης ἔλεγεν, ἑαυτὸν ἀφειλκυκότος καὶ τοῖς θεοῖς ὑποτεταχότος ἑαυτὸν καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων προκηδομένου· εἰ τούτου πάντα τὰ ἄλλα μικρότερα καὶ εὐτελέστερα εὑρίσκεις, μηδενὶ χώραν δίδου ἑτέρῳ, πρὸς ὃ ῥέψας ἅπαξ καὶ ἀποκλίνας οὐκέτι ἀπερισπάστως τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἐκεῖνο, τὸ ἴδιον καὶ τὸ σόν, προτιμᾶν δυνήσῃ. ἀντικαθῆσθαι γὰρ τῷ λογικῷ καὶ πολιτικῷ ἀγαθῷ οὐ θέμις οὐδʼ ὁτιοῦν ἑτερογενές, οἷον τὸν παρὰ τῶν πολλῶν ἔπαινον ἢ ἀρχὰς ἢ πλοῦτον ἢ ἀπολαύσεις ἡδονῶν· πάντα ταῦτα, κἂν πρὸς ὀλίγον ἐναρμόζειν δόξῃ, κατεκράτησεν ἄφνω καὶ παρήνεγκεν. σὺ δέ, φημί, ἁπλῶς καὶ ἐλευθέρως ἑλοῦ τὸ κρεῖττον καὶ τούτου ἀντέχου· “κρεῖττον δὲ τὸ συμφέρον.” εἰ μὲν τὸ ὡς λογικῷ, τοῦτο τήρει· εἰ δὲ τὸ ὡς ζῴῳ, ἀπόφηναι, καὶ ἀτύφως φύλασσε τὴν κρίσιν· μόνον ὅπως ἀσφαλῶς τὴν ἐξέτασιν ποιήσῃ.

members.text:
If thou shalt intend that which is present, following the rule of
right and reason carefully, solidly, meekly, and shalt not intermix
any other businesses, but shall study this only to preserve thy spirit
unpolluted, and pure, and shall cleave unto him without either hope
or fear of anything, in all things that thou shalt either do or speak,
contenting thyself with heroical truth, thou shalt live happily; and
from this, there is no man that can hinder thee.
members.english: If you do the work that is present, following right reason, earnestly, vigorously, with good will, and with nothing as a side business, but keep your own spirit standing pure, as if you had to give it back this very moment; if you join this together, waiting for nothing and fleeing nothing, but content with the present work that is according to nature and with heroic truth in what you say and utter, you will live well. And there is no one who can prevent this.
members.greek: Ἐὰν τὸ παρὸν ἐνεργῇς ἑπόμενος τῷ ὀρθῷ λόγῳ, ἐσπουδασμένως, ἐρρωμένως, εὐμενῶς, καὶ μηδὲν παρεμπόρευμα, ἀλλὰ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ δαίμονα καθαρὸν ἑστῶτα τηρῇς, ὡσεὶ καὶ ἤδη ἀποδοῦναι δέοι· ἐὰν τοῦτο συνάπτῃς μηδὲν περιμένων μηδὲ Φεύγων, ἀλλὰ τῇ παρούσῃ κατὰ Φύσιν ἐνεργείᾳ καὶ τῇ ὧν λέγεις καὶ Φθέγγῃ ἡρωικῇ ἀληθείᾳ ἀρκούμενος, εὐζωήσεις. ἔστι δὲ οὐδεὶς ὁ τοῦτο κωλῦσαι δυνάμενος.

members.text:
To live happily is an inward power of the soul, when she is affected
with indifferency, towards those things that are by their nature
indifferent. To be thus affected she must consider all worldly objects
both divided and whole: remembering withal that no object can of itself
beget any opinion in us, neither can come to us, but stands without
still and quiet; but that we ourselves beget, and as it were print in
ourselves opinions concerning them. Now it is in our power, not to print
them; and if they creep in and lurk in some corner, it is in our
power to wipe them off. Remembering moreover, that this care and
circumspection of thine, is to continue but for a while, and then thy
life will be at an end. And what should hinder, but that thou mayest do
well with all these things? For if they be according to nature, rejoice
in them, and let them be pleasing and acceptable unto thee. But if
they be against nature, seek thou that which is according to thine own
nature, and whether it be for thy credit or no, use all possible speed
for the attainment of it: for no man ought to be blamed, for seeking his
own good and happiness.
members.english: To live life through in the finest way: this power is in the soul, if a person is indifferent toward the things that are indifferent. And a person will be indifferent if they look at each of these things taken apart and as a whole, and remember that none of them puts a judgment about itself into us, nor comes to us, but the things stay still, and it is we who produce the verdicts about them and, as it were, write them in ourselves, when it is in our power not to write them, and in our power, even if one somehow escapes notice, to wipe it out at once; and remember that this kind of attention will be for a short time, and after that life will be over. But what is hard in it, if these things are otherwise? For if they are according to nature, rejoice in them and let them be easy for you. And if they are contrary to nature, look for what there is for you that is according to your own nature and hurry toward that, even if it brings no reputation. For there is pardon for everyone who looks for their own good.
members.greek: Κάλλιστα διαζῆν, δύναμις αὕτη ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ, ἐὰν πρὸς τὰ ἀδιάφορά τις ἀδιαφορῇ. ἀδιαφορήσει δέ, ἐὰν ἕκαστον αὐτῶν θεωρῇ διῃρημένως καὶ ὁλικῶς καὶ μεμνημένος ὅτι οὐδὲν αὐτῶν ὑπόληψιν περὶ αὐτοῦ ἡμῖν ἐμποιεῖ οὐδὲ ἔρχεται ἐφ’ ἡμᾶς, ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν ἀτρεμεῖ, ἡμεῖς δέ ἐσμεν οἱ τὰς περὶ αὐτῶν κρίσεις γεννῶντες καὶ οἷον γράφοντες ἐν ἑαυτοῖς, ἐξὸν μὲν μὴ γράφειν, ἐξὸν δέ, κἄν που λάθῃ, εὐθὺς ἐξαλεῖψαι· ὅτι ὀλίγου χρόνου ἔσται ἡ τοιαύτη προσοχὴ καὶ λοιπὸν πεπαύσεται ὁ βίος. τί μέντοι δύσκολον ἄλλως ἔχειν ταῦτα; εἰ μὲν γὰρ κατὰ φύσιν ἐστί, χαῖρε αὐτοῖς καὶ ῥᾴδια ἔστω σοι· εἰ δὲ παρὰ φύσιν, ζήτει τί ἐστί σοι κατὰ τὴν σὴν φύσιν καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦτο σπεῦδε, κἂν ἄδοξον ᾖ· παντὶ γὰρ συγγνώμη τὸ ἴδιον ἀγαθὸν ζητοῦντι.

members.text:
Never esteem of anything as profitable, which shall ever constrain
thee either to break thy faith, or to lose thy modesty; to hate any man,
to suspect, to curse, to dissemble, to lust after anything, that
requireth the secret of walls or veils. But he that preferreth before
all things his rational part and spirit, and the sacred mysteries of
virtue which issueth from it, he shall never lament and exclaim, never
sigh; he shall never want either solitude or company: and which is
chiefest of all, he shall live without either desire or fear. And as for
life, whether for a long or short time he shall enjoy his soul thus
compassed about with a body, he is altogether indifferent. For if even
now he were to depart, he is as ready for it, as for any other action,
which may be performed with modesty and decency. For all his life long,
this is his only care, that his mind may always be occupied in such
intentions and objects, as are proper to a rational sociable creature.
members.english: Never value as a benefit to yourself anything that will one day force you to break faith, to abandon your self-respect, to hate someone, to suspect, to curse, to play a part, to desire something that needs walls and curtains. For whoever has preferred their own mind and spirit, and the rites of its virtue, does not make a tragedy of things, does not groan, will need neither solitude nor a crowd. Greatest of all, they will live neither pursuing nor fleeing. Whether they will have the use of the soul, enclosed in the body, for a longer stretch of time or a shorter one matters to them not at all. For even if they have to depart this moment, they will go as free of ties as if they were about to do any other of the things that can be done with self-respect and in good order, on their guard through their whole life against this one thing only: that their thought should take any turn foreign to a living being that has mind and is civic.
members.greek: Μὴ τιμήσῃς ποτὲ ὡς συμφέρον σεαυτοῦ, ὃ ἀναγκάσει σέ ποτε τὴν πίστιν παραβῆναι, τὴν αἰδῶ ἐγκαταλιπεῖν, μισῆσαί τινα, ὑποπτεῦσαι, καταράσασθαι, ὑποκρίνασθαι, ἐπιθυμῆσαί τινος τοίχων καὶ παραπετασμάτων δεομένου. ὁ γὰρ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ νοῦν καὶ δαίμονα καὶ τὰ ὄργια τῆς τούτου ἀρετῆς προελόμενος τραγῳδίαν οὐ ποιεῖ, οὐ στενάζει, οὐκ ἐρημίας, οὐ πολυπληθείας δεήσεται· τὸ μέγιστον, ζήσει μήτε διώκων μήτε φεύγων, πότερον δὲ ἐπὶ πλέον διάστημα χρόνου τῷ σώματι περιεχομένῃ τῇ ψυχῇ ἢ ἐπ’ ἔλασσον χρήσεται, οὐδ᾽ ὁτιοῦν αὐτῷ μέλει· κἂν γὰρ ἤδη ἀπαλλάσσεσθαι δέῃ, οὕτως εὐλύτως ἄπεισιν, ὡς ἄλλο τι τῶν αἰδημόνως καὶ κοσμίως ἐνεργεῖσθαι δυναμένων ἐνεργήσων, τοῦτο μόνον παρ’ ὅλον τὸν βίον εὐλαβούμενος, τὸ τὴν διάνοιαν ἔν τινι ἀνοικείῳ νοεροῦ καὶ πολιτικοῦ ζῴου τροπῇ γενέσθαι.

members.text:
Herein doth consist happiness of life, for a man to know
thoroughly the true nature of everything; what is the matter, and what
is the form of it: with all his heart and soul, ever to do that which is
just, and to speak the truth. What then remaineth but to enjoy thy life
in a course and coherence of good actions, one upon another immediately
succeeding, and never interrupted, though for never so little a while?
members.english: What keeps a life safe: to see each thing through and through, what it is in itself, what in it is the material and what the cause; with the whole soul to do what is just and to say what is true. What is left but to enjoy living, joining one good to another so as to leave not even the shortest gap?
members.greek: Σωτηρία βίου ἕκαστον δι’ ὅλου αὐτὸ τί ἐστιν ὁρᾶν, τί μὲν αὐτοῦ τὸ ὑλικόν, τί δὲ τὸ αἰτιῶδες· ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς τὰ δίκαια ποιεῖν καὶ τἀληθῆ λέγειν. τί λοιπὸν ἢ ἀπολαύειν τοῦ ζῆν συνάπτοντα ἄλλο ἐπ’ ἄλλῳ ἀγαθόν, ὥστε μηδὲ τὸ βραχύτατον διάστημα ἀπολείπειν;

members.text:
As one who is altogether governed by nature, let it be thy care to
observe what it is that thy nature in general doth require. That
done, if thou find not that thy nature, as thou art a living sensible
creature, will be the worse for it, thou mayest proceed. Next then thou
must examine, what thy nature as thou art a living sensible creature,
doth require. And that, whatsoever it be, thou mayest admit of and do
it, if thy nature as thou art a reasonable living creature, will not be
the worse for it. Now whatsoever is reasonable, is also sociable, Keep
thyself to these rules, and trouble not thyself about idle things.
members.english: Watch what your nature asks for, taking yourself as something governed by nature only. Then do it and accept it, unless your nature as an animal is going to be put in a worse state. Next you must watch what your nature as an animal asks for, and all of this is to be taken up, unless your nature as a rational animal is going to be put in a worse state. And what is rational is by that very fact also civic. Using these rules, then, do not busy yourself with anything further.
members.greek: Παρατήρει τί σου ἡ φύσις ἐπιζητεῖ ὡς ὑπὸ φύσεως μόνον διοικουμένου· εἶτα ποίει αὐτὸ καὶ προσίεσο, εἰ μὴ χεῖρον μέλλει διατίθεσθαί σου ἡ ὡς ζῴου φύσις. ἑξῆς δὲ παρατηρητέον τί ἐπιζητεῖ σου ἡ ὡς ζῴου φύσις, καὶ πᾶν τοῦτο παραληπτέον, εἰ μὴ χεῖρον μέλλει διατίθεσθαι ἡ ὡς ζῴου λογικοῦ φύσις· ἔστι δὲ τὸ λογικὸν εὐθὺς καὶ πολιτικόν. τούτοις δὴ κανόσι χρώμενος μηδὲν περιεργάζου.

members.text:
These things thou must always have in mind: What is the nature
of the universe, and what is mine--in particular: This unto that what
relation it hath: what kind of part, of what kind of universe it is: And
that there is nobody that can hinder thee, but that thou mayest always
both do and speak those things which are agreeable to that nature,
whereof thou art a part.
members.english: These things must always be remembered: what the nature of the whole is, and what mine is, and how this one stands to that one, and what kind of part it is of what kind of whole; and that there is no one who prevents you from always doing and saying what is in keeping with the nature of which you are a part.
members.greek: Τούτων ἀεὶ δεῖ μεμνῆσθαι, τίς ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις καὶ τίς ἡ ἐμὴ καὶ πῶς αὕτη πρὸς ἐκείνην ἔχουσα καὶ ὁποῖόν τι μέρος ὁποίου τοῦ ὅλου οὖσα καὶ ὅτι οὐδεὶς ὁ κωλύων τὰ ἀκόλουθα τῇ φύσει, ἧς μέρος εἶ, πράσσειν τε ἀεὶ καὶ λέγειν.

members.text:
Contract thy whole life to the measure and proportion of one single
action. And if in every particular action thou dost perform what is
fitting to the utmost of thy power, let it suffice thee. And who can
hinder thee, but that thou mayest perform what is fitting? But there may
be some outward let and impediment. Not any, that can hinder thee, but
that whatsoever thou dost, thou may do it, justly, temperately, and
with the praise of God. Yea, but there may be somewhat, whereby some
operation or other of thine may be hindered. And then, with that very
thing that doth hinder, thou mayest he well pleased, and so by this
gentle and equanimious conversion of thy mind unto that which may be,
instead of that which at first thou didst intend, in the room of that
former action there succeedeth another, which agrees as well with this
contraction of thy life, that we now speak of.
members.english: You must put your life together one action at a time, and if each action does its own part as far as it can, be content. And no one at all can prevent you from having it do its own part. “But something from outside will stand in the way.” Nothing will, at least not in the way of acting justly, with self-control and with good sense. Some other kind of activity will perhaps be prevented; but through being well pleased with the very thing that prevents it, and through moving over with good grace to what is given, another action at once takes its place, one that will fit into the putting together of which we are speaking.
members.greek: Συντιθέναι δεῖ τὸν βίον κατὰ μίαν πρᾶξιν καὶ εἰ ἑκάστη τὸ ἑαυτῆς παρέχει ὡς οἷόν τε, ἀρκεῖσθαι· ἵνα δὲ τὸ ἑαυτῆς παρέχῃ, οὐδὲ εἷς σε κωλῦσαι δύναται.—ἀλλʼ ἐνστήσεταί τι ἔξωθεν.—οὐδὲν εἴς γε τὸ δικαίως καὶ σωφρόνως καὶ εὐλογίστως, ἄλλο δέ τι ἴσως ἐνεργητικὸν κωλυθήσεται, ἀλλὰ τῇ πρὸς αὐτὸ τὸ κώλυμα εὐαρεστήσει καὶ τῇ ἐπὶ τὸ διδόμενον εὐγνώμονι μεταβάσει εὐθὺς ἄλλη πρᾶξις ἀντικαθίσταται ἐναρμόσουσα εἰς τὴν σύνθεσιν, περὶ ἧς ὁ λόγος.

members.text:
They will say commonly, Meddle not with many things, if thou wilt
live cheerfully. Certainly there is nothing better, than for a man
to confine himself to necessary actions; to such and so many only, as
reason in a creature that knows itself born for society, will command
and enjoin. This will not only procure that cheerfulness, which from the
goodness, but that also, which from the paucity of actions doth usually
proceed. For since it is so, that most of those things, which we either
speak or do, are unnecessary; if a man shall cut them off, it must needs
follow that he shall thereby gain much leisure, and save much trouble,
and therefore at every action a man must privately by way of admonition
suggest unto himself, What? may not this that now I go about, be of the
number of unnecessary actions? Neither must he use himself to cut off
actions only, but thoughts and imaginations also, that are unnecessary
for so will unnecessary consequent actions the better be prevented and
cut off.
members.english: “Do few things,” he says, “if you mean to be cheerful.” Might it not be better to do what is necessary, and whatever the reason of a living being that is civic by nature requires, and in the way it requires? For this brings not only the cheerfulness that comes from doing things well, but also the cheerfulness that comes from doing few things. For most of what we say and do is not necessary, and if a person strips it away they will have more leisure and be less troubled. So on each occasion one must also remind oneself: “Is this perhaps one of the things that are not necessary?” And one must strip away not only the actions that are not necessary but impressions too, for then superfluous actions will not follow after them either.
members.greek: ʽὈλίγα πρῆσσε, φησίν, εἰ μέλλεις εὐθυμήσειν.ʼ μήποτε ἄμεινον τἀναγκαῖα πράσσειν καὶ ὅσα ὁ τοῦ φύσει πολιτικοῦ ζῴου λόγος αἱρεῖ καὶ ὡς αἱρεῖ; τοῦτο γὰρ οὐ μόνον τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ καλῶς πράσσειν εὐθυμίαν φέρει, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ ὀλίγα πράσσειν. τὰ πλεῖστα γὰρ ὧν λέγομεν καὶ πράσσομεν οὐκ ἀναγκαῖα ὄντα ἐάν τις περιέλῃ, εὐσχολώτερος καὶ ἀταρακτότερος ἔσται. ὅθεν δεῖ καὶ παῤ ἕκαστα ἑαυτὸν ὑπομιμνῄσκειν· μήτι τοῦτο τῶν οὐκ ἀναγκαίων; δεῖ δὲ μὴ μόνον πράξεις τὰς μὴ ἀναγκαίας περιαιρεῖν, ἀλλὰ καὶ φαντασίας· οὕτως γὰρ οὐδὲ πράξεις παρέλκουσαι ἐπακολουθήσουσιν.

members.why: Its subject is that I am a part of the whole and kin to those of my own kind, and so welcome what the whole allots and do nothing unsocial; Articles 1 and 3 say this, and it does not speak of what is best or of what no one can prevent.
members.text:
Either with Epicurus, we must fondly imagine the atoms to be the
cause of all things, or we must needs grant a nature. Let this then be
thy first ground, that thou art part of that universe, which is governed
by nature. Then secondly, that to those parts that are of the same kind
and nature as thou art, thou hast relation of kindred. For of these,
if I shall always be mindful, first as I am a part, I shall never be
displeased with anything, that falls to my particular share of the
common chances of the world. For nothing that is behoveful unto the
whole, can be truly hurtful to that which is part of it. For this
being the common privilege of all natures, that they contain nothing in
themselves that is hurtful unto them; it cannot be that the nature of
the universe (whose privilege beyond other particular natures, is,
that she cannot against her will by any higher external cause be
constrained,) should beget anything and cherish it in her bosom that
should tend to her own hurt and prejudice. As then I bear in mind that
I am a part of such an universe, I shall not be displeased with anything
that happens. And as I have relation of kindred to those parts that
are of the same kind and nature that I am, so I shall be careful to
do nothing that is prejudicial to the community, but in all my
deliberations shall they that are of my kind ever be; and the common
good, that, which all my intentions and resolutions shall drive unto,
as that which is contrary unto it, I shall by all means endeavour to
prevent and avoid. These things once so fixed and concluded, as thou
wouldst think him a happy citizen, whose constant study and practice
were for the good and benefit of his fellow citizens, and the carriage
of the city such towards him, that he were well pleased with it; so must
it needs be with thee, that thou shalt live a happy life.
members.english: Whether it is atoms or nature, let this first be laid down: that I am a part of the whole, which is governed by nature. Next, that I stand in a kind of kinship to the parts that are of the same kind as I am. For if I remember these things, then insofar as I am a part, I will not be displeased with anything that is allotted from the whole. For nothing that is good for the whole is harmful to the part. For the whole has nothing that is not good for itself. All natures have this in common, but the nature of the universe has this in addition, that it is not even forced by any cause from outside to produce anything harmful to itself. So by remembering that I am a part of a whole of this kind, I will be well pleased with everything that comes about. And insofar as I stand in a kind of kinship to the parts of the same kind, I will do nothing unsocial. Rather I will make those of my own kind my aim, and I will lead my every impulse toward what is good for all in common and lead it away from the opposite. When these things are carried through in this way, life must flow well, just as you would think that a citizen’s life flows well when that citizen goes forward through actions that profit the citizens, and welcomes whatever the city allots.
members.greek: Εἴτε ἄτομοι εἴτε φύσις, πρῶτον κείσθω ὅτι μέρος εἰμὶ τοῦ ὅλου ὑπὸ φύσεως διοικουμένου· ἔπειτα, ὅτι ἔχω πως οἰκείως πρὸς τὰ ὁμογενῆ μέρη. τούτων γὰρ μεμνημένος, καθότι μὲν μέρος εἰμί, οὐδενὶ δυσαρεστήσω τῶν ἐκ τοῦ ὅλου ἀπονεμομένων· οὐδὲν γὰρ βλαβερὸν τῷ μέρει ὃ τῷ ὅλῳ συμφέρει. οὐ γὰρ ἔχει τι τὸ ὅλον ὃ μὴ συμφέρει ἑαυτῷ, πασῶν μὲν φύσεων κοινὸν ἐχουσῶν τοῦτο, τῆς δὲ τοῦ κόσμου προσειληφυίας τὸ μηδὲ ὑπό τινος ἔξωθεν αἰτίας ἀναγκάζεσθαι βλαβερόν τι ἑαυτῇ γεννᾶν. κατὰ μὲν δὴ τὸ μεμνῆσθαι ὅτι μέρος εἰμὶ ὅλου τοῦ τοιούτου, εὐαρεστήσω παντὶ τῷ ἀποβαίνοντι, καθόσον δὲ ἔχω πως οἰκείως πρὸς τὰ ὁμογενῆ μέρη, οὐδὲν πράξω ἀκοινώνητον, μᾶλλον δὲ στοχάσομαι τῶν ὁμογενῶν καὶ πρὸς τὸ κοινῇ συμφέρον πᾶσαν ὁρμὴν ἐμαυτοῦ ἄξω καὶ ἀπὸ τοὐναντίου ἀπάξω. τούτων δὲ οὕτως περαινομένων ἀνάγκη τὸν βίον εὐροεῖν, ὡς ἂν καὶ πολίτου βίον εὔρουν ἐπινοήσειας προιόντος διὰ πράξεων τοῖς πολίταις λυσιτελῶν καὶ ὅπερ ἂν ἡ πόλις ἀπονέμῃ, τοῦτο ἀσπαζομένου.

members.text:
Thou mayest always speed, if thou wilt but make choice of the
right way; if in the course both of thine opinions and actions, thou
wilt observe a true method. These two things be common to the souls, as
of God, so of men, and of every reasonable creature, first that in their
own proper work they cannot be hindered by anything: and secondly, that
their happiness doth consist in a disposition to, and in the practice of
righteousness; and that in these their desire is terminated.
members.english: You can always have your life flow well, if indeed you can also travel a good road, if indeed you can also judge and act step by step, as along a road. These two things are common to the soul of god, and of a human being, and of every rational living being: not to be hindered by anything else; and to have its good in a just disposition and just action, and to have its desire stop there.
members.greek: Δύνασαι ἀεὶ εὐροεῖν, εἴ γε καὶ εὐοδεῖν, εἴ γε καὶ ὁδῷ ὑπολαμβάνειν καὶ πράσσειν. δύο ταῦτα κοινὰ τῇ τε τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τῇ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου καὶ παντὸς λογικοῦ ζῴου ψυχῇ· τὸ μὴ ἐμποδίζεσθαι ὑπ’ ἄλλου καὶ τὸ ἐν τῇ δικαικῇ διαθέσει καὶ πράξει ἔχειν τὸ ἀγαθὸν καὶ ἐνταῦθα τὴν ὄρεξιν ἀπολήγειν.

members.text:
Let thy course ever be the most compendious way. The most
compendious, is that which is according to nature: that is, in all both
words and deeds, ever to follow that which is most sound and perfect.
For such a resolution will free a man from all trouble, strife,
dissembling, and ostentation.
members.english: Always run to the short road. And the short road is the one according to nature, so that you say and do everything in the soundest way. For a purpose of this kind frees you from toil and from hanging back, and from all contriving and affectation.
members.greek: Ἐπὶ τὴν σύντομον ἀεὶ τρέχε· σύντομος δὲ ἡ κατὰ φύσιν, ὥστε κατὰ τὸ ὑγιέστατον πᾶν λέγειν καὶ πράσσειν. ἀπαλλάσσει γὰρ ἡ τοιαύτη πρόθεσις κόπων καὶ στραγγείας καὶ πάσης οἰκονομίας καὶ κομψείας.

members.text:
No man can hinder thee to live as thy nature doth require. Nothing
can happen unto thee, but what the common good of nature doth require.
members.english: No one will prevent you from living according to the reason of your own nature. Nothing will happen to you contrary to the reason of the common nature.
members.greek: Κατὰ τὸν λόγον τῆς σῆς φύσεως βιοῦν σε οὐδεὶς κωλύσει· παρὰ τὸν λόγον τῆς κοινῆς φύσεως οὐδέν σοι συμβήσεται.

members.text:
if any should put this question unto thee, how this word Antoninus
is written, wouldst thou not presently fix thine intention upon it, and
utter out in order every letter of it? And if any shall begin to gainsay
thee, and quarrel with thee about it; wilt thou quarrel with him again,
or rather go on meekly as thou hast begun, until thou hast numbered out
every letter? Here then likewise remember, that every duty that belongs
unto a man doth consist of some certain letters or numbers as it were,
to which without any noise or tumult keeping thyself thou must orderly
proceed to thy proposed end, forbearing to quarrel with him that would
quarrel and fall out with thee.
members.english: If someone sets you the question how the name Antoninus is written, surely you will not strain as you bring out each of its letters? What then if they get angry: surely you will not get angry back? Will you not gently go on counting off each of the letters? So here too, remember that every duty is made complete out of certain counted parts. These you must keep to, and, without being thrown into confusion and without answering those who are annoyed with annoyance of your own, carry through step by step what lies before you.
members.greek: Ἐάν τίς σοι προβάλῃ πῶς γράφεται τὸ Ἀντωνίνου ὄνομα, μήτι κατεντεινόμενος προοίσῃ ἕκαστον τῶν στοιχείων; τί οὖν ἐὰν ὀργίζωνται, μήτι ἀντοργιῇ; μήτι οὐκ ἐξαριθμήσῃ πρᾴως προιὼν ἕκαστον τῶν γραμμάτων; οὕτως οὖν καὶ ἐνθάδε μέμνησο ὅτι πᾶν καθῆκον ἐξ ἀριθμῶν τινῶν συμπληροῦται. τούτους δεῖ τηροῦντα καὶ μὴ θορυβούμενον μηδὲ τοῖς δυσχεραίνουσιν ἀντιδυσχεραίνοντα περαίνειν ὁδῷ τὸ προκείμενον.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 3.7 is 3.6, 3.8 is 3.7, 3.13 is 3.12, 11.15 is 11.16, 12.22 is 12.29, 2.6 is 2.9, 8.30 is 8.32, 4.20 is 4.24, 4.43 is 4.51, 5.28 is 5.34, 6.53 is 6.58, 6.24 is 6.26; 10.2 and 10.6 are the same.

Reads 3.7’s “if nothing appears better than the spirit” as the answer Marcus expects, and states it in claim 1 as my view; 3.7’s open side is the said-once item under doubt. Under “Why” the section gives the statement’s two halves at length (claims 1 and 2), not an argument for them.

Claim 2 gathers four passages that each say “no one can prevent”, though each names a different thing that cannot be prevented: living well, doing and saying what fits nature, living by my own nature’s reason, each action doing its part. The claim puts living well first and names the others after it; only “No one can prevent me” is said by all four.

Claim 4 pairs 3.7’s question (does it benefit me as a rational being or as an animal?) with 10.2’s ladder of natures, and places it under “In action”, not under doubt, though in 3.7 it answers an objection.
articles.limit: Article 8’s claim 4 already says that nothing that happens prevents me from being good and just, and Article 2 that reason leads my work; what this article adds is the ranking, that nothing is better than the spirit within and its virtue. Article 17’s claim 4 allows that the people around me may not let me live according to nature, so “no one can prevent me” in claim 2 is read here as holding of the inner act, not of my outward life; the said-once item on verdicts (11.15) repeats Article 7’s claims 2 and 3 and Article 8’s claim 2. 3.7 carries much of the article, which asserts that nothing is better and does not argue it; Seneca’s item under “Why” and the statement clause come close to Article 5, which already quotes Ep. 76.8 and has an item on 76.10 and 41.8, and what they add here is 76.9’s comparison with animals.

articles.title: Living with the gods

statement.t: I live with the gods and meet their power always, revere both them and reason, and keep before me the dawn sky and a good person of old.

parts.words: I live with the gods and meet their power always
revere both them and reason
keep before me the dawn sky and a good person of old

statement.kind: A way of living with the gods, what I revere, and two exercises of reminding
statement.form: Claim 1 says that I live with the gods and experience their power all the time, and what living with them consists in. Claim 2 names what is revered: the gods, reason and the unseen soul. Claim 3 gives two exercises of reminding, and the statement names what each keeps before me: the dawn sky I look at (11.25) and the good person I am reminded of (11.24). No passage joins the three, so the statement lists them with “and” and draws no conclusion from one to another. Its first part sets what 5.21 says (living with the gods) beside what 12.21 says (meeting their power), joined by what both say: “always”, which stands for 12.21’s “on every occasion” and 5.21’s “constantly”. It closes the first part so that it covers that part only: 11.25 is an exercise at dawn, and 4.13 gives no frequency.

groups.name: Why
groups.asks: The ground for the statement.

groups.name: In action
groups.asks: What follows for what I do.

groups.name: Practice
groups.asks: An exercise I can repeat.

groups.name: When it breaks
groups.asks: What failing looks like, and the way back.

groups.name: If I doubt it
groups.asks: What still holds if the statement is not true.
groups.empty: No passage in this section asks what still holds if there are no gods; 12.21 answers those who ask where Marcus has seen them with grounds for revering them, which stand under Why.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, claim 1 gains a second author for calling the spirit, which is reason, a fragment of the divine, and claim 3 a second author for keeping one good person in mind. The article gains what Marcus leaves out here: God as a witness within me, what worship consists in, the chosen person as a watcher, an example of what I turn back from when I return to reason, and what holds if no guardian was given to me. He limits claim 3: I need the person as a guard over me only until I respect myself.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains two watchers: God, who is a witness of my soul, and the good person of old, whom I treat as if he were watching me. He sets a term to the second: once I have come to respect myself, I need no longer keep that person over me as a guard.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Reason, however, is nothing else than a portion of the divine spirit set in a human body
piece.follows: Human reason is a portion of the divine spirit, placed in a human body.
piece.context: Letter 66 argues that all goods are equal, since the divine is of one nature. “Reason” is human reason; it matches claim 1 through 5.21, where the spirit is each person’s mind and reason.
gives: a fragment of himself

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Cherish some man of high character, and keep him ever before your eyes
piece.follows: The counsel is to pick one man of high character, hold him dear and keep him always in view.
piece.context: The closing motto of Letter 11, which Seneca gives as the counsel of Epicurus. “Some man of high character” is a man one chooses; the motto does not say that he must be of old.
gives: I constantly remind myself of one
who practised virtue

items.label: why
items.t: God is near me, with me and within me. A holy spirit lives within me that marks my good and bad deeds and is my guardian, and as I treat this spirit, so it treats me. Nothing is shut off from the sight of God: he is a witness of my soul and comes into the midst of my thoughts.
items.why: Marcus says that I show the gods my soul and that the spirit is my protector and leader. He does not say that the spirit marks what I do, that it treats me as I treat it, or that nothing in me can be kept from the sight of God.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: God is near you, he is with you, he is within you.
support.follows: God is near a person, with that person and within that person.
support.context: The opening of Letter 41: Lucilius need not pray at a temple for sound understanding, since he can get it from himself. “You” is Lucilius, and through him anyone.
gives: God is near me, with me and within me

support.author: seneca
support.quote: a holy spirit indwells within us, one who marks our good and bad deeds, and is our guardian. As we treat this spirit, so are we treated by it.
support.follows: A holy spirit within us notes our good and bad deeds and guards us, and it treats us as we treat it.
support.context: Letter 41, just after “God is within you”. “This spirit” is the holy spirit dwelling in each person; no one, Seneca adds, is good without God’s help.
gives: A holy spirit lives within me that marks my good and bad deeds and is my guardian
as I treat this spirit, so it treats me

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Nothing is shut off from the sight of God. He is witness of our souls, and he comes into the very midst of our thoughts
support.follows: God sees everything, is a witness of our souls and enters into our thoughts.
support.context: The opening of Letter 83: Lucilius asked for an account of Seneca’s whole day. One should live and think as if seen, since God sees into our souls and thoughts.
gives: Nothing is shut off from the sight of God: he is a witness of my soul and comes into the midst of my thoughts

items.label: action
items.t: The first way I worship the gods is to believe in them, and the next is to acknowledge their majesty and their goodness. God is worshipped by those who truly know him.
items.why: Marcus says that he reveres the gods and stands in awe of them; in this section he does not say what worship consists in. Seneca does, and he begins where the questioners of 12.21 begin: with holding that the gods exist.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The first way to worship the gods is to believe in the gods; the next to acknowledge their majesty, to acknowledge their goodness without which there is no majesty.
support.follows: Worship of the gods begins with believing in them and goes on to acknowledging their majesty and their goodness.
support.context: Letter 95 holds that rules for ritual are useless without a right idea of God. This sentence begins Seneca’s own account of what worshipping the gods is.
gives: The first way I worship the gods is to believe in them, and the next is to acknowledge their majesty and their goodness

support.author: seneca
support.quote: God is worshipped by those who truly know Him
support.follows: The people who worship God are those who truly know him.
support.context: Letter 95, on worship: Seneca would forbid lamps, morning calls at temples and gifts to Jupiter’s and Juno’s statues, and sets knowing God against these rites.
gives: God is worshipped by those who truly know him

items.label: practice
items.t: I choose a Cato, or, if Cato seems too severe a model, a gentler Laelius. I live as if he were watching me and order all my actions as if he saw them. With a witness standing near when I am likely to go wrong, I can get rid of most of my faults.
items.why: 11.24 gives the Epicurean rule in one line: remind yourself of a person of old. Seneca gives a similar counsel, which he quotes from Epicurus and comments on. In it the person is more than a reminder: he is a witness, and I act as if he saw me. Seneca also names whom to choose.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Choose therefore a Cato; or, if Cato seems too severe a model, choose some Laelius, a gentler spirit.
support.follows: The person to choose is a Cato, or, for someone who finds Cato too severe, the gentler Laelius.
support.context: Letter 11: Seneca applies Epicurus’s counsel to keep a good man always before one’s eyes. Cato and Laelius are Romans of earlier centuries, offered as that man.
gives: I choose a Cato, or, if Cato seems too severe a model, a gentler Laelius

support.author: seneca
support.quote: living as if he were watching you, and ordering all your actions as if he beheld them
support.follows: One should live and arrange every action as if the chosen man were looking on.
support.context: The second half of a motto that Seneca quotes from Epicurus at the end of Letter 11. “He” is the man of high character whom one is to keep before one’s eyes.
gives: I live as if he were watching me and order all my actions as if he saw them

support.author: seneca
support.quote: We can get rid of most sins, if we have a witness who stands near us when we are likely to go wrong.
support.follows: Having a witness close by at the moment of going wrong removes most wrongdoing.
support.context: Letter 11, Seneca’s comment on Epicurus’s counsel to keep a good man before one’s eyes. The “witness” is here the man one pictures watching, as in the motto.
gives: With a witness standing near when I am likely to go wrong, I can get rid of most of my faults

items.label: breaks
items.t: When I have been striving for what is not my own, such as bodily strength, which nature has given in greater degree to cattle and wild beasts, I come back to the good that is really mine. I am a reasoning animal, and the good that lies within me is perfect reason. The greatest service my teacher can do me is to show me that good, to take me out of the class of dumb animals and place me on a level with God.
items.why: 4.13 says that I pass from seeming a beast to seeming a god if I turn back to the principles and to reverence for reason; it does not say what I had turned to instead. Seneca gives an example: bodily strength, which cattle and wild beasts have in greater degree. He speaks of what I am, where 4.13 speaks of how I seem to others.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Why, pray, do you foster and practise your bodily strength? Nature has granted strength in greater degree to cattle and wild beasts.
support.follows: Seneca asks why anyone cultivates bodily strength, when nature has given more of it to cattle and wild beasts.
support.context: Near the end of Letter 124, on the Good as grasped by reason. Seneca asks Lucilius why he cultivates strength, beauty, hair and speed, in each of which some animal surpasses him.
gives: such as bodily strength, which nature has given in greater degree to cattle and wild beasts

support.author: seneca
support.quote: striving as you are for something that is not your own—and come back to the Good that is really yours
support.follows: Whoever is striving for something not his own is asked to come back to the good that really is his.
support.context: Letter 124: Seneca has asked why Lucilius trains strength, beauty and speed, in which animals surpass him. Those are the things “not your own”; the Good is a clear mind.
gives: When I have been striving for what is not my own
I come back to the good that is really mine

support.author: seneca
support.quote: You are a reasoning animal. What Good, then, lies within you? Perfect reason.
support.follows: A human being is a reasoning animal, and the good that lies within one is perfect reason.
support.context: The close of Letter 124. “You” is Lucilius as a human being; Seneca’s answer to his own question is that a human’s good is reason brought to perfection.
gives: I am a reasoning animal, and the good that lies within me is perfect reason

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I can be of no greater benefit to you than by revealing the Good that is rightly yours, by taking you out of the class of dumb animals, and by placing you on a level with God
support.follows: Seneca’s greatest service to Lucilius is to show him his own good, take him out of the class of animals and set him level with God.
support.context: The end of Letter 124, which argues that the Good is grasped by reason and not by the senses. Seneca says what use the argument is to Lucilius, the “you”.
gives: The greatest service my teacher can do me is to show me that good, to take me out of the class of dumb animals and place me on a level with God

items.label: doubt
items.t: I can set aside for the present the belief that a god is assigned to each of us as an attendant. Whether I have been allotted a guardian or am neglected and left to Fortune, the heaviest curse on me would be to be at enmity with myself.
items.why: No passage of Marcus in this section asks what holds if no spirit was given to me. Seneca sets that belief aside and says what holds either way: the worst thing is to be at enmity with myself. He doubts only the guardian assigned to each person, not the gods; and in Letter 41 he himself says that a holy spirit within us is our guardian.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Lay aside for the present the belief of certain persons—that a god is assigned to each one of us as a sort of attendant
support.follows: The belief that each person has a god assigned as an attendant can be left aside for now.
support.context: The opening of Letter 110, just after the greeting. Seneca sets aside, for the moment, the popular belief in a lesser god attached to each person, which Roman ancestors held.
gives: I can set aside for the present the belief that a god is assigned to each of us as an attendant

support.author: seneca
support.quote: whether we are allotted to special guardians, or whether we are neglected and consigned to Fortune, you can curse a man with no heavier curse than to pray that he may be at enmity with himself
support.follows: With guardians or without them, no curse on a person is heavier than enmity with himself.
support.context: Letter 110: Seneca leaves open whether gods attend to individuals. “Special guardians” are gods assigned to each person; either way enmity with oneself is the worst curse.
gives: Whether I have been allotted a guardian or am neglected and left to Fortune, the heaviest curse on me would be to be at enmity with myself

items.t: Claim 3 says that I constantly remind myself of a person of old, by a rule from the writings of the Epicureans. Seneca gives a similar Epicurean practice an end: the man is a guard set over me until I have come to respect myself, and then I may send him away (Ep. 25.6). This limits the claim and does not contradict it; he does not say that the reminding ever does harm. Letter 11 sets no such term: at its end he says to picture the chosen man always.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: when you have progressed so far that you have also respect for yourself, you may send away your attendant; but until then, set as a guard over yourself the authority of some man
support.follows: The imagined guard is to be kept until one respects oneself; after that he may be dismissed.
support.context: Letter 25, on Epicurus’s saying “Do everything as if Epicurus were watching you”. The “attendant” is the good man one imagines as a guard over oneself.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: picture him always to yourself as your protector or your pattern
support.follows: The chosen man is to be pictured always, as a protector or as a pattern; no end to this is named.
support.context: The last lines of Letter 11, after the advice to choose a Cato or a Laelius. “Him” is that chosen man, by whom one regulates one’s character as by a ruler.

amend.t: ; God is a witness of my soul, and I live as if the good person of old were watching me
; but once I have come to respect myself, I need no longer keep this person over me as a guard

passages.title: The epistles of seneca
passages.text: Mortal things decay, fall, are worn out, grow up, are exhausted, and replenished. Hence, in their case, in view of the uncertainty of their lot, there is inequality; but of things divine the nature is one. Reason, however, is nothing else than a portion of the divine spirit set in a human body. If reason is divine, and the good in no case lacks reason, then the good in every case is divine. And furthermore, there is no distinction between things divine; hence there is none between goods, either. Therefore it follows that joy and a brave unyielding endurance of torture are equal goods; for in both there is the same greatness of soul relaxed and cheerful in the one case, in the other combative and braced for action.

passages.title: On the blush of modesty
passages.text: But my letter calls for its closing sentence. Hear and take to heart this useful and wholesome motto: “Cherish some man of high character, and keep him ever before your eyes, living as if he were watching you, and ordering all your actions as if he beheld them.”

passages.title: On the god within us
passages.text: You are doing an excellent thing, one which will be wholesome for you, if, as you write me, you are persisting in your effort to attain sound understanding; it is foolish to pray for this when you can acquire it from yourself. We do not need to uplift our hands towards heaven, or to beg the keeper of a temple to let us approach his idol’s ear, as if in this way our prayers were more likely to be heard. God is near you, he is with you, he is within you.

passages.title: On the god within us
passages.text: This is what I mean, Lucilius: a holy spirit indwells within us, one who marks our good and bad deeds, and is our guardian. As we treat this spirit, so are we treated by it. Indeed, no man can be good without the help of God. Can one rise superior to fortune unless God helps him to rise? He it is that gives noble and upright counsel. In each good man A god doth dwell, but what god know we not.

passages.title: On drunkenness
passages.text: You bid me give you an account of each separate day, and of the whole day too; so you must have a good opinion of me if you think that in these days of mine there is nothing to hide. At any rate, it is thus that we should live,—as if we lived in plain sight of all men; and it is thus that we should think,—as if there were someone who could look into our inmost souls; and there is one who can so look. For what avails it that something is hidden from man? Nothing is shut off from the sight of God. He is witness of our souls, and he comes into the very midst of our thoughts—comes into them, I say, as one who may at any time depart.

passages.title: On the usefulness of basic principles
passages.text: The first way to worship the gods is to believe in the gods; the next to acknowledge their majesty, to acknowledge their goodness without which there is no majesty. Also, to know that they are supreme commanders in the universe, controlling all things by their power and acting as guardians of the human race, even though they are sometimes unmindful of the individual. They neither give nor have evil but they do chasten and restrain certain persons and impose penalties, and sometimes punish by bestowing that which seems good outwardly. Would you win over the gods? Then be a good man. Whoever imitates them, is worshipping them sufficiently.

passages.title: On the usefulness of basic principles
passages.text: Precepts are commonly given as to how the gods should be worshipped. But let us forbid lamps to be lighted on the Sabbath, since the gods do not need light, neither do men take pleasure in soot. Let us forbid men to offer morning salutation and to throng the doors of temples; mortal ambitions are attracted by such ceremonies, but God is worshipped by those who truly know Him. Let us forbid bringing towels and flesh-scrapers to Jupiter, and proffering mirrors to Juno; for God seeks no servants. Of course not; he himself does service to mankind, everywhere and to all he is at hand to help.

passages.title: On the blush of modesty
passages.text: Choose therefore a Cato; or, if Cato seems too severe a model, choose some Laelius, a gentler spirit. Choose a master whose life, conversation, and soul-expressing face have satisfied you; picture him always to yourself as your protector or your pattern. For we must indeed have someone according to whom we may regulate our characters; you can never straighten that which is crooked unless you use a ruler. Farewell.

passages.title: On the blush of modesty
passages.text: Such, my dear Lucilius, is the counsel of Epicurus; he has quite properly given us a guardian and an attendant. We can get rid of most sins, if we have a witness who stands near us when we are likely to go wrong. The soul should have someone whom it can respect,—one by whose authority it may make even its inner shrine more hallowed. Happy is the man who can make others better, not merely when he is in their company, but even when he is in their thoughts! And happy also is he who can so revere a man as to calm and regulate himself by calling him to mind! One who can so revere another, will soon be himself worthy of reverence.

passages.title: On the true good as attained by reason
passages.text: Why, pray, do you foster and practise your bodily strength? Nature has granted strength in greater degree to cattle and wild beasts. Why cultivate your beauty? After all your efforts, dumb animals surpass you in comeliness. Why dress your hair with such unending attention? Though you let it down in Parthian fashion, or tie it up in the German style, or, as the Scythians do, let it flow wild—yet you will see a mane of greater thickness tossing upon any horse you choose, and a mane of greater beauty bristling upon the neck of any lion. And even after training yourself for speed, you will be no match for the hare.

passages.title: On the true good as attained by reason
passages.text: Are you not willing to abandon all these details—wherein you must acknowledge defeat, striving as you are for something that is not your own—and come back to the Good that is really yours? And what is this Good? It is a clear and flawless mind, which rivals that of God, raised far above mortal concerns, and counting nothing of its own to be outside itself. You are a reasoning animal. What Good, then, lies within you? Perfect reason. Are you willing to develop this to its farthest limits—to its greatest degree of increase?

passages.title: On the true good as attained by reason
passages.text: Do you ask now whither our argument is tending, and of what benefit it will be to your mind? I will tell you: it exercises and sharpens the mind, and ensures, by occupying it honourably, that it will accomplish some sort of good. And even that is beneficial which holds men back when they are hurrying into wickedness. However, I will say this also: I can be of no greater benefit to you than by revealing the Good that is rightly yours, by taking you out of the class of dumb animals, and by placing you on a level with God.

passages.title: On true and false riches
passages.text: From my villa at Nomentum I send you greeting and bid you keep a sound spirit within you—in other words, gain the blessing of all the gods, for he is assured of their grace and favour who has become a blessing to himself. Lay aside for the present the belief of certain persons—that a god is assigned to each one of us as a sort of attendant—not a god of regular rank, but one of a lower grade—one of those whom Ovid calls “plebeian gods.” Yet, while laying aside this belief, I would have you remember that our ancestors, who followed such a creed, have become Stoics; for they have assigned a Genius or a Juno to every individual.

passages.title: On true and false riches
passages.text: Later on we shall investigate whether the gods have enough time on their hands to care for the concerns of private individuals; in the meantime, you must know that whether we are allotted to special guardians, or whether we are neglected and consigned to Fortune, you can curse a man with no heavier curse than to pray that he may be at enmity with himself. There is no reason, however, why you should ask the gods to be hostile to anyone whom you regard as deserving of punishment; they are hostile to such a person, I maintain, even though he seems to be advanced by their favour.

passages.title: On reformation
passages.text: And when you have progressed so far that you have also respect for yourself, you may send away your attendant; but until then, set as a guard over yourself the authority of some man, whether your choice be the great Cato or Scipio, or Laelius,—or any man in whose presence even abandoned wretches would check their bad impulses. Meantime, you are engaged in making of yourself the sort of person in whose company you would not dare to sin. When this aim has been accomplished and you begin to hold yourself in some esteem, I shall gradually allow you to do what Epicurus, in another passage, suggests: “The time when you should most of all withdraw into yourself is when you are forced to be in a crowd.”

claims.role: With the gods at every moment
claims.t: I live with the gods and experience their power all the time. I constantly show them my own soul, content with what is allotted and doing all that is wanted by the spirit Zeus gave me as protector and leader, a fragment of himself.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of dealings with the gods that never stop. In 12.21 Marcus experiences their power “on every occasion”; in 5.21 the one who lives with the gods shows them their own soul “constantly”. “All the time” stands for both. Only 5.21 calls this living with the gods.
claims.changed: 12.21 gives this experience as the way Marcus knows that the gods exist; the claim takes from it only that the experience comes on every occasion, and sets it beside living with the gods without making it a part of that life. 5.21 says “each person” and “their own soul”; the claim says “me” and “my own soul”.

support.quote: the one who lives with the gods is the one who constantly shows them their own soul, content with what is allotted and doing all that the spirit wants, the spirit that Zeus has given to each person as protector and leader, a fragment of himself
support.follows: To live with the gods is to show them, constantly, a soul content with its lot that does all that the spirit given by Zeus wants.
gives: I live with the gods
all the time
I constantly show them my own soul, content with what is allotted and doing all that is wanted by the spirit Zeus gave me as protector and leader, a fragment of himself

support.quote: from what I experience of their power on every occasion
support.follows: Marcus experiences the power of the gods on every occasion.
gives: experience their power
all the time

claims.t: I revere the gods and reason, and I honour my own soul, though I have never seen it.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of reverence, with words from one Greek root: in 12.21 Marcus is asked why he should “revere” the gods, and 4.13 calls for “reverence for reason”. 12.21 adds a third thing that is honoured, the soul that he has never seen.
claims.changed: In 12.21 the word “revere” is spoken by those who question Marcus; his answer accepts it and ends with his awe of the gods. 4.13 does not say whether the reason to be revered is a person’s own or the reason of the whole, and the claim leaves that open as well.

support.quote: that you revere them as you do
support.follows: Those who question Marcus take it as a fact that he reveres the gods.
gives: I revere
the gods

support.quote: reverence for reason
support.follows: Reason is something to be revered.
gives: I revere
reason

support.quote: I have not seen my own soul either, and yet I honour it
support.follows: Marcus has never seen his own soul, and he honours it all the same.
gives: I honour my own soul, though I have never seen it

claims.t: I give myself reminders, by rules taken from schools of philosophy. At dawn I turn my eyes to the sky and am reminded of those in the sky that always complete their own work in the same way; and I constantly remind myself of one of the people of old who practised virtue.
claims.shared: Both passages give a rule for reminding oneself, and both use the same verb: 11.25 “so that we are reminded”, 11.24 “to remind oneself”. Both name the school the rule comes from: “The Pythagoreans” in 11.25, “the writings of the Epicureans” in 11.24. Each names something to be reminded of that does its part well: those in the sky that always complete their own work, and a person of old who practised virtue.
claims.changed: The claim takes both rules as my own and says “schools of philosophy” for the Pythagoreans and the Epicureans. 11.25 says “we” and 11.24 “oneself”; the claim says “I”. Only 11.24 uses the word “rule”; 11.25 gives the Pythagoreans’ instruction without a verb. 11.25 says “those”; the claim says “those in the sky”, since the passage has just named the sky.

support.quote: The Pythagoreans: to turn our eyes to the sky at dawn, so that we are reminded of those that always complete their own work along the same lines and in the same way
support.follows: The Pythagoreans’ instruction is to look at the sky at dawn, as a reminder of those in the sky that always complete their own work in the same way.
gives: I give myself reminders
by rules taken from schools of philosophy
At dawn I turn my eyes to the sky and am reminded of those in the sky that always complete their own work in the same way

support.quote: In the writings of the Epicureans a rule was laid down: to remind oneself constantly of one of the people of old who practised virtue
support.follows: The Epicureans had a written rule: keep reminding yourself of one of the people of old who practised virtue.
gives: I give myself reminders
by rules taken from schools of philosophy
I constantly remind myself of one of the people of old who practised virtue

single.quote: this spirit is each person’s mind and reason
single.label: What the spirit is
single.t: The spirit that Zeus gave me as my leader is my own mind and reason.
single.why: Only this passage says what the spirit is. 4.13 names reason and does not connect it with a spirit or with Zeus, so the two are not fused.
single.follows: The spirit that the passage has just described is each person’s own mind and reason.

single.quote: they are visible even to the eye
single.label: Seen with the eye
single.t: The gods can be seen, even with the eye.
single.why: Only this passage says that the gods are visible, and it does not say which gods. 11.25 looks at the sky but does not call what is seen there gods, so the two are not fused.
single.follows: Marcus’s first answer to those who ask where he has seen the gods is that they can be seen with the eye.

single.quote: from that I both grasp that they exist and stand in awe of them
single.label: Known by their power
single.t: It is from my experience of their power that I grasp that the gods exist, and I stand in awe of them.
single.why: Only this passage says how I know that the gods exist. No other passage of the section argues for it.
single.follows: Marcus’s ground for holding that the gods exist, and for his awe of them, is what he has just named: his experience of their power.

single.quote: and of their order, their purity and their nakedness. For a star has no veil.
single.label: What the sky shows
single.t: The sky at dawn also reminds me of order, of purity and of nakedness: a star has no veil in front of it.
single.why: Only this passage names order, purity and nakedness. 5.21 speaks of showing the gods my soul, but it does not say that the soul is shown uncovered, so the two are not fused.
single.follows: Those in the sky are also a reminder of order, purity and nakedness, since a star has nothing hung in front of it.

single.quote: Within ten days you will seem a god to the very people to whom you now seem a beast and an ape, if you turn back to the principles
single.label: From beast to god
single.t: To the very people to whom I now seem a beast and an ape, I shall seem a god within ten days, if I turn back to the principles.
single.why: Only this passage says what it looks like to have left the principles, and that there is a way back. It speaks of how I seem to people, not of living with the gods, so it is not fused with 5.21. Its last words, “reverence for reason”, are counted in claim 2.
single.follows: Whoever turns back to the principles will soon seem a god to the same people who now take him for a beast and an ape.

members.text:
To them that ask thee, Where hast thou seen the Gods, or how
knowest thou certainly that there be Gods, that thou art so devout in
their worship? I answer first of all, that even to the very eye, they
are in some manner visible and apparent. Secondly, neither have I ever
seen mine own soul, and yet I respect and honour it. So then for the
Gods, by the daily experience that I have of their power and providence
towards myself and others, I know certainly that they are, and therefore
worship them.
members.english: To those who ask: “Well, where have you seen the gods, or from what have you grasped that they exist, that you revere them as you do?” First, they are visible even to the eye. Second, though, I have not seen my own soul either, and yet I honour it. So with the gods too: from what I experience of their power on every occasion, from that I both grasp that they exist and stand in awe of them.
members.greek: Πρὸς τοὺς ἐπιζητοῦντας· ποῦ γὰρ ἰδὼν τοὺς θεοὺς ἢ πόθεν κατειληφὼς ὅτι εἰσὶν οὕτως σέβεις; πρῶτον μὲν καὶ ὄψει ὁρατοί εἰσιν· ἔπειτα μέντοι οὐδὲ τὴν ψυχὴν τὴν ἐμαυτοῦ ἑώρακα καὶ ὅμως τιμῶ· οὕτως οὖν καὶ τοὺς θεούς, ἐξ ὧν τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτῶν ἑκάστοτε πειρῶμαι, ἐκ τούτων ὅτι τε εἰσὶ καταλαμβάνω καὶ αἰδοῦμαι.

members.text:
To live with the Gods. He liveth with the Gods, who at all times
affords unto them the spectacle of a soul, both contented and well
pleased with whatsoever is afforded, or allotted unto her; and
performing whatsoever is pleasing to that Spirit, whom (being part of
himself) Jove hath appointed to every man as his overseer and governor.
members.english: “To live with the gods.” And the one who lives with the gods is the one who constantly shows them their own soul, content with what is allotted and doing all that the spirit wants, the spirit that Zeus has given to each person as protector and leader, a fragment of himself. And this spirit is each person’s mind and reason.
members.greek: ʽΣυζῆν θεοῖς.ʼ συζῇ δὲ θεοῖς ὁ συνεχῶς δεικνὺς αὐτοῖς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὴν ἀρεσκομένην μὲν τοῖς ἀπονεμομένοις, ποιοῦσαν δὲ ὅσα βούλεται ὁ δαίμων, ὃν ἑκάστῳ προστάτην καὶ ἡγεμόνα ὁ Ζεὺς ἔδωκεν, ἀπόσπασμα ἑαυτοῦ. οὗτος δέ ἐστιν ὁ ἑκάστου νοῦς καὶ λόγος.

members.text:
Within ten days, if so happen, thou shalt be esteemed a god of
them, who now if thou shalt return to the dogmata and to the honouring
of reason, will esteem of thee no better than of a mere brute, and of an
ape.
members.english: Within ten days you will seem a god to the very people to whom you now seem a beast and an ape, if you turn back to the principles and to reverence for reason.
members.greek: Ἐντὸς δέκα ἡμερῶν θεὸς αὐτοῖς τούτοις δόξεις οἷς νῦν θηρίον καὶ πίθηκος, ἐὰν ἀνακάμψῃς ἐπὶ τὰ δόγματα καὶ τὸν σεβασμὸν τοῦ λόγου.

members.text:
The Pythagoreans were wont betimes in the morning the first thing
they did, to look up unto the heavens, to put themselves in mind of them
who constantly and invariably did perform their task: as also to put
themselves in mind of orderliness, or good order, and of purity, and of
naked simplicity. For no star or planet hath any cover before it.
members.english: The Pythagoreans: to turn our eyes to the sky at dawn, so that we are reminded of those that always complete their own work along the same lines and in the same way, and of their order, their purity and their nakedness. For a star has no veil.
members.greek: Οἱ Πυθαγόρειοι· ἕωθεν εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀφορᾶν, ἵν’ ὑπομιμνῃσκώμεθα τῶν ἀεὶ κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ καὶ ὡσαύτως τὸ ἑαυτῶν ἔργον διανυόντων καὶ τῆς τάξεως καὶ τῆς καθαρότητος καὶ τῆς γυμνότητος· οὐδὲν γὰρ προκάλυμμα ἄστρου.

members.text:
In the ancient mystical letters of the Ephesians, there was an
item, that a man should always have in his mind some one or other of the
ancient worthies.
members.english: In the writings of the Epicureans a rule was laid down: to remind oneself constantly of one of the people of old who practised virtue.
members.greek: Ἐν τοῖς τῶν Ἐπικουρείων γράμμασι παράγγελμα ἔκειτο συνεχῶς ὑπομιμνῄσκεσθαι τῶν παλαιῶν τινος τῶν ἀρετῇ χρησαμένων.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay those of the 1634 edition. In modern editions 12.21 is 12.28, 5.21 is 5.27, 4.13 is 4.16, 11.25 is 11.27 and 11.24 is 11.26.

Sets living with the gods (5.21) and experiencing their power (12.21) side by side, in claim 1 and in the first part of the statement, joined by the one thing both say: that it goes on all the time. Only 5.21 speaks of living with the gods, and 12.21 mentions the experience to explain how Marcus knows that the gods exist. Claim 1 is headed “With the gods at every moment”, not as a definition, and neither it nor the statement says that the experience is part of living with them.

Takes “I revere the gods” from words that 12.21 gives to Marcus’s questioners (“that you revere them as you do”), because they share a Greek root with “reverence for reason” in 4.13. Marcus’s own verbs in 12.21 are “honour”, of his soul, and “stand in awe”, of the gods.

Does not say that the reason I revere is the reason that leads me. 4.13 says “reverence for reason”, and its Greek leaves open whether a person’s own reason or the reason of the whole is meant; 5.21 says that the spirit leads and is mind and reason, but not that it is revered. The two stand side by side: the reverence in claim 2 and in the statement, the leading spirit in claim 1 and in the said-once item from 5.21.

Reads “those that always complete their own work” (11.25) as the stars, as the passage’s last sentence suggests, but writes “those in the sky” in the claim and does not name them. Does not join them to the gods who are “visible even to the eye” in 12.21: neither passage says that the stars are gods.

Says in claim 3 that both rules come from schools of philosophy. For 11.24 this follows the edition’s text, “Epicureans”; the translators’ note says, from memory and unchecked, that the manuscripts read “Ephesians” and that “Epicureans” is an editor’s correction.
articles.limit: Article 4 already says that what rules in me is of one kind with the reason that governs the world, and that I honour what is supreme in myself (5.18); Article 3 already says that I accept what happens, which here is “content with what is allotted”. What this article adds is that life with the gods goes on all the time, that it consists in what I show them, and two exercises of reminding. Of Seneca’s additions, the one on what I come back from (w4) comes near Article 5’s Seneca item from Ep. 76.10, that reason is what is peculiar to me; what it adds here is the turning back from what is not my own. It is weakest where it joins its parts: the section holds three passages on the gods and reason and two on reminders, and no passage connects the two groups; the statement only sets them side by side.

articles.title: Blaming no one for what is not up to me

statement.t: I do not let what is not up to me make a difference to me, and I blame no one for it, neither the gods nor people.

statement.kind: A ground and the conduct that follows from it
statement.form: Claims c1 and c3 are the ground: I count only what is up to me as good or bad, and the gods go wrong in nothing. Claims c2 and c4 are the conduct that follows: no one is to be blamed, and my own wrong is what I can stop. 6.36 itself draws the line from the ground to the conduct, so the “and” of the statement needs no inference of the editor’s. Claim c5 is the failure and the way back.
