single.quote: But you have come out of old habit. I am not angry with you. Only go away.
single.label: A practice
single.t: When an impression comes out of old habit, I am not angry with it. I only tell it to go away.
single.why: Only this passage gives words to say. It adds two things no other passage has: the impression comes out of old habit, and it is sent away without anger.
single.follows: The impression has come out of old habit; Marcus is not angry with it and only tells it to go away.

single.quote: An exile is whoever exiles themselves from the reason that belongs to citizens.
single.label: An exile by my own act
single.t: I am an exile when I exile myself from the reason that belongs to citizens.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of exile. “The reason that belongs to citizens” is, by the translators’ note, the reason of those who live together as citizens of the one city that all rational beings share. The passage does not say that the exile is against what happens, so the exile is not joined to claim 3.
single.follows: A person becomes an exile by exiling themselves from the reason that belongs to citizens.

single.quote: Blind is whoever shuts the eye of the mind.
single.label: Blind by my own act
single.t: I am blind when I shut the eye of my own mind.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of sight. It does not say what the eye of the mind should be looking at, so it is not joined to 2.5 on keeping track of my own soul.
single.follows: To be blind, in the sense meant here, is to shut the eye of the mind.

single.quote: But enough.
single.label: Breaking off
single.t: When I catch myself going over all I endured because I was not content with my ruling part, I stop: enough.
single.why: Only this passage ends with an order to stop, the nearest thing in the section to a way back. The first half of the line comes from the sentence of 9.24 just before these words, which is quoted under the claim on being content. The Greek does not say what there has been enough of. The line takes it as enough of going over what was endured; it could also be enough of the enduring itself.
single.follows: Marcus breaks off with two words: but enough.

members.text:
He is a true fugitive, that flies from reason, by which men are
sociable. He blind, who cannot see with the eyes of his understanding.
He poor, that stands in need of another, and hath not in himself all
things needful for this life. He an aposteme of the world, who by being
discontented with those things that happen unto him in the world,
doth as it were apostatise, and separate himself from common nature's
rational administration. For the same nature it is that brings this
unto thee, whatsoever it be, that first brought thee into the world. He
raises sedition in the city, who by irrational actions withdraws his own
soul from that one and common soul of all rational creatures.
members.english: An exile is whoever exiles themselves from the reason that belongs to citizens. Blind is whoever shuts the eye of the mind. A beggar is whoever is in need of another and does not have from themselves everything that is useful for life. An abscess standing apart from the universe is whoever stands apart and separates themselves from the reason of the common nature by being displeased with what happens: for that nature brings this forth, the same one that brought you forth too. A piece split off from the city is whoever splits their own soul off from the soul of rational beings, which is one.
members.greek: φυγὰς ὁ φεύγων τὸν πολιτικὸν λόγον· τυφλὸς ὁ καταμύων τῷ νοερῷ ὄμματι· πτωχὸς ὁ ἐνδεὴς ἑτέρου καὶ μὴ πάντα ἔχων παρ’ ἑαυτοῦ τὰ εἰς τὸν βίον χρήσιμα· ἀπόστημα κόσμου ὁ ἀφιστάμενος καὶ χωρίζων ἑαυτὸν τοῦ τῆς κοινῆς φύσεως λόγου διὰ τοῦ δυσαρεστεῖν τοῖς συμβαίνουσιν· ἐκείνη γὰρ φέρει τοῦτο, ἣ καὶ σὲ ἤνεγκεν· ἀπόσχισμα πόλεως ὁ τὴν ἰδίαν ψυχὴν τῆς τῶν λογικῶν ἀποσχίζων, μιᾶς οὔσης.

members.text:
For not observing the state of another
man's soul, scarce was ever any man known to be unhappy. Tell whosoever
they be that intend not, and guide not by reason and discretion the
motions of their own souls, they must of necessity be unhappy.
members.english: Hardly anyone has been seen to be unhappy through not attending to what goes on in another person’s soul. But those who do not keep track of the movements of their own soul are bound to be unhappy.
members.greek: Παρὰ μὲν τὸ μὴ ἐφιστάνειν, τί ἐν τῇ ἄλλου ψυχῇ γίνεται, οὐ ῥᾳδίως τις ὤφθη κακοδαιμονῶν· τοὺς δὲ τοῖς τῆς ἰδίας ψυχῆς κινήμασι μὴ παρακολουθοῦντας ἀνάγκη κακοδαιμονεῖν.

members.text:
What is εὐδαιμονία, or happiness: but ἀγαθὸς δαίμων, or, a good
dæmon, or spirit? What then dost thou do here, O opinion? By the Gods
I adjure thee, that thou get thee gone, as thou earnest: for I need thee
not. Thou earnest indeed unto me according to thy ancient wonted manner.
It is that, that all men have ever been subject unto. That thou camest
therefore I am not angry with thee, only begone, now that I have found
thee what thou art.
members.english: Happiness is a good spirit, or a good ruling part. So what are you doing here, impression? Go away, by the gods, as you came: for I do not need you. But you have come out of old habit. I am not angry with you. Only go away.
members.greek: Εὐδαιμονία ἐστὶ δαίμων ἀγαθὸς ἢ ἡγεμονικὸν ἀγαθόν. τί οὖν ὧδε ποιεῖς, ὦ φαντασία; ἀπέρχου, τοὺς θεούς σοι, ὡς ἦλθες· οὐ γὰρ χρῄζω σου. ἐλήλυθας δὲ κατὰ τὸ ἀρχαῖον ἔθος. οὐκ ὀργίζομαί σοι· μόνον ἄπιθι.

members.text:
Infinite are the troubles and miseries, that thou hast already
been put to, by reason of this only, because that for all happiness
it did not suffice thee, or, that thou didst not account it sufficient
happiness, that thy understanding did operate according to its natural
constitution.
members.english: You have endured countless things because you were not content with your ruling part doing the kind of things it is made to do. But enough.
members.greek: Ἀνέτλης μύρια διὰ τὸ μὴ ἀρκεῖσθαι τῷ σῷ ἡγεμονικῷ ποιοῦντι ταῦτα, οἷα κατεσκεύασται. ἀλλὰ ἅλις.

members.text:
He that runs away from his master is a fugitive. But the law is
every man's master. He therefore that forsakes the law, is a fugitive.
So is he, whosoever he be, that is either sorry, angry, or afraid, or
for anything that either hath been, is, or shall be by his appointment,
who is the Lord and Governor of the universe. For he truly and properly
is Νόμος, or the law, as the only νέμων, or distributor and dispenser
of all things that happen unto any one in his lifetime--Whatsoever then
is either sorry, angry, or afraid, is a fugitive.
members.english: Whoever flees from their master is a runaway slave. And the law is master, so whoever breaks the law is a runaway slave too. But whoever is distressed or angry or afraid, too, does not want one of the things appointed by the one who governs all things to have happened, or to be happening, or to be going to happen; and the one who governs all things is law, as the one who deals out all that falls to each. So whoever is afraid or distressed or angry is a runaway slave.
members.greek: Ὁ τὸν κύριον φεύγων δραπέτης· κύριος δὲ ὁ νόμος καὶ ὁ παρανομῶν οὖν δραπέτης. ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ λυπούμενος ἢ ὀργιζόμενος ἢ φοβούμενος οὐ βούλεταί τι γεγονέναι ἢ γίνεσθαι ἢ γενήσεσθαι τῶν ὑπὸ τοῦ τὰ πάντα διοικοῦντος τεταγμένων, ὅς ἐστι νόμος, νέμων ὅσα ἑκάστῳ ἐπιβάλλει. ὁ ἄρα φοβούμενος ἢ λυπούμενος ἢ ὀργιζόμενος δραπέτης.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of the 1634 edition. In modern editions 4.24 is 4.29 without its first sentence, 2.5 is 2.8, 7.14 is 7.17 and 9.24 is 9.26; 10.25 is the same.

Keeps “a good ruling part” and leaves “a good spirit” (7.14) to the quote. The Greek word for happiness contains the word for spirit, which English cannot show, and the “or” between the two names can also mean “that is”.

Turns two descriptions of a failure into a rule: 9.24’s “you were not content” becomes “I am content”, and 4.24’s beggar, who is “in need of another”, becomes “I need nothing besides”. Neither passage states the rule in the positive.

Reads the common nature that “brings this forth” (4.24) and the one who governs all things, who is law (10.25), as what sends what happens; “the very thing that sends it” (claim 3), “nature and the law that send it” (the statement) and “I desert” are the editor’s words for what the two say. Keeps 4.24’s exile out of that claim, because the exile leaves the reason that belongs to citizens and is not said to be against what happens.

Leaves out two sentences of quoted passages. The last sentence of 4.24, on splitting one’s own soul off from the one soul of rational beings, is about my tie to other people, which Article 1 states. The step in 10.25 about whoever breaks the law is the middle of the argument and is not about what happens to me; the conclusion it leads to is quoted.
articles.limit: Article 1 already says that resenting what happens cuts me off from the whole, and Article 3 that I accept what happens and do not complain. Claim 3’s “Displeased with it, I stand apart and separate myself from the common nature” is close to Article 3’s item from 5.8, that each time I am displeased with what happens I cut through the connection of the whole, and its “brought me forth too” is close to Article 3’s first claim, that what happens comes from the same causes that produced me. Claim 2 is close to Article 2, whose fourth claim says that doing my work makes me content and whose item from 7.30 says that my mind then has all that belongs to it, and it is nearly the same as Article 18’s first claim, that a good state of soul and good actions are enough for me. The same words of Seneca’s Ep. 98.2 back that claim and this article’s claim 1. Claims 1 and 2 are also near Article 12, which says that I keep watch over what is within me rather than guess what others think, and that I am content with my present state. What this article adds is that my happiness or unhappiness is decided in my own soul, and that distress, anger and fear are a flight from a master. The section has two strands that no passage joins: 2.5, 7.14 and 9.24 are about my own soul, 10.25 is about the law of the whole, and only 4.24 touches both, so it feeds two claims. Claim 1 rests on two short passages, each of which gives one side of it.

statement.kind: A fact faced, and how to live under it
statement.form: Claims 1 and 2 are the ground: death is near, and dying is nothing much. Claims 3 and 4 say how to live meanwhile: without pretence, and here as anywhere. The said-once items give a way to stay free, a daily exercise, two pictures of failing and the way back, and an argument by cases that holds whether or not death comes.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four claims gain a second author: that death is near, that I am ready to go, that I do not pretend, and, in claim 4, both “wherever I am” and preferring death to living another way. He adds what can serve as a reason for the article, though he does not offer it as one: death will show whether my brave words were felt or a pretence. He adds words to say each night, and he limits the readiness to die: not in haste, and not from a longing for death.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains what can serve as a reason, though Seneca does not offer it as one: death will show whether my brave words were really felt or a pretence.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: But who is not near death? It is ready for us in all places and at all times.
piece.follows: Everyone is near death, since death is ready for us everywhere and always.
piece.context: Letter 30: Seneca reports the old, failing Bassus on the fear of death. The words say that death, “it”, is near to everyone, in all places and at all times.
gives: any moment now I will be dead

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: I shall never be frightened when the last hour comes; I am already prepared
piece.follows: Seneca will not be afraid when his last hour comes, because he is already prepared for it.
piece.context: Letter 54: Seneca has just come through an attack of asthma, which doctors call rehearsing death. “The last hour” is the hour of his own death.
gives: I am ready to go

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Surely you are aware that dying is also one of life’s duties?
piece.follows: Dying is one of the duties of life.
piece.context: Letter 77, on taking one’s own life: someone says he wants to live on because of the honourable duties he is fulfilling. Seneca answers that dying is a duty too.
gives: one of the acts of my life

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: At whatever point you leave off living, provided you leave off nobly, your life is a whole.
piece.follows: A life that ends nobly is whole, wherever it ends.
piece.context: Letter 77, on taking one’s own life: a journey stopped halfway is incomplete, Seneca says, but a life is not incomplete if it is honourable.
gives: whenever death comes my life is not cut off unfinished

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Never shall this flesh drive me to feel fear, or to assume any pretence that is unworthy of a good man.
piece.follows: Seneca will never let his body drive him into fear or into a pretence unworthy of a good man.
piece.context: Letter 65: Seneca calls his body a chain on his freedom. “This flesh” is his body, and the pretence is one he might put on to protect it.
gives: I do not pretend or play a part

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: I am not born for any one corner of the universe; this whole world is my country.
piece.follows: Seneca is not born for one corner of the universe; the whole world is his country.
piece.context: Letter 28: Lucilius travels to shake off his gloom, and Seneca says it goes with him. This is the belief he tells him to live by instead.
gives: wherever I am

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: It is not a question of dying earlier or later, but of dying well or ill. And dying well means escape from the danger of living ill.
piece.follows: What matters is dying well, and dying well is escaping the danger of living badly.
piece.context: Letter 70, on the proper time to end one’s life: the wise man lives as long as he ought; Seneca then blames a captive who chose to live on in a tyrant’s cage.
gives: I would rather die
than live another way

items.label: why
items.t: What I have shown so far, in word or deed, proves nothing. I leave it to death to judge what progress I have made: on that day, without stage paint, I will see whether my brave words were really felt or a pretence.
items.why: In this section Marcus sets the nearness of death beside a life without pretence and does not say why the two belong together. Seneca says that death will test whether his brave words against fortune were felt or a pretence; reading that as the reason is the editor’s link.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The showing which we have made up to the present time, in word or deed, counts for nothing.
support.follows: Nothing we have shown so far, in words or deeds, proves anything.
support.context: Letter 26, on old age and death: the old Seneca speaks to himself as if the day that judges all his years had come. “The showing” is what he has said and done.
gives: What I have shown so far, in word or deed, proves nothing

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I shall leave it to Death to determine what progress I have made.
support.follows: Seneca leaves it to death to decide how far he has progressed.
support.context: Letter 26, on old age and death: the progress is Seneca’s progress in philosophy, which, he says, his words so far cannot prove.
gives: I leave it to death to judge what progress I have made

support.author: seneca
support.quote: putting aside all stage artifice and actor’s rouge, I am to pass judgment upon myself,—whether I am merely declaiming brave sentiments, or whether I really feel them; whether all the bold threats I have uttered against fortune are a pretence and a farce.
support.follows: On that day, with the stage paint off, Seneca will judge whether his brave words were felt or a pretence.
support.context: Letter 26, on old age and death: the day Seneca is making ready for is the day of his death, when he judges himself without the actor’s make-up.
gives: on that day, without stage paint, I will see whether my brave words were really felt or a pretence

items.label: practice
items.t: When I go to sleep, I go gladly and say: “I have lived; the course that fortune set for me is finished.” If God adds another day, I welcome it gladly.
items.why: 7.40 says to live through every day as the last, and gives no words for it. Seneca gives words to say when each day ends, and a way to take the next morning.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: let us go to our sleep with joy and gladness; let us say: I have lived; the course which Fortune set for me Is finished.
support.follows: We should go to sleep glad and say that we have lived and that the course fortune set us is finished.
support.context: Letter 12, on old age: Pacuvius held his own funeral feast every evening; Seneca turns the custom to a good use. The course is the course of one’s life.
gives: When I go to sleep, I go gladly and say
I have lived; the course that fortune set for me is finished

support.author: seneca
support.quote: And if God is pleased to add another day, we should welcome it with glad hearts.
support.follows: If God adds another day, we should welcome it gladly.
support.context: Letter 12, on old age: said right after the bedtime words “I have lived”. The added day is the next morning, taken as a gift.
gives: If God adds another day, I welcome it gladly

items.t: Seneca agrees that leaving life can be right, but he limits it. The brave and wise man does not beat a hasty retreat from life, and above all he avoids the lust for death that seizes even noble spirits. Marcus says to leave if others will not allow a life by nature; Seneca adds that the leaving must not be hasty or come from a longing to die. The limit concerns going to death rather than waiting for it; it limits the claim and does not contradict it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The brave and wise man should not beat a hasty retreat from life; he should make a becoming exit.
support.follows: A brave and wise man does not leave life in haste; he leaves it in a fitting way.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death: having argued against fearing death, Seneca warns that even when reason advises ending life, one must not act headlong.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: And above all, he should avoid the weakness which has taken possession of so many,—the lust for death.
support.follows: Above all, a brave and wise man avoids the longing to die that has seized so many.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death: “the lust for death” is an unreflecting pull toward dying, which Seneca says seizes the noble and the craven alike.

amend.t: ; death will show whether my brave words were really felt or a pretence
; but I do not go to death in haste, and I keep clear of a longing to die

passages.title: On conquering the conqueror
passages.text: Bassus kept saying: “It is due to our own fault that we feel this torture, because we shrink from dying only when we believe that our end is near at hand.” But who is not near death? It is ready for us in all places and at all times. “Let us consider,” he went on to say, “when some agency of death seems imminent, how much nearer are other varieties of dying which are not feared by us.”

passages.title: On asthma and death
passages.text: Accept this assurance from me: I shall never be frightened when the last hour comes; I am already prepared and do not plan a whole day ahead. But do you praise and imitate the man whom it does not irk to die, though he takes pleasure in living. For what virtue is there in going away when you are thrust out? And yet there is virtue even in this: I am indeed thrust out, but it is as if I were going away willingly. For that reason the wise man can never be thrust out, because that would mean removal from a place which he was unwilling to leave; and the wise man does nothing unwillingly. He escapes necessity, because he wills to do what necessity is about to force upon him. Farewell.

passages.title: On taking one’s own life
passages.text: “But,” says one, “I wish to live, for I am engaged in many honourable pursuits. I am loth to leave life’s duties, which I am fulfilling with loyalty and zeal.” Surely you are aware that dying is also one of life’s duties? You are deserting no duty; for there is no definite number established which you are bound to complete.

passages.title: On taking one’s own life
passages.text: An expedition will be incomplete if one stops half-way, or anywhere on this side of one’s destination; but life is not incomplete if it is honourable. At whatever point you leave off living, provided you leave off nobly, your life is a whole. Often, however, one must leave off bravely, and our reasons therefore need not be momentous; for neither are the reasons momentous which hold us here.

passages.title: On the first cause
passages.text: Never shall this flesh drive me to feel fear, or to assume any pretence that is unworthy of a good man. Never shall I lie in order to honour this petty body. When it seems proper, I shall sever my connexion with it. And at present, while we are bound together, our alliance shall nevertheless not be one of equality; the soul shall bring all quarrels before its own tribunal. To despise our bodies is sure freedom.

passages.title: On travel as a cure for discontent
passages.text: That trouble once removed, all change of scene will become pleasant; though you may be driven to the uttermost ends of the earth, in whatever corner of a savage land you may find yourself, that place, however forbidding, will be to you a hospitable abode. The person you are matters more than the place to which you go; for that reason we should not make the mind a bondsman to any one place. Live in this belief: “I am not born for any one corner of the universe; this whole world is my country.”

passages.title: On the proper time to slip the cable
passages.text: It is not a question of dying earlier or later, but of dying well or ill. And dying well means escape from the danger of living ill. That is why I regard the words of the well-known Rhodian as most unmanly. This person was thrown into a cage by his tyrant, and fed there like some wild animal. And when a certain man advised him to end his life by fasting, he replied: “A man may hope for anything while he has life.”

passages.title: On old age and death
passages.text: “The showing which we have made up to the present time, in word or deed, counts for nothing. All this is but a trifling and deceitful pledge of our spirit, and is wrapped in much charlatanism. I shall leave it to Death to determine what progress I have made. Therefore with no faint heart I am making ready for the day when, putting aside all stage artifice and actor’s rouge, I am to pass judgment upon myself,—whether I am merely declaiming brave sentiments, or whether I really feel them; whether all the bold threats I have uttered against fortune are a pretence and a farce.

passages.title: On old age
passages.text: Thus Pacuvius had himself carried out to burial every day. Let us, however, do from a good motive what he used to do from a debased motive; let us go to our sleep with joy and gladness; let us say: I have lived; the course which Fortune set for me Is finished. And if God is pleased to add another day, we should welcome it with glad hearts. That man is happiest, and is secure in his own possession of himself, who can await the morrow without apprehension. When a man has said: “I have lived!”, every morning he arises he receives a bonus.

passages.title: On despising death [ 1 ]
passages.text: The brave and wise man should not beat a hasty retreat from life; he should make a becoming exit. And above all, he should avoid the weakness which has taken possession of so many,—the lust for death. For just as there is an unreflecting tendency of the mind towards other things, so, my dear Lucilius, there is an unreflecting tendency towards death; this often seizes upon the noblest and most spirited men, as well as upon the craven and the abject. The former despise life; the latter find it irksome.

claims.t: My time is short: very soon I will leave all this behind, and any moment now I will be dead. What is left now is little.
claims.shared: All three say that the end is close, each in its own words: “very soon” (10.12), “any moment now” (4.30), “what is left now is little” (10.17).
claims.changed: 10.12 speaks of “such a person” and 4.30 speaks to “you”; the claim says “I”. 10.17 does not say what is left; the claim takes it to be time.

support.quote: having taken in that very soon they will have to leave all these things behind as they go from among people
support.follows: The person described has understood that very soon they must leave all this behind and go from among people.
gives: My time is short
very soon I will leave all this behind

support.quote: Any moment now you will be dead
support.follows: Marcus tells himself that he will be dead any moment now.
gives: My time is short
any moment now I will be dead

support.quote: What is left now is little.
support.follows: Marcus tells himself that little is left now.
gives: My time is short
What is left now is little

claims.t: I am ready to go, and I go as one who suffers nothing bad: dying is nothing much, one of the acts of my life. If my mind has been disciplined and cleaned out, then whenever death comes my life is not cut off unfinished.
claims.shared: 5.23 and 6.2 both say that dying matters little: “Why do you think it anything much?” (5.23) and “Let it make no difference to you whether you do what is fitting … whether dying” (6.2). 5.23 and 3.9 both describe someone ready to leave: “There is smoke, and I leave” (5.23), a life that fate does not overtake unfinished (3.9).
claims.changed: 5.23 says that one should go out of life as one who suffers nothing bad; the claim keeps this as the manner of going, and takes for any death the calm that 5.23 speaks of when others do not allow one to live rightly. 6.2 says only that dying should make no difference to doing what is fitting; “dying is nothing much” is wider. “I am ready to go” is said without 3.9’s condition; the claim’s last sentence keeps it.

support.quote: as one who is suffering nothing bad
support.follows: If one has to go out of life, one goes as someone who is suffering nothing bad.
gives: I go as one who suffers nothing bad

support.quote: There is smoke, and I leave. Why do you think it anything much?
support.follows: When there is smoke, Marcus leaves, and he asks why one should think leaving any great matter.
gives: I am ready to go
dying is nothing much

support.quote: Let it make no difference to you whether you do what is fitting shivering or warm, and whether drowsy or having slept enough, and whether spoken ill of or praised, and whether dying or doing some other kind of act.
support.follows: Whether I am dying or doing something else, as with cold or praise, it should make no difference to doing what is fitting.
gives: dying is nothing much

support.quote: For this too is one of the acts of life, the one in which we die.
support.follows: Dying is one of the acts of life.
gives: one of the acts of my life

support.quote: In the mind of someone who has been disciplined and thoroughly cleansed you would find nothing full of pus
support.follows: A mind that has been disciplined and cleansed has nothing festering in it.
gives: If my mind has been disciplined and cleaned out

support.quote: Nor does fate overtake their life while it is unfinished, as one might say of a tragic actor who leaves before finishing and playing the play through.
support.follows: Whenever death comes to such a person, their life is not left unfinished, like a play an actor walks out of.
gives: I am ready to go
whenever death comes my life is not cut off unfinished

claims.t: I do not pretend or play a part. The finer thing is to leave this life without ever having tasted pretence, with nothing affected or hidden in me.
claims.shared: 9.2 and 7.40 both refuse pretence: “any pretence” (9.2) and “nor to play a part” (7.40). In the Greek the two are one word, the noun ὑπόκρισις and its verb.
claims.changed: 9.2 says that going without having tasted pretence would have been the finer course, one already missed; the claim names it as the finer thing, and says “leave this life” for 9.2’s “go from among people”, and does not say that I can still have it. 9.2 names lying, luxury and vanity beside pretence; the claim keeps pretence. From 3.9’s longer list the claim keeps “affected” and, as “hidden”, “lurking in a hole”.

support.quote: It would have been the mark of a finer man to go from among people without having tasted lying, or any pretence or luxury or vanity.
support.follows: It would have been finer to leave life without ever having tasted lying, pretence, luxury or vanity.
gives: I do not pretend or play a part
The finer thing is to leave this life without ever having tasted pretence

support.quote: nor to play a part
support.follows: A perfect character does not play a part.
gives: I do not pretend or play a part

support.quote: nothing slavish, nothing affected, nothing tied to anything, nothing split off, nothing liable to be called to account, nothing lurking in a hole
support.follows: In a cleansed mind there is nothing slavish, affected or hidden, and nothing that has to answer for itself.
gives: with nothing affected or hidden in me

claims.t: The place makes no difference: I can live here the way I mean to live, according to nature, wherever I am. If the people around me do not allow it, I would rather die than live another way.
claims.shared: Both say that the life one means to live can be lived where one is: “you can live that way here” (5.23), “it makes no difference whether there or here” (10.17). Both call it a life by nature, and both say what to do if others will not have it: “if they do not allow it, then go out of life” (5.23), “If they do not bear it, let them kill that person” (10.17).
claims.changed: 5.23 speaks of going out of life oneself, 10.17 of being killed by others; the claim says only “die”. In 10.17 “that way” is open: it may mean living as those people live. 10.17 says that the place makes no difference if a person lives in the universe as in a city; the claim does not repeat that condition.

support.quote: The way you have in mind to live once you have gone out, you can live that way here.
support.follows: The life one plans to live after leaving can be lived here already.
gives: The place makes no difference
I can live here the way I mean to live

support.quote: Live as on a mountain. For it makes no difference whether there or here, if a person, wherever they are, lives in the universe as in a city.
support.follows: One can live as on a mountain anywhere, since the place makes no difference to someone whose city is the universe.
gives: The place makes no difference
I can live here the way I mean to live
wherever I am

support.quote: Let human beings see, let them study, a true human being living according to nature.
support.follows: Marcus asks that people see and study a true human being living according to nature.
gives: according to nature

support.quote: And I want what accords with the nature of the rational and social living creature.
support.follows: What Marcus wants is what fits the nature of a rational and social creature.
gives: according to nature

support.quote: But if they do not allow it, then go out of life as well
support.follows: If others do not let one live that way, one should go out of life.
gives: If the people around me do not allow it
I would rather die

support.quote: If they do not bear it, let them kill that person. For that is better than to live that way.
support.follows: If people cannot bear a person who lives by nature, being killed by them is better than living that way.
gives: If the people around me do not allow it
I would rather die
than live another way

single.quote: But as long as nothing of that kind leads me out, I stay, free, and no one will prevent me from doing what I want.
single.label: Free while I stay
single.t: As long as nothing leads me out of life, I stay, free, and no one will prevent me from doing what I want.
single.why: Only 5.23 says that staying is free. “Of that kind” in the quote refers to the smoke just before it: something that makes staying impossible. 10.23’s first case, living here and being used to it, is about staying too, but it does not say that staying is free.
single.follows: Until something like the smoke leads Marcus out, he stays, free, and no one stops him from doing what he wants.

single.quote: Perfection of character has this: to live through every day as the last, and neither to be feverish nor to go numb
single.label: Every day as the last
single.t: I live through every day as if it were my last, neither feverish nor numb.
single.why: Only 7.40 in this section gives an exercise for each day. Its last words, on playing no part, feed claim 3.
single.follows: A perfect character lives each day as the last, without agitation and without numbness.

single.quote: But at any rate to breathe one’s last having at least grown sick of these things is the next best course. Or have you chosen to stay sitting beside vice, and does not even experience yet persuade you to flee from the plague? For the corruption of the mind is a plague, far more so than any such unhealthy mixture and change of this air that is poured around.
single.label: The next best course
single.t: If I have tasted lying and pretence, the next best thing is at least to be sick of them when I die. I do not stay sitting beside vice: a corrupt mind is a worse plague than any sickness of the air.
single.why: Only 9.2 gives a way back for someone who has already failed: to grow sick of these things before the end and to flee the plague.
single.follows: Having tasted these vices, the next best course is to die sick of them, since staying with vice is staying with a worse plague.

single.quote: Picture everyone who is pained or displeased at anything whatever as like the piglet that is being sacrificed and kicks and squeals. Like it too is the one who laments on their little bed, alone, in silence.
single.label: The piglet at the sacrifice
single.t: When I am pained or displeased at anything, I am like the piglet at the sacrifice that kicks and squeals, and no less so when I lament alone on my bed, in silence.
single.why: Only 10.28 pictures what failing looks like. Its last sentence, on following what happens willingly, is left to Article 10.
single.follows: Whoever is pained or displeased at what happens is like a sacrificial piglet kicking, even when they lament in silence.

single.quote: Either you live here, and by now you are used to it; or you are going out from here, and that is what you wanted; or you are dying, and you have completed your service. Besides these there is nothing. So be of good heart.
single.label: Three cases
single.t: Either I go on living here, and I am used to it by now; or I go away from here, as I wanted; or I die, and my service is complete. There is no other case, so I can be of good heart.
single.why: Only 10.23 argues by cases, and it holds whether or not death comes soon, so it stands under doubt. Its “completed your service” is close to 3.9, but it is kept whole here. Its “so” is Marcus’s own.
single.follows: Whether one lives on here, goes away or dies, there is no fourth case, and in each one can be of good heart.

members.text:
It were indeed more happy and comfortable, for a man to depart out
of this world, having lived all his life long clear from all falsehood,
dissimulation, voluptuousness, and pride. But if this cannot be, yet it
is some comfort for a man joyfully to depart as weary, and out of love
with those; rather than to desire to live, and to continue long in those
wicked courses. Hath not yet experience taught thee to fly from the
plague? For a far greater plague is the corruption of the mind, than any
certain change and distemper of the common air can be. This is a plague
of creatures, as they are living creatures; but that of men as they are
men or reasonable.
members.english: It would have been the mark of a finer man to go from among people without having tasted lying, or any pretence or luxury or vanity. But at any rate to breathe one’s last having at least grown sick of these things is the next best course. Or have you chosen to stay sitting beside vice, and does not even experience yet persuade you to flee from the plague? For the corruption of the mind is a plague, far more so than any such unhealthy mixture and change of this air that is poured around. For the latter is a plague of living creatures, in so far as they are living creatures; the former is a plague of human beings, in so far as they are human beings.
members.greek: Χαριεστέρου μὲν ἦν ἀνδρός, ἄγευστον ψευδολογίας καὶ πάσης ὑποκρίσεως καὶ τρυφῆς καὶ τύφου γενόμενον ἐξ ἀνθρώπων ἀπελθεῖν. τὸ δ’ οὖν κορεσθέντα γε τούτων ἀποπνεῦσαι δεύτερος πλοῦς. ἢ προῄρησαι προσκαθῆσθαι τῇ κακίᾳ καὶ οὔπω σε οὐδὲ ἡ πεῖρα πείθει φεύγειν ἐκ τοῦ λοιμοῦ; λοιμὸς γὰρ διαφθορὰ διανοίας πολλῷ γε μᾶλλον ἤπερ ἡ τοῦ περικεχυμένου τούτου πνεύματος τοιάδε τις δυσκρασία καὶ τροπή· αὕτη μὲν γὰρ ζῴων λοιμός, καθὸ ζῷά ἐστιν, ἐκείνη δὲ ἀνθρώπων,καθὸ ἄνθρωποί εἰσιν.

members.text:
He hath got loose from the bonds of his body, and perceiving that
within a very little while he must of necessity bid the world farewell,
and leave all these things behind him, he wholly applied himself, as to
righteousness in all his actions, so to the common nature in all things
that should happen unto him. And contenting himself with these two
things, to do all things justly, and whatsoever God doth send to like
well of it: what others shall either say or think of him, or shall do
against him, he doth not so much as trouble his thoughts with it. To go
on straight, whither right and reason directed him, and by so doing to
follow God, was the only thing that he did mind, that, his only business
and occupation.
members.english: Such a person has stripped off the body and, having taken in that very soon they will have to leave all these things behind as they go from among people, has given their whole self over: to justice in what they do themselves, and to the nature of the whole in the other things, those that happen. What anyone will say or think about them, or do against them, they do not even let into their mind, being content with these two things: if they themselves act justly in what is being done now, and if they love what is being allotted to them now. They have let go of all busyness and all eager pursuits, and want nothing else than to keep a straight course right through, by way of the law, and to follow god, who keeps a straight course right through.
members.greek: ἐξεδύσατο τὸ σῶμα καὶ ἐννοήσας ὅτι ὅσον οὐδέπω πάντα ταῦτα καταλιπεῖν ἀπιόντα ἐξ ἀνθρώπων δεήσει, ἀνῆκεν ὅλον ἑαυτὸν δικαιοσύνῃ μὲν εἰς τὰ ὑφ’ ἑαυτοῦ ἐνεργούμενα, ἐν δὲ τοῖς ἄλλοις συμβαίνουσι τῇ τῶν ὅλων φύσει. τί δ’ ἐρεῖ τις ἢ ὑπολήψεται περὶ αὐτοῦ ἢ πράξει κατ’ αὐτοῦ, οὐδ’ εἰς νοῦν βάλλεται, δύο τούτοις ἀρκούμενος, εἰ αὐτὸς δικαιοπραγεῖ τὸ νῦν πρασσόμενον καὶ φιλεῖ τὸ νῦν ἀπονεμόμενον ἑαυτῷ· ἀσχολίας δὲ πάσας καὶ σπουδὰς ἀφῆκε καὶ οὐδὲν ἄλλο βούλεται ἢ εὐθεῖαν περαίνειν διὰ τοῦ νόμου καὶ εὐθεῖαν περαίνοντι ἕπεσθαι τῷ θεῷ.

members.text:
Thou art now ready to die, and yet hast thou not attained to
that perfect simplicity: thou art yet subject to many troubles and
perturbations; not yet free from all fear and suspicion of external
accidents; nor yet either so meekly disposed towards all men, as thou
shouldest; or so affected as one, whose only study and only wisdom is,
to be just in all his actions.
members.english: Any moment now you will be dead, and you are not yet simple, nor untroubled, nor free of the suspicion that you could be harmed from outside, nor gracious towards everyone, nor someone who places wisdom only in acting justly.
members.greek: Ἤδη τεθνήξῃ καὶ οὔπω οὔτε ἁπλοῦς οὔτε ἀτάραχος οὔτε ἀνύποπτος τοῦ βλαβῆναι ἃν ἔξωθεν οὔτε ἵλεως πρὸς πάντας οὔτε τὸ φρονεῖν ἐν μόνῳ τῷ δικαιοπραγεῖν τιθέμενος.

members.text:
In the mind that is once truly disciplined and purged, thou canst
not find anything, either foul or impure, or as it were festered:
nothing that is either servile, or affected: no partial tie; no
malicious averseness; nothing obnoxious; nothing concealed. The life of
such an one, death can never surprise as imperfect; as of an actor, that
should die before he had ended, or the play itself were at an end, a man
might speak.
members.english: In the mind of someone who has been disciplined and thoroughly cleansed you would find nothing full of pus, nor indeed anything stained, nor anything festering under the skin. Nor does fate overtake their life while it is unfinished, as one might say of a tragic actor who leaves before finishing and playing the play through. And further, nothing slavish, nothing affected, nothing tied to anything, nothing split off, nothing liable to be called to account, nothing lurking in a hole.
members.greek: Οὐδὲν ἂν ἐν τῇ διανοίᾳ τοῦ κεκολασμένου καὶ ἐκκεκαθαρμένου πυῶδες οὐδὲ μὴν μεμολυσμένον οὐδὲ ὕπουλον εὕροις· οὐδὲ ἀσυντελῆ τὸν βίον αὐτοῦ ἡ πεπρωμένη καταλαμβάνει, ὡς ἄν τις εἴποι τὸν τραγῳδὸν πρὸ τοῦ τελέσαι καὶ διαδραματίσαι ἀπαλλάσσεσθαι· ἔτι δὲ οὐδὲν δοῦλον οὐδὲ κομψὸν οὐδὲ προσδεδεμένον οὐδὲ ἀπεσχισμένον οὐδὲ ὑπεύθυνον οὐδὲ ἐμφωλεῦον.

members.text:
Either thou dost Continue in this kind of life and that is it,
which so long thou hast been used unto and therefore tolerable: or thou
doest retire, or leave the world, and that of thine own accord, and then
thou hast thy mind: or thy life is cut off; and then mayst thou
rejoice that thou hast ended thy charge. One of these must needs be.
Be therefore of good comfort.
members.english: Either you live here, and by now you are used to it; or you are going out from here, and that is what you wanted; or you are dying, and you have completed your service. Besides these there is nothing. So be of good heart.
members.greek: Ἤτοι ἐνταῦθα ζῇς καὶ ἤδη εἴθικας· ἢ ἔξω ὑπάγεις καὶ τοῦτο ἤθελες· ἢ ἀποθνῄσκεις καὶ ἀπελειτούργησας. παρὰ δὲ ταῦτα οὐδέν. οὐκοῦν εὐθύμει.

members.text:
So live as indifferent to the world and all worldly objects, as
one who liveth by himself alone upon some desert hill. For whether here,
or there, if the whole world be but as one town, it matters not much for
the place. Let them behold and see a man, that is a man indeed, living
according to the true nature of man. If they cannot bear with me, let
them kill me. For better were it to die, than so to live as they would
have thee.
members.english: What is left now is little. Live as on a mountain. For it makes no difference whether there or here, if a person, wherever they are, lives in the universe as in a city. Let human beings see, let them study, a true human being living according to nature. If they do not bear it, let them kill that person. For that is better than to live that way.
members.greek: Ὀλίγον ἐστὶ τὸ ὑπολειπόμενον τοῦτο. ζῆσον ὡς ἐν ὄρει· οὐδὲν γὰρ διαφέρει ἐκεῖ ἢ ὧδε, ἐάν τις πανταχοῦ ὡς ἐν πόλει τῷ κόσμῳ. ἰδέτωσαν, ἱστορησάτωσαν οἱ ἄνθρωποι ἄνθρωπον ἀληθινὸν κατὰ φύσιν ζῶντα. εἰ μὴ φέρουσιν, ἀποκτεινάτωσαν· κρεῖττον γὰρ ἢ οὕτως ζῆν.

members.text:
Then hath a man attained to the estate of perfection in his life and
conversation, when he so spends every day, as if it were his last day:
never hot and vehement in his affections, nor yet so cold and stupid as
one that had no sense; and free from all manner of dissimulation.
members.english: Perfection of character has this: to live through every day as the last, and neither to be feverish nor to go numb nor to play a part.
members.greek: Τοῦτο ἔχει ἡ τελειότης τοῦ ἤθους, τὸ πᾶσαν ἡμέραν ὡς τελευταίαν διεξάγειν καὶ μήτε σφύζειν μήτε ναρκᾶν μήτε ὑποκρίνεσθαι.

members.text:
'Where there shall neither roarer be, nor harlot.' Why so? As
thou dost purpose to live, when thou hast retired thyself to some such
place, where neither roarer nor harlot is: so mayest thou here. And if
they will not suffer thee, then mayest thou leave thy life rather than
thy calling, but so as one that doth not think himself anyways wronged.
Only as one would say, Here is a smoke; I will out of it. And what a
great matter is this! Now till some such thing force me out, I will
continue free; neither shall any man hinder me to do what I will, and
my will shall ever be by the proper nature of a reasonable and sociable
creature, regulated and directed.
members.english:
Neither a tragic actor nor a prostitute.

The way you have in mind to live once you have gone out, you can live that way here. But if they do not allow it, then go out of life as well, yet as one who is suffering nothing bad. There is smoke, and I leave. Why do you think it anything much? But as long as nothing of that kind leads me out, I stay, free, and no one will prevent me from doing what I want. And I want what accords with the nature of the rational and social living creature.
members.greek: Οὔτε τραγῳδὸς οὔτε πόρνη. Ὡς ἐξελθὼν ζῆν διανοῇ, οὕτως ἐνταῦθα ζῆν ἔξεστιν· ἐὰν δὲ μὴ ἐπιτρέπωσι, τότε καὶ τοῦ ζῆν ἔξιθι, οὕτως μέντοι ὡς μηδὲν κακὸν πάσχων. καπνὸς καὶ ἀπέρχομαι· τί αὐτὸ πρᾶγμα δοκεῖς; μέχρι δέ με τοιοῦτον οὐδὲν ἐξάγει, μένω ἐλεύθερος καὶ οὐδείς με κωλύσει ποιεῖν ἃ θέλω· θέλω δὲ κατὰ φύσιν τοῦ λογικοῦ καὶ κοινωνικοῦ ζῴου.

members.text:
Be it all one unto thee, whether half frozen or well warm; whether
only slumbering, or after a full sleep; whether discommended or
commended thou do thy duty: or whether dying or doing somewhat else; for
that also 'to die,' must among the rest be reckoned as one of the duties
and actions of our lives.
members.english: Let it make no difference to you whether you do what is fitting shivering or warm, and whether drowsy or having slept enough, and whether spoken ill of or praised, and whether dying or doing some other kind of act. For this too is one of the acts of life, the one in which we die. So in this too it is enough to manage well what is at hand.
members.greek: Μὴ διαφέρου πότερον ῥιγῶν ἢ θαλπόμενος τὸ πρέπον ποιεῖς, καὶ πότερον νυστάζων ἢ ἱκανῶς ὕπνου ἔχων, καὶ πότερον κακῶς ἀκούων ἢ εὐφημούμενος, καὶ πότερον ἀποθνῄσκων ἢ πράττων τι ἀλλοῖον· μία γὰρ τῶν βιωτικῶν πράξεων καὶ αὕτη ἐστί, καθ’ ἣν ἀποθνῄσκομεν· ἀρκεῖ οὖν καὶ ἐπὶ ταύτης τὸ παρὸν εὖ θέσθαι.

members.text:
As a pig that cries and flings when his throat is cut, fancy to
thyself every one to be, that grieves for any worldly thing and takes
on. Such a one is he also, who upon his bed alone, doth bewail
the miseries of this our mortal life. And remember this, that Unto
reasonable creatures only it is granted that they may willingly and
freely submit unto Providence: but absolutely to submit, is a necessity
imposed upon all creatures equally.
members.english: Picture everyone who is pained or displeased at anything whatever as like the piglet that is being sacrificed and kicks and squeals. Like it too is the one who laments on their little bed, alone, in silence. Picture also how we are bound, and that to the rational living creature alone it has been given to follow willingly what happens, while simply to follow is a necessity for all.
members.greek: Φαντάζου πάντα τὸν ἐφ’ ᾡτινιοῦν λυπούμενον ἢ δυσαρεστοῦντα ὅμοιον τῷ θυομένῳ χοιριδίῳ καὶ ἀπολακτίζοντι καὶ κεκραγότι· ὅμοιος καὶ ὁ οἰμώζων ἐπὶ τοῦ κλινιδίου μόνος σιωπῇ. τὴν ἔνδεσιν ἡμῶν καὶ ὅτι μόνῳ τῷ λογικῷ ζῴῳ δέδοται τὸ ἑκουσίως ἕπεσθαι τοῖς γινομένοις, τὸ δὲ ἕπεσθαι ψιλὸν πᾶσιν ἀναγκαῖον.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 10.12 is 10.11b, 4.30 is 4.37, 3.9 is 3.8, 10.23 is 10.22, 10.17 is 10.15, 7.40 is 7.69 and 5.23 is 5.28b–29; 9.2, 6.2 and 10.28 are the same.

Joins 5.23 and 10.17 in claim 4 although one speaks of going out of life oneself and the other of being killed; both say that dying is the answer when others will not allow a life by nature. In 10.17 “that way” is open, and the claim’s “another way” keeps it open.

Takes 9.2’s “pretence” and 7.40’s “play a part” as one thing, because the Greek uses one word for both. 3.9’s “affected” is a different word, smart or showy in a bad sense, and backs only its own part of claim 3.

Leaves to Article 10 the claim that acting justly now and taking what is allotted are enough, though 10.12 (“content with these two things”), 4.30 (“wisdom only in acting justly”), 6.2 (“it is enough to manage well what is at hand”) and 10.28 (“follow willingly what happens”) say it here too. Leaves out as well: 5.23’s opening “Neither a tragic actor nor a prostitute”, which closes a part of the chapter on anger and has no verb; 10.12’s “What anyone will say or think about them … they do not even let into their mind” and the rest of 4.30’s list, which concern what others do and belong with Articles 8 and 12; 9.2’s last sentence, which only explains the two plagues; and 10.28’s “Picture also how we are bound”, whose Greek does not construe as it stands.
articles.limit: Much of this section is said elsewhere: Article 10 already says that death is near and that justice in what I do and peace with what is allotted are enough, Article 3 that I accept what happens, and Article 6 that nothing comes too early; 7.40’s every day as the last is Article 9’s claim 4 and Article 10’s claim 2, the refusal of pretence is in Article 9’s claim 1, a life complete whenever it ends is Article 31’s claim 5 (without this article’s condition), and Articles 12 and 18 already say that where I am makes no difference. What this article adds is the readiness to go, the refusal of pretence set beside death, and the indifference of place joined to a willingness to die rather than live otherwise. In claim 4, “do not allow” means the outward conditions of a life, where and among whom I live, not the power to act justly, which Article 13 (claim 2) and Article 8 (claim 4) say no one can take from me; and the article states that dying is nothing much without arguing for it beyond calling it one of the acts of life.

articles.title: Content wherever I am put

statement.t: Wherever I am put, and equally whatever is given me or taken back, a good state of soul and good actions are enough for me.

parts.words: Wherever I am put
whatever is given me or taken back
a good state of soul and good actions
are enough for me

inferences.why: No passage joins the place I am put in to what is given and taken back; setting 8.43 and 5.30 beside 10.16 under one “enough” is the editor’s step.

statement.kind: A ground, the rule it supports, and words to say
statement.form: Claim 1 is the ground: wherever I am, a good lot is one I assign myself, and a good state of soul and good actions are enough. Claim 2 is the rule for those two things: what I do is for other people, and what happens I accept. Claim 3 gives words that hand the choice of gifts, losses and place to another. The statement joins the “wherever” of 8.43 and 5.30 to the giving and taking back of 10.16; that joining is the editor’s.

groups.name: Why
groups.asks: The ground for the statement.

groups.name: In action
groups.asks: What follows for what I do.

groups.name: Practice
groups.asks: An exercise I can repeat.

groups.name: When it breaks
groups.asks: What failing looks like, and the way back.

groups.name: If I doubt it
groups.asks: What still holds if the statement is not true.
groups.empty: No passage in this section asks what holds if a good state of soul and good actions are not enough for me, or if nothing gives and takes back.

near.chapter: The whole and my place in it

What happens can be borne and does not harm me

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, all three claims gain a second author. For the first: any land I am driven to can be a hospitable home, the soul by its own power makes a life happy or wretched, and the real good comes from a good conscience, honourable purposes and right actions. For the second: a good man bears whatever happens to him as the result of divine law. For the third: a prayer hands to Jupiter the choice of where I am led. The article gains two grounds (the person matters more than the place; a spirit within treats me as I treat it), two things under “In action” (how to hold what is given; making something of whatever fortune I find) and a rehearsal of poverty and exile. Nothing is added under “If I doubt it”. He limits the first claim: some places harm a mind still recovering, and where he may choose he avoids them.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a ground: the person I am matters more than the place I go to. His limit on the first claim touches the statement’s “wherever” too: for a mind not yet sound some places are harmful, and where I may choose I avoid them.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: though you may be driven to the uttermost ends of the earth, in whatever corner of a savage land you may find yourself, that place, however forbidding, will be to you a hospitable abode
piece.follows: Once the mind’s trouble is removed, even the most forbidding place I am driven to will be a hospitable home to me.
piece.context: Letter 28, on travel that does not cure a gloomy mind: Lucilius needs a change of soul, not of scene. “That place” is any land, once the mind’s trouble is removed.
gives: Wherever I am put
I can be content there

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: For the soul is more powerful than any sort of Fortune; by its own agency it guides its affairs in either direction, and of its own power it can produce a happy life, or a wretched one.
piece.follows: The soul is stronger than Fortune and by its own power makes a life happy or wretched.
piece.context: Letter 98, on not depending on Fortune’s gifts. Seneca has just said that Fortune hands us only the raw material of goods and ills; the soul turns it to good or ill.
gives: A good lot is one I assign myself

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: it comes from a good conscience, from honourable purposes, from right actions
piece.follows: The real good comes from a good conscience, honourable purposes and right actions.
piece.context: Letter 23, on true joy: rejoice only in what comes from your own store. “It” is the real good; these are the first three of the five sources Seneca names for it.
gives: a good state of soul
good actions

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: he will endure with an unruffled spirit whatever happens to him; for he will know that it has happened as a result of the divine law
piece.follows: A good man bears calmly whatever happens to him, because he knows it happened by the divine law.
piece.context: Letter 76, on the honourable as the only good. “He” is the good man, who owes the gods the highest duty; the divine law is the one that moves all creation.
gives: What happens to me, I accept
whatever it is
as something that comes from the gods

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Lead me, O Master of the lofty heavens, My Father, whithersoever thou shalt wish. I shall not falter, but obey with speed.
piece.follows: The speaker asks Jupiter to lead him wherever Jupiter wishes, and promises to obey at once.
piece.context: Letter 107, on obeying the order of the universe, ends with lines of the Stoic Cleanthes that Seneca has put into Latin. They are spoken to Jupiter.
gives: I hand the choice over

items.label: why
items.t: The person I am matters more than the place I go to, and for that reason I do not bind my mind to any one place. I am not born for one corner of the universe: the whole world is my country.
items.why: Marcus says that he will be content wherever he is thrown and gives as the ground the state of the divinity within him. He does not say in this section, as Seneca does, that the person counts for more than the place, or that the whole world is my country.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The person you are matters more than the place to which you go; for that reason we should not make the mind a bondsman to any one place.
support.follows: Who I am counts for more than where I go, so the mind should not be tied to any one place.
support.context: Letter 28, on travel that fails to cure a gloomy mind. Seneca has just said that, once the mind’s trouble is gone, any land is hospitable; “you” is Lucilius.
gives: The person I am matters more than the place I go to
for that reason I do not bind my mind to any one place

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I am not born for any one corner of the universe; this whole world is my country.
support.follows: I should live in the belief that I was not born for one corner of the universe and that the whole world is my country.
support.context: Words Seneca gives Lucilius to live by, in a letter saying that a restless traveller needs a change of soul. “This whole world” is set against any one place.
gives: I am not born for one corner of the universe
the whole world is my country

items.label: why
items.t: A holy spirit dwells within me as my guardian and marks what I do well and badly. As I treat this spirit, so it treats me.
items.why: 8.43 says that wherever I am thrown the divinity within me will be gracious, and that it is content if its state and its actions follow from its make-up; the fused claim keeps the state and the actions and leaves the divinity out. Seneca too speaks of a spirit within, and says what Marcus does not say here: it marks what I do, and how it treats me depends on how I treat it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: a holy spirit indwells within us, one who marks our good and bad deeds, and is our guardian. As we treat this spirit, so are we treated by it.
support.follows: A holy spirit lives in each of us as guardian and witness of our deeds, and it treats us as we treat it.
support.context: Letter 41 opens by telling Lucilius not to pray to heaven for a sound mind: God is near him, with him, within him. “This spirit” is that god within each person.
gives: A holy spirit dwells within me as my guardian and marks what I do well and badly
As I treat this spirit, so it treats me

items.label: action
items.t: What I am given I use but do not boast of, as something left with me for safe-keeping that will be withdrawn. I do not let it stick fast to me, so that when it is withdrawn it tears no part of me away.
items.why: 8.31 says to take without conceit and to let go readily, and does not say what is taken. 10.16 says that nature gives and takes back. Seneca names the things, the advantages that opinion calls goods, and says how to hold them between the giving and the taking back.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Let us use these things, but not boast of them, and let us use them sparingly, as if they were given for safe-keeping and will be withdrawn.
support.follows: I should use such things sparingly and without boasting, as things given into my keeping that will be withdrawn.
support.context: From Letter 74, on virtue as the only good. “These things” are the advantages that opinion calls goods, which Seneca says are in our possession but outside ourselves.
gives: What I am given I use but do not boast of
as something left with me for safe-keeping that will be withdrawn

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Let everything of this nature be added to us, and not stick fast to us, so that, if it is withdrawn, it may come away without tearing off any part of us.
support.follows: Such things should be added to me without sticking fast, so that losing them tears no part of me away.
support.context: Letter 74, on virtue as the only good. Seneca has just said that what opinion calls goods are only “advantages”, our chattels and not parts of us; “everything of this nature” means these.
gives: I do not let it stick fast to me
when it is withdrawn it tears no part of me away

items.label: action
items.t: I develop virtue in my own country if that is possible and in exile if it is not, in sound health if that is possible and enfeebled if it is not. Whatever fortune I find, I make something noteworthy of it, as Phidias would have made the best statue that his material permitted.
items.why: Marcus says here that I act for the good of others and accept what happens; he does not say what I do with the place or the fortune I am handed. Seneca does: I work with it as a sculptor works with the material he is given. He grants with his “if possible” that one fortune is preferable to another, which no passage of Marcus in this section does.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: So the wise man will develop virtue, if he may, in the midst of wealth, or, if not, in poverty; if possible, in his own country—if not, in exile; if possible, as a commander—if not, as a common soldier; if possible, in sound health—if not, enfeebled. Whatever fortune he finds, he will accomplish therefrom something noteworthy.
support.follows: The wise man develops virtue at home if he can and in exile if he cannot, and makes something noteworthy of whatever fortune he finds.
support.context: Letter 85, on the wise man and misfortune: what Seneca draws from Phidias, who made the best statue each material allowed. Poverty, exile and illness are the poorer materials.
gives: I develop virtue in my own country if that is possible and in exile if it is not, in sound health if that is possible and enfeebled if it is not
Whatever fortune I find, I make something noteworthy of it

support.author: seneca
support.quote: If you had given him marble, or a still meaner material, he would have made of it the best statue that the material would permit.
support.follows: Given marble or something meaner, Phidias would have made the best statue that the material allowed.
support.context: Letter 85, on the wise man and misfortune: he is not weighed down by evils but makes use of them. “Him” is the sculptor Phidias, who worked in bronze as well as ivory.
gives: as Phidias would have made the best statue that his material permitted

items.label: practice
items.t: I think of everything that can happen as something that will happen. If I become poor, I shall be one among many; if I am exiled, I shall regard myself as born in the place I am sent to.
items.why: Marcus’s words are said to whoever throws him, and they leave the place open. Seneca thinks of each thing that can happen before it does, and for poverty and exile he gives the answer to have ready; his answer to exile is to regard the new place as my birthplace.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Let us think of everything that can happen as something which will happen.
support.follows: Whatever can happen should be thought of as something that is going to happen.
support.context: Letter 24, on the fear of a lawsuit. Seneca reminds Lucilius that death, exile and grief have hung over him since birth, and that he was born to these perils.
gives: I think of everything that can happen as something that will happen

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I may become a poor man; I shall then be one among many. I may be exiled; I shall then regard myself as born in the place to which I shall be sent.
support.follows: If I become poor I shall be one among many, and if I am exiled I shall treat the place I am sent to as my birthplace.
support.context: Letter 24, to Lucilius, who fears losing a case in court. Seneca has told him to turn from his own case to what can befall anyone; “I” is anyone saying this.
gives: If I become poor, I shall be one among many
if I am exiled, I shall regard myself as born in the place I am sent to

items.t: Seneca agrees that any land can be a home once the mind is at peace (Ep. 28.4), but he does not treat all places alike. Some places are unwholesome for a mind that is recovering and not yet sound, and he says we ought to choose where we live with our character in mind. This limits the claim and does not contradict it. The harm he names does not depend on choosing: some places are unwholesome for a mind not yet sound, whether or not it chose them. His remedy does depend on it: where he may arrange things himself he keeps away from such places, and where he may not, he says that one can live quietly even in the Forum if necessary.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: there are some places which are also unwholesome for a healthy mind which is not yet quite sound, though recovering from its ailment
support.follows: Some places are bad for a mind that is recovering but is not yet fully sound.
support.context: Letter 28, on travel. Seneca likens such places to pestilential regions that attack even the strongest body; the mind meant is one still mending from its faults, not yet sound.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Of course, if one were allowed to make one’s own arrangements, I should flee far from the very sight and neighbourhood of the Forum.
support.follows: Given the choice, Seneca would keep far away from the Forum.
support.context: Letter 28, on travel. Seneca has just said that one can live quietly even in the Forum, the most confused of places, if necessary; this is what he adds at once.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: We ought to select abodes which are wholesome not only for the body but also for the character.
support.follows: I should choose where I live with my character in mind as well as my body.
support.context: Letter 51, on Baiae, which Seneca left the day after he came because luxury has claimed it. He says the wise man avoids such places without hating any place as such.

amend.t: ; the person I am matters more than the place I go to
; but some places harm a mind still recovering, and where I may choose I pick a place that is wholesome for my character

passages.title: On travel as a cure for discontent
passages.text: That trouble once removed, all change of scene will become pleasant; though you may be driven to the uttermost ends of the earth, in whatever corner of a savage land you may find yourself, that place, however forbidding, will be to you a hospitable abode. The person you are matters more than the place to which you go; for that reason we should not make the mind a bondsman to any one place. Live in this belief: “I am not born for any one corner of the universe; this whole world is my country.”

passages.title: On the fickleness of fortune
passages.text: All things that Fortune looks upon become productive and pleasant, only if he who possesses them is in possession also of himself, and is not in the power of that which belongs to him. For men make a mistake, my dear Lucilius, if they hold that anything good, or evil either, is bestowed upon us by Fortune; it is simply the raw material of Goods and Ills that she gives to us—the sources of things which, in our keeping, will develop into good or ill. For the soul is more powerful than any sort of Fortune; by its own agency it guides its affairs in either direction, and of its own power it can produce a happy life, or a wretched one.

passages.title: On the true joy which comes from philosophy
passages.text: Do you ask me what this real good is, and whence it derives? I will tell you: it comes from a good conscience, from honourable purposes, from right actions, from contempt of the gifts of chance, from an even and calm way of living which treads but one path. For men who leap from one purpose to another, or do not even leap but are carried over by a sort of hazard,—how can such wavering and unstable persons possess any good that is fixed and lasting?

passages.title: On learning wisdom in old age
passages.text: A good man, you will admit, must have the highest sense of duty toward the gods. Hence he will endure with an unruffled spirit whatever happens to him; for he will know that it has happened as a result of the divine law, by which the whole creation moves. This being so, there will be for him one good, and only one, namely, that which is honourable; for one of its dictates is that we shall obey the gods and not blaze forth in anger at sudden misfortunes or deplore our lot, but rather patiently accept fate and obey its commands.

passages.title: On obedience to the universal will
passages.text: Lead me, O Master of the lofty heavens, My Father, whithersoever thou shalt wish. I shall not falter, but obey with speed. And though I would not, I shall go, and suffer, In sin and sorrow what I might have done In noble virtue. Aye, the willing soul Fate leads, but the unwilling drags along.

passages.title: On the god within us
passages.text: This is what I mean, Lucilius: a holy spirit indwells within us, one who marks our good and bad deeds, and is our guardian. As we treat this spirit, so are we treated by it. Indeed, no man can be good without the help of God. Can one rise superior to fortune unless God helps him to rise? He it is that gives noble and upright counsel. In each good man A god doth dwell, but what god know we not.

passages.title: On virtue as a refuge from worldly distractions
passages.text: Let everything of this nature be added to us, and not stick fast to us, so that, if it is withdrawn, it may come away without tearing off any part of us. Let us use these things, but not boast of them, and let us use them sparingly, as if they were given for safe-keeping and will be withdrawn. Anyone who does not employ reason in his possession of them never keeps them long; for prosperity of itself, if uncontrolled by reason, overwhelms itself. If anyone has put his trust in goods that are most fleeting, he is soon bereft of them, and, to avoid being bereft, he suffers distress. Few men have been permitted to lay aside prosperity gently. The rest all fall, together with the things amid which they have come into eminence, and they are weighted down by the very things which had before exalted them.

passages.title: On some vain syllogisms
passages.text: Do you suppose that he is weighed down by evils? He makes use of them. It was not of ivory only that Phidias knew how to make statues; he also made statues of bronze. If you had given him marble, or a still meaner material, he would have made of it the best statue that the material would permit. So the wise man will develop virtue, if he may, in the midst of wealth, or, if not, in poverty; if possible, in his own country—if not, in exile; if possible, as a commander—if not, as a common soldier; if possible, in sound health—if not, enfeebled. Whatever fortune he finds, he will accomplish therefrom something noteworthy.

passages.title: On despising death [ 1 ]
passages.text: Ponder these words which you have often heard and often uttered. Moreover, prove by the result whether that which you have heard and uttered is true. For there is a very disgraceful charge often brought against our school,—that we deal with the words, and not with the deeds, of philosophy. What, have you only at this moment learned that death is hanging over your head, at this moment exile, at this moment grief? You were born to these perils. Let us think of everything that can happen as something which will happen.

passages.title: On despising death [ 1 ]
passages.text: I may become a poor man; I shall then be one among many. I may be exiled; I shall then regard myself as born in the place to which I shall be sent. They may put me in chains. What then? Am I free from bonds now? Behold this clogging burden of a body, to which nature has fettered me! “I shall die,” you say; you mean to say “I shall cease to run the risk of sickness; I shall cease to run the risk of imprisonment; I shall cease to run the risk of death.”

passages.title: On travel as a cure for discontent
passages.text: Can there be any spot so full of confusion as the Forum? Yet you can live quietly even there, if necessary. Of course, if one were allowed to make one’s own arrangements, I should flee far from the very sight and neighbourhood of the Forum. For just as pestilential places assail even the strongest constitution, so there are some places which are also unwholesome for a healthy mind which is not yet quite sound, though recovering from its ailment.

passages.title: On baiae and morals
passages.text: We ought to select abodes which are wholesome not only for the body but also for the character. Just as I do not care to live in a place of torture, neither do I care to live in a café. To witness persons wandering drunk along the beach, the riotous revelling of sailing parties, the lakes a-din with choral song, and all the other ways in which luxury, when it is, so to speak, released from the restraints of law not merely sins, but blazons its sins abroad,—why must I witness all this?

claims.t: Wherever I am put, my lot can be good and I can be content there. A good lot is one I assign myself: a good state of soul and good actions. These are enough for me.
claims.shared: 8.43 and 5.30 both say “wherever”, and both say that I am well off there: in 8.43 the divinity within me is gracious, in 5.30 my lot is good. Both then name what that rests on, and both name how the soul is and how it acts (8.43: “the state it is in and the way it acts”; 5.30: “good turnings of the soul, good impulses, good actions”). 8.43’s “content” and 9.5’s “It is enough” are the same verb in the Greek.
claims.changed: The claim says “soul” where 8.43 says “the divinity within me” and 5.30 says “the soul”. 8.43 does not call the state good; it says the state and the way of acting “follow from its own make-up”. 5.30 lists three things; the claim drops “good impulses”, which stand between the soul’s turnings and its actions. In 8.43 it is the divinity within me that is content, and the claim says that I am, and that these are enough for me. The span quoted from 9.5 names only the judgment; in the passage the same “It is enough” also governs the social action and the well-pleased disposition, which are quoted in claim 2. 5.30 says “yourself”; the claim says “myself”.

claims.t: What I do, I do for the good of other people. What happens to me, I accept, whatever it is, as something that comes from the gods.
claims.shared: All three passages set what I do beside what happens to me and give one rule for each. For what happens, 8.22 and 12.8 both say “accept” and both name the gods or god; 12.8 and 9.5 both say “everything”. For what I do, 8.22 says “the doing of good to human beings” where 9.5 says “social”.
claims.changed: 9.5 says “well pleased”, which is warmer than “accept”; the claim keeps the word that 12.8 and 8.22 share. 9.5 names “the external cause” and not the gods. 12.8 measures what I do by god’s praise, not by the good of other people; that half of 12.8 stands alone under “Why”.

claims.role: Words that hand over the choice
claims.t: I hand the choice over: to nature I say “Give what you want, take back what you want”, and about where I am put I say “Pick me up and throw me wherever you want”. The words to nature I say in obedience to it and good will toward it, not in bold defiance.
claims.shared: Both passages are spoken to a “you”, and both leave the choice to it in nearly the same words: “what you want” (10.16) and “wherever you want” (8.43). The Greek verb is the same in both.
claims.changed: 10.16 is about things given and taken back, 8.43 about the place I am thrown to; the claim keeps the two sayings apart. 8.43 does not say who is addressed, and the claim does not make it nature. Only 10.16 says in what spirit its words are said, so the last sentence speaks of the words to nature alone and rests on that passage alone. 8.43 names no spirit; its next words state a confidence, that the divinity within will be gracious there too.
