single.quote: How great a power a human being has: to do nothing other than what god is going to praise
single.label: A great power
single.t: To do nothing but what god is going to praise is in my power, as it is in every human being’s, and it is a great power.
single.why: Only this passage calls the rule a power, and only it measures what I do by god’s praise; 8.22 and 9.5 measure it by the good of other people. The same sentence goes on to accepting what god assigns, which is quoted under “In action”.
single.follows: A human being has the power to do only what god is going to praise, and it is a great power.

single.quote: To take without conceit, and to let go readily.
single.label: Taking, letting go
single.t: I take without conceit, and I let go readily.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of how I take and how I let go. It does not say what is taken, so it is not fused with 10.16, where it is nature that gives and takes back.
single.follows: Whatever is taken should be taken without conceit and let go readily.

single.quote: How easy it is to push away and wipe out every impression that is troublesome or out of place, and at once to be in a complete calm.
single.label: When I am troubled
single.t: When an impression troubles me or is out of place, I can push it away and wipe it out, and at once be completely calm. This is easy.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of an impression that troubles me and of calm. It is kept as what losing my contentment looks like, with the way back.
single.follows: A troublesome or out-of-place impression is easy to push away and wipe out, and complete calm follows at once.

members.text:
How happy is man in this his power that hath been granted unto
him: that he needs not do anything but what God shall approve, and
that he may embrace contentedly, whatsoever God doth send unto him?
members.english: How great a power a human being has: to do nothing other than what god is going to praise, and to accept everything god assigns to them, whatever it is.
members.greek: Ἡλίκην ἐξουσίαν ἔχει ἄνθρωπος μὴ ποιεῖν ἄλλο ἢ ὅπερ μέλλει ὁ θεὸς ἐπαινεῖν, καὶ δέχεσθαι πᾶν ὃν νέμῃ αὐτῷ ὁ θεός.

members.text:
Take me and throw me where thou wilt: I am indifferent. For there
also I shall have that spirit which is within me propitious; that is
well pleased and fully contented both in that constant disposition, and
with those particular actions, which to its own proper constitution are
suitable and agreeable.
members.english: Pick me up and throw me wherever you want. For there too I will have the divinity within me gracious, that is, content if the state it is in and the way it acts follow from its own make-up.
members.greek: Ἆρόν με καὶ βάλε, ὅπου θέλεις. κἀκεῖ γὰρ ἕξω τὸν ἐμὸν δαίμονα ἵλεων, τουτέστιν, ἀρκούμενον, εἰ ἔχοι καὶ ἐνεργοίη κατὰ τὸ ἑξῆς τῇ ἰδίᾳ κατασκευῇ.

members.text:
If my present apprehension of the object be right, and my present
action charitable, and this, towards whatsoever doth proceed from God,
be my present disposition, to be well pleased with it, it sufficeth.
members.english: It is enough that the present judgment should have a firm grasp of what is there, that the present action should be social, and that the present disposition should be well pleased with everything that happens from the external cause.
members.greek: Ἀρκεῖ ἡ παροῦσα ὑπόληψις καταληπτικὴ καὶ ἡ παροῦσα πρᾶξις κοινωνικὴ καὶ ἡ παροῦσα διάθεσις εὐαρεστικὴ πρὸς πᾶν τὸ παρὰ τῆς ἐκτὸς αἰτίας συμβαῖνον.

members.text:
Give what thou wilt, and take away what thou wilt, saith he that is
well taught and truly modest, to Him that gives, and takes away. And it
is not out of a stout and peremptory resolution, that he saith it, but
in mere love, and humble submission.
members.english: To nature, which gives everything and takes everything back, the person who is educated and modest says: “Give what you want. Take back what you want.” And that person says this not in bold defiance, but only in obedience to it and good will toward it.
members.greek: Τῇ πάντα διδούσῃ καὶ ἀπολαμβανούσῃ φύσει ὁ πεπαιδευμένος καὶ αἰδήμων λέγει· δὸς ὃ θέλεις· ἀπόλαβε ὃ θέλεις. λέγει δὲ τοῦτο οὐ καταθρασυνόμενος, ἀλλὰ πειθαρχῶν μόνον καὶ εὐνοῶν αὐτῇ.

members.text:
Shall I do it? I will; so the end of my action be to do good unto
men. Doth anything by way of cross or adversity happen unto me? I accept
it, with reference unto the Gods, and their providence; the fountain of
all things, from which whatsoever comes to pass, doth hang and depend.
members.english: Am I doing something? I do it, referring it to the doing of good to human beings. Is something happening to me? I accept it, referring it to the gods and to the spring of all things, from which everything that comes about is wound together.
members.greek: Πράσσω τι; πράσσω ἐπ’ ἀνθρώπων εὐποιίαν ἀναφέρων. συμβαίνει τί μοι; δέχομαι ἐπὶ τοὺς θεοὺς ἀναφέρων καὶ τὴν πάντων πηγήν, ἀφ’ ἧς πάντα τὰ γινόμενα συμμηρύεται.

members.text:
Let death surprise me when it will, and where it will, I may be
εὔμοιρος, or a happy man, nevertheless.

For he is a happy man, who in his lifetime dealeth unto himself a happy
lot and portion. A happy lot and portion is, good inclinations of the
soul, good desires, good actions.
members.english: … wherever caught, a person whose lot is good. And “whose lot is good” means having assigned yourself a good lot; and good lots are good turnings of the soul, good impulses, good actions.
members.greek: ὁπουδήποτε καταληφθείς, εὔμοιρος ἄνθρωπος· τὸ δὲ εὔμοιρος, ἀγαθὴν μοῖραν σεαυτῷ ἀπονείμας· ἀγαθαὶ δὲ μοῖραι ἀγαθαὶ τροπαὶ ψυχῆς, ἀγαθαὶ ὁρμαί, ἀγαθαὶ πράξεις.

members.text:
How easy a thing is it for a man to put off from him all turbulent
adventitious imaginations, and presently to be in perfect rest and
tranquillity!
members.english: How easy it is to push away and wipe out every impression that is troublesome or out of place, and at once to be in a complete calm.
members.greek: Ὡς εὔκολον ἀπώσασθαι καὶ ἀπαλεῖψαι πᾶσαν φαντασίαν τὴν ὀχληρὰν ἢ ἀνοίκειον καὶ εὐθὺς ἐν πάσῃ γαλήνῃ εἶναι.

members.text:
Receive temporal blessings without ostentation, when they are sent
and thou shalt be able to part with them with all readiness and facility
when they are taken from thee again.
members.english: To take without conceit, and to let go readily.
members.greek: Ἀτύφως μὲν λαβεῖν, εὐλύτως δὲ ἀφεῖναι.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of the 1634 edition. In modern editions 12.8 is the first part of 12.11, 8.43 is the first part of 8.45, 9.5 is 9.6, 10.16 is 10.14, 8.22 is 8.23, 5.30 is the end of 5.36 and 8.31 is 8.33; 5.2 is the same.

Says “a good state of soul” for two different things: the state of the divinity within me, when it follows from its own make-up (8.43), and good turnings of the soul (5.30). Only 5.30 uses the word “good”. The translators note that Marcus elsewhere treats the divinity within as one’s own mind and reason.

Reads 8.43’s “content if …” as naming what the divinity within is content with: its state and its way of acting. The translators give another reading, “content, provided that …”, which makes the clause a condition on the whole promise. “These are enough for me” leans on the first reading; 9.5’s “It is enough” backs the same words independently.

Reads 5.30 from where the 1634 edition cuts it, in the middle of a sentence. The opening words, “Once I was”, stand in the passage before, so “wherever caught, a person whose lot is good” has no verb here. The claim takes it with the definition that follows, which is complete, and says only that my lot “can be” good.

Joins 8.43 to 10.16 because both hand the choice to a “you”. The Greek of 8.43 does not say who that is, and the article does not make it nature. The obedience and good will of 10.16 are kept to the words spoken to nature.
Places the calm of 5.2 under “When it breaks”. The passage does not mention place or lot; it is read as the way back when an impression disturbs my contentment.

Keeps the translators’ reading of 12.8, ὃ ἂν νέμῃ (“whatever he assigns”), for the transmitted ὃν, which does not construe. Their note says the edition’s text was given from memory and is unchecked, and no printed edition could be consulted for this article; the English of 1634 (“whatsoever God doth send”) reads it the same way. Claim 2’s “whatever it is” does not rest on 12.8 alone: 9.5’s “everything that happens” backs the same words.
articles.limit: Much of this article is said elsewhere. Claim 2 repeats Article 3 (I accept whatever happens) and Articles 1 and 2 (what I do aims at the common good), and adds only that the two stand side by side as one rule. Claim 1’s “wherever” is already Article 17’s claim 4 (I can live as I mean to wherever I am) and Article 12’s claim 1 (where I am is like any retreat); its “enough” is Article 16’s claim 2 (what I have in myself is enough), and Article 2 says that doing my own work makes me content. Claim 3 stands near Article 6, which already takes the universe’s side; and the said-once 5.2a is Article 7’s claim 3 (when I take away the judgment there is calm) and Article 21’s claim 3 (I keep wiping out impressions). What this article adds is that a good lot is one I assign myself, and that the same measure holds for whatever is given or taken back as for the place; claim 3 adds the spoken words that hand over gifts, losses and place. That part rests mainly on 5.30, a fragment cut from a sentence in the past tense, and on 10.16. No passage joins “wherever I am put” to “whatever is given or taken back” in one sentence; the statement does, and its “equally” is marked as the editor’s. In the statement, “taken back” is said by 10.16 alone; 12.8 backs only “whatever is given me”.
